At least one person was killed while four others suffered injuries after an oxygen cylinder exploded near a community hall in Okhla Phase-1 of Delhi on Wednesday, PTI reported.
The incident was reported at around 11 am. Three water tenders and a multi-casualty first responder vehicle were rushed to the spot after the incident.
The four injured have been shifted to a nearby hospital.
Police said a Tata 407 carrying commercial oxygen cylinders had arrived at the premises from Ghaziabad. The vehicle was registered in the name of SM Traders, which has been using the premises as a godown.
How did the blast happen?
According to the preliminary inquiry, workers were unloading the cylinders and shifting them into the godown when one oxygen cylinder fell from the vehicle onto the road and immediately exploded.
Police said only one cylinder exploded in the incident.
However, the exact cause of the explosion has not yet been ascertained as of yet.
1 dead, 4 injured
The deceased has been identified as Mohit Singh, 35, who worked as a helper at SM Traders. Police said he had been working with the firm for around three years and died at the spot.
The injured have been identified as Umesh, Arvind, Manoj and Pankaj.
What police found about SM Traders
According to the preliminary inquiry, SM Traders is engaged in the trading and local distribution of industrial oxygen cylinders. The firm has reportedly been operating from the rented premises for around one to two years and has three to four workers.
Police said no oxygen-filling plant was found or reported at the premises. The cylinders were reportedly received in filled condition from Ghaziabad through a supplier identified as Ram Avtar and then supplied to local traders and industries, particularly in the Okhla area.
The firm reportedly handles around 70-80 cylinders a day, although police said the figure is yet to be verified through stock registers, purchase and sale records, invoices and other documents.
Police are also verifying the ownership and source of the cylinders, the credentials of the supplier and the statutory permissions and licences applicable to their storage, handling and transportation.
The spot has been secured and further investigation is underway, police said.

NEW DELHI: Philippines defence secretary Gilberto C Teodoro publicly rebuked China at a defence forum in Seoul after a note outlining Beijing's position on the South China Sea arbitration was handed to him while he was speaking.
Teodoro was addressing maritime challenges and the South China Sea at the Seoul Defence Dialogue when a man approached him from behind and placed a sheet of paper on the table. Teodoro paused, picked up the note and asked whether it had come from China before reading parts of it aloud. "I have a note here. I think this is from China. And may I read it?" he said.
As Teodoro read the note, he interrupted its argument with a blunt response: "They have no position." The note stated that China's position on the South China Sea arbitration was "clear, consistent and firm" and argued that the arbitration violated fundamental principles of international law.
Teodoro then challenged the legal argument contained in the note, referring to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), under which the Philippines had brought the arbitration case against China. "So what you signed unclause. 
You mean violates international law. That's what you mean," he said.
The note further described the arbitration ruling as illegal, null and void and said it had no binding force. The 2016 arbitration tribunal rejected China's expansive historic-rights claims in the South China Sea and found no legal basis for Beijing's claims to resources within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone. China has rejected the ruling and maintained that the tribunal had no jurisdiction.
The Philippine defence chief then turned the incident into a broader criticism of Beijing's conduct, questioning the decision to deliver the message while he was addressing an international audience.
"How can you deal with a country in an international forum beyond the question asked to me disrespecting the organizers of this forum, how do you expect to deal with it civilly?" Teodoro said.
He argued that the episode went beyond the legal dispute and amounted to a lack of respect for the forum's organisers and South Korea, which was hosting the event.
"If this is a Chinese position sent to me, it not only disrespects international law throwing uncloths to the floor and trampling upon it, but it also disrespects the basic decency accorded that should be accorded to our most gracious hosts, the Republic of Korea and the rest of the audience here," he said.
Teodoro then accused China of using pressure against the Philippines, saying, "Perhaps basic decency and behavior is what China needs to do now."
He said he would retain the note as a reminder of what he described as Beijing's weakness in making its case.
"I will keep this paper as a memento of how desperate China is and how ineffective its position is in the face of a free audience," Teodoro said.
He also directed a sarcastic remark at the person who had handed over the note, saying, "You just done your country a great service. Thank you. And I hope you don't suffer in a gulag for it."
What initially appeared to be a deliberate interruption was later reported to have resulted from a mix-up.
According to forum organisers, the note had been sent by a Chinese military attache with the Chinese Embassy in Seoul, Yonhap News Agency reported. The attache reportedly handed it to a forum staff member with instructions that it be passed to Teodoro.
The staff member apparently mistook it for a message from Teodoro's own delegation and handed it to him while he was speaking.
Teodoro targets China's South China Sea claims
Teodoro used the episode to reiterate Manila's concerns over China's activities in the South China Sea, particularly in areas that the Philippines considers part of its exclusive economic zone.
"I think it is well known to the public, to everyone here, about the Philippine situation where we face challenges daily from the People's Republic of China, which tries to occupy and illegally assert its presence over our territory and especially our exclusive economic zone," he said.
He said the Philippines had responded by strengthening its defence arrangements and alliances.
"We live in a very interconnected world, and there is no right for any state of that matter to appropriate an international common for its exclusive use or right, contrary to what the international norms clearly state," Teodoro said.
China later sought to distance itself from the circumstances surrounding the note while reiterating its established position on the arbitration case.
"We advise some people in the Philippines to stop trying to stir up trouble, stop undermining bilateral ties and stability in the South China Sea," the Chinese Foreign Ministry said, without naming Teodoro.
The incident, which began with a single sheet of paper being placed on Teodoro's table, quickly became a public confrontation over China's position on the South China Sea and the Philippines' refusal to accept Beijing's claims.

Meta announced Tuesday the release of Muse, a personal AI agent that people can message to automate digital tasks in a secure cloud environment, all while relying on security and privacy that the company says is “built into it” from the start.
Meta says Muse is rolling out today for iOS and Android users in a dedicated Muse app, as well as the website Muse.ai. The company also says users can directly message Muse in WhatsApp to interact with the agent. Meta says users of its AI glasses will soon be able to interact with its Muse agent as well. Meta says people can try out Muse for free, but users who want to automate lots of digital tasks will need one of the company’s AI subscription plans.
Muse is Meta’s latest attempt to compete with viral AI agents such as OpenClaw and Instinct, which users can message with to automate digital tasks. Muse is a product of Meta Superintelligence Labs, the AI unit CEO Mark Zuckerberg formed roughly a year ago to catch up with OpenAI and Anthropic, offering some researchers eye-popping compensation packages to join. The unit was built on the belief that AI agents will transform how everyday users navigate the internet, as well as Meta’s products.
WIRED previously reported that Meta has been testing Muse internally under the codename “Hatch,” and that employees have been using it to autonomously operate third-party applications and browse the web on their behalf.
Meta claims in a blog post that anyone can use Muse out of the box, and that the product was designed “so there’s no learning curve.” The company says users can prompt Muse in natural language, and the agent will work on its own to send emails, book travel, or even help sell a car on a user’s behalf.
Muse is also capable of making purchases on behalf of users, checking out using special payment infrastructure designed by Stripe. The payment tool, which Stripe calls Link, issues a single-use card number so that agents aren’t going around entering a person’s real financial information across the internet. Meta says Muse is the first AI agent covered by Link’s purchase protections for agents, which guarantees no-fee returns.
Meta is late to release a personal agent, but it seems to be seeking to differentiate itself by focusing on security and privacy features for Muse. The agent is debuting with an architecture for all users dubbed Secure VM, which is meant to isolate each user’s activity in a so-called virtual machine to keep untrusted data from the web and any integrations separate from the part of the agent that can actually take action on a user’s behalf.
A personal AI agent requires a lot of user trust, something Meta in particular has struggled with significantly over the years. To get users to try out Muse—and allow the agent to be integrated with users’ third-party apps and services—Meta is attempting to convince people that they can trust the company to handle their data appropriately.
“We know it’s really important, if we’re going to build a product like this that can access a lot of sources of personal data, that we’re really responsible with that, so we’ve designed this system very deliberately,” says David Singleton, Meta Superintelligence Lab’s vice president of engineering for consumer products. “And we’ve built what we call the Sentinel that actually looks out for everything that’s moving out of the VM and either matches it to an existing policy where the user or the system has given permission for that to happen or presents a human-in-the-loop dialog to ask you to approve the action it’s going to take.”
Singleton notes that these check-in prompts for humans come directly to the user and aren’t filtered through the model, to protect against attacks like prompt injections.
While Secure VM is built to maintain user security and privacy, it is not a truly locked box. Singleton notes that while Meta is barred by policy from accessing user Muse data, it would still be technically possible. Users can opt out of allowing their data to be used for training.
The architecture of Secure VM is noteworthy from a privacy standpoint, if only as a way to set a new industry standard for AI agents. Eventually, Meta will also offer Muse “Confidential VM,” designed so each VM runs in a “trusted execution environment” and users manage their own access keys locally on their devices. This way no one else, including Meta, can access that user’s agent VM.
Confidential VM comes as part of Meta’s work with Moxie Marlinspike, creator of the end-to-end encrypted messaging app Signal who also developed the privacy-focused AI platform Confer in recent years.
WIRED viewed an advance draft of a technical white paper describing Confidential VM. In addition to structuring the system so the user controls their access keys, Meta is also giving select security firms access to the Confidential VM source to regularly audit and verify its privacy guarantees. Meta will also publish the Confidential VM binaries (machine-readable instruction files) and a transparency log, so users can verify the validity and integrity of their connection to Muse.
Singleton emphasizes that Muse Secure VM has already been extensively vetted, including by Meta’s human and agentic red teams as well as through the company’s private bug bounty. And now Meta is adding Muse to the scope of its public bounty as well, with payouts up to $300,000 for valid vulnerability findings, including up to $130,000 for successful prompt injection attacks that affect a single user.

SpaceX's recovered Starship 40 will take months to get back to Texas
The rocket spent 24 days at sea before recovery efforts began.
SpaceX's Starship 40 is one fast rocket, having traveled thousands of miles from Texas to the Indian Ocean in around 65 minutes. Its journey home is, well, slightly slower: The company says it will take several months.
Starship 40 launched from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on July 24. The spacecraft deployed 20 Starlink V3 satellites during its roughly 65-minute flight. However, this was a suborbital mission, and after briefly linking up with SpaceX's network, the satellites reentered and burned up about 20 minutes after deployment. That was the intended result as it wasn't an operational satellite launch. Instead, it was designed to test Starship's payload deployment system (among other things) as SpaceX inches toward a fully reusable launch system.
What came as a surprise was that, unlike previous Starship upper stages, Starship 40 survived its splashdown intact. Although it's likely in no shape to be reused, the salvaged spacecraft gives engineers something to study in detail rather than deduce from telemetry or scraps of debris.
Lifting Starship out of the water
Getting the 171-foot spacecraft from the Indian Ocean to Texas is a massive undertaking. Step one was moving it into calmer waters. After about 24 days at sea, SpaceX's recovery team guided Starship 40 toward the coast of Christmas Island, an Australian territory that lies south of Indonesia. The almost 300-foot Normand Ranger, which tugged the spacecraft from its splashdown site, held Starship 40 near the island until a 710-foot-long transport ship named Forte arrived to take over.
Crews tethered the upper stage alongside Forte as the transport ship filled its ballast tanks, lowering its cargo deck beneath the surface. From there, it was a matter of lining up the spacecraft with a custom-built cradle on the submerged deck. Forte then pumped the ballast water back out, slowly rose beneath the spacecraft and lifted it into place.
Although performing such a feat with a rocket may be a first, shipping expert and history professor Sal Mercogliano noted that ships like Forte are no strangers to such tasks with other cargo. "Ships like Forte do this every day," he said on his What's Going On With Shipping? YouTube channel. "This is a very common occurrence in the shipping industry, whether it's large objects like this, barges, cranes, ships — you name it."
The journey back to Texas
Next comes the really slow part. SpaceX hasn't shared the exact route Forte will take to get the spacecraft back to Texas, but it has described the trip as a "several month journey." Current ship tracking suggests that may be a conservative estimate, with Forte reportedly broadcasting an October 8 arrival to the Port of Brownsville, Texas. Mercogliano says the ship's westward course points toward the Cape of Good Hope as a plausible route.
Engineers have already collected heat-shield samples, gaining "vital insight" "vital insight" into how the upper stage handled reentry. The data should help the company improve future Starship designs and missions. SpaceX's goal is to eventually make Starship missions return to its Starbase Texas HQ for a tower catch rather than taking another rather considerable detour via the Indian Ocean.

How to use the AI Clean Up tool in iOS 27 to remove unwanted objects in iPhone Photos
Remove those photobombers with even more accuracy than before.
Apple is adding a bunch of new AI features in iOS 27, with one of the most essential apps, Photos, getting some cool AI upgrades too. There's one feature in particular that's getting much better with iOS 27: Clean Up. This tool has been around since iOS 18 redesigned the Photos app, though it's always lagged far behind its competitors. But thanks to Apple's new AI models, Clean Up is now much better at removing objects from your photos.
Before you can use the upgraded Clean Up, your iPhone needs iOS 27. If you've already installed the update, the next step is to enable Apple Intelligence if it's not already. That means you need an iPhone 15 Pro or later. If you have an older iPhone, you won't be able to take advantage of this feature.
Removing objects from your photos with Clean Up
If you've used Clean Up before, you'll know where to find it in iOS 27. The difference is that it now has some extra controls. To start, choose a photo you want to adjust in the Photos app and tap the Edit button at the bottom. Select Tools and choose Clean Up. You'll see an Auto button at the top, which lets you change the processing type. Leave this set to Auto to have your phone choose between the other two modes depending on how complex the image is.
Fast retouches your photos with a smaller AI model. It gets the job done much faster, but it's not ideal for more complex retouching. Say you have a photo of a landscape and you want to remove a trash can in the background. Or maybe you need to hide the wiring on the street lights. These are the kinds of edits that the Quick model is most likely to handle well.
But where Apple's Clean Up feature has always struggled is with more complex edits. When there are a bunch of people behind you ruining your selfie, that's where the High Quality option comes in. More advanced AI models can better understand the context of an image. But this improved processing comes at the cost of taking longer and using more battery.
Clean Up often tries to recognize unknown objects that you'll want to remove from your photo. This doesn't always work as it should, so it's more accurate to circle what you want to remove.
Extending and reframing photos
For other cases where a photo didn't come out like you intended, iOS 27 introduces two extra photo-editing features: Extend and Reframe. Extend uses AI to expand the area around your photo. Imagine you took a selfie, but it's too close to your face. Extend can fix this by understanding the context to generate more of the image around it, filling in what's already in the photo. Just pinch to zoom out as much as you want. It may take a while before you see the results, but that's normal.
Reframe is different: it changes the perspective and angle from which you originally took the photo. For example, maybe you weren't looking at the camera when the picture was taken. Reframe lets you change that without retaking the photo. The results are hit or miss, though. Some photos appear natural. Others end up looking like AI slop, with the model hallucinating objects or even people who weren't originally there. It's worth a try if you really don't like the original photo, but don't get your hopes up. Improving your smartphone photography in the first place should have better results.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
- Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark 
  - Published7 June
- Antonelli says he still has questions to answer 
  - Published11 June
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Expressing grave concern over the high prevalence of child marriages resulting in underage pregnancies and deliveries in the State, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday (September 7, 2026) said that the State had recorded nearly 60,000 underage institutional deliveries in the first six months of 2026.
Details of underage institutional deliveries from January 1, 2026 to June 30, 2026 had been obtained from the State Health Department, and the numbers were alarming, Mr. Adhikari said.
“As a result of the previous government, we are now number one in two criteria across the country — marriage of girls below 18 years of age, and deliveries before 18 years of age. These numbers are so high that there aren’t enough jails in which to put these people,” the Chief Minister said, addressing media persons at the State Secretariat.
Mr. Adhikari read out the provisions of the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, adding that the law prohibited marriage with a child below 18 years of age. In such cases, “Police action will be initiated and arrests will be made,” he said.
The Chief Minister emphasised that the practice of child marriage could not be allowed to prevail, and the State Health Department would issue a show-cause notice to the offenders, especially the husband, who would have to provide documentary evidence within a month that both he and his ‘wife’ were adults in accordance with the law.
“If he fails to do so, the DGP (Director General of Police), who is sitting right next to me, will take action as per the law,” Mr. Adhikari said. The State government would stop delivering benefits under all Central and State government welfare schemes to these families, he said. Action would be taken against the priest and qazi who solemnised the marriage, and against other family members, he added.
Sharing district-wise details of cases of underage pregnancies, the Chief Minister said 12,847 institutional childbirths by underage girls were recorded in Murshidabad district alone, followed by South 24 Parganas at 4,178.
West Bengal has recorded the highest number of child marriages over the past few years, despite schemes rolled out to keep girls in schools. According to the Sample Registration Survey report published in September 2025, West Bengal recorded 6.3% of females getting married before the age of 18 years, whereas at the national level, 2.1% of females got married before the age of 18 years. Murshidabad remains a hotspot for child marriages. About 55.4% women in the district aged 20 to 24 years said they were married before the age of 18 years, according to the National Family Health Survey-5.
Experts working on the ground, however, say that child marriage is a complex issue involving not only parental or social pressure but also cases of elopement, and minor grooms. They warn that the arrest of husbands may result in placing a strain on already marginalised families, and impact marital relations adversely.

A video purporting to be the first-ever helicopter view of Mount Kailash in Tibet is being shared on social media (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of Mount Kailash in Tibet, filmed from a helicopter.
Fact: The viral video is not of Mount Kailash, but of Mount Assiniboine in Canada. China has closed the airspace around Mount Kailash, and helicopters are completely banned from flying there. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using the keyframes of the viral video led us to photos showing the same mountain on various photography and tourism websites, where it was identified as Mount Assiniboine in Canada. We also compared the mountain seen in the viral video with available photographs of Mount Kailash and found that the two mountains are clearly different.
Additionally, videos filmed by tourists visiting Mount Assiniboine can be viewed here and here. These videos also feature the lake seen in the viral footage. On the other hand, the Government of China has prohibited planes, helicopters, and drones from flying over Mount Kailash, located in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. As the airspace around Mount Kailash is closed for security and religious reasons, tour operators in neighbouring Nepal offer special Kailash Darshan charter flights. These flights operate at around 27,000 feet within Nepali airspace, allowing pilgrims to view Mount Kailash from a distance without entering Tibetan airspace.
To sum up, a video of Canada’s Assiniboine Mountains is being shared as a view of Mount Kailash.

A team of Indian researchers has produced the first comprehensive molecular and functional profile of the venom gland of Stegodyphus sarasinorum, a colonial spider species found across the Indian subcontinent, to identify numerous proteins and small molecules that could serve as promising leads for future drug discovery.
Published in Springer Nature’s peer-reviewed, open-access journal Scientific Reports, the study identifies bioactive compounds associated with anti-cancer, antimicrobial and immune-related functions, while also demonstrating that venom gland extracts can kill cancer cells under laboratory conditions.
The researchers caution, however, that the findings represent an early stage of biomedical research and require extensive validation before any clinical application becomes possible.
Lead researcher A.P. Ajay Kumar of the Department of Zoology at Sree Neelakanta Government Sanskrit College, Pattambi, led the multidisciplinary study.
Unlike most spiders, which are solitary hunters, S. sarasinorum lives in permanent colonies, constructs communal silk nests and captures prey cooperatively. It is among only a small number of permanently social spider species known worldwide, thereby making it an important model for studying both spider behaviour and venom biology.
Although spider venom has long attracted scientific interest for their diverse biological activities, this is the first study to comprehensively analyse the molecular composition of the venom gland of this species using an integrated multi-omics approach, the researchers emphasise.
The research team combined transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and Confocal Raman Spectroscopy to examine the spider’s venom gland in great detail. Their analysis identified 31 protein components through transcriptomic profiling and 32 proteins through proteomic analysis. In addition, Ultra High-Performance Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (UHPLC-MS) detected 81 metabolites, including amino acids, biogenic amines and organic acids to provide a detailed molecular inventory of the venom gland.
To investigate the biological activity of these molecules, the researchers tested venom gland extracts against Dalton’s Lymphoma Ascites (DLA) cancer cells in laboratory experiments. The extracts exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, meaning that higher concentrations destroyed a greater proportion of cancer cells.
The findings suggest that the venom gland contains molecules with anti-cancer potential, the experiments were conducted only in cultured cells. Nonetheless, further studies involving additional cancer models, healthy cells, animals and eventually clinical trials will be required before any therapeutic use can be considered.
Among the most significant discoveries was the identification of several protein families that are already known for their biomedical relevance. These include hemocyanin proteins, which are known to stimulate immune responses and have attracted considerable interest in cancer immunotherapy research. The study also detected U12 and U20 lycotoxins, peptide molecules that can disrupt the membranes of bacteria and cancer cells, making them promising templates for the future development of antimicrobial peptides and targeted anti-cancer compounds.
The experimental work was carried out by research scholar Veena Venugopal, with contributions from collaborators from Calicut University, S.N. College, Nattika, St. Joseph’s College, Devagiri, PSG Institute of Advanced Studies, Coimbatore; GITAM University, Andhra Pradesh; and Ajman University, UAE.

Singapore’s prime minister has been given a $1m pay rise as the affluent city-state announced a dramatic one-off salary boost for government ministers.
The pay increases add more than 60% to what are already the world’s highest ministerial salaries.
Singapore has justified high-end salaries for its political leaders, arguing they attract talent and ensure good governance. The issue is nevertheless politically sensitive, with cabinet members’ income far exceeding that of most ordinary citizens.
Prime minister Lawrence Wong’s benchmark annual salary will rise from S$2.2m ($1.7m) to S$3.6m ($2.8m).
The deputy prime minister’s benchmark will lift from S$1.8m to S$3m. Cabinet ministers will get between S$1.8m and S$2.8m, depending on the seniority and weight of their portfolio.
Wong said he would donate the entire increase of his salary to “suitable good causes” during his term.
Even before the raise, the Singaporean prime minister’s paycheck vastly outstripped the wages of many other leaders, including in the US and other G7 nations. The US president earns $400,000 a year, while the UK prime minister is paid about $230,000 annually.
“Political salaries are a difficult and emotive issue,” said Wong, whose long-ruling People’s Action Party dominates Singapore’s parliament and its 21-member cabinet. “The sums involved are more than what most citizens earn, so I understand why Singaporeans scrutinise them closely, and why many feel strongly about the matter.”
However, the issue is “ultimately about whether Singapore will continue to have the quality of political leadership we need to take our country forward” in the decades ahead, he said.
“Our starting point is this: good government depends on good leadership.”
The South-east Asian nation, which last adjusted ministerial salaries 15 years ago, is regularly ranked among the world’s least corrupt countries.
Wong said the pay raises were recommended by an independent committee, adding that existing office holders would not be moved immediately to the new benchmarks.
They will receive a one-off adjustment of up to 9% from 15 October, depending on individual circumstances, including performance.

In 2007, a piece of space debris punched a bullet-like hole through the radiator panel of the US space shuttle Endeavor. The shuttle program ended in 2011, but the space debris problem has only intensified as we launch more and more satellite constellations, telescopes, and spacecraft into orbit. That’s why Chinese scientists have devised a new aluminum material inspired by eggshells that they believe could offer enhanced protection against debris fragments, according to a new paper published in the Journal of Applied Physics.
Eggshells have long fascinated scientists because of their mechanical properties. For instance, it’s well known that cracking an egg requires applying just enough force to the center to achieve a clean break without completely shattering the shell. In 2012, MIT mechanical engineer Pedro Reis co-authored a paper demonstrating the link between an egg’s ovoid geometry and its rigidity, a major factor when predicting how much force an object can endure before cracking. (As I wrote for Slate at the time, rigidity is related to, but distinct from, strength. If one eggshell has tiny cracks and the other doesn’t, both shells have different strengths—the cracked one will break more easily—but the same rigidity.)
Reis started studying eggshells after participating in a popular physics demonstration: walking on cartons of eggs without breaking them. The key, he learned, was to align the eggs with their narrow tip (the most crack-resistant part) pointing up, and then carefully place one’s feet to distribute one’s weight over the entire surface area. This ensures that no single egg is overloaded. While it takes around 5.5 pounds of force to crack an egg, that depends on the direction in which the force is applied, as well as its distribution over the shell’s surface.

In the wake of the passing of Dolly Parton in August 2026, a story we previously debunked in December 2025 about Parton opening an animal sanctuary resurfaced. Parton's real acts of charity were well documented throughout her career, yet this false story still made the rounds.
This was a type of claim we refer to "glurge," a term originating in the 1990s that we've defined as "a sentimental or heart-rending story that undermines its own inspirational message by distorting — or ignoring — the facts."
Tales like the one about Parton's supposed animal shelter would indeed be inspiring ... if they were true.
These stories often recirculate when a celebrity makes real headlines for something unrelated — and the spread of generative artificial intelligence tools that can fabricate text and realistic images makes it harder than ever to sort through the noise and find the truth.
We dug into the Snopes archives to collect 15 false stories about celebrities doing (fake) acts of kindness.

The mystery at the heart of Trump’s trade war
There is no prominent think tank, industry or pundit that wants an all-out clash with Canada. So why is Trump obsessed?
I spent Labor Day weekend in Montreal, and signs of the trade war were everywhere.
On Google Maps, which — at least until we crossed over the border — jarringly displayed the label “Lake America” where “Lake Ontario” used to be. Along Highway 2, which runs beside the St. Lawrence River, and where lawns sprouted signs with slogans like “Canada, strong and free.” On the TV in the hotel lobby, where a brisk CBC segment reported that Canadians overwhelmingly support Prime Minister Mark Carney’s retaliatory tariffs against the US.
Those tariffs, incidentally, went into effect this morning — targeting roughly $20 billion in US products.
The levies are Canada’s response to the 50 percent tariffs that President Donald Trump slapped on Canadian goods in late August, after trade talks between the two countries collapsed. They’ll make it harder for American businesses to sell goods ranging from cheese to golf clubs in Canada, and they’ll make those goods more expensive for Canadians.
More worryingly, the new tariffs inflame an ugly dispute that, as I unpack more below, has no apparent upside for the US. President Donald Trump’s aggression toward our northern neighbor has both damaged the country’s international reputation and made life more expensive for average Americans.
Go a little deeper
Launching a trade war against America’s closest ally is self-evidently…unusual, let’s say. But the strangest thing about Trump’s campaign against Canada is how few people are riding this particular train.
No think tank is churning out anti-Canada papers. No industry is lobbying for 50% tariffs. No prominent influencer, even, has caught Trump’s eye with dreams of northern conquest.
This sets Canada apart from virtually all of Trump’s other unpopular, fringe positions, which at least have some constituency behind them. Since Trump began musing about Canadian annexation 18 months ago, however, reporters have repeatedly gone out in search of the intellectual and political roots of that fixation…and come back empty-handed.
My colleague Zack Beauchamp made another go of it just last month and concluded, in a word: ¯\_(ツ)_/¯. Zack talked to a ton of trade experts, political scientists, and Republican strategists and found that — even in industries that have long-standing trade disputes with Canada, and even at think tanks that support economic nationalism more broadly — no one is advocating for the full-scale trade war we’re now experiencing.
That vacuum has led many analysts to conclude that Trump’s animus toward Canada is personal, not strategic. And while armchair-psychologizing about this president is risky, his posts about Canada certainly give the impression that he’s after personal and geopolitical domination more than anything else.
On Sunday, Trump posted a cartoon that shows him and Carney dressed as hockey players, with Carney sprawled on the rink in apparent distress. Trump glowers over him: “GET UP, GOVERNOR,” a speech bubble says.
It might be the most insight we get into the real motivations for a trade war that’s steadily intensifying, with no resolution in sight.
One link for later
➨ Ditch the plastic food packaging. A new peer-reviewed study concluded that it’s impossible to evaluate the safety of most chemicals used in food processing and packaging — companies just don’t make enough data public for that. So in the absence of regulation that mandates more disclosure, you’re probably better off storing your food in an eclectic collection of tiny jars.

At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

Some of the hottest software this year revolves around capturing voices. Whether it’s the sharp dictations of Wispr or the always-listening ears of Granola, voice-centered software currently feels inescapable. Voice dictation is getting so sharp, in fact, that I often write drafts in my notepad and then dictate aloud to my laptop.
Some prognosticators have declared this to be a dramatic end-of-the-keyboard moment, where legions of white-collar workers will soon be quietly whispering into desk microphones rather than clacking away at keyboards. I disagree, but I do think these changes could upend how customers give feedback.
I rarely email customer support unless something substantially negative has happened and I’m fishing for a refund. I’m much more open to giving feedback by blabbering for 20 seconds into my phone, good or bad, than I am to waiting on hold for who knows how long until someone answers.
“In the last two years, we hit a tipping point,” says Karan Gupta, CEO of Voicebox, a startup designed to collect feedback via voice. “That voice could now be accurate. It could be fast.” His previous startup also relied on voice technology—an app called Alice designed for secure transcription.
Giving feedback through Voicebox is simple. Shoppers can scan a QR code or tap their phone to an NFC chip posted in a store and then say whatever they want. The feedback is automatically transcribed and sent to the company’s dashboard, with a sentiment analysis. Companies can also follow up over email, if needed. Voicebox has partnered with airport terminals so that travelers can give their two bits about bathroom messiness or gate directions.
Gupta wants this type of feedback to extend beyond corporate experiences. Earlier this year, Lena Dunham held an event in San Francisco for her book Famesick and flashed a Voicebox QR code on the screen. Numerous attendees gave feedback, sharing emotional messages about how they empathized with her medical journey. He sees this as an example of the public wanting to share more feedback more easily on topics they feel passionate about.
As part of this larger vision, Voicebox recently launched its “directory,” so feedback can be sent in from anywhere and, in future iterations, users can discover what other people are saying publicly about a specific business. I could give a quick opinion about my haircut on my way out of the barbershop by just whispering into my phone, or share advice for future visitors about navigating some hospital’s parking situation.
The directory expands Voicebox’s potential from a customer-complaint vehicle centered around business needs into something more like Google Maps, with crowd-spoken reviews. This voice-centric approach mirrors other popular software trends, where the future of dictation feels so natural that using your thumbs to tap away on a smartphone may feel cumbersome and outdated.
After chatting with Gupta, I opened the Voicebox directory and searched for, well, Voicebox. It was time for my voice to be heard. Though I’m still waiting for the couple sitting next to me at the airport to leave so I don’t feel awkward about whispering into my phone.

Google will 'degrade' Search in Europe to avoid EU fines
The company was accused of favoring its own content in search engine results.
Google said it will change its Search services in the EU in an effort to sidestep some of the €890 million (~$1 billion) in fines levied by the European Commission earlier this summer. The EU charged a fine of €460 million (~$534 million) on claims that Google had abused its dominance in search to prioritize the brand's other services when displaying query results.
That sanction was the latest salvo between the EU government and a US tech company for infringing on its Digital Markets Act. The debate centers on the DMA requirement that major tech brands "must not treat their own services more favorably in ranking than third-party services."
Google first laid out some of its planned changes to its services in response to the Digital Markets Act in March 2024. Later that month, though, the EC said it was investigating the company, as well as Apple and Meta, for continuing to favor their own services with practices such as putting Google Flights information above competitors in travel-related Google Search queries. A year later, the Commission charged its first fines to Google for the alleged self-preferencing. Reports in October 2025 suggested that Google had offered to make changes to how its search results were displayed in order to meet the bloc's rules.
Which brings us to today's news. According to Reuters, Google's revised search results "will highlight one specialized search engine at the top of the page, followed by two others with fewer details. A carousel of hotels, airlines and restaurants, for example, will sit below them with key features such as real-time prices stripped out." Those specialized engines include sites like Expedia or Hotels.com, also known as vertical search services, so European users may soon see those aggregators and comparison sites prioritized more highly than individual businesses' websites in their results. Reuters noted that "the rankings will be determined by Google's algorithm," meaning the tech company still holds a lot of control over how results are displayed. The EC had given Google 60 days to comply with its rules, but the company has not specified an exact timeline for when European users will start seeing the changes.
Google leadership has framed DMA compliance as forcing it to deliver lower quality search results. The company told Reuters that the changes will amount to the largest decrease in service quality in the search engine's history. "These changes degrade the user experience for Europeans — boosting online intermediaries at the expense of local businesses, and removing helpful features people rely on every day," Nick Fox, senior vice-president of knowledge and information at Google, said in a statement to the publication. Reuters added that according to Google, its past search changes for DMA compliance were tied to a 30 percent decrease "in free, direct booking traffic to European businesses," and the company suggested there would be another drop with the new updates.

Prashanth Fertility launched ‘Prashanth Fertility at Home’, an initiative to provide select IVF-related support services at patients’ homes across Chennai.
The service is aimed at helping patients maintain continuity during fertility treatment, particularly those who may find it difficult to make frequent visits to the fertility centre because of work and other commitments.
Under the initiative, a dedicated team will provide services such as injection administration, eligible monitoring, follow-ups and treatment coordination at home, while patients continue to remain under the supervision of their treating fertility specialists.
A dedicated vehicle and team will operate across Chennai. Patients can schedule eligible services through the Prashanth Fertility app, which also allows them to manage appointments, follow-ups and treatment-related medical records.
Speaking at the launch, actor Khushbu Sundar, the chief guest, highlighted the stigma and emotional challenges associated with infertility and fertility treatment. She said couples often have to navigate not only the physical and financial demands of treatment, but also social expectations and questions around parenthood.
Samhitha Moturi, Director, Prashanth Group of Hospitals, said fertility treatment involves multiple appointments, medication schedules, monitoring and follow-ups, and repeated travel to a fertility centre can be an additional challenge for couples. “The initiative has been conceived to take appropriate, clinically supervised aspects of care closer to the patient,” she said, adding that reducing practical barriers could help patients stay on track with treatment.
Geetha Haripriya, Chairman, Prashanth Group of Hospitals, said the initiative was intended to make fertility care “more accessible, more personalised, and more connected to the patient”.
The service is currently available across Chennai. Patients can contact the 24x7 helpline 044-2888-2888 for details about eligibility and scheduling.

Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction
- Published
Once the undisputed giant of Nigerian politics, the Peoples Democratic Party now finds itself on the brink of extinction.
A question hanging over the campaign for January's general election, which officially kicked off this week, is whether the PDP can survive.
A factional struggle that has ended up in the courts over who exactly is in charge could end up rendering it irrelevant at the ballot box.
It is a remarkable fall for the party, founded in 1998, which appeared impregnable after the end of military rule a year later - so much so that its chairman boasted in 2008 that it would govern for six decades.
For 16 years, it controlled the presidency - in the shape of Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and then Goodluck Jonathan - and the vast majority of the country's 36 states.
But the 2015 federal election was a seismic shock.
The PDP lost the presidential vote to Muhammadu Buhari and the newly formed All Progressives Congress (APC) - a coalition of opposition parties and disgruntled former members.
Thrust into the political wilderness the party's national leaders were bewildered - familiar with the trappings of federal power they had to work out what to do in opposition.
This was the beginning of the end, according to political analyst Ishaq Buhari.
"They were a party that was so used to power, being in opposition was a new challenge they struggled with from the start," he told the BBC.
If 2015 was a major blow, 2025 was the year the party's foundations were left in ruins.
It was marked by a dizzying wave of defections and bitter internal conflicts.
A group of state governors switched party allegiance, which had a particularly devastating effect.
At the start of that year, the PDP still held eight states. But by December, five state governors - from Delta, Akwa Ibom, Enugu, Bayelsa and Rivers - had gone over to the ruling APC.
They cited the PDP's declining viability and a desire for better co-operation with the federal government as reasons for their departure.
Early this year, the PDP held three states but that is now down to zero - with the Oyo governorship slipping from the party's hands just last month.
Internal power struggles, factionalism, insistence that power rotates through the regions and disciplinary measures have all added to the sense of disillusionment within the party.
The PDP has been robbed of high-profile figures and talent, including the loss of former Vice-President Atiku Aubakar last year.
The crisis was intensified by a debilitating leadership tussle.
In November 2025, a faction of the party, which observers say represented the majority of members, held a contentious national convention in Ibadan, Oyo state, despite court orders attempting to stop it.
The convention expelled Nyesom Wike, a prominent PDP member who is serving in President Bola Tinubu's APC-led government.
Wike, who helped found the party, heads a rival faction creating a political stand-off that has paralysed the PDP.
He had controversially helped the APC win Rivers state in the last presidential election leading to accusations that he had betrayed the PDP.
But in the eyes of the law the faction that he heads is the legitimate party.
This means that it has been able to submit its slate of presidential and parliamentary candidates to the electoral commission leaving the rival faction without any representatives on the ballot.
Despite the chaos, some die-hard loyalists remain optimistic.
Politician and staunch PDP member Aminu Adamu, part of the anti-Wike faction, believes a return to its former glory is possible.
He cites examples from Thailand and Argentina, where parties have bounced back after years in the wilderness.
"We have seen it happen before," he tells the BBC. "All we need to do is put our house in order and start to build from there.
"If we make all the necessary corrections, by 2032 I really think PDP can be a major force again."
Others point out that the party still has a grassroots network - essential to win and sustain power - with offices, activists, supporters and local leaders. But by 2032 it may be too late.
With the party in such disarray and candidates backed by Wike on the ballot - voters are unlikely to trust them.
Analyst Deji Olarenwaju believes the only thing that could save the once-mighty party is an alliance with the African Democratic Congress - now seen as the biggest opposition group or Peter Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.
"Because on their own they are going nowhere," he says.

The DSA’s Problem Isn’t ‘Media Training’
Authoritarian extremists are speaking for American socialists, and a lot of people don’t like what they say.
American socialists are convinced that they have a media-training problem.
In the past year, members of the Democratic Socialists of America, the country’s largest leftist organization, have won electoral victories in places such as New York City and Michigan, drawing a spotlight that the group has struggled to handle.
Last month, the DSA’s co-chairs, Megan Romer and Ashik Siddique, gave several high-profile interviews that even many of their most fervent supporters agree were disastrous. The two leaders struggled to give straight answers to simple questions, and they defended outlandish policies, such as abolishing prisons and police. They seemed to present socialists exactly the way their opponents caricature them: as extremist, unserious, and unprepared.
In damage-control mode, many of DSA’s defenders on social media are repeating the phrase media training as though it were a mantra. If only the group’s leaders had been better prepared to deal with media outlets, the thinking goes, they would have avoided this train wreck. The DSA’s communications director, Priscilla Yeverino, recently told Axios, “Our leaders aren’t politicians. They’re working-class people and new to doing media.”
The idea that the DSA’s troubles on prime-time television are a technical matter solvable by the right training is surely comforting, but it is also wrong. The group has a bigger problem: It is led by unpractical extremists whose views are a far cry from those that its electorally successful figures, such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, espouse.
This disconnect is partly explained by a sharp division within the DSA. One wing engages in mass politics and includes AOC, Mamdani, and other socialists committed to democratic principles. The other wing is sectarian and extremist: It evinces little commitment to democracy and includes open admirers of Hamas, the Iranian regime, and historical dictators such as Mao Zedong. If the interviews with the DSA’s co-chairs were embarrassing, that’s a result not of a lackluster media performance but of the actual positions the group has embraced.
A closer look at the interviews confirms this. Romer, who belongs to the sectarian wing, evidently did not know what the 2000 Camp David Summit was and could not say what “taxing the hell out of millionaires,” as she demanded, would look like in practice. When asked about authoritarianism in Cuba, she praised the country’s constitution and suggested that Americans should learn from it.
Maybe media training could have taught Romer what happened at Camp David and what a tax policy might entail. It still wouldn’t have made the pro-authoritarian politics she shares with her faction of the DSA more palatable. In December, Romer’s Red Star caucus, a self-declared Marxist-Leninist faction of the DSA, posted quotes from a speech by Mao in “celebration” of the Chinese Communist leader’s 132nd birthday. Members of the faction study the works of Mao and the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin as part of their political education. Red Star has declared its unequivocal sympathy for Hamas and praised the “good judgement” of “our socialist siblings” in Palestine for working with the Islamist organization and “external groups like Iran, Hezbollah, and Ansarallah under a principle they call unity of the fields.” In other words, Red Star is an admirer of Iran’s notorious “Axis of Resistance.”
That Romer wouldn’t critique authoritarianism in Cuba is not a lapse but an expression of her faction’s politics. Red Star’s stated policy couldn’t be any clearer about this: “To publicly critique a government or movement that stands in opposition to the American government is to do the U.S. State Department’s work for them, from Iran to Palestine.”
In other words, any state or group that opposes the American government should be beyond criticism. Liberation, the DSA’s “Marxist-Leninist-Maoist caucus,” likewise declares the United States to be “not a nation” but a “prison-house of nations, with the Euro-Americans being the jailer.”
Unlike Romer, Siddique belongs to the mainstream wing of the DSA, but he is bound by the group’s statements and broader culture. The sectarian wing currently dominates the DSA: The group’s convention in Chicago last year rejected a resolution opposing “all governments that engage in the repression of democratic rights.” Thus, when asked repeatedly what he thought of Fidel Castro, whom the DSA had praised in an earlier statement, Siddique awkwardly referred to “inequality in the United States” and criticized U.S. policy—deflecting the question and offering sound bites instead of engagement, much as an establishment pol might do.
This pro-left-authoritarian orientation explains why DSA electoral observers shamefully reported no fraud when they were dispatched to monitor the electoral sham organized by Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in 2024. Those results were so bogus that even the left-wing governments of Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay couldn’t accept them. Yet at a DSA session on the subject, a pro-Maduro organization’s assessment that Venezuela’s electoral system was “one of the very best in the world” was presented as fact, as was the false claim that Venezuela’s main opposition candidates were “fascist.”
The two wings of the DSA are committed to wildly different methods. Mamdani governs New York City partly as a technocrat, and AOC has sought to influence the Democratic Party from within. One of the DSA’s sectarian factions, by contrast, recently suggested that socialist lawmakers “should do everything in their power to disrupt any Congressional business that does not benefit the working class or advance the socialist program.” They should, it went on, “creatively abuse their powers to make it difficult to conduct legislative business,” for instance by packing the galleries of Congress with hecklers. This faction seems to view elected lawmakers as “tribunes” for the socialist movement rather than as people who, you know, make laws.
The sectarian wing got the DSA to drop its endorsement of AOC and refuse to support Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Red Star argued against endorsing AOC unless she withdrew her support for Joe Biden (then the Democratic nominee), and it refused to fundraise for the Democratic leadership or central congressional campaign. But ultimately, the DSA dropped AOC on the grounds that she was not sufficiently anti-Israel—a singular obsession of the sectarian wing. (The foreign-policy section of the DSA’s political platform discusses the details of only one country’s politics, and that’s Israel and Palestine, in which it calls for the self-determination of Palestinians without making a similar provision for Israeli Jews.)
For all of the extremist wing’s influence, however, my years of research into the group suggest that the DSA’s members are mostly not members of any caucuses. The average DSA member probably has more in common with AOC than with Mao or Hamas, and the nonsectarians seem especially dominant in the group’s large urban chapters—such as in New York City, where the DSA has more than 15,000 of its approximately 120,000 members. More than 80 percent of DSA members in the Bronx and Queens voted in 2024 to endorse AOC. The sectarian wing came to control much of the organization’s leadership by manipulating internal processes, which is one reason it opposes organizational referenda and other one-member-one-vote procedures.
The DSA’s mainstream wing includes thinkers who are committed to democracy, critical of authoritarianism (including that of socialist regimes, past and present), and who reject some of the signature policies of the sectarian wing, such as police abolition. These figures have been vocal in response to last month’s media fiasco.
Eric Blanc, a labor historian at Rutgers, sharply criticized Romer for “falling into a trap being set by the establishment,” which seeks “to paint DSA as extreme.” Like others in his wing, Blanc advocates for adopting a Nordic-style social democracy as a step toward overcoming capitalism. This position is also shared by the Jacobin founder and former DSA Vice Chair Bhaskar Sunkara, whose 2019 Socialist Manifesto explores Swedish social democracy in envisioning a socialism for the 21st century.
Reacting to the DSA’s recent media debacles, Ben Burgis, a philosopher and Jacobin writer, opined: “We don’t do ourselves any favors by refusing to say anything too negative about left-wing dictatorships targeted by US foreign policy,” especially “if we’re trying to argue that the failures of authoritarian state socialism in the twentieth century shouldn’t mean that capitalism is the best humanity will ever be able to do.” The group has failed to reassure its critics of its commitment to multiparty democracy, Burgis added.
Thinkers in this wing of the DSA take seriously the imperative to reconcile socialist commitments to economic justice with democratic and liberal values. Burgis, Sunkara, and the economist Mike Beggs have co-authored a forthcoming book called The Blueprint: How Socialism Can Work in the Real World, which attempts to offer a “realistic model” of a post-capitalist economic system. Drawing on the work of the liberal philosopher John Rawls, as well as detailed economic research, the book takes the Soviet Union to task for a “record of systematic economic failure, not just political repression” and suggests a model that mixes social ownership with a significant role for the market. It also engages the arguments of well-known critics of socialism, such as Friedrich Hayek and Ludwig von Mises. This work puts the flippancy of Romer’s “taxing the hell out of millionaires” comment to shame.
But if the likes of AOC, Sunkara, Burgis, and Blanc wish for the American public to give their notions of an economically rigorous and democratically committed socialism a chance, they need to break with the fans of Mao and Hamas. So long as they share an organization with the DSA’s sectarians, they can’t complain when the media associates the DSA—and American socialism—with the extreme positions that it formally adopts and that its leaders espouse. No amount of media training can solve that.

COMIC: If we fight, is our love doomed? And other honest questions about conflict
Life Kit
Want more intimacy in your relationships? Conflict could help
Should we argue with the people we love? For Priya Parker, author of a book published in September, The Art of Fighting: The Transformative Power of Conflict, the answer is yes.
While many people dread conflict, it's not necessarily a bad thing. In fact, it's necessary if we want to be in close, authentic relationships, says Parker. So when you have a moment of misalignment with someone, try thinking of it as a signal. There's something here to talk about.
"We assume if the heat is rising, this must be bad. But the reframe is that there's something relevant here. I should pay attention," she says.
Parker, who has been a conflict resolution facilitator for 20 years, shares advice about common questions you may have about getting into fights — whether that's with a partner, a family member or a friend.
