Ukraine has been trying to bring the war to Russia. More Russians are beginning to feel it
Summer was marked by fuel shortages and drone attacks on warehouses
As Kyiv reeled Tuesday from another night of deadly strikes by ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, Russia's state-controlled media didn't report on the damaged highrise buildings or the cars that were set ablaze.
Instead, Russian broadcasters reported that several military facilities in Ukraine had been successfully targeted, while at home, the country's air defences had intercepted more than 380 Ukrainian drones.
But Russia's own vulnerability has become harder to conceal.
Local officials reported that two civilians were killed in Russia during the overnight strikes. And there are reports in the country's media that Moscow plans to allow postal workers to arm themselves with anti-drone weapons.
The measures are another sign of how Ukraine's expanding drone campaign is bringing the war deeper into Russian territory — and increasingly into the lives of ordinary Russians.
A summer of strikes
For nearly five years, the Kremlin has tried to shield much of the population from the realities of its full-scale war against Ukraine, as well as its economic consequences.
But Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries, energy facilities and e-commerce warehouses this summer have been a blunt reminder that Russia is not impenetrable.
"After the active drone raids on Russia — on Moscow and the Moscow region in particular — anxiety has increased greatly," said Tatiana, 66, who wanted to be identified only by her first name. "We were driving to the dacha with the children and saw a huge column of smoke. Naturally, that also causes fear."
- Russia reports large-scale Ukrainian drone attack across 12 regions
- Ukraine hits Moscow oil refinery again, part of massive drone wave inside Russia
Tatiana, like others CBC News spoke with for this story, communicated through voice memos sent on a messaging app. No one wanted to give their last names for fear of being punished for speaking to foreign media about the war.
She said she sometimes lies to her grandchildren when they wake up at night because of the noise, telling them it is construction work because she does not want them to be afraid.
At her dacha, a country home, she said people talk about the fear caused by the buzzing of drones overhead.
Ukrainian attacks on refineries and energy facilities have contributed to a fuel shortage in Russia, leading to long lines at gas stations, fuel rationing and public frustration. Videos posted on social media showed fights and arguments breaking out at some stations.
The government has taken steps to stabilize supplies, including importing fuel from countries such as India. It's a significant move given that Russia is one of the world's largest oil exporters.
The shortage has also helped fuel the popularity of GdeBENZ (Where is the Benzine), an app that directs motorists to gas stations with available fuel.
Measuring the mood
Denis Volkov, director of the Moscow-based research and polling organization Levada Center, said as the fuel crisis intensified earlier in the summer, surveys showed rising anxiety and a decline in approval of the Russian government.
But he said the mood has softened somewhat as fuel supplies have improved.
Levada’s August survey, published on Thursday, was conducted through video calls with 1,600 people across Russia. About one-quarter said they were experiencing tension and fear, while nearly 60 per cent described themselves as being in a normal mood.
About two-thirds said they had experienced problems with mobile internet access, messaging apps or fuel. One-third said the fuel shortage had seriously affected their lives.
"The main concerns are, of course, economic, but also the overall continuation of hostilities," Volkov said in a phone interview with CBC News from Moscow.
Ksenia, 41, a single mother who works in the civil service in the Russian capital, said the drones do not frighten her terribly. But she is struggling with rising prices.
"It feels as though no salary or freelance work is enough to cover expenses anymore," she said in a message to CBC News.
"Is there any light at the end of the tunnel? Who knows."
Beleaguered economy
The Russian economy is expected to grow by just 0.4 per cent this year, while many non-military sectors are stagnating or shrinking. If Ukraine continues striking Russian targets, including its oil and grain export infrastructure, the country's economic growth could be pushed down further.
Last month, Andrei Klepach, chief economist at Russia’s state development bank, lost his job after giving a public speech about the economic problems created by the war.
Last week, the Kremlin envoy for international development, Boris Titov, was quoted as saying the Russian economy could go "berserk" if the country continues on a steadfast war footing.
In August, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree allowing the government to take control of infrastructure deemed critical if it is considered inadequately protected from drone attacks.

- Wildberries is the Amazon of Russia. Ukraine is trying to destroy it
"The country is spiralling into a terrifying abyss. Especially when you look at the economic results of the last five years, it makes you want to cry," said Vitaliy, 40, a businessman from Noginsk, about 40 kilometres east of Moscow.
Vitaliy runs a business supplying spare parts to chemical plants. He said Western sanctions have made it difficult to obtain foreign-made parts, forcing the supply chain to shift toward what he described as the buying of "domestic crap."
"The business is going under. I am not down to my last piece of bread, but I am deeply worried about the future of myself, my family and my loved ones."
Vitaliy said he was also saddened by the attacks on e-commerce warehouses because of the losses they represent for other business owners.
The one thing that gives him some solace, he said, is that his ID card says he is fit for military service "with restrictions." He hopes that will be enough to keep him from being swept up if the government launches another mobilization.
In recent weeks, rumours have circulated that Russia is preparing for another mobilization. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also speculated that it could happen after Russia's parliamentary elections scheduled for Sept. 18 to 20.
The Kremlin has denied that it is about to start another large-scale draft, but fear persists, and the New York Times recently spoke with men who are making plans to leave the country just in case.

On September 5, Saurav Das, the co-convener of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), shared a photo on X that attributed a quote to BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia, under the label of ‘NBT’, which presumably referred to the news outlet, NavBharat Times.

He now faces criminal charges under Sections 115(2), 126(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, along with provisions of the POCSO Act and SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, with an attempt-to-murder charge also invoked in the case. Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the viral quote attributed to Gaurav Bhatia, we ran relevant keyword searches to see if any verified news outlet reported on it, but could find none.

It took only 83 minutes for the post to be deleted. Unqualified apology still remains. Tomorrow will be a day of FIR if no unqualified apology is tendered. Can’t spread propaganda and then just delete and run. https://t.co/oTXLR6ZwKe

How the Government Wastes Our Time
What do we lose in the hours spent filling out paperwork?
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts
Americans are bogged down in paperwork for reasons that are sometimes necessary, sometimes thoughtless—and, at times, nefarious. In her new book, The Time Tax: How the Government Wastes Our Time—And How to Fix It, my colleague Annie Lowrey looks at all those hours spent looking for tax documents or trying to certify income for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, or the FAFSA and finds that things don’t have to be this way.
A time tax is an infliction of “paperwork, effort, delay, and aggravation” that Americans suffer to get the rights they are guaranteed. We have the right to vote in a democracy; a time tax creates obstacles to those rights and makes realizing them cumbersome: They show up as extra identification requirements, when voter fraud is incredibly rare—or, in Jim Crow, as literacy tests.
So many things are easy now. If I get hungry, I can order food from just about anywhere with just a few swipes of my thumb; one click at midnight, and diapers can be at the door before the sun rises. Why is there still such sludge in our bureaucratic systems? On this episode of Radio Atlantic, Annie joins me to discuss how these time taxes show up in our lives and waste our time, and how to make our government more efficient.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Annie Lowrey: I think if instead of saying, This is about the poor people getting this program, or This is about making sure that these programs are secure, we could have a politics that says, This is malign; this is bad policy making. We give the government $8 trillion a year, and it passes back this garbage? No! No.
[Music]
Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and today we need to think about all of the ways that the government wastes our time.
I’m only half-joking. If you’ve ever thought to yourself while filling out your taxes or trying to cancel a gym membership that This is taking too long! Don’t they already have this information? There has to be a better way!—you’re not alone.
My colleague Annie Lowrey has a name for these cumbersome processes: She calls them “time taxes.” She wrote about the phenomenon for The Atlantic in 2021, and in her new book, The Time Tax: How the Government Wastes Our Time—And How to Fix It, she explores how and why our time is squandered when it does not have to be.
So, what gets lost in the hours spent filling out paperwork? And how do we fix it?
 
 Annie joins me now to discuss. Annie, welcome to the show.
Annie Lowrey: Thank you for having me, Adam.
Harris: So, I wanna start by talking about the DMV.
Lowrey: Yeah.
Harris: Because, right, it’s Labor Day, government offices are closed, but tomorrow across the country, DMVs are gonna be full of people trying to renew their car registrations, get Real IDs, change their addresses, change their names—whatever it might be.
But those long lines at the DMV, I think, are the most trenchant example of what you call a “time tax.” So what are time taxes, and how do they show up in everyday lives, even outside of the DMV?
Lowrey: So time taxes, these show up everywhere you are encountering the government, and really everywhere you’re interacting with businesses, right? It doesn’t necessarily have to be the government. And a time tax—or what’s called in the academic literature “an administrative burden”—is merely the person who is being bureaucratized, their experience of bureaucracy. So how much work they have to do to apply to something; how much work they have to do to research it; the fees that they might have to pay in some cases; and also their psychological or emotional experience, whether that’s DMV-level frustration or emotional anguish in a welfare program, or even a sense of civic pride that you might get when you’re interacting with a service that makes you feel good about yourself.
Harris: So this is how people sort of interact with different things, right? So like you said, it’s not just the government—it can also be canceling a gym membership. In your new book, The Time Tax, you write about the idea that we see some of the most cumbersome examples of these time taxes as they relate to sort of social-safety-net programs. Food stamps, Medicaid, Social Security—things that people in need of help need to survive.
So why is that? Why do we see a structure where the time taxes seem so cumbersome in those social-safety-net programs?
Lowrey: We see time taxes as a general point, I think, being bigger, more onerous, more expensive in a broad sense of the word for programs that are affecting people with less social status, for whatever reason that might be—people with a history of being discriminated against, people viewed with some kind of skepticism by the state. So that could be people who weren’t born here, immigrants. That could be people with a history of interaction or involvement with the criminal-justice system. That could be different racial groups. White Americans are treated very differently than Black Americans. And absolutely, high-income Americans are treated very different than low-income Americans.
And importantly, I don’t think that’s because low-income Americans are the recipients of this generosity that high-income Americans aren’t. So high-income Americans, they absolutely use programs like Social Security retirement benefits. They use tax programs like the 529 college-savings program or the Home Mortgage Interest Deduction. They benefit from the exclusion of employer-sponsored health benefits in some cases. But we don’t think of those as benefits, right? Those are tax policies—that’s not a benefit. It absolutely is. To the government, in accounting terms, it’s the same thing. It’s just that we’re not asking you to pee in a cup for it, which we do for a lot of benefits where you have to apply and reapply and come face-to-face with a social worker and perhaps fill out forms that might be a hundred pages long. And none of those policies interact with each other; they’re really cumbersome.
And I think that’s because we want to dissuade low-income people from using these, because we believe that some share of them are applying fraudulently. And there’s this thought that, you know, Maybe if you’re low income, you need to get a little bit better at paperwork in your life. You need to straighten up and figure yourself out. And this is an imposition of that moral onto you.
Harris: Yeah, and it’s interesting that you mentioned all the paperwork, and that’s even if they know that the programs exist to help them, right?
Lowrey: Absolutely. Yes.
Harris: And that doesn’t—as you write, that’s not by accident, that historically these sort of cumbersome processes have been used as a form of social control that is as old as data itself.
So can you explain that idea a little bit? That these time taxes aren’t something that popped up in the middle of the 1950s and 1960s with an explosion of bureaucracy.
Lowrey: Absolutely not. So a really clear example of these are the voting rules set out in Jim Crow. They are all hypothetically race-neutral. Or perhaps not all, but mostly, right? They are race-neutral.
But, you know, a poll tax is gonna hit lower-income people, namely Black people, way harder than it’s gonna hit higher-income people. Property rules—if you’re a property owner, that isn’t gonna be applied equally. And something like a grandfather clause is instead going to allow white people, white men, to be able to vote, whereas Black men whose ancestors were enslaved are not going to be able to vote.
And so even now, if we scoot forward, look at some of the rules in the SNAP program, which is food stamps. You can’t buy prepared food with your SNAP benefits. So the rotisserie chickens at Costco or at your grocery store? You cannot get those. Right now, there’s a lot of debate over ensuring that SNAP benefits only go to “healthy food.” So we’re saying, This can only be for nutrition as the state sees it, and we’re worried that you’re buying junk food and eating it.
Never mind the fact, I don’t know, maybe somebody is a runner or a diabetic. Maybe they have reasons to access that. Maybe poor kids should be able to have birthday cakes—that seems fine to me. But that is why it’s a tool of social control. We’re making people know that we are skeptical of their spending habits and we’re attempting to control those spending habits through these little time taxes in the program. And I feel like once you see these, you see them everywhere.
Again, I think it’s actually really good to compare it with the home-mortgage interest deduction that, like, if you have a mortgage, you get it. That’s it. They’re not like, Oh, are you living in a floodplain? Are you designing your home in this way? There isn’t that kind of paternalism in there, where there’s a lot of paternalism in a lot of other benefits.
Harris: During COVID, there were so many programs that were intended to simply help people who were struggling, right? Additional tax benefits and things like that. A lot of those programs were very clearly designed so that they reached the most people with the greatest ease, and they worked. Like the children’s tax credit—things like that worked.
Why don’t we do more things like that?
Lowrey: I think often we have multiple goals in mind with a program. So take TANF, which is the cash-welfare program. Its stated goal, or its original goal, is to end child poverty. TANF as it is currently constructed has no effect on the child-poverty rate, which is remarkable to me. That’s in part because it’s a small program. It’s also because the goal of TANF is to control the behavior of the mostly mothers who are using it. There’s very strict work requirements. If you screw up in TANF, you get sanctioned. You are treated as a fraud risk. You are in trouble in some way. Which is not true—even with the IRS, if you screw your taxes up a bit, they’ll ask for the money or they’ll send you the money if you screwed up in the wrong way. But there isn’t this implication that this was a fraudulent act—unless you’re outright committing tax fraud; I’m just saying if you’ve miscalculated something.
And so this is a way that we shrink public programs, where we’re saying, if we’re looking at the example of means-tested programs, the question is not only, Do you have certain characteristics? Do you fall below a certain income line, taking into account the size of your family and some other things? It’s saying, Okay, but we also need you to be good enough at performing for the state, at filling out this paperwork, meeting with this counselor at this given time.
And it’s just, you know, I don’t know that that’s a really legitimate way to go about it, as opposed to simply saying, Yeah, if you meet the income target, you should have this.
Harris: When we come back we talk with Annie about how to address the time tax.
[Music]]
Harris: So there were about 4 million people in the U.S. when the Constitution was signed in 1787. There are about 350 million people in the country now. And so, as the nation has grown, so has its bureaucracy and the systems that it uses. And over time, those systems age.
It makes sense to want to update them, to want to make them better as technology improves. And at the beginning of the second Trump administration, the president established DOGE, the Department of Government Efficiency; appointed Elon Musk to head it up; charged it with cleaning up the government, modernizing old systems, and making it more efficient. You were working on this book when that began. What did you think of that effort at the time?
Lowrey: A few things. So one was that this was presented as a novel thing. And no, no—there’s, like, more than a hundred years of presidents attempting to do this, saying, The systems have gotten too complicated; we’re gonna clean things up; we’re gonna make the entire system more efficient. So it wasn’t new.
I think that the fundamental idea was a good one. I think that the way that they went about it was, like, I would call it clown college if it weren’t so destructive and cruel. They were just firing civil servants at random. They made all of the federal civil servants send a five-point email explaining what they had done every week.
Harris: Wasting their time.
Lowrey: Yeah, exactly—wasting their time. There was no effort to look at the voluminous reports that we have from inspectors general, for instance, or the government’s various accountability offices to say, Okay, can we actually improve procurement contracts? Or, Could we find out the places where we’re really overspending on something, or, you know, We need some deep improvement. There was none of that.
They hurt service delivery by getting rid of some critical people. They created all kinds of busywork. Not just the [five-point] emails. They slowed things down such that some agencies couldn’t get essential components that they would have needed without the approval of a political operative. So for instance, NASA had to get approval for, like, bolts. I’m pretty sure that NASA knows how to buy bolts, right? That is not the problem with an inefficiency in government. And they never considered the citizen experience. Do we really need to wait this long to vote? Do we have to do our own taxes? We don’t, by the way—the IRS would like to do them for us.
And so it was just this all-out assault on the civil service. And it was the second time that we’ve seen it from President Trump, where he just believes that civil servants are a malign politicized force, that they’re there to take sinecures and draw money away from the taxpayer, when many of them, they just love their work—and they’re actually earning less than they would in private industry—because they’re really dedicated to their jobs and they’re very specialized at what they do.
So, yes, DOGE—good idea. And I hope that that idea carries forward, but I hope that they do it much more effectively and efficiently going around the next time. I’d also note that the great sin of DOGE, too, is that it might end up costing the government money because it caused so many lawsuits. They did so many things without the appropriate permissions, without the legal changes that they needed, that they’ve just been mired in lawsuits.
Harris: So when you say we don’t have to do our taxes. The IRS would like to do our taxes for us? What do you mean by that?
Lowrey: Yes, you have to pay your taxes; you have to do your taxes. What I mean is that nine in 10 American households take the standard deduction, which means that they’re not itemizing their taxes. Generally, it’s because their tax situation is pretty straightforward. And so the IRS has all of the information it needs already to do your taxes for you. They have your payroll data from your employer. If you have a retirement account, they’ll have those financial records from the institution, from your bank or your lender. They’ll have local data as well. So they could merely pre-fill your 1040 for you and send it to you to look over, or they could just send you a summary and say, Okay, if you agree with this, just let us know. You don’t really have to do anything. We’ll send you your refund, or there won’t be any money exchanging hands at all.
And so this is the way that taxes work in a lot of our peer countries with high incomes. In Japan, if you’re earning a salary, for the most part you don’t have to do anything. In some countries in Europe, you can do it all by text message. And the IRS is legally prevented from doing this, such that the average American spends 12 hours a year on the 1040 and spends roughly $300 on tax-preparation services. It’s silly. It’s silly. And there’s some people with very complicated tax situations. Fine. The IRS might have some requests for information. Did you have another kid this year? Did you take out another mortgage? Something like that. But they don’t need these endless, endless, endless, endless forms. They don’t need you to do them or hire somebody else to do them. They could do it.
Harris: To that point, are there other ways that we could be doing things? Is there a better way outside of these time taxes? How can the U.S. make government programs more accessible?
Lowrey: There’s a million and one. And it’s almost—there’s so many options out there that I feel like sometimes it’s hard for me to summarize.
So one straightforward thing is that there are different income standards and eligibility standards that target the same group of people using the same programs, many of whom use multiple programs. So for instance, Medicaid and SNAP—they have different income standards. In some cases, they have different standards of qualifying income, and you can’t cross enroll. So you can’t say, Okay, if I’m eligible for this, then I’ll maybe also be eligible for that. Sometimes that’s because of a difficult reason, so consider jobless insurance, which people often use if they’ve lost their job. That goes to the individual, where SNAP is really aimed at households instead. So that’s actually kind of a technical thing. But just unifying these standards and making such that you could cross-enroll in programs would be a wonderful, wonderful thing to do.
Holding states and offices and DMVs and everything else accountable for counting how much paperwork they’re putting on people, how many people they are not serving or are churning off and on programs because the paperwork is too much, and then saying, Okay, we want you to bring these numbers down—that would be really helpful. We don’t do that.
In terms of health care, dealing with hospitals and insurers and doctors is absolute misery. There’s a lot of common-sense regulation that could prevent health-care providers and insurers from denying procedures that should have been approved, or making sure that your medical bill is actually accurate—which half of them aren’t—preventing them from providing you with what you are paying for through simple paperwork and attrition and frustration, as opposed to some other legitimate tool. So those are just some ideas, but there are a lot out there.
Harris: Well, I guess if there are so many ideas out there, why hasn’t the government used some of those ideas, utilized the modern technology in the same way that, if I wanted a burger right now, I could pull my phone forward and just order it from DoorDash and it’s here in 15 minutes. If I needed a car to get somewhere, it’s, like, two clicks and I’ve got it. We have all of this modern technology. Why haven’t they used that modern technology to streamline a lot of this stuff?
Lowrey: Because the government is not really very good at reforming itself.
A lot of these changes would have to be made by Congress, and Congress doesn’t really care; it doesn’t see itself as a benefits administrator. And we’ve screwed up the lines of responsibility here. So if you’re not getting a benefit that you were supposed to be receiving, who’s at fault? Is that the state administrator? Is that the office that you’re working with, where if you complain, you are concerned that you might be retaliated against? Is that the governor? Is that the president? Because he’s the administrator of the programs, right? Is that Congress?
And I also think that there’s these broken feedback loops, by which I mean: If you get Social Security retirement benefits, we have decades of beautiful political-science research showing that it makes you feel like a citizen; it makes you feel like a good person; it makes you more likely to vote; it makes you more likely to be civically engaged in lots of ways. And seniors, when there are threats to Social Security, they come out and they demand that politicians stop it.
But there’s so many other little, tiny problems that relate to other programs that I don’t think that we have a mass politics demanding this. And so that’s why I think it’s hard. Nevertheless, when politicians do this stuff and make things easier, I think often it goes really well. It’s been really popular for, for instance, Zohran Mamdani in New York City. And I think that to a certain extent, we’re still operating under this understanding that these administrative burdens are demanded by the broad public because they’re so afraid of fraud in these programs. But there’s not that much fraud in these programs. We have really good ways to detect it. Giving more money to the civil service such that they could stamp fraud out would be a way to do it. And I just, I don’t know that people are voting on the basis of the way that the IRS is administering audits to other taxpayers. I don’t think that they are.
Harris: I mean, they might be.
Lowrey: Some of it. Everybody’s voting for something.
Harris: About the sort of weaponization of data that we’ve seen over the last year and a half, and the counterargument to The government should do more things to make lives better with our data is that the government can also take our data and do things that are nefarious if they so chose to, right? You can look at the Stasi; you can look at the Pinochet regimes.
How do you balance those concerns? Or does the government just already have so much data that they don’t necessarily factor in?
Lowrey: I think it’s a real concern and a real threat, since we are in an environment of democratic backsliding. This is one of the reasons that mixed-status families with citizen children and perhaps undocumented parents don’t get safety-net benefits that they have every right to get. That kid is a citizen; they’re allowed to get it. It’s because they don’t want to invite this state that could be very threatening to them into their lives.
I think one way to think about this is to give Americans the choice and to give the government permission: Okay, if I want this benefit, I feel comfortable with this office getting my data from the IRS. Something like that, so that it is elective and so that people can decide.
Harris: You point to Estonia in the book as a sort of prime example of a place that’s successfully easing the administrative burden on their citizens. But you also mentioned that they’re a small country. And as you were talking about, the gargantuan task of making the systems talk to each other in the United States, it makes me think that we have a scale problem here, that we might just be too big to eliminate some of the cumbersome bureaucracy. But how do you square the Estonian example with our context in the U.S.?
Lowrey: Yeah, Estonia is something we can aspire to, but I don’t think it’s ever gonna be something that we’re gonna have. So the thing about Estonia is they build a completely new government after they break away from the Soviet Union and regain their independence.
So Estonia regains its independence in the summer of 1991, and they form a government completely de novo, from scratch, at that point. And they do so during a climate where they want Estonians to trust the government because so many didn’t due to the Soviet influence.
And so they create the most elegant system of benefits that are all controlled by an ID number on all of these databases that are designed and updated constantly to talk to each other, such that Estonia has this policy that if you tell the government, any part of the government, a piece of information about yourself once, everything updates.
So for instance, if you tell the voting authority, My address has changed, all of the hospitals know it. All the schools, everything knows it. All of your mail goes to your new address. It’s nothing like that in the United States at all. So I don’t think that we are gonna become that—again, a very small homogenous country that started in the 1990s functionally. But I think that we can become more Estonia-like. And they’ve also had some issues with data security. They take it really seriously. So maybe there’s some lessons from Estonia to us, too, about setting these systems up in a way that is secure.
Harris: What would it take to implement some of those ideas from there? Is this just a political-will question?
Lowrey: Yeah, I do think it is a political-will question. And I think it’s a political-framing question. Because very often, administrative burdens are framed as necessary to prevent fraud. They’re not terribly good at preventing fraud. They’re much better at preventing people from getting needed benefits. But I think if instead of saying, This is about the poor people getting this program, or this is about making sure that these programs are secure, we could have a politics that says, This is malign; this is bad policy making. We give the government $8 trillion a year, and it passes back this garbage? No! No. Right? At least do the obvious stuff here.
And I also think that there’s ways of thinking about new policy changes that could be administratively light. So for instance, there’s always been this idea to put children up to the age of 18 on Medicare, which comes and goes and comes and goes. That’s a nice thing to do because it would mean that just kids are on Medicare. You never have to worry if your kid gets a broken bone or, God forbid, a cancer, that they’re always gonna be able to get treatment. But more than that, it’s just elegant. It’s simple. It’s the government taking work away from you.
I think about this a lot in terms of free school meals as well. That’s not only a benefit for lower-income families that might be having nutritional challenges. It’s also like, If you don’t have food in the house just because you forgot, oh great, the school’s just gonna feed your kid and you don’t have to worry about it. It’s just a nice thing in terms of reducing those burdens.
And so I think that a lot of that could be really popular. One thing I think about a lot is: We focus so much on reducing unnecessary burdens on businesses. Can we think about it in terms of reducing unnecessary burdens on families? Whether that’s these insurers that are not really insuring us, or this tax authority that makes us do our own taxes, or any other program where it’s just hard to grapple with.
Harris: Annie, here is to hoping that that burden is alleviated. Thank you so much for joining.
Lowrey: Thank you. I do hope. Thank you so much, Adam.

Tebogo says late mother 'always there' ahead of emotional return to Budapest
- Published
Olympic 200m champion Letsile Tebogo will return to Budapest for the Ultimate Championships next week, but the Hungarian capital is more than just another stop on the athletics calendar for the Botswana sprinter.
It is the city where the 23-year-old announced himself to the world and where his mother Seratiwa watched him make history for his country by claiming two medals at the 2023 World Championships.
This time Seratiwa will not be cheering on her son from the stands, having passed away in May 2024 after a short illness.
Having shared a close relationship with his mother - one she described as being more like a "brother and sister bond" - Tebogo admits that returning without her is difficult.
"I haven't really looked into the fact that I'm going now to Budapest without my mom," he said.
"It's just been a bumpy ride having to think about it and having to continue with the grind."
Three years ago, Seratiwa surprised her son by travelling to Budapest to watch the then 20-year-old compete in his first senior global championships.
Tebogo won silver in the 100m and bronze in the 200m - the first World Championship medals claimed by a male athlete from Botswana. He also became the first African man to win a World Championship medal in the 100m.
Seratiwa told BBC Sport Africa at the time that she was "proud" of what her son had achieved.
For all the memories the city holds, Tebogo says there is also a source of strength in returning to the place where his mother witnessed one of the defining moments of his career.
"I believe she's always there with me in spirit and in days where giving up is an option," he said.
"She pushes me to give my absolute best and I believe the memories that we had in Budapest, they will still come again."

Teaching 'unwavering sportsmanship'
Those memories now sit alongside everything that has happened since for Tebogo.
A year on from his success at the 2023 World Championships, Tebogo scaled greater heights by becoming Botswana's first Olympic champion when he won the 200m at the Paris 2024 Games, carrying his mother's initials on both his shoes and fingernails as a tribute.
He returns to Budapest as one of the faces of a new competition created to bring together the sport's best performers.
The Ultimate Championships is a biennial global event designed to crown the best of the best in a track and field season.
The three-day end-of-season competition includes Olympic champions, world champions, Diamond League winners and the year's other leading performers.
The inaugural edition in Budapest, which runs from 11-13 September, has a $10m (£7.41m) prize pot - the highest in track and field history according to organisers World Athletics - with each gold medallist taking home $150,000 (£111,000).
Tebogo, who helped Botswana to gold in the 4x400m at the World Relays on home soil earlier this year before registering 200m wins at the Diamond League events in Oslo and Lausanne, says the 200m in Budapest will not only be about looking back.
He is one of the team captains for the Kids' Athletics Ultimate Challenge, where young people from across the city will be invited to participate in activities at the Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre the day before the Ultimate Championships begin.
That will give him the chance to share some of the lessons he has learned since first stepping onto the global stage.
"I believe firstly you should start with accountability," he said.
"Think about your preparation, how you want your journey or your season to be, and then also think of unwavering sportsmanship.
"I would love them to have that unwavering sportsmanship, so that they can share lanes, they can cheer for one another."

When Muhammad Shaheem, 17, from Karnataka was diagnosed with severe thalassemia at just five months old, regular blood transfusions became a part of his childhood. Years of transfusions, however, led to severe iron overload that affected his heart and liver, making a stem cell transplant a particularly high-risk procedure.
A possible way out came from within his own family when Shaheem’s younger sister, Zara, 7, was identified as a full Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA)-matched donor. After extensive preparation and counselling at the Sankalp-Bhagwan Mahavir Jain Hospital in Bengaluru, his family decided to proceed with the transplant.
Their mother, Zareena, who lives with thalassemia major, said, “I continue to undergo treatment and regular blood transfusions. Though it was a difficult decision to make in my son’s case, it has ultimately given my son a second chance for better life without being troubled much by the disease.”
Mr. Shaheem is among 1,000 children who have undergone paediatric stem cell transplants with help from Sankalp India Foundation, DKMS, and Cure2Children. The procedure is both risky and expensive, and the treatment cost in India ranges from ₹12 lakh to ₹40 lakh.
On Friday (September 4), Sankalp, along with international nonprofit organisation DKMS and medical partner Cure2Children Foundation, completed 1,000 stem cell transplants for children suffering from thalassemia.
Of these transplants, DKMS has supported the transplantation costs of more than 820 children. On the other hand, Sankalp currently provides care to more than 3,000 children through 30 thalassemia day-care centres and operates paediatric bone marrow transplant centres in Bengaluru and Ahmedabad.
Rajat Kumar Agarwal, president of Sankalp India Foundation, said, “For us, these 1,000 transplants are 1,000 beginnings and proof that cure can be made accessible when organisations combine their strengths with a shared purpose. It shows how centres in resource-constrained settings can still achieve success in medicine and internationally recognised quality while keeping transplantation affordable and accessible.”

Whatever happened to the floating schools of Bangladesh?
In September 2018, we posted a story from flood-prone Bangladesh, 'Floating Schools' Make Sure Kids Get To Class When The Water Rises. Did the floating schools actually work, and what happened to the children who attended them? This story is part of our annual series, Whatever happened to …
We're revisiting some of our past global health and development stories to see "Whatever happened to ..."
Eight years ago, NPR correspondent Jason Beaubien visited a riverside village in the northwest of Bangladesh and found a small beige boat tied up in tall grass beside the Atrai River.
The boat was packed with narrow benches, which in turn were jammed with children. About 29 third-grade students sat shoulder to shoulder in front of a blackboard on this very first floating school of Bangladesh, which started its journey 24 years ago.
The floating schools were a response to a longstanding local problem of seasonal floods and impassable, muddy roads that kept children from reaching conventional schools. Now, as we come back in 2026, climate-related disruptions are affecting schooling on a much larger scale, and that practical local solution has become more necessary and more relevant beyond Bangladesh.
The schools were designed for one flood-prone region, but they now offer a model for how communities can preserve essential services as the environment changes. International recognition highlights the project's growing relevance.
Poetry on board
On a visit to one of the boat schools this summer, 27 students sat on benches and recited Bangla poetry with their teacher.
"This school picks me up from my house in the morning and, after class, drops me off beside my house," says Mahiya Khatun, a 12-year-old fourth grader. "Other schools are not too close; it is tough to reach there during the rainy season because of floods and mud. The teacher teaches us with care in this school, and I love to learn the rhymes."
Then she recites a Bangla rhyme written by the famous poet and author Farrukh Ahmad.
Another fourth grader, Himel Hasan, says he doesn't like the government-run primary school because it is too far from his house, so he loves coming to the boat school.
"I have five friends here in this class, and we enjoyed learning together," says Himel.
Mosammat Hosne Ara Khatun has been teaching in the boat school for the last 10 years.
"My house is near this school. Like me, most of the students are from nearby villages.. I enjoyed this job because the workplace is easy to commute to, and I think I am doing a noble job teaching underprivileged students," says Hosne Ara. [so the convention is to use the two middle names and not the last name?We can write the first name Mosammat
Suman Mia, who drives the boat, says "I didn't get the chance to study in my childhood, and now I am earning my livelihood by operating this engine boat. I dream that someday my son and daughter will be educated in those boat schools, and they will do a good job after growing up."
Student success stories
Rabbi Hossain started his schooling at the floating school, studying there from 2005 to 2010.
After completing grade five, Rabbi later went to a local high school and college. He now studies engineering at Dhaka University of Engineering & Technology, located in Gazipur.
"My life started from the boat school. I want to be an engineer after completing my studies," says Rabbi, whose father is a farmer and mother is a school teacher.
He credits the boat school for an important step in his schooling: "Just imagine, in 2005 we got the opportunity to learn computers."
Rabbi has many schoolmates who are in established positions after starting their education at the boat school.
Nahid Hossain, a classmate, received his education at the same floating school and is now a soldier in the Bangladesh Army.
For him, the boat school was more than just an educational institution.
"Boat school was an emotional place for me. I learned my basic education from that floating school," says Nahid. Without the floating school, he says, he would never have moved ahead in life.
To collect students, the boat school goes from one ghat — one docking place — to another, enabling children in difficult-to-reach areas to attend classes.
Even when there are storms and heavy rain, he says, classes generally went on.
"Flooding was a serious issue for conventional schools in that area because roads and communication lines would become unusable and muddy, school grounds might be flooded, and students' education would be disrupted. In contrast, the floating school could keep going and reach the children where they were," says Nahid.
Another successful student is Surovi Khatun, an undergrad student currently studying at Nawab Siraj-Ud-Dowla Government College of Natore, a neighboring district of Pabna.
Surovi was raised in a small village named Bolighati in Singra Upazila, Natore, and started her first schooling at a floating school.
She studied at the boat school at the primary level from 2012 to 2016; later, she was admitted to a local high school and college, and is now working toward a degree in English.
"The foundation that I achieved from the boat school advanced me in the English language, as teachers were so caring about teaching a second language in our early schooling days," she says.
She wishes the floating schools would go beyond grade 5.
"The education was free at boat schools. In addition, they provided us with textbooks, notebooks and even a pen. But after completing primary level, it required coaching tuition fees, school fees and educational material fees at the higher secondary level, which parents often cannot bear, and they sent their female children to marry at an early age."
Apart from formal education, the boat schools also taught tailoring skills to Surovi and her mother, and now the mother and daughter can make their own clothes and sometimes make clothes for neighbors to earn extra income.
Plans for the future
The floating boat school initiatives are run by Shidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha, a local nonprofit group.
The initiative received the UNESCO Confucius Literacy Prize 2025, in recognition of its efforts to deliver education to children in the flood-prone Chalan Beel wetlands.
"Bangladesh has had a remarkable journey from the lowest literacy rate globally in 1971 at only 17.6% to around 76% in 2026. The work of groups like Shidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha have made this possible," says Susan Vize, UNESCO representative to Bangladesh. "Their outreach to women and rural communities, the remaining pockets where literacy is lowest, is striving to ensure this journey continues."
Shidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha hopes to reach additional parts of the country with floating schools.
The founder of the group, Mohammed Rezwan, is designing a larger boat that could serve as a floating community hub, hosting classes as well as health care and other services and also serving as a shelter for up to 150 people during flood seasons.
He also hopes to build a global network of people working with this floating school model. Other flood-prone countries, including Cambodia, Vietnam, India, Malaysia, the Philippines and Brazil, have started similar floating school programs.
Ali Asif Shawon is the chief reporter at Dhaka Tribune in Bangladesh, where he covers politics, security, climate change, migration and global health. He can be reached on LinkedIn.

Larger sensors provide clearer, sharper video. Low-light performance improvements. 8K/50 fps 360 video. Shoot both 4K linear files and 8K 360 video simultaneously. Smaller body. Built-in storage and microSD card slot.
TIRED
Unresponsive haptic buttons. Mediocre pro recording features.
The combination of good video quality and user-friendly software has kept Insta360 at the forefront of the 360 camera world even as competitors like DJI and GoPro have carved out their own niche. With its latest camera, the Insta360 X6, the company is hoping to leap ahead of the pack again.
The Insta360 X6 brings a slightly larger sensor, faster video frame rates, better low-light performance, and tools to help you spend less time editing and more time filming. While it’s not a huge leap over its predecessor, the X6 is a solid improvement with several new features that might make upgrading worth it for some users.
What’s New
The X6 looks a little bit like if the X5 and the GoPro Max 2 had a baby. It’s shorter, squatter, and a tad bit wider than the X5, but not as small as the Max 2. That might sound like I’m setting it up to say it’s the Goldilocks size, but that’s not really the case. I actually like the individual sizes of the X5 and Max 2 better, the first for its narrower profile and the second for its much smaller overall size.
Along with the smaller size come two other major changes from the X5: the screen is smaller, and the physical buttons at the bottom are gone. Though there is noticeably less coverage, I didn’t find the smaller screen to make much difference. I could still see what I wanted to shoot, but the point of a 360 camera is you don’t need to frame shots. The main thing I use the screen for is making sure that the stitch line isn’t on my main subject.
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
I do miss the X5’s physical buttons on the front, one to record and the other for the menu. There is still a record button, now on the side of the X6, but the onscreen buttons just aren’t as good. They provide haptic feedback (the buttons vibrate when you press them), but they don’t respond 100 percent of the time. I found them noticeably harder to activate compared to the X5’s physical buttons, and I prefer the X5’s front button to start recording.
Another change to the outside is one of the better things about the X6: There are now power contact points on the bottom, which means you can attach a powered selfie stick and charge your camera while you use it. This is a great new feature that I hope other manufacturers copy. And don’t worry, the standard 1/4-inch tripod mount is still there.
Insta360 also says the X6’s new replaceable lens covers are harder than those on previous models. I have never scratched the lenses on my X5, nor did I acquire any scratches during the couple of months I tested the X6. The camera has an IP68 rating, and it’s dustproof and waterproof down to 66 feet.
Speaking of batteries, perhaps my favorite thing about the redesigned X6 is that the battery is now … just a battery. In older X-series cameras, the battery door was part of the battery, which always seemed unnecessary and meant there was no chance of ever using the same battery in another Insta360 camera, like the Ace Pro 2. Now that is potentially possible. If you’re listening, Insta360, give us the same battery for the Ace Pro 3 that’s in the X6. Battery size has also increased from 2,400 mAh to 2,600 mAh compared to the X5.
New Innards
The X6 uses a larger 1/1.1-inch sensor, the same size as the one in the DJI Osmo 360. That’s up from the 1/1.28-inch sensor in the X5 (and note that 360 cameras have two sensors since they have two lenses), and it gives you marginally sharper, clearer video. I did not notice a huge difference when recording in 360 mode. Of the Insta360, GoPro, and DJI cameras I’ve tested, I still find the GoPro Max 2 footage to be the best quality overall, and to GoPro’s point when it launched the Max 2, the X6 only records 7.2K video versus the Max 2’s 8K video.
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
At night, though, the X6 wins. It’s much brighter than the X5 or the GoPro for starters, and while sometimes it does render colors a little wonky, with blues tending toward green and yellows going more orange than they are in real life, it still produces the best 360-degree low-light footage I’ve shot. The Osmo 360 is a close second, but at times I find it has quite a bit of weird blur-like artifacts in low light.
One of the more exciting new features is single-lens mode, which, at least on the spec sheet, goes a long way to making the X6 a viable action camera replacement. I dream of one camera that can do it all, and the X6 is definitely closer than other 360 cameras in fulfilling that wish.
The X6 can now record up to 5K video in single-lens mode (up from 4K in the X5), but even better is the new InstaFrame 2.0 feature, which is Insta360’s name for the ability to record both 360 video and a single-lens shot at the same time. This greatly simplifies editing since you have a flat file to work from, and if you miss the shot in that one, you have the 360 footage to fall back on. This was always a great feature, but in the X5 the non-360 file was capped at 1080p, which made it less than useful. The X6 bumps that footage to 4K for the single-lens recording and up to 8K at 30 frames per second for the 360 footage recorded simultaneously, which makes this very usable and is, in fact, how I shot most of the time.
As I have said many times, no one wants to see raw 360 footage (yeah, yeah, I know VR is going to catch on one day, but I am not holding my breath), and while InstaFrame makes editing it down to a traditional linear video file about as easy as is possible, it is still kind of a pain. Advanced users will also find it annoying that you cannot use Insta360’s I-Log format (video log modes are to video what a RAW file is to still images, and capture a much wider dynamic range) with InstaFrame 2.0, but there are some pretty good preset color modes, and I recommend using them for everyday shots.
With I-Log, the X6 supports 10-bit recording when recording in 360 mode. In single-lens mode, you can only shoot in 8-bit I-Log. The higher the bit rate, the more color information is available (1,024 shades in 10-bit versus 256 in 8-bit). That’s a shame because, at least for my needs, this stops the X6 from replacing an action camera in my kit. Perhaps we’ll get this in the X7. For non-pro users, this is likely a moot point.
Photograph: Scott Gilbertson
Other new features in the X6 include 47 GB of internal storage. There’s still a microSD card slot, which is what I used in almost all my testing, but it’s nice to have the internal storage for those times that you forget an SD card, as I do from time to time. Even though I don’t use the internal storage, I love that it’s there as a backup.
The photo tools also got a bump, with 120-megapixel images (up from 72 MP in the X5) and a new AI reframing feature. In this mode, just press the shutter button and the camera will take three photos, one facing you, one facing out at (presumably) your subject, and one of those tiny world images. (I find the first two photo styles useful, but the latter is lame.) You also get the original 360 photo.
To my mind, useful software-driven features, like the triple-photo feature and InstaFrame 2.0, are what have always separated Insta360 from GoPro and DJI. They make it easier to get usable images and video out of the camera.
Finally, I’d like to point out something I haven’t seen mentioned much, but I love how fast the X6 starts up. You press power, and it’s up and running in about 200 milliseconds, which is the fastest start-up time of any action or 360 camera I’ve tested.
360 for Newbies
If you already own the X5, this is very much an incremental update. The new features are nice to have, but the basic video quality is comparable to the X5. If you’ve been thinking of getting a 360 camera but haven’t pulled the trigger yet, the X6 is worth considering. While I prefer the GoPro Max 2 in many shooting scenarios, the X6 wins in low light. I also love the ability to use it as a 5K action camera when you don’t need the 360 footage, as well as the option to shoot 4K and 360 video at the same time, neither of which is possible with the GoPro Max 2. Throw in the very nice editing software Insta360 offers, and you’ve got a great option for 360 camera newcomers.

Indonesia volcano eruption leaves 270,000 stranded as airports extend closure
- Published
Some 270,000 passengers have been left stranded across Indonesia after a volcanic eruption grounded more than 2,000 flights and forced airports to suspend operations for a second day.
Anak Krakatau, located 150km (90mi) from Jakarta, began erupting late on Friday, producing lava fountains and sending volcanic ash into the capital and the Lampung province. It stayed seismically active throughout the weekend.
Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International and three other airports have extended closures till 18:00 local time on Monday after volcanic ash was detected in airspaces near them.
Schools in the region moved classes online while some shipping operations were also disrupted.
Snaking queues formed at the departure halls in Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly.
A newly wed Malaysian couple, who had just spent a week in Bali, said they were told that the next flight back to Kuala Lumpur wouldn't be until 11 September.
"What are we going to do here for another five days? We only prepared enough money for our honeymoon and [were supposed] to go home yesterday," Amir Hamzah told Malaysia's national news agency Bernama.
"We thought we would just sleep at the airport for a few hours and then take the morning flight home [on Monday]. We never thought we would end up being stuck here for days," the 29-year-old said.
Suhardi, 58, was due to travel from Jakarta to Lampung for work.
"This is nature, after all. So I have to accept it, because when it comes to nature, there's no choice. Now I'm just waiting for the next update from the airline," he tells Reuters news agency.
On Monday, Indonesia's Geological Agency warned that "the probability of further eruptions in the coming periods remains high".
Volcanic ash reached as high as 6,000m on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000m on the Sumatra side and in some parts of Java's westernmost province Banten, the meteorological agency BMKG said.
Anak Krakatau sits on the Sunda Strait about midway between the islands of Java and Sumatra.
The most recent eruption occurred at 20:23 on Sunday, according to the agency.
"We cannot ascertain when this will end due to the dynamic weather," Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said in relation to the temporary closures of the affected airports.
Dudy said on Sunday that authorities across the airports have been conducting tests every 30 minutes "to anticipate whether the ash spread is widening or subsiding".
Authorities have warned against approaching or engaging in activities within a 3km radius from the active crater, while ships passing through the Sunda Strait have also been prohibited from entering an exclusion zone of 3km radius from it.
Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano.
Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.
The volcano collapsed in December 2018 triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java.
Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high.
The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand.
Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that's 452 individual active volcanoes.

The genetics of one's personality, or gene variants that predict it, could be more relevant to human experience and associated with health, education, career paths, among other major life outcomes, new research suggests.
An international team of researchers forming the Revived Genomics of Personality Consortium combined results from 46 distinct cohorts around the world to study the genetic basis of personality.
Findings published in the journal Nature show that more than 1,200 gene variants are associated with the Big Five personality traits -- openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism -- and that the personality genetics are linked to dozens of life outcomes, including health behaviours.
The DNA of two randomly selected people is approximately 99.9% identical -- differences in the remaining 0.1 per cent of the genome can influence individual traits, including appearance, disease risk, and the body's response to medications, the researchers said.
The small amount of genetic variation may also be linked to several personality traits, they found.
The authors wrote, "(Genetic) analyses indicate that personality traits have widespread, potentially causal associations with consequential behaviours and life outcomes." "There is no single 'personality gene'," lead author Ted Schwaba, faculty at Michigan State University's Department of Psychology, said.
"Personality traits are associated with many genetic variants, but even the largest effects of individual genetic variants are still very small. However, even though any individual genetic variant makes very little difference in personality, the effects of many variants together can be more sizeable," Schwaba said.
For example, the same variants linked to extraversion in a young adult in the Netherlands also predicted extraversion in an older adult retiree in the U.S., the study found.
The researchers used methods that compared relatives to one another and "confirmed" that the genetic links weren't actually the byproduct of a shared upbringing.
However, despite the genetic associations, environment was still found to play a major role in personality.
For example, the study found that common genetic variants linked to openness to experience predicted that a person would move to more cosmopolitan neighbourhoods. In turn, living in those neighbourhoods may reinforce and further shape that same trait.
The researchers noted that the genetics of personality are relevant to many parts of the human experience.
The genetic variants that predict personality can also partially predict mental and physical health, longevity, education, career paths and outcomes and even how people are perceived by close others, they said.
Genetic variants linked to conscientiousness were associated with being more active during the day, while variants linked to openness to experience and extraversion were linked to being more of a night owl.
"Personality seems to be relevant nearly everywhere you look. We hope this study will encourage many other scientists to incorporate personality traits into their fields of study," Schwaba said.
"For example, genetic variants associated with neuroticism predict more time spent in the hospital, which is relevant to physicians and health researchers, and variants associated with openness to experience are linked to income and switching jobs, which is relevant to vocational researchers," Schwaba said.

25 years since 9/11: Terror's new faces and India's evolving security challenges
Lessons from 9/11 attack remain unlearnt as terror networks evolve, use sophisticated recruitment and retain political utility, argues Shishir Gupta.
Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks transformed the global security landscape, terrorism remains far from defeated. In a conversation with Senior Anchor Aayesha Varma on Point Blank, Hindustan Times Executive Editor Shishir Gupta argued that while the methods, networks and technologies used by terrorist groups have changed, the underlying political purpose of terrorism remains the same: to seize influence, spread fear and advance ideological goals through violence.
The discussion came against the backdrop of the approaching 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, in which 2,977 people were killed after al-Qaeda hijackers weaponised commercial aircraft and struck the World Trade Centre, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania. For many, 9/11 remains a deeply personal memory—not only of loss and horror, but also of the fear, racism and suspicion that followed, particularly affecting non-white communities in the United States in the aftermath of the brazen strikes.
Gupta’s central argument was that the world has not fully absorbed the lessons of 9/11. Terrorism may no longer dominate global headlines in the way it did during the “war on terror” era, but its networks have adapted, its recruitment methods have become more sophisticated, and its political utility for state and non-state actors persists.
ALSO READ | The forgotten attack that came before 9/11: How a van bomb nearly brought down the Twin Towers
From 9/11 to a changing global threat
The 9/11 attacks were not an isolated event. They followed the September 9, 2001 assassination of Ahmad Shah Massoud, the anti-Taliban commander in Afghanistan, by al-Qaeda operatives posing as journalists. Two days later, al-Qaeda carried out the attacks on the United States, pushing Washington into a war in Afghanistan aimed at dismantling the Taliban regime that had hosted Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda.
The consequences were immediate and global. Terrorism, Gupta said, was suddenly placed at the centre of international security thinking. Countries such as India, which had already faced years of cross-border terrorism in Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir and elsewhere, found that the wider world was finally paying attention to a threat New Delhi had long highlighted.
Within months, India itself was targeted in the December 13, 2001, attack on Parliament. Seven years later came the November 26, 2008, Mumbai attacks, in which Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorists launched coordinated assaults across the city, killing more than 160 people.
But despite the post-9/11 global focus, the problem did not disappear. Instead, it fragmented. Large organisations such as al-Qaeda and the Islamic State continue to operate, directly or through affiliates. At the same time, terrorism has become more decentralised, with local cells, online recruits, lone attackers and loosely connected ideological networks replacing the rigid hierarchy of earlier militant organisations.
ALSO READ | 9/11: A fourth plane was headed for Washington, until 40 people stopped it
Gupta pointed to militant activity in the Sahel and Maghreb regions of Africa, the continuing presence of al-Shabaab, Boko Haram, Islamic State affiliates and Iranian-backed armed groups across West Asia. He also highlighted alliances that cut across sectarian divides, arguing that terrorism is often driven less by theology than by political power.
The result is a threat environment in which organisations with differing religious identities or regional goals can cooperate when their strategic interests align. In this view, terror is not merely a tactic of isolated extremist groups; it is also a tool deployed in wider struggles for influence, territory and political legitimacy.
India and Pakistan-based terror networks
For India, the most persistent concern remains Pakistan-based terrorism. Gupta said groups including Lashkar-e-Taiba, Jaish-e-Mohammed, al-Qaeda-linked organisations and Islamic State Khorasan Province continue to pose a danger, despite repeated crackdowns, international sanctions and Pakistan’s assurances of action against terror financing.
The central challenge, he argued, is that India remains a target for groups that view terrorism as a way to pursue Pakistan’s long-standing claims over Kashmir and to challenge India’s rise. The pattern has stretched across decades: separatist militancy in Punjab during the 1980s, terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir through the 1990s, and high-profile attacks in Indian cities and institutions in subsequent years.
Gupta contrasted India’s earlier approach with the more overtly retaliatory posture adopted after 2014. He cited the 2016 surgical strikes, the 2019 Balakot airstrike and Operation Sindoor as examples of India signalling that cross-border terrorism would not be met only through diplomacy or defensive measures.
However, deterrence does not eliminate the risk. Terror groups can exploit ideological networks, encrypted communication platforms, financial channels, criminal syndicates and vulnerable individuals. As Gupta noted, the task for India is not simply to respond after an attack but to remain proactive enough to prevent one.
That requires understanding how militant networks recruit, communicate, finance themselves and activate dormant cells. Terrorism, he said, works through “nodes”: narcotics trafficking can fund weapons purchases, weapons can sustain militant modules, and those modules can then be activated for attacks. The objective of counterterrorism, therefore, must be to disrupt the entire ecosystem rather than merely arrest individuals after violence has taken place.
Different posture
Global terror networks are entering the 25th anniversary of 9/11 in a fundamentally different posture than the immediate post-2001 threat picture. There is no longer a single "paramount" threat; instead, the terror landscape has shifted to become increasingly complex and unpredictable involving formal groups, loose networks, and lone actors. Al-Qaeda affiliates and Islamic State provinces continue to pose the greatest threat in West Asia and Africa, many of them growing in strength. Both organisations are expected to keep exploiting conflict zones and ungoverned spaces to expand geographic reach and operational tempo.
The Sahel remains one of the fastest-growing terrorism hotspots and Islamic State West Africa Province is assessed as probably the largest IS province worldwide. Groups in this belt are also adopting new capabilities, with terrorist organizations making increasing use of unmanned aerial systems and artificial intelligence.
ALSO READ | 9/11, 25 years on: The terror threat is not gone and US is struggling with the lesson
Despite their organisational degradation, al-Qaeda and Islamic State continue to operationally engage, a dynamic visible in lethal but rare attacks like the New Orleans truck attack on New Year's Day 2025. When it comes to effective organisational resurgence, the Afghanistan-Pakistan theatre carries the risk of formal reconstitution. The region continues to serve as a safe haven for Islamic State Khorasan Province, which keeps signaling interest in external operations. On the other hand, al-Qaeda maintains a quieter presence in the region, but carries a serious risk that it could slowly rebuild its ranks, including by working with al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS) fighters.
Adoption of AI
Islamic State has treated online platform resilience as a core operational priority. Telegram remains its primary long-term home for both official media and supporter-generated content. The newer shift is into AI: IS-Khorasan's English-language magazine Voice of Khorasan, in June 2025, presented AI literacy as an individual religious duty for every Muslim. The same publication also warned about deepfakes, surveillance, and data collection, while offering practical guidance for self-protection — indicating the group is simultaneously weaponising AI for propaganda/translation and coaching its own operatives on counter-surveillance tradecraft.
Terror supporters have all begun actively using artificial intelligence technologies in their propaganda output. Al-Qaeda's digital architecture is more centralised around branded news infrastructure than Islamic State's diffuse channel model. Al-Qaeda-linked media were circulating likely AI-generated images as early as 2023, alongside AI tools to translate its messaging into multiple languages.
The online radicalisation challenge
One of the most consequential changes since 2001 is the growth of online radicalisation. Terrorist recruitment no longer necessarily begins in a training camp, a seminary or a face-to-face meeting. It can begin with an online message, a social-media interaction, propaganda video, gaming platform, encrypted chat group or a carefully cultivated ideological grievance.
Gupta described a process in which potential recruits are profiled, approached and gradually drawn into a worldview built around victimhood. Recruiters assess their vulnerabilities, reinforce grievances, provide ideological validation and, in some cases, direct them toward violence.
Artificial intelligence, deepfakes and increasingly sophisticated digital propaganda could make this challenge harder. Manipulated videos and synthetic voices can be used to spread inflammatory narratives, impersonate trusted figures and intensify communal or political tensions. Terrorist groups can reach recruits across borders without physically moving people, money or instructions in the ways security agencies once learned to monitor.
This makes counter-radicalisation as important as counterterrorism. Gupta identified intelligence-sharing, community engagement and structured counter-radicalisation programmes as essential components of any long-term strategy. Countries such as the United Arab Emirates, Jordan and India have developed frameworks intended to counter extremist messaging, but he argued that a broader international effort is required.
The principle, he suggested, should be straightforward: political differences cannot justify attacks on civilians. The distinction between “freedom fighter” and “terrorist” becomes indefensible when innocents are deliberately targeted.
Intelligence failures and the need to “join the dots”
The most difficult aspect of counterterrorism is often not the absence of intelligence, but the failure to interpret and connect available warnings. Gupta’s assessment was blunt: every successful terror attack is, in some sense, an intelligence failure.
That does not mean agencies never prevent attacks. Security services may disrupt numerous plots that never become public. But even a single missed threat can cause mass casualties and reshape national policy, public confidence and regional geopolitics.
The 9/11 attacks are widely seen as a case where different warning signs existed but were not assembled into a complete picture. Gupta made a similar point about the 26/11 Mumbai attacks, saying information and maritime alerts had been available but did not translate into effective prevention.
The October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel likewise demonstrated how an adversary can exploit complacency, miscalculation and institutional blind spots. Gupta described it as both an intelligence and enforcement failure, noting that an operation of that scale could not have been organised overnight.
The lesson is that intelligence cannot rely only on surveillance technology. Signals intelligence, data analysis and digital monitoring are indispensable, but human intelligence—sources embedded in networks, local knowledge and on-ground assessment—remains critical. Gupta pointed to the operations that located Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad and Ayman al-Zawahiri in Kabul as examples of the continuing importance of human intelligence.
Terrorism remains a political tool
The broader point emerging from the conversation is that terrorism cannot be understood only as a law-and-order issue. It is tied to geopolitics, proxy conflicts, state support, regional rivalries and struggles for political power.
Gupta argued that Pakistan has repeatedly benefited from support or strategic accommodation from major Western powers, even as India has raised concerns about terror groups operating from Pakistani soil. In this reading, global powers often treat terrorism selectively, prioritising their own regional interests over consistent action against extremist infrastructure.
For India, that means expecting no permanent external solution. The country must strengthen intelligence capabilities, improve coordination among agencies, expand cross-border information-sharing and maintain the ability to pre-empt threats before they materialise.
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the world is dealing with wars in Ukraine, Gaza and West Asia, alongside great-power rivalry and economic uncertainty. Terrorism may no longer occupy the top spot in every global conversation, but it remains a persistent, adaptive and deadly challenge.
The enduring lesson of 9/11 is not simply that terrorism can strike without warning. It is that preventing it requires vigilance long before the attack—through better intelligence, stronger institutions, credible deterrence and a refusal to treat violence against civilians as politically acceptable.
