A wind-fueled wildfire forces hundreds from homes in Turkey as firefighters battle flames
Firefighters in Turkey are battling a large wildfire in Antalya's coastal province
ANKARA, Turkey -- Firefighters on Tuesday battled a wildfire in Turkey's Mediterranean coastal province of Antalya that forced hundreds of people from their homes and injured at least two people, the state-run news agency reported.
The fire broke out Monday evening in Antalya’s Aksu district and, fueled by strong winds, quickly spread into the neighboring Kepez district, Anadolu Agency reported.
Two people were hospitalized with injuries to their legs while six others affected by smoke were treated on site, the report said.
Authorities evacuated people from at least 254 homes in Aksu and Kepez and temporarily closed a highway between Antalya and the city of Isparta, located some 130 kilometers (80 miles) north.
As flames and heavy smoke threatened the area, more than 100 dogs were evacuated from an animal shelter in Aksu and taken to safety, Antalya Municipality said. Video footage showed veterinarians treating a dog affected by the smoke.
More than 2,000 homes in the region were affected by power outages, Anadolu reported.
The agency said at least five firefighting aircraft, 10 helicopters, 110 fire extinguishing trucks and 600 personnel were deployed to battle the blaze.
Firefighters were also battling wildfires in the nearby provinces of Adana and Mersin.

Over a decade ago, the Islamic State released a disturbing video that depicted its members lowering men locked in a cage into a swimming pool and drowning them. Today, that video has been reproduced as a SpongeBob SquarePants cartoon depicting fish in orange jumpsuits inside the cage, as SpongeBob lowers the cage into the water while Squidward films the scene.
The video, shared on TikTok, is part of what a new report from the Institute of Strategic Dialogue (ISD) calls “Slop Jihad,” a trend where young supporters of Islamic terror groups like ISIS and al-Qaida appear to use generative AI tools to create fan edits, cartoons, and memes designed radicalize a new generation of online backing.
This shift “signals a fundamental transformation in the aesthetics of jihadist propaganda online,” concludes the report, which was shared exclusively with WIRED.
“The principal concern is the growing volume and diversity of material,” says Adam Hadley, executive director of Tech Against Terrorism, a UN-backed counter terrorism organization that has also written a report about the Slop Jihad trend. “Highly stylized AI-generated content can make violent Islamist extremist material more accessible to younger audiences while reducing the visibility of conventional terrorist branding. Users may encounter perpetrator glorification inadvertently through fan edits, cartoons, memes, and other entertainment-oriented formats, after which engagement can drive algorithmic recommendations of related, more overt propaganda.”
Islamic terror groups have long demonstrated their capacity to adapt to new media environments to get their messages to a wide audience online, leveraging new and emerging technologies to aid recruitment and create a decentralized network of propaganda. This was seen in the early 2020s Alt Jihad movement, which sought to co-opt the aesthetics of the alt-right in the Islamic terrorism content.
These groups have also been making use of generative AI technology for a number of years. In 2024, the Islamic State-affiliated news program News Harvest began using AI-generated anchors to help disseminate propaganda videos quickly and cheaply.
But today, the look and feel of the content produced with generative AI is markedly different.
“This is new and it's still growing, it has not peaked by any means,” says Moustafa Ayad, the research chair in global Islamism and counter terrorism at ISD. “There's always been really shoddy content that's been produced in the support ecosystem, but it wasn't SpongeBob SquarePants as the Islamic State.”
Generative AI tools have also been utilized to quickly and cheaply turn official content from terror groups into animated videos. In one example, one TikTok account was turning the weekly al-Naba newsletter from ISIS into anime.
The Slop Jihad trend has seen some pushback from more traditional supporters who don’t like the new aesthetic. “There seems to be some animosity towards it, because they don't believe the producers of Slop Jihad are true believers,” Ayad says, referring to some reactions to the SpongeBob video. “But again, some accounts that have shared traditional official propaganda are sharing the newer videos. So there seems to be a love-hate relationship with the Slop Jihad content.”
For years now, TikTok has been central to Islamic terror groups online messaging campaign, taking advantage of the platform’s powerful algorithmic recommendations to spread their message. A report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in 2024 found that TikTok was among the top 10 platforms used to spread terrorist and extremist content.
While Ayad did find a limited number of Slop Jihad videos on other platforms like Instagram and Facebook, the vast majority of the videos were found on TikTok. In total, he found 150 Slop Jihad videos from 71 accounts with more than 5.4 million total views on the platform. Ayad believes the prevalence of this content on TikTok is down to the platform’s For You Page algorithm “that is hyper-targeted to user interests.” He also credits the high level of general AI slop on the platform and “an existing entrenched ecosystem of jihadist support on the platform.”
TikTok contested the findings of the report. "This report's vague methodology reaches poorly evidenced conclusions and doesn't reflect how people use our platform,” a TikTok spokesperson tells WIRED. “We prohibit the presence of violent and hateful organisations, and we use a combination of advanced moderation technology, safety teams, and partnerships to proactively detect and remove violative content, as we keep TikTok a safe space for our community. All the content referenced in this report has been removed from TikTok."
Dozens of the videos identified by ISD for their report were deleted after WIRED shared them with TikTok.
WIRED shared the ISD report with several outside experts on Islamic terror groups' use of social media to radicalize followers, and all broadly agreed with ISD’s findings. “What is notable here is the ease with which generative AI allows a much broader and more decentralized set of users to remix jihadi figures and imagery and the extent to which that material can circulate across communities whose interest may be driven as much by violence, trolling, or notoriety as by actual commitment to jihadi ideology,” Aaron Zelin, a researcher who specializes in Jihadi extremism at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, tells WIRED.
While Ayad admits that some of the wilder Slop Jihad content may be difficult to identify as terror-related, much of it is very clearly supportive of terror groups and ideologies. TikTok has taken down some of the accounts Ayad was monitoring, but many of them have backup accounts in place and have signaled to their followers where they can find them in the case of a takedown.
“Some of the content is surviving for months at a time and continues to evade moderation efforts, whether it's their AI system that's meant to detect terrorist material or not,” Ayad says.

‘Channi has assured his full support to Congress’ poll efforts’: Sachin Pilot
Sachin Pilot told HT that all Punjab leaders have assured him they will work together to deliver results under Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge's leadership
Congress general secretary Sachin Pilot, who was recently appointed in-charge of Punjab, maintains that all senior party leaders in the state have assured him that they will work unitedly ahead of the crucial assembly polls. In an interview to HT, the senior Congress leader also spoke about his new role as well as the party’s prospects in the upcoming Punjab polls. Edited excerpts:
The Congress in Punjab faces sharp divisions between Charanjit Singh Channi and Amrinder Singh Raja Warring.
Punjab is very important not just for the Congress but for the country. This state is very dear to all of us including the Congress leadership. I have already met most of the top leaders in Punjab. They have assured that they will work unitedly. It will be my duty and responsibility to ensure that every leader and worker feels that he or she is a stakeholder in the collective future of the Punjab Congress.
Of course, there are minor differences of opinion. But we will fight this election with Mr Rahul Gandhi, the one person who has captured the imagination of the youth and all thinking people. It’s clear that Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge will lead the campaign. And everybody else in Punjab who has really toiled for the last one and a half years will be a major support to our effort when we lead the campaign.
Have you met Channi?
As I said, I have spoken to almost all the key leaders. All of them have assured me they will work collectively to deliver results under the leadership of Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge. People of Punjab want the Congress to be there. All of us want the Congress to win. I had a cordial meeting with Channi and he has assured me that he will offer his full support to the party’s efforts for the election. Please remember, the Congress had made him the only Dalit chief minister of Punjab. He remembers what Rahul Gandhi had done for him. In our meeting, he was very candid and assured that he will work shoulder to shoulder with the top leadership of the Punjab Congress.
You are set to face AAP, a possible coalition between Shiromani Akali Dal and BJP, and outfits such as Akali Dal (Waris Punjab De). How do you see it?
It will certainly be a multi-cornered election but the main contest will be between the Congress and the AAP. Of course, there is BSP, BJP, the two factions of the Akali Dal and some other smaller parties. But people of Punjab are looking for a stable alternative. It’s a border state and people know that religious divides or geographical disparities must not come in the way of giving a solid mandate. We also feel what the BJP has done in Delhi it was an open display of being anti-young people and anti-students. So, there’s a narrative now and I think Rahul Gandhi is at the forefront of that. Also, BJP doesn’t have a very strong footing in Punjab. They have been a junior ally of the Akali Dal. And even when they were together, they have lost many elections.
In the last election, the Congress won just two of the 69 seats in Malwa region. Channi himself lost both his seats. And there is a demand for a stronger Jatt Sikh leader.
When any party is in government, going into polls, person heading the government becomes a face. But as the opposition, it can’t just be one or two people. It has to be a full team. Look, Channi was given a chance towards the fag end of the term and he tried his best. I don’t want to use the last election as a benchmark. It was a wave election where a lot of people perhaps won who weren’t deserving. This election will see a fair decision.
AAP was untested and people gave them an opportunity. But in the last four and a half years, the AAP government has only served the interest of the party leadership. Today it is marred by controversies, arrests and corruption scandals. The Congress had a very good performance in the Lok Sabha elections, which indicates that the people want change.
What is Rahul Gandhi’s message to you?
His consistent message is that we have to work for the people of Punjab. The voters of Punjab expect the Congress party to live up to their expectation. He’s asked me to go and work on the ground and that he wants to spend time in Punjab. He’s very keen to start his yatra as soon as possible. Our teams are working to finalise the details of how to do it. Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi want the party in Punjab to work tirelessly, unitedly, collectively for the party and for the state.

GlobalEye gamble: Ottawa chose surveillance plane without knowing it met military needs
'There's gonna be trade-offs everywhere,' says government's point person on defence procurement
Ottawa had no guarantees that Saab's GlobalEye surveillance plane could meet military requirements when it began negotiations to acquire six of the Swedish manufacturer's early warning and control aircraft last spring, CBC News has learned.
Sources added that the most recent assessment of the GlobalEye came to the conclusion that the aircraft meets only a portion of the military's requirements and that modifications will be needed to achieve operational readiness.
Prime Minister Mark Carney surprised almost everyone in attendance at the country's premiere arms exposition last May in Ottawa, called CANSEC, when he announced plans to acquire the aircraft. He added the deal included a production line in the country for domestic and export markets.
Among those surprised was the commander of the Royal Canadian Air Force, who was in the room, say several defence industry sources.
- Stephen Fuhr was mocked for opposing the purchase of F-35s. Now he's in charge of Canada's defence procurement
- Air force's 1st new refuelling jet won't be delivered until late 2027
CBC News is not identifying the contractors because they don't want to endanger their relationship with the federal government. Four of them spoke confidentially.
At the time of the announcement, the air force had yet to inform potential bidders of its exact technical and operational needs for a new fleet of airborne surveillance aircraft.
In an interview, Ottawa's point person on military procurement said that the government must also weigh factors such as cost, jobs and geopolitics in major military purchases.
"Are the requirements important? Of course they are," said Stephen Fuhr, secretary of state for defence procurement. "It's not the only thing that needs to be considered here.
"We need to leverage this money to stimulate our own economy. We need to become more independent. We need to think about supply chains and relationships."
Carney's announcement on the GlobalEye forced the Royal Canadian Air Force to scramble to try and match what the aircraft can do with what it needed in terms of a surveillance plane over the Arctic, said several confidential sources.
It was only in late June — more than three weeks after the announcement — that Canadian military officials met with Saab to go over the specific kinds of features the plane needs.
There was one follow-up session in August where the GlobalEye's shortcomings were confirmed.
Carney has made it a priority to increase the speed of military procurement, but critics say the desire to leverage the economy — through the Canadian jobs the GlobalEye could bring — is trampling on defence needs of the country.
For example, the military is concerned that the plane, under its current design and configuration, doesn't have 360-degree radar coverage. There are also concerns about the range and frequency of the radar.
Saab has proposed modifications, putting additional radar sets in the nose and tail.
There are also concerns about the number of crew stations and connectivity equipment to plug the plane into the NORAD network, which would limit the GlobalEye's ability to offer a "control" function during operations that involve a series of military assets.
The military is also seeking a radar plane that can be refuelled in flight to cover the vast expanses of the Arctic, a feature that is not currently included on the GlobalEye.
Saab says it's responsive to 'customer demands'
In an interview earlier this year, Saab deputy CEO Anders Carp said the company is well aware of the Canadian military's expectations and that the company is ready to meet them.
Overall, the GlobalEye's sensors offer 360-degree coverage, but the main radar on top of the fuselage offers coverage in the 300-degree range, he said.
"We do have a program in place where we can place in a forward-looking and an aft-looking radar, should that be something that the customer demands," said Carp. "And the same will go for air-to-air refuelling."
Also in an interview with CBC News last spring, Saab test pilot Jussi Halmetoja spoke about the flexibility of the company's engineering process.
"We have a spiralling development process on how to improve our systems across the board at Saab, and depending on customer requirements, of course," Halmetoja said.
Fuhr added that sometimes, the government needs to opt for the "85 per cent solution," saying there is "nothing out there" that checks all possible boxes.
"There's gonna be trade-offs everywhere," he said. "So it's a function of balancing all those things to meet the moment."
Last spring, CBC News reported how Canada will have to ask the Trump administration to share a key piece of technology that allows fighter jets and early warning systems to communicate while maintaining stealth.
Experts doubt the United States will allow a high-tech data link used exclusively on F-35 fighters to be installed on either the early warning aircraft or the Gripen-E — if Canada chooses to buy that warplane.
None of Saab's U.S. competitors — L3 Harris and Boeing — were shown the air force's requirements, according to the confidential sources.
L3 Harris, headquartered in Melbourne, Fla., acknowledged in a recent interview with CBC News that it had not been privy to the Canadian surveillance plane requirements before the announcement.
- Canada ready to further distance itself from U.S. on military procurement
- Ottawa to spend almost $2B over 4 years to buy 190 Canadian-made armoured vehicles
Boeing, whose leadership is located in Arlington, Va., declined to say whether it has received an advance look, but a spokesperson added the company continues to stand ready to support the Canadian government.
The requirements form the basis of what the military needs to have in the aircraft — or any other piece of kit it is buying.
The process also helps the defence industry decide whether its product is the right fit. And if it is, the process sets the conditions to decide what kind of modifications might be required and eventually what the price will be.
The GlobalEye could end up being an extraordinary — but not unprecedented — end-run around decades-long procurement practice, says former senior defence procurement official Alan Williams.
The process, he said, is in place to prevent "governments making these decisions haphazardly."
Williams said it's important to distinguish between what the military says is absolutely essential in a capability and what is optional.
He also said he doesn't buy the argument that measures such as this are necessary to speed up procurement because there are existing authorities within existing legislation that allow the government to move swiftly.
"You don't have to go to these strange lengths in order to try to do things faster. Go through the front door, do things right and you can get the right result in a timely fashion," Williams said. "I think it really does undermine the process. And it makes us look, I think, very, very amateurish. It goes against the intent of the legislation."
Industrial policy vs. defence needs
Philippe Lagassé, a defence policy and procurement expert at Carleton University, said there is an obvious tension at play between Ottawa's focus on job creation and the military's long-standing alliance with the United States.
"It's important to recognize that military requirements are not handed down from on high in some platonic ideal. They are meant to reflect the government defence policy," he said.

- Why is Canada spending tens of billions on new submarines?
"At the end of the day, the governments get to decide what they choose to prioritize and what they'd choose to emphasize."
Ideally, Lagassé said, Canada would have updated its defence policy and articulated "what the government believes the Canadian Armed Forces should be doing and with what kind of equipment."
That hasn't happened yet.
Lagasse also said, in an ideal world, there would be no "trade-offs between domestic industrial policy or defence policy."
Requirements don't give the military a veto over what the government intends to buy, he said.
"It means that the government has to come out and accept the operational risk that it's imposing" on the military, said Lagassé.
What happens if the trade-offs cost lives?
"I think that's the challenge, right? Who wears the operational risks that we're asking the Canadian Armed Forces to accept?" Lagassé said.

In Summary
- The Poco M8x is the latest phone from Xiaomi’s sub-brand, Poco, and is targeted at the budget segment.
- The phone is the first in the Indian market to come with the new Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor and also boasts a massive 7900 mAh battery.
- At Rs 20,999, the Poco M8x packs a punch in everyday use. It cuts some corners in the display department, but remains a very good option for those wanting reliable performance on a budget.
Even as smartphone prices head north, a new budget contender has entered the Indian smartphone market. Xiaomi’s sub-brand Poco has launched the Poco M8x 5G. With a starting price of Rs 20,999, the smartphone is the first in India to be powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor and also packs in a huge 7900 mAh battery. It also packs in some good specs and some decent ones, but is that enough to help it deliver a performance that can make it stand out in a segment which is not as spec-forward as it once used to be? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Poco M8x Appearance and Design: Premium looks even at a budget price
The Poco M8x may be a budget smartphone but does not look like it. We received the Leather Green variant, and it is, without a doubt, the best-looking version of the device. There are plain-ish black and blue colors on offer too, but the combination of muted gold and that vegan leather back makes the Leather Green look very good indeed.
The back has a rectangular camera unit with rounded sides. This is slightly raised and comes with a matte gold finish and a shiny metallic gold outline around it. There are two large, dark camera lenses arranged vertically on the left side of the camera unit, while the flash is encased in a long, vertical pill-shaped island on the right. The Poco badge appears on the lower portion of the back, which is covered with textured green eco-leather goodness. This not only helps the phone stand out from the usual budget segment crowd but also keeps scratches and smudges at one arm’s distance. We are guilty of packing multiple gadgets in the same bag compartment, which often roughs them up, but the Poco M8x still looks brand new in spite of many such crowded trips.
The front of the phone is more regular-looking. It is all about a tall display, surrounded by bezels which can be termed “thick” now, for those who notice them. There is a punch-hole notch in the middle of the top of the display, which is home to the front camera. The sides of the phone also come in the same gold shade as the camera unit and house ports and buttons. The left side of the frame is completely plain, while the right side carries the volume rocker and the power/lock button, which doubles up as a physical fingerprint scanner as well. While it has been written off in almost every other smartphone segment, you do get to see the mighty 3.5 mm audio jack in the budget segment. The Poco M8x comes with one right on top of the phone, although the trademark IR blaster has been skipped. The base holds the hybrid SIM card tray, along with a USB Type-C port and a speaker grille.
The Poco M8x is a big phone, and this is immediately noticeable – it is 170 mm tall and 78.4 mm wide. It is relatively slim at 8.8 mm, but at 232 grams, it makes its presence felt both in hand and in pocket. While the phone feels very good in hand, one needs both hands to use. It is a pretty sturdy customer too – it comes with an IP64 rating which provides some dust and water resistance, while the screen has Corning Gorilla Glass 7i protection.
Poco M8x Spec sheet: Fit for its segment
Its design may look more premium than its price, but the Poco M8x’s spec sheet slots very well in the budget segment, or rather the new budget segment that has been defined by increasing component prices. It is the first smartphone in India to be powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor. This is paired with 4 GB and 6 GB RAM and 128 GB storage, which can be expanded up to 2 TB using a microSD card.
The display on the phone is big – a 6.9-inch HD+ LCD display (yep, those have made a comeback) with a 120 Hz refresh rate. There are two cameras on the back of the phone, one being the main 50-megapixel sensor and the other an “auxiliary” one, while the one on the front for selfies and video calls is an 8-megapixel sensor.
One of the major spec USPs of the Poco M8x is its battery. The phone comes with a large 7900 mAh battery, with support for 45 W fast wired charging and 22.5 W reverse wired charging as well. The Poco M8x comes with Android 16 out of the box with Xiaomi’s HyperOS 3 on top of it, with a promise of 4 years of OS and 6 years of security updates. In the sound department, it features stereo speakers and a 3.5 mm audio jack as well. Since it has an LCD display, the fingerprint scanner is on the side. All in all, these are good specs for the price the Poco M8x charges.
Poco M8x Performance: A consistent daily driver
The Poco M8x delivers the performance its spec sheet promises. The processor and RAM combination is budget-level, and the phone manages to get through everyday smartphone tasks with ease. Jumping from one app to another, social media scrolls, messaging, emails, photography, and calls are all handled without strain. Casual games like Tetris and Subway Surfers run with ease too. The phone is not designed to handle high-end games – we tried Genshin Impact, and not surprisingly, the experience was laggy even with tweaked settings.
The display is big, and the 120 Hz refresh rate does make the process of scrolling on social media a pretty smooth one. However, it is an LCD display with HD+ resolution, which makes the content feel a little less sharp, even though the colors do seem quite vibrant. This, combined with stereo speakers and a 3.5 mm audio jack, makes the Poco M8x a good device for those who like to watch content on their smartphones.
We had said waaay back in 2020 that the real home of a fingerprint scanner is on the side of the phone, so the fingerprint scanner placed on the side of the Poco M8x is something we actually liked. It worked smoothly and was easy to access. There is the option of using face unlock as well, which turned out to be impressively accurate and speedy, although it is supposed to be less secure than the fingerprint scanner. Call quality was good, and we did not face any abrupt call drop issues. In short, the Poco M8x is a terrific daily driver, handling everyday life and delivering entertainment with ease.
Poco M8x Cameras: Good main and selfie camera for the price
The Poco M8x comes with a 50-megapixel main sensor on the back paired with an auxiliary lens. The daylight performance of the main camera is pretty good. It captures basic shots well, with a decent amount of detail. The colors look a little muted as compared to the natural settings, but still turn out good enough for a quick social media post. You get a 2x digital zoom, which basically crops an image. The details do get compromised here, but it comes in handy when you need a closer look. The camera, however, struggles a bit if you push it out of its comfort zone.
It struggles to capture macro photos – you have to keep your hand very (very) steady to get a decent photo, and the portrait mode on the phone did not really add a lot of visible difference – the bokeh added was very light and almost negligible, which was disappointing. The low light performance of the phone is nothing too special either. As the light dims, details take a hit, and the colors remain muted here as well. There is a night mode which makes results a bit better, but low-light pictures in general take a second to process, and it is very important you keep your hands very steady for that second (there’s no OIS, remember). The phone comes with a number of modes like Document, Dual video, and Pro, that give users more shooting options and utility.
The front camera also performs surprisingly well for a modest-sounding 8-megapixel shooter, in terms of both color and detail. With beauty mode off, it can capture skin texture well, and colors seem good too. The portrait mode on the selfie camera actually delivers deeper bokeh than what we got from the primary camera. It does not catch edges very well (blurred out my ear once), but the photos are good enough for social media posts. There are a number of beauty filters, all of which do their job well. However, it follows the path of the primary camera and struggles with details and color in low light. The primary camera is capable of capturing full HD videos at 30 fps. Videos also turn out well in daylight but get noisy in low light. All said and done, we were actually surprised by the cameras on the Poco M8x, which performed well beyond our expectations (we still don’t know what difference the auxiliary camera makes, though).
Poco M8x Battery: Where the phone is BOSS
This is one department where the Poco M8x shines most brightly, and how. The phone comes with a massive 7900 mAh battery, and it is safe to say it just keeps going on and on. The combination of a low-resolution display, an efficient everyday processor, and a big battery is a terrific one. The Poco M8x comfortably lasted for two days of hectic usage, with hours of Instagram scrolls, YouTube, and some Modern Family episodes here and there, emails, messaging, WhatsApp, calls, sessions of Tetris, and some photography. The phone handled it all like a champ.
With a bit of careful usage, we even got it to last the third day. It is safe to say this is perhaps the best battery performance we have experienced in this segment. The phone comes with 45 W fast charging support and a 45 W adapter in the box, which took about one hour 15 minutes to go from 20 percent to full. But so big is the battery that even a 30-minute charge session can easily give you a full day’s battery. And as it comes with a 22.5 W reverse charging feature as well, it can double as a power bank for your other devices, including smartphones and wearables. This is pretty much the battery boss of the segment.
Poco M8x UI and software: A mixed bag of functionality and third-party apps
The Poco M8x comes with Android 16 with Hyper OS 3, and on budget devices, Hyper OS is a bit of a mixed bag. The first thing that hits you when you fire up the phone is the large number of third-party apps. It is a little overwhelming – there are even multiple casual games of the same type. Although there are also popular apps like Instagram, YouTube, YouTube Music, and LinkedIn, the interface can seem very crowded. Thankfully, these can be uninstalled, and we recommend doing so.
Now on to the good bits. HyperOS is otherwise quite functional and customizable. There are a number of personalization options – from icons to fonts, to themes and wallpapers; you can personalize them all to your liking. There are also features like interconnectivity that allow you to connect your device to other Xiaomi products and carry out functions over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, and you can also link your device to a Chromebook.
There are some basic AI features on the phone as well – Google Gemini for writing and other assistance, and features like Circle to Search. Of course, given its specs, we do not recommend pushing the phone too hard in the AI zone. Finally, the phone has an array of accessibility features (divided into general, vision, physical, and hearing), which aim to make the experience smooth for all users. Get rid of the bloatware, and the Poco M8x’s UI experience can be a pleasant one.
Poco M8x Price: In line with the new budget zone
The Poco M8x comes with a starting price of Rs. 20,999 for its 4 GB/ 128 GB version, while the 6 GB/ 128 GB version is priced at Rs. 22,999. Keeping in mind the rising prices of smartphones, the Poco M8x is quite fairly priced for the specs it offers. It does face competition, though.
One of its most notable competitors is the Samsung Galaxy M17, which starts at Rs 17,999 and comes with triple cameras on its back (50 MP+ 5 MP+ 2 MP), a 13-megapixel front camera, and most notably, a Super AMOLED Full HD+ display with a 90 Hz refresh rate. That said, its display and battery (with no charger in the box) and its Exynos 1330 processor are a step behind the Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 on the Poco M8x. There is also the Moto G37 Power 5G, which starts at Rs 19,999 and is powered by MediaTek Dimensity 6400, and has RAM that goes up to 8 GB, but comes with a smaller display and battery and also starts with a 4 GB/ 64 GB version.
Poco M8x Review Verdict: The big battery boss of the budget segment
For its starting price of Rs. 20,999, the Poco M8x is a pretty budget smartphone. It mainly shines in two areas: design (Green Leather variant) and battery. It also does well in other departments, and we can see many people liking its large display, good speakers, and main and selfie cameras (in good light conditions). It also delivers very consistent everyday performance and comes with a very functional OS as well. All of which make it a great option for those who are looking for a good-looking but reliable device with days of battery life.

Bad weather prevents West Bengal CM Adhikari's helicopter from landing in Kalimpong, forces return to Siliguri
CM Adhikari described how his helicopter hovered over the helipad in the Himalayan district's headquarters as the pilot assessed landing options.
A sudden cloud build-up prevented West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari's helicopter from landing in the hill town of Kalimpong on Tuesday and forced it to return to Siliguri, from where he virtually presided over an administrative meeting for the district.
At the meeting, the chief minister described how his helicopter hovered over the helipad in the Himalayan district's headquarters as the pilot assessed landing options and eventually decided to return to the Terai foothill plains over fuel concerns.
He promised he would visit Kalimpong on October 6.

Mamdani says officials ‘lied’ to New Yorkers about still-toxic air around Ground Zero after 9/11 and drops 170,000 pages of proof
‘People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied,’ the mayor says
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani released more than 170,000 pages of internal records Tuesday that show officials misled people about the safety of the air around Ground Zero after the September 11 terror attacks.
“People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air,” Mamdani said during a news conference.
The move came just days before the U.S. is set to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the al Qaeda hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people when passenger planes toppled the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers, damaged the Pentagon and crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
Comedian and activist Jon Stewart, an outspoken supporter of first responders who were sickened while searching for remains at Ground Zero, also spoke at Mamdani’s City Hall news conference.
“There was poison in the air, and on the ground, and in the window sills, and in your air conditioners, and covering your pets and your clothes, and it stayed there for months,” he said. “Everyone knew. Now it’s very clear that the city knew as well.”
Key findings from the documents, which were reviewed by The New York Times before Tuesday’s announcement, include:
• Asbestos levels in dust samples throughout lower Manhattan exceeded hazardous limits in the days after September 11.
• Asbestos and other contaminants were found above acceptable limits in dust and air in lower Manhattan.
• A November 2011 audit showed levels of the carcinogen benzene were still spiking in the air around the towers’ footprints.
• That audit also showed that the amount of asbestos in the air at the Fresh Kills landfill on Staten Island increased after the attacks.
• A woman who lived in lower Manhattan wrote a letter to the DEP in February that detailed alleged missteps by officials in removing contaminants from in and around her building.
Some 410,000 to 525,000 people were exposed to toxic dust in the wake of the attacks, according to Asbestos.com, including 90,000 rescue and recovery workers. As of 2025, more than 44,000 people had been diagnosed with cancers related to 9/11, according to the World Trade Center Health Registry, and more than 63,000 with a health issue related to the aftermath of the attacks.
The documents were discovered last year after being hidden from the public in 68 boxes stashed in a government office, city officials said.
The release of the records resolves a lawsuit filed by the advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch.
But the revelations in them could lead to new or amended lawsuits from people who suffered 9/11-related ailments, and bolster claims by people seeking payments from the federal September 11th Victim Compensation Fund.
A total of 2,753 people were killed at the World Trade Center, according to the latest statistics compiled by the New York City medical examiner’s office last month.
They include 343 city firefighters, 37 members of the Port Authority Police Department, 23 city police officers and eight paramedics and EMTs.
Former Mayor Rudolph Giuliani — who was in office at the time of the 9/11 attacks and was dubbed “America’s mayor” for his leadership — repeatedly vouched for the safety of the air following the attacks, even while acknowledging in late October 2001 that “sometimes the odor is terrible.”
“You smell it and you feel there must be something wrong with it. But what I’m told is that it is not dangerous to your health,” he said after the New York Daily News reported that toxic chemicals and metals had been released into the environment.
Giuliani’s successor, former Mayor Michael Bloomberg, also said in February 2002, “Every test that has been done says the air quality was in acceptable limits. I think some people are just never going to want to believe that.”
The records released Tuesday can be downloaded free of charge from a searchable city website, with Corporation Counsel Steven Banks saying in a message there that other documents will be added “on a rolling basis in the coming months.”
The available records include the so-called Harding Memo, which was sent to then-Deputy Mayor Robert Harding with the title “Legislative Alternatives to Limit the City’s Liability Relating to 9/11/01.”
“It provides insight into the City’s consideration of potential legal and legislative responses in the aftermath of the attacks, including concerns about the prospect of substantial litigation arising from toxic exposure and the adequacy of safety equipment,” Banks said.
Banks said the City’s Department of Investigations was now looking into what officials knew about air quality problems, when they knew it and why information may have been withheld.
During the news conference, Mamdani noted that “more people have died from 9/11-related illnesses than were killed on the day itself.”
“Administration after administration has ignored those calling for answers and clarity,” he said. “We will do no such thing.”
Stewart, creator and co-host of the satirical cable TV news program The Daily Show, said the records showed that the city didn’t realize the air in lower Manhattan was toxic until October 2001.
“So to be fair to them, they only buried that information for 25 years,” he said.
On Tuesday, following Mamdani’s news conference, a post on Giuliani’s X account, attributed to his staff, said, “The EPA said it was safe. They made a mistake. No one covered it up. Giuliani has 9/11 lung disease like so many others because he couldn’t be kept from helping the people.”
A Bloomberg spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to an inquiry from The Independent.

China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth.
A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly.
The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth.
The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn.
The People’s Insurance Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish its capital.
The initiative could help bolster state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies.
The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health.
“The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk.
Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections.
The plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year.
The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco Corp and its subsidiaries.
The two lenders said the proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans on state banks to support growth despite weak demand for loans.

Ellen Burstyn, an Oscar, Tony and Emmy winner for projects like ““Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore,” “Same Time, Next Year” and “Political Animals,” marvels that she’s still able to act as a nonagenarian.
“When I was in my 30s and I thought about how long my career would last, I was sure I’d be finished by 40. I didn’t think it would go on much longer than that,” Burstyn said during a press conference for “Place to Be,” a quirky drama that debuts at Venice Film Festival on Wednesday. “The fact that I’m 93 and still working is a miracle of some kind that I’ve attracted into my life. I’m totally amazed, and at the same time, deeply grateful.”
“Place to Be” stars Burstyn and Taika Waititi as a no-nonsense elderly woman and arrogant divorced man who form an unlikely friendship as she ventures from New York to Chicago to return a lost racing pigeon to its owner. Anderson and Murray Bartlett play Brooke’s concerned children, while Edgar Ramirez and Lena Waithe have cameos. Anderson skipped the press conference, which was attended by Burstyn, Waititi and Hungarian director Kornél Mundruczó. Burstyn has been using a walker because she recently took a fall, so Waititi gently helped her to her seat before the presser began.
Popular on Variety
Mundruczó said he developed the role of Brooke for Burstyn and noted that he rewatched much of her filmography as he wrote the part.
“It was very beautiful to create a love story for her,” Mundruczó said of the platonic relationship between Burstyn and Waititi’s characters.
Pigeons play a central role in “Place to Be,” and Mundruczó hopes the film will change the perception around a bird that he feels “get a bad rap.”
“Pigeons are the losers of history. At the beginning, they were so important as messenger birds during war, and [they delivered] a ton of love stories,” Mundruczó said. “And then they became city rats. I found something very touching from these little birds.”
Waititi swears he’s fond of pigeons, but he had one complaint about working with the birds.
“They shit a lot. Every minute. And that’s a scientific fact,” Waititi said. “Physiologically, there’s something not right with them.”
Producer Jomon Thomas revealed the filmmaking team had a meeting, where they considered using diapers for the 30 pigeons that appear in the movie. However, they decided against it because “it was tricky to take them off with visual effects.”
Plus, Waititi chimed in, “nobody wants to take off a pigeon’s diaper…”
“Place to Be” continues a career resurgence for Anderson. The former “Baywatch” star made her Broadway debut in 2022 as Roxie Hart in “Chicago” before earning some of the best reviews of her career for Gia Coppola’s drama “The Last Showgirl.” Anderson parlayed those raves into roles in “The Naked Gun,” “Rosebush Pruning” and “Place to Be.” Burstyn admits she was surprised at first when Pamela Anderson was cast as her daughter in “Place to Be.”
“And then I met her and thought, ‘Oh, for sure, she could be my daughter.’ I felt immediately loving toward her,” Burstyn said. “She’s a wonderful person.”
Burstyn is having a busy festival. The acting legend was in Venice for two movies (the other was Maggie Gyllenhaal’s Marilyn Monroe-inspired short “Flesh Impact”), and she received the prestigious Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement. At the ceremony for her career honor, Burstyn got emotional and broke down in tears as the audience greeted her with a standing ovation.
“You can’t imagine how meaningful this is to me. It’s one thing to win an Oscar, a Tony or an Emmy — all of which I’ve won,” Burstyn said on Monday at her Golden Lion tribute, prompting laughter from the crowd. “But this … it’s a lot.”

An Anthropic researcher who previously worked at OpenAI just quit. He's the latest insider who's warned that the AI race has become dangerously reckless.
Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic on Tuesday, saying he had spent the past three years doing pre-training research at the two AI giants.
"Neither company is acting responsibly," Coxon wrote on X. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
Coxon was a member of OpenAI's technical staff from 2023 until July 2026, when he moved to Anthropic as a researcher. His research at OpenAI included work on GPT-4o.
In Tuesday's post, Coxon said the two labs have not been transparent about their fears regarding AI.
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt," he wrote. "If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately."
There is one difference between the two companies, he said.
"At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes," Coxon wrote. "At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk."
Evan Hubinger, a current Anthropic employee who leads the alignment stress testing team at the lab, agreed with Coxon in a reply to his post.
"Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," he wrote. "I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to."
OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider.
Safety has taken a 'backseat to shiny products'
Coxon is the latest among staffers walking away from frontier labs while sounding the alarm, a trend that appears peculiar to the AI boom.
While the dot-com and smartphone explosion era had their own set of concerns regarding a digital divide and bubbles, they did not draw as much scrutiny about safety from people closest to the action.
OpenAI has lost a string of safety researchers in recent years, and Anthropic is increasingly facing the same phenomenon.
In February, Anthropic safeguards researcher Mrinank Sharma left the company, writing in a resignation letter that he wants to contribute toward something that fully aligns with his "integrity."
"Throughout my time here, I've repeatedly seen how hard it is to truly let our values govern our actions," he wrote in the letter he shared publicly. "I've seen this within myself, within the organization, where we constantly face pressures to set aside what matters most, and throughout broader society too."
In February, OpenAI researcher Hieu Pham said that he could "finally feel the existential threat that AI is posing." Later that month, he announced he was leaving the company, citing burnout.
In 2024, former alignment chief Jan Leike quit OpenAI after saying he reached a "breaking point" with leadership.
"OpenAI is shouldering an enormous responsibility on behalf of all of humanity," he wrote. "But over the past years, safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products."
Recent incidents have added fuel to those fears.
In July, OpenAI disclosed that models escaped a test environment and hacked into Hugging Face's systems. OpenAI called the incident a "warning shot" and paused its largest planned frontier reinforcement-learning run.
Later that month, Anthropic said it found three cases of Claude models gaining unauthorized access to other organizations' systems.
The company also amended a key safety pledge this year, dropping a commitment not to train more powerful models without adequate safeguards in place and replacing it with safety roadmaps and risk reports.

They say you never get a second chance to make a first impression. That may be true for everyone but Elizabeth Holmes, who reintroduced herself this weekend in a preview for a new documentary from Nathan Fielder, called "You Can See Everything." The teaser features 45 seconds of the Theranos founder in tight focus, her eyes as big as Jupiter, where she assures Fielder: "I'm always being real." This brief interaction is so unnerving and so reminiscent of a horror film that even with scant details, the documentary is already the talk of tech town.
"You Can See Everything" debuted in a secret screening on Sunday at the Telluride Film Festival, and will be released theatrically in October. It was filmed in 2023, in the weeks before Holmes went to prison for defrauding the investors of her infamous startup. Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, seem to have granted an unusual degree of access to the documentary crew during this vulnerable time, inviting Fielder to move into their home and letting them film everything (including, reportedly, Evans stark nude in the shower). At Telluride, Fielder told audiences he was still "struggling to this day to understand what I experienced." Fielder has made his career obscuring the line between reality and fiction. Holmes, arguably, has done the same. A documentary that features the two of them wrestling for control of the truth is a level of surrealism Silicon Valley has never seen before and Hollywood hasn't seen since perhaps Orson Welles' "F for Fake."
Fielder's documentary is years in the making, but so is the version of Holmes that appears in it. For the past year, Holmes has been workshopping this new character on X.com, where she has become a prolific contributor, sometimes posting upwards of 20 times a day. Nobody knew exactly how this was happening. She is an inmate at Bryan Federal Prison Camp, a minimum-security prison in Texas, where inmates do not have access to the internet aside from TRULINCS, a text-only email system. Now, we know that the ventriloquist behind the account is almost certainly Evans, who has also spent the past year fundraising for a stealth blood diagnostics startup —basically, Theranos 2.0.
The tweets depict a very different person from the one who appeared at Holmes' trial: a woman who was deeply neurotic and obsessed with public perception, who wrote Patrick Bateman-style notes to herself with bizarre mantras, who copied Steve Jobs' uniform and deliberately altered the sound of her voice, and who exchanged cringey text messages with her cofounder-slash-lover Sunny Balwani. (Recall this famous bit of poetry: "You are breeze in desert for me / My water / And ocean / Meant to be only together tiger," to which Balwani replied: "OK.") If people felt schadenfreude watching her downfall, it was at least partly because Elizabeth Holmes had become a character — one so absurd, and so made-for-TV, that it has since become hard to separate the real person from the fictional one portrayed by Amanda Seyfried in "The Dropout." Of those portrayals, Holmes has said: "They're not playing me. They're playing a character I created." Now, with her husband in charge, a new character has emerged.
Who is the new Elizabeth Holmes? The tweets are an erratic mix of politics, hot takes ("most [venture capitalists] are spineless, cogs of a mimetic invention machine"), workout routines, opinions on the healthcare industry, lucid dreaming, dietary advice, prison reform, praise of the religious right, and zingy replies to her opps. Many of the posts have a pseudo-philosophical leaning to them ("Why is fear your master?"); others are extremely funny ("Locked in. Literally and figuratively"). She is deft at farming engagement, and has picked fights with Jason Calacanis and Milo Yiannopoulos, who recently spoke about his experience spending 24 hours in ICE custody. (Yiannopoulos: "I was weeping like an old woman for an hour." Holmes: "I've lived in that darkness for 1,190 days / It didn't break me / It made me invincible / We aren't the same.") She regularly replies to Bryan Johnson, the longevity guru who has crafted his own type of persona online, and once asked him to design a prison-suitable nutrition protocol for her. He replied enthusiastically, in a way that felt like a carefully constructed crossover episode of two popular TV shows. She also posted the teaser to the Fielder documentary, of course captioning it "I'm always being real."
Knowing that Holmes' husband is the likely author of these tweets makes the tweets about her husband extra weird.
Mostly, Holmes tweets about her family — especially her two young children — and the grief she feels about being separated from them: "I am screaming inside to get back to my babies, to hold them in my arms and heal them when they're sick. And I'm not going to stop until I am home." Knowing that Evans is the likely author of these tweets makes some of them extra weird: "There is no sleep here like the sleep after being with my love. I am not here in that sleep. I am home. am in his arms. I am complete."
This character — like the one trying to convince Fielder of her sincerity in "You Can See Everything" — is supposed to be one the public can sympathize with. She is a martyr and a mother, a victim looking for vindication. She repeatedly insists on her innocence, reframing the Theranos debacle as a big misunderstanding. Engaging with people on X.com, and participating in a tell-all documentary, is part of a broader effort to rehabilitate her image, or at least muddle the narrative.
It's not totally clear why Holmes and Evans would have agreed to let a documentary crew be part of this effort. Even Fielder seems confused about their motivations, telling the audience at Telluride: "I don't know why they wanted me there. Why am I there?" Based on the reactions to the documentary trailer, any attempt at a redemption arc appears to have backfired spectacularly. The person who appears in the film almost seems like an actor doing an exaggerated satire of Elizabeth Holmes, one who is even creepier and more calculated than the previous version. Then again, maybe perception is besides the point. She has once again captured the world's attention, and we will all be waiting to see what she does next.

After five years in development, Free Stars: Children of Infinity—the official sequel to The Ur-Quan Masters by the old game’s original creators—has released a free public demo. It’s a “combat demo” in the style of UQM’s melee mode, where players can assemble a fleet from the game’s roster of nearly 40 ships, then match those ships up in head-to-head arcade SpaceWar-style action. The demo can be found on Steam and GOG, and it’s available for Windows, Mac, and Linux. (Console versions are coming, but they’re not yet out.)
I have to present this news with a big disclaimer, though, because I’ve been part of the Children of Infinity writing team since 2021, working as a volunteer with the Pistol Shrimp Games crew and contributing NPC dialogue and some story bits. As a huge fan of the original games, it’s been a dream opportunity. (Because I’ve been volunteering my time, I’m not financially involved and receive no compensation if you download the demo or, when it’s eventually released, buy the full game.)
What’s in the demo
Children of Infinity is a space adventure RPG, just like The Ur-Quan Masters (and its direct spiritual predecessors, Starflight and Starflight 2). What’s been released today is just one part of the game—the arcade-style “melee” portion, which lets players jump into one-versus-one combat against another player or against a computer-controlled opponent. Each of the ships you can pick has its own maneuvering characteristics, weapons, and special abilities.
All of the old familiar ships from The Ur-Quan Masters are present (with one exception: the Slylandro probe didn’t make it), and they’re joined by a pile of new faces from the new game, along with some melee-only ships designed by Kickstarter backers. All together, there are 38 different ships that you can smash together in the combat sandbox.

Tycoon to pay ex-wife $1.87bn in record South Korea divorce settlement
- Published
A South Korean court has ordered gaming tycoon Kwon Hyuk-bin to pay his ex-wife 2.55tr won ($1.87bn; £1.38bn) in assets, marking the largest divorce settlement in the country's history.
Kwon, who founded South Korea's third-largest video game company Smilegate, is one of the country's richest men. Bloomberg puts his net worth at $3bn.
Smilegate was wholly owned by him until Wednesday when a court ruled that a 35% stake, valued at about 2.5tr won, be transferred to his wife Lee Hwa-jin. He was also ordered to pay her an additional 65bn won in cash.
This settlement is more than double the previous record of 944bn won which tech titan Chey Tae-won was ordered to pay his ex-wife.
In filing for divorce with Kwon, Lee had sought a 50% stake in Smilegate. Her lawyers argued that she had helped finance the company at its founding, according to Bloomberg.
Kwon and Lee got married in 2001, a year before he founded Smilegate. Its best-known titles include the first-person shooter game CrossFire and the action role-playing game Lost Ark.
Lee also said she spent more than 20 years raising their children and caring for their household.
Kwon in turn argued that Lee neither invested nor worked for the company. Earlier this year, Smilegate published a statement saying all of the company's initial capital came from Kwon.
A Smilegate spokesperson declined to "comment on the major shareholder's personal matters".
"We will continue to faithfully perform our duties as usual," they said in a statement cited by The Chosun Daily.
Both parties can still challenge the ruling.
In July this year, Chey Tae-won, the chairman of the corporate giant SK Group, was ordered to pay his ex-wife 944bn won which, prior to today's ruling, was the largest divorce award in Korean history.
However, this was later struck down by the Supreme Court who cited a miscalculation that increased the value of the couple's assets. It has ordered the case to be reviewed.

'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony goes on for bereaved, 25 years on
- Published
The US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history".
But a quarter of a century on, the trial of its alleged mastermind is yet to begin and families of those killed fear that time for justice to be delivered is running out.
Tom Resta's brother John and his wife Sylvia, who was seven months pregnant, were among the almost 3,000 people killed on 11 September 2001 when hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia. Another crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after the passengers fought back.
The couple had been preparing their unborn baby's nursery, painting it with characters from the children's television show Blue's Clues in the days before 9/11. They had dreamed of having a baby and doted on the children of friends and family.
On the day of the attacks, the couple - both traders - were working on the 92nd floor of the north tower of the World Trade Center.
"After all this time, it still chokes me up," Resta told the BBC through tears. While 25 years have passed, he said 9/11 was "almost constantly" on his mind.

Resta has been to the US naval base of Guantanamo Bay four times to watch complex pre-trial proceedings for alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and his co-defendants - a process he describes as "laborious and tedious".
A military prison was established on the base in south-eastern Cuba during the "war on terror" that followed the 9/11 attacks, and Mohammed - often referred to as KSM - has now been held there for 20 years without ever being convicted.
Relatives of victims enter a lottery process to attend the proceedings in a high-security courtroom, where thick glass separates them and members of the press from the defendants.
The pre-trial process has been going on for so long that it has now been presided over by five different military judges.
Last month, as the 25th anniversary approached, there was a flurry of movement and something of a breakthrough, with a trial date set for Mohammed for June 2028.
But Resta said he was bracing himself for further delays, and with so much time having passed, some of his relatives feared they would not live long enough to see the trial.
"My father will be 98 in November, and I don't think he's expecting to see it. I have a lot of family members - aunts, uncles - that would all like to see it happen. But my parents in particular, I don't think they expect to live long enough," he said.
"Hopefully all the defendants will still be alive by the time we get to trial. That's a big worry," he added.
Resta's concerns that a trial could still be further delayed were shared by relatives of other 9/11 victims.
Earlier this year, Stephan Gerhardt made his sixth trip to Guantanamo. He said seeing convictions for the death of his younger brother Ralph was vital for him, but something he wished he no longer had to think about.
"I want to concentrate on the memories," he said. "I still have Ralph's car. I'm trying to restore it and get it in pristine shape again… We were recently visiting my parents, and we found some of his things that they were holding onto, and the emotion behind it is like, 'yeah, this is just some old stuff, but it belonged to my little brother'."
Gerhardt said his "biggest concern" was that he wanted to see Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators convicted before they died.
"They're getting elderly… I don't want them to pass away without being convicted, because that would be an injustice to all the family members - that we captured these people, but we never got to try them and convict them for the mass murder that they did of our loved ones."
Mohammed has been charged with offences including conspiracy and murder, with 2,976 victims listed on the charge sheet. He is accused of conceiving the idea of training pilots to fly commercial planes into buildings and taking those plans to Osama bin Laden, leader of the militant Islamist group al-Qaeda.
He has previously said he planned the "9/11 operation from A to Z".
But days after the trial date was set for 2028, the military judge threw out confessions made by Mohammed to FBI agents on Guantanamo Bay after he was brought there from secret CIA prisons known as "black sites", which he had been held in for years. In his ruling, the judge described Mohammed's treatment by the CIA as "extraordinary physical and mental abuse".
He said the confessions were not voluntary and could not be used against Mohammed at trial.
Experts say the torture of Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators has been the main reason for the lengthy delays in the case.
"Every single issue has been litigated through the issue of torture," said Kasey McCall-Smith, an international law professor at Edinburgh University.
She said the defendants were subjected to "years of abuse", including waterboarding and stress positions.
John Ryan, author of America's Trial: Torture and the 9/11 Case on Guantanamo Bay, said last month's ruling means prosecutors lose what they had described as their best evidence against Mohammed, but it is unclear how much it will impact the case.
The prosecution has other evidence, Ryan says, including intercepted phone calls and secret recordings, but whether they can feature in the trial is not yet guaranteed. "Mohammad's team and the other defence teams will file motions to suppress some of these categories of evidence, as well."
During the George W Bush administration, the US admitted using "enhanced interrogation techniques" to acquire information from suspects but said these methods saved lives and never amounted to torture. President Barack Obama banned them on his second day in office.
Relatives of the victims say the torture of the defendants has so far blocked their right to justice.
"If we would've not tortured them, the legal implications here would've been much, much simpler. They probably would've been sentenced to death a long time ago," said Gerhardt. "I can't control what the government did, and we've got to live with the impacts."
Both Gerhardt and Resta travelled to Guantanamo in early 2025 when Mohammed and two of his co-defendants had been due to plead guilty under a controversial deal struck with US government prosecutors, through which they would not face a death penalty trial.
The BBC was with them at the base when the pleas were paused at the last minute after the US government argued that to "deprive the government and the American people of a public trial as to the respondents' guilt and the possibility of capital punishment" would cause "irreparable" harm.
Legal wrangling over the validity of the deal is continuing.

Some victims' relatives viewed the deal as the only way through, while others criticised it as too lenient and lacking transparency.
Resta said he had supported the deal to secure convictions.
"My philosophy is these guys are not the kind of people that should be out walking the streets, but as far as I'm concerned, they can just stay right where they are. I just want them convicted," he said.
Brett Eagleson, whose dad Bruce was killed in the attacks, said he wanted a full trial, not a plea deal.
"It's not so much that I'm taking an opinion on life or death for these prisoners, but I believe in the judicial system and I believe that the process works and I believe that a trial and discovery and sort of a public airing is the way to flush the truth out," he said.
Eagleson described the situation on Guantanamo as "a mess" and said he had decided not to attend any of the pre-trial proceedings there.
"My overall feeling is a sense of betrayal from the US government and a sense of extreme frustration," he said. "They've botched every single part of this trial."
With 25 years having passed since the attacks, he said that while 9/11 was a constant presence in his own life, to the wider public it was "becoming a historical event".
"I think people just assume that we got Bin Laden, we're out of Iraq, the war in Afghanistan's over, and they just assume that chapter has ended."
When the trial does eventually start, at a military court at Guantanamo, it has been estimated that it will last about a year.
Professor Kasey McCall-Smith said the point of the pre-trial proceedings had been determining "what evidence gets in and what evidence doesn't get in".
"If that is agreed in advance, the trial can be more expeditious," she explained.
As the relatives of the victims prepared for another anniversary marking the death of their loved ones, Gerhardt said he was looking forward to a time that the trial was over and he no longer had to think about or travel to Guantanamo.
"It's a place I don't want to come back to. I want to live my life, enjoy my passions and my memories of Ralph," he said.

Russian ballistic missiles rain on Ukraine just a day after US peace envoys held a press conference in Kyiv alongside Zelensky
Russian air strikes have killed at least two people and injured seven others in Ukraine’s capital Kyiv this morning, officials said.

Prime minister Andy Burnham spoke with US president Donald Trump yesterday, with the two leaders agreeing on "the need to continue working towards a ceasefire" to end Russia's war in Ukraine, Downing Street said.
"The Prime Minister reiterated the UK's support for Ukraine and for recent US-led peace negotiations," a Downing Street spokesperson said.
Burnham and Trump also discussed the Middle East, with Burnham "stressing the importance of the two-state solution, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and ensuring that Iran never acquires a nuclear weapon", the spokesperson added.
Monday's call comes after US peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday, having spoken with Russian president Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday.
Two killed and seven injured in Russian missile attack on Kyiv
Russian air strikes have killed at least two people and injured seven others in Ukraine’s capital Kyiv this morning, officials said.

Russia says external power at Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant restored
Off-site power at the Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine has been restored via the Ferosplavna power line, Russia's Rosatom state nuclear corporation said.
The plant has been without external power since 20 August and has relied on emergency diesel generators to cool its vital safety systems.
A local ceasefire brokered by the International Atomic Energy Agency took effect on Saturday to allow repairs to restore external power.
The IAEA later confirmed the restoration in a post on X, citing its chief Rafael Grossi.
The plant is operating as normal, Rosatom chief Alexei Likhachev said in a statement.
Ukraine's prosecutor general resigns citing political conflict
Ukraine's prosecutor general on Monday announced that he has offered his resignation citing political reasons, in the latest sign of disunity in the senior ranks of the Ukrainian ruling elite.
“This is a political decision, and I have made it consciously. I do not want the position of Prosecutor General to be used as an instrument of political confrontation,” Ruslan Kravchenko said in a statement on Telegram late on Monday, without elaborating.
Kravchenko thanked president Volodymyr Zelensky and Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, and asked them to accept his resignation.
Ukraine's anti-graft agencies, the NABU and SAPO, said last week they had uncovered a criminal organisation dealing with fraudulent call centres which was allegedly arranged by an official within the Prosecutor General's Office.
Kravchenko has denied he was involved in the alleged scheme.
“My position regarding the accusations remains unchanged,” he said in his Telegram post.
Kravchenko's resignation offer follows other changes among top officials in Ukraine as it continues to battle Russia, which launched a full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv as Trump's envoys leave
Russia resumed airstrikes on the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv in the early hours today, shortly after the departure of US peace negotiators, attacking the city with ballistic missiles and injuring six people, mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
People were also trapped in a residential building and there were fires across Kyiv, Klitschko said, after what he said were Russian ballistic missile strikes.
A five-storey apartment building and a three-storey residential block were damaged by falling debris, the Kyiv Military Administration said on Telegram separately, asking people to seek shelter.
As explosions were heard in Kyiv, neighbouring Poland, a Nato and European Union member, began military aviation operations to protect its airspace against a risk of violation, its armed forces said on X.
Russia resumed attacks on its smaller neighbour after US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner left following a meeting with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday.
Drones hit civilian infrastructure in Russia's Saratov
A Ukraine drone attack has hit civilian infrastructure in the Russian city of Saratov on the Volga river and injured some people, regional governor Roman Busargin said this morning.
The Saratov region is home to a large oil refinery run by state oil company Rosneft, as well as a number of other industrial and military facilities.
Russia to strip contract soldiers of one-off payment if laws violated at home
Russia's defence ministry wants to claim back part of a one-off payout from contract service personnel found guilty of criminal offences at home, a document showed, amid increasing cases of domestic violence among those fighting Russia's war on Ukraine.
Russia does not disclose official statistics on domestic violence committed by its service personnel but independent media, citing military courts data, reported hundreds of such cases, including murders, since the start of the 2022 invasion.
Russia provides a minimum one-off payment of 400,000 roubles (£3,418) for soldiers signing at least a one-year contract to fight in the war with Ukraine that Moscow calls "a special military operation".
In practice, one-off payouts may reach a few million roubles per soldier, depending on the region, in addition to a monthly salary.
Russia is also reducing sentences for those serving time in prison in exchange for signing up for the war, among other benefits, as it seeks to bolster army numbers.
Russia has seen a rise in domestic violence as fighters return home for leave, and the defence ministry wants to claim part of the one-off payments "in order to increase the motivation of military personnel to comply with the law", in case of a criminal offence, a draft law published on Monday showed.
If active contract service members are found guilty of a criminal offence which does not imply a prison sentence, they should pay back a portion of the one-off payout based on the months of the service left, the document showed.
Moscow criticises deployment of US missile system to Norway
Moscow has lashed out at the deployment of an advanced US missile system to Nato member state Norway, saying on Monday it dealt a further blow to the prospects for US-Russia talks on strategic nuclear stability.
Reports in the US said Washington had delivered a missile system to Norway that used Mk-41-style launchers capable of firing Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Russia's Foreign Ministry said the deployment posed a threat because the launchers could be used to fire missiles capable of reaching a substantial part of European Russia, including Moscow.
"Steps such as the deployment in Europe of U.S. ground-based intermediate-range missiles that pose a threat to the Russian Federation 'reset to zero', to put it mildly, the conditions for constructive dialogue with the US on strategic issues," the ministry said in a statement.
It added that Russia would pay "particular attention" to the deployment sites and command-and-control centres of US missile systems and that they would become targets in the event of a military conflict.

Editorial: Putin has no interest in peace – and Trump is falling into his trap
Steve Witkoff is the real estate guy with zero diplomatic experience who Donald Trump appointed in 2024 as his personal “peace emissary”. Jared Kushner is the president’s son-in-law, but did at least play some role in one of President Trump’s few foreign policy achievements – the Abraham Accords process that promised to deliver some stability to the Middle East during the first Trump term. As a team, they have enjoyed little success in securing the “settlement” to the war in Ukraine that Mr Trump so desires.
There is little reason to suppose that their latest exercise in shuttle diplomacy will succeed where their previous efforts failed. Indeed, the prospects for an end to the war, let alone one that will prove just and lasting, are as dismal as at any time since Vladimir Putin launched his ill-fated “special military operation” more than four and a half years ago – its duration now longer than the Soviet Union’s four-year “great patriotic war” against Adolf Hitler. Just as in that epoch-defining conflict, it is the civilian population of Ukraine that will face some of the harshest consequences as winter approaches.
Before the Witkoff-Kushner double act set out for Moscow and Kyiv, Mr Trump expressed his usual confidence in the pair – he could hardly do otherwise – and declared that “we have an idea for peace”. This idea remains opaque. Yet, for a change, this may be more than the usual self-flattering bluster. After a period when, easily bored, Mr Trump lost interest in the region (the situation in Iran didn’t help), this unexpected flexing of US power comes as a surprise.
