Approximately one in eight girls/women, experienced rape or sexual assault before turning 18, according to UNICEF 2024 estimates. Global estimates have also documented substantial sexual abuse among boys. Child sexual abuse is predominantly seen as a social evil and crime against humanity, but it is equally a serious public health problem. Yet our response understandably revolves around the perpetrator. Was the crime reported? Has the accused been arrested? Will the prosecution succeed? What punishment will follow?
For the young person or child, however, punishment of the offender does not reverse what has happened. There may be physical injuries to treat, infections to prevent, pregnancy to consider and psychological wounds that may surface immediately or years later. Healthcare must begin even if justice is delayed.
The first contact with the healthcare system is crucial. Depending on the nature and timing of the assault, the child may require treatment for physical injuries, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, and assessment of the risk of HIV. When indicated, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis should be started as early as possible and within 72 hours. Emergency contraception can be offered to girls at risk of pregnancy who present within 120 hours. Hepatitis B and HPV vaccination, STI prophylaxis or treatment and pregnancy-related care may also be required. This is why medical examination after sexual assault cannot become merely an exercise in collecting evidence for a criminal case. Evidence matters, but the survivor is also simultaneously a patient sitting in front of the doctor.
Unseen injuries
The immediate psychological response to sexual abuse may include fear, confusion, shame, anger, numbness, disturbed sleep or silence. A child may not even have the vocabulary to explain what has happened. The first psychological intervention, therefore, is not necessarily psychotherapy, but safety. The child must be protected from further abuse, listened to without blame and helped to regain a sense of security and normalcy. Repeatedly asking the child to recount traumatic details can itself cause distress.
While some children recover with family support and appropriate care, others may develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, anxiety, nightmares, intrusive memories, hypervigilance or dissociation. Self-harm, suicidal thoughts, eating disorders, substance misuse and behavioural problems can also occur. Longer-term difficulties may involve self-worth, emotional regulation, trust, intimacy and relationships.
Experiencing trauma does not automatically mean developing a psychiatric disorder. Outcomes vary with age, developmental stage, duration of abuse, relationship with the perpetrator and support following disclosure. This is why every survivor should receive a baseline mental health assessment covering mood, sleep, behaviour, schooling, relationships, self-harm and suicidality. Its purpose is not to label the child as mentally ill, but to establish a clinical reference point from which recovery or emerging difficulties can be followed.
Trauma over time
Sexual abuse is also not invariably a single traumatic incident. For most children, particularly when the perpetrator has regular access or authority, abuse may recur for months or years. What clinicians encounter may therefore be the cumulative effect of repeated exposure.
Even after the abuse stops, recovery is not governed by a calendar. Memories, family responses, seeing the perpetrator, investigation and court proceedings can reactivate distress. Childhood is also the period during which emotional regulation, self-concept and ideas about safety and relationships are developing. Trauma occurring during these formative years can become entangled with these processes.
Healing consequently means more than making traumatic memories disappear. It means helping the child resume development. Returning to school, playing, sleeping normally, rebuilding relationships and recovering a sense of safety and control can themselves be important parts of recovery.
Paths to recovery
Treatment must be individualised. Supportive psychotherapy and counselling may be sufficient for some. Children with significant symptoms require assessment by trained mental health professionals. Cognitive behavioural therapy helps identify connections between thoughts, emotions and behaviour and develops healthier ways of responding to distress.
For children and adolescents with post-traumatic stress symptoms or PTSD, trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy, or TF-CBT, is an important evidence-based option. It can teach skills to manage anxiety, gradually and safely process traumatic memories, challenge beliefs such as self-blame and help restore normal functioning.
Other interventions, including interpersonal psychotherapy for appropriate emotional disorders and EMDR for PTSD, may have a role depending on clinical assessment. The principle is that every survivor deserves an assessment and access to care, but not every survivor needs the same treatment.
Families matter
Recovery also rarely happens in the consulting room alone. A supportive, non-offending parent or caregiver can be one of the child’s greatest protective resources. Families need guidance on how to respond to disclosure, avoid blaming or repeatedly questioning the child, recognise warning signs, and restore ordinary routines without pretending that nothing happened.
Where safe and appropriate, caregivers can participate in trauma-focused therapy. They, too, may require psychological support. A parent discovering that their child has been sexually abused may experience guilt, anger, helplessness and enormous distress. Helping the caregiver can indirectly strengthen the child’s recovery.
Building capacity
This requires more than appointing counsellors. The system needs to facilitate frontline doctors, paediatricians, gynaecologists, nurses and counsellors to provide immediate trauma-informed care. District services need access to clinical psychologists and psychiatrists, with clear referral pathways for children requiring specialised interventions. The healthcare providers themselves also need protection. Listening repeatedly to accounts of sexual violence can result in secondary or vicarious trauma. Supervision, manageable caseloads, debriefing, peer support, and periods away from continuous trauma work should be built into services rather than regarded as luxuries.
Eventually, the success of our response cannot be measured only by whether justice was set in motion: it is whether the infection was prevented, whether reproductive healthcare was provided, whether the child’s mental health was assessed, whether treatment was available when needed, whether the family knew how to support the child, whether the child returned to school and, ultimately, whether that child was able to move forward.
A humane health system must, at first, ask what needs to happen for the child, while law simultaneously addressing what needs to happen for justice.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

A ground report from Satya Niketan highlights the ongoing plight of college students facing severe distress in paying guest accommodations. Faculty and student volunteers from Maitri College have mobilised relief efforts, conducting donation drives to distribute essential supplies and providing temporary shelter along with meals in the college hostel. Representatives on the ground state that several PG owners have restricted outside communication, locked premises, and instructed residents not to alert authorities or media due to fears of eviction following compliance checks. Caretakers and owners in multiple facilities have reportedly abandoned the premises without providing regular meals or refunding security deposits. While basic amenities like clothes and drinking water have seen partial restoration, stranded students continue to face acute food shortages and difficulty vacating their accommodations amidst the crisis.
Following the building collapse in Delhi's Satya Niketan that killed seven Delhi University students, police have arrested five people, including building owner Hariram Gupta, his family members, a PG operator, and a labour contractor. Municipal Corporation of Delhi officials have faced suspensions, and civic authorities have initiated a phased demolition of the adjacent dilapidated Kanak Lata PG building. Dilapidated structures in Laxmi Nagar and Pandav Nagar are also facing scrutiny. Additionally, the government has announced curbs on paying guest accommodations, mandating registration, rent caps, CCTV cameras, night guards, and limiting security deposits to three months.

Hawaii’s western islands hit by fierce winds from Hurricane Lowell as thousands lose power
Strong winds uprooted trees and caused widespread blackouts on the island of Kauai
Severe gales and heavy rain triggered by Hurricane Lowell battered the western islands of Hawaii on Tuesday, severing power to thousands and tearing up stretches of coastal roads.
Along the Southern California coast, dangerous surf conditions created by the remnants of Hurricane Marie are expected to linger for several days.
In Hawaii, high winds uprooted trees and caused widespread blackouts on Kauai, home to 73,000 residents. The Kauai Island Utility Cooperative stated that nearly all of its roughly 35,000 members were left without power early on Tuesday.
Emergency officials asked residents to conserve water and stay off the roads as authorities assessed the damage.
Waves that crashed onto Kauai's southern coast tore apart a road along the coast and pushed piles of sand and lava rocks into a beachside park, said Rochelle Ballard, a former professional surfer who runs a surf school across from the park.
It will take weeks of cleanup, she said. Her family’s surf shop and neighboring restaurant came away without damage, but she said a friend’s house was destroyed.
“It's going to take awhile. I think we'll be fine,” Ballard said. “We've been through this before.”
Hurricane Lowell didn't make a direct hit on Hawaii
The center of the storm passed west of the islands in the overnight hours Tuesday and moved farther away throughout the day.
The storm's tropical storm-force winds extended well beyond the center, the National Hurricane Center said. On Kauai, sustained winds measured just above 50 mph (80 kph) at Lihue Airport, the island's only commercial airport that was closed after the storm.
Hurricane warnings for Kauai and the tiny island of Niihau, which has less than 100 permanent residents, were no longer in place by Tuesday morning local time. A tropical storm warning was also lifted for Oahu, the state's most populated island with close to 1 million residents.
But flooding and mudslides will continue to be a risk through the day, said Eric Blake, of the National Hurricane Center.
Some wind gusts reached 80 mph (130 kph), according to the hurricane center. But the force of the sustained winds had decreased by early Tuesday and later the storm weakened and was no longer a hurricane. Lowell is expected to continue weakening in the coming days.
Storm left a mess on Kauai and Oahu
There was extensive damage across Kauai, and crews were using heavy equipment to push trees and debris off the roads, said Derek Kawakami, mayor of Kauai County. About 300 people were staying in shelters on Kauai.
Kauai real estate agent Lori Benkert, who lives in Lihue, said she endured a loud, windy night after her power went out Monday evening. The storm downed trees next to her house, and the community’s main road was closed because of fallen trees, she said.
“We’re fine. My house did great with no boarded-up windows,” Benkert said. “But there are a lot of downed power lines.”
On Oahu, road crews were clearing sand and rocks from a major route along the island's western edge after floodwaters topped a coastal highway, north of Honolulu.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green closed schools and government offices on the three islands for Tuesday ahead of the storm.
Rainfall totals could reach up to 24 inches (60 centimeters) in some areas on Kauai. Oahu, Maui and the Big Island also could see large amounts of rain.
Last month, Tropical Storm Lala brushed past Hawaii and stirred up landslides, washing away about 100 homes and causing widespread power outages.
Marie downgraded but still being felt in California
What's left of Hurricane Marie was downgraded again and is no longer considered a tropical storm.
But it was still creating dangerous surf conditions along the coast of Mexico’s Baja California and Southern California. Swells with life-threatening surf and rip current conditions will continue for the next few days, the hurricane center said.
In Malibu, where big waves were pounding the shore, the driveway of a beachfront home that sits on pylons collapsed into a sinkhole Tuesday morning, the Los Angeles County Fire Department said.

Quick Answer
John Ternus faces the tough task of balancing Steve Jobs’ product-first innovation with Tim Cook’s business success. As Apple’s new CEO, he must revive innovation, fix its AI struggles, manage rising costs, and keep Apple at the top.
It is September, and around this time of year my stories usually start with “Tis the iPhone season” (not kidding, you can check). While the new iPhones are still coming early in September, this story is not about the iPhone but rather about the people behind it, or rather Apple in general.
After 15 years of taking care of CEO business, Tim Cook finally bid farewell to Apple. On his last day in the role, on 31 August 2026, he penned an emotional memo addressed to “Team”. Cook has not cut ties with Apple completely but will now serve as the Executive Chairman of Apple’s Board of Directors.
John Ternus has taken over the reins as Apple’s new CEO. He has been with Apple since 2001 and has climbed the corporate ladder, all the way from being a member of the product design team to the CEO position in 2026. In case you do not know him well, we got you covered.
A full circle moment for Apple
This change in command feels like Apple’s life has come full circle. The company was started/ headed mainly by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, who were known as product people through and through. It seemed to be teetering on the verge of closing down when Jobs returned to turn it around in 1997. He was succeeded by Tim Cook, who, as Jobs himself mentioned, is “not a product person” but focused more on scaling the business and made Apple the first trillion-dollar company in the world under his tenure. And now Cook has given the Apple empire to Ternus to take care of.
Many believe Ternus has been handed a golden spoon— Jobs laid the groundwork in his second coming, made products that became aspirational and industry benchmarks, and then Cook followed by scaling the business in a way no one had ever imagined could be done. Many think Ternus can just pass his tenure enjoying the fruits of their labor.
I respectfully would like to disagree. If anything, I believe he has an uphill battle in front of him.
From Jobs to Cook – from being insanely innovative to being a world champ
Steve Jobs focused on products and features that were not created to blend in. Under him, Apple’s product portfolio was slim and streamlined. People who have recently started following tech may find it hard to believe, but under Steve Jobs, Apple back then was generally launching just one iPhone a year. Just one. The idea was to focus on user experience, bringing out products that made the lives of its users easier, developing interfaces that would make using a device a simple process – in short, innovation that would make a difference. Apple was actually ‘thinking different’.
Under Tim Cook, that rulebook was respectfully thrown out of the window. Whatever Jobs did, it seemed Cook was doing the opposite. From launching just one iPhone a year, Apple started to launch multiple ones, sometimes more than once a year. It also had multiple watches, earbuds, headphones, iPads, iMacs, MacBooks, Mac Minis, HomePods, and, believe it or not, even a cleaning cloth (there are two generations of it now). It is safe to say Apple’s product portfolio expanded (some would say “exploded”) under Tim Cook.
It may have gotten extremely hard to keep track of all of Apple’s products, but under Cook, Apple became the most valuable company in the world. During his time as CEO, Apple’s shares went up a whopping 2,275 percent! When Cook gained control in 2011, Apple was valued at USD 350 billion (a very healthy number), and with his strategy of diversifying the portfolio and expanding into new markets, Cook took Apple all the way up to a valuation of USD 5 trillion, becoming only the second company in history to do so (Nvidia was the first).
Jobs and Cook thus both played very vital but very different roles in making Apple what it has become today. One focused on innovation, the other on expansion.
Ternus has got some big shoes to fill
Now, Ternus has stepped into the CEO’s role, and he has some really big shoes to fill. Not just in terms of his immediate predecessor, but the one before him too.
Let me explain: Ternus is a product person, and for all these years when Cook was in the office, many Apple purists were disappointed by his constant efforts to make the brand more mainstream. Cook’s efforts were not about making the brand more accessible or democratizing it (even though the number of Apple products has vastly expanded, they still remain premium), but were more about relentlessly releasing products and their variants. While this did increase Apple’s revenues and profits exponentially, many believed it had deflected the brand from its core values, the values Jobs believed in: innovation, user experience, and product design. According to many critics, Apple’s designs became repetitive, software became buggy, and its innovation arc felt more like a flat line of late, with the odd bump here and there.
So naturally, now that Ternus has assumed office, this lobby has new hope. Hope that perhaps as a “product person,” he will take Apple back to what they insist were its ‘golden days’ under Jobs. That he will channel all of Apple’s energy into making more innovative products and not just products that seem to exist to make numbers.
What this lobby, however, forgets is that Jobs is not the only legacy Ternus has to live up to. Cook may have done things very differently (some might say he really did ‘think different’ but in a different sphere of business), but under his leadership Apple soared and found its way to the top. Today, it stands at the very pinnacle of the tech world; some would even say it is the most important company in the world. While topping this would be difficult, Ternus can certainly not let it slide off this pedestal.
Now it’s Ternus’ turn to think different
This means John Ternus basically has to find a balance between the Jobs method and the Cook method or come up with something completely new. And that too at a very difficult time for the industry. With demand for memory driving up prices of all things tech – smartphones, laptops, computers, hard drives – it will be a challenge for Ternus to manage prices, even while bringing in the big sales numbers that many now associate with Apple. There is also the matter of Apple’s struggle with AI for the past couple of years, which has become quite a spectacle, one which Ternus needs to solve as soon as possible.
Many would kill to be in Ternus’ position, as it seems like the guy has got it all made and simply has to carry it forward, but if you ask me, I do not envy him his place or task. He has to deal with the shadows of two illustrious predecessors and an industry crisis, as well as a deeply polarised community, apart from, of course, intense competition from the likes of Microsoft, Google, Meta and Samsung. To be fair, it was not easy for either Jobs or Cook. Jobs took over Apple in 1997, with many confident that the company would not last another year. When Jobs passed away in 2011, an equally large number of people felt that a non-product person like Cook would not be able to succeed. Both of them defied their detractors and added a new dimension to Apple in different ways. It is Ternus’ turn to put his own spin on Apple. It will not be easy. Will he, too, Think Different, differently? Only time will tell.

Australians question US commitment to Aukus submarine deal in crowdfunded inquiry
Under the Australia-UK-US security pact, Canberra will get eight nuclear-powered submarines at an estimated cost of up to US$266 billion
At an Aukus public inquiry in Canberra last week, one of Australia’s leading submarine experts, retired Rear Admiral Peter Briggs, called the plan “flawed and undeliverable”.
Australia scrapped an agreement for France to supply Attack-class submarines in favour of the Aukus sale in 2021. Briggs said the French deal was the better option, arguing that US shipyards, already struggling to meet the domestic demands, could not deliver the promised nuclear-powered submarines on time.
At the same inquiry, former civil servants dealing with national security Michael Keating and Jon Stanford said joining Aukus meant Australia was significantly more likely to be dragged into a conflict with China and potentially targeted with nuclear weapons. Australia had “sacrificed considerable sovereignty” to the US while leaving the country vulnerable without a guaranteed security safety net, they said.

India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.

There’s a lingering notion that Indian menswear-forward brands have to look a certain way or that they somehow can’t occupy the same conversation, say as The Row or Lemaire. Gathering proves otherwise. The clothes have this organic ease to them: earthy tones, flattering cuts, natural fabrics, with much of the dyeing done traditionally in Jaipur. The sort of brand you want to gate keep until everyone discovers it and you can say: “Oh, I’ve known them for ages.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing
Rs 8,452 crore
The Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations Fund (PM Cares), set up during the coronavirus pandemic, had a balance of £647m (Rs 8,452 crore) at the end of the 2025 financial year, prompting questions about why such a large sum remained unused instead of being put towards relief work. Pradeep Bhandari, a spokesperson for the Bharatiya Janata party, countered the charge in a debate on Times Now, saying the PM Cares fund provides for long-term rehabilitation instead of immediate relief during disasters.
Vibe check
For choreographer and director Usha Jey (@usha_jey), learning bharatanatyam at the age of 20 was a way to connect to her culture. Jey, who is French and of Sri Lankan Tamil heritage, has since developed her own movement language. Hybrid bharatham, as she calls it, fuses the Indian classical dance form with hip-hop but is careful to retain the integrity of both. There is an interplay of abandon and elegance in her choreographic works. Actor Maitreyi Ramakrishnan features in her latest video, Hide N Seek. Directed by Jey and her longtime partner, Gavin Emishka, the film is a striking visual treat featuring two dance forms in fluid negotiation.

Singapore is set to increase pay for its political leaders by more than 60 per cent, taking the world's already highest ministerial salaries up another notch, Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong told parliament on Tuesday, according to news agency AFP.
The affluent city-state has justified high-end salaries for its political leaders, arguing they attract talent and ensure good governance. The Southeast Asian nation, which last adjusted ministerial salaries 15 years ago, is regularly ranked among the world's least corrupt countries.
The issue is nevertheless politically sensitive, with cabinet members' income far exceeding that of most ordinary citizens.
"Political salaries are a difficult and emotive issue," said Wong. "The sums involved are more than what most citizens earn, so I understand why Singaporeans scrutinise them closely, and why many feel strongly about the matter."
However, Wong maintained that the issue is “ultimately about whether Singapore will continue to have the quality of political leadership we need to take our country forward” in the decades ahead, adding, “Our starting point is this: good government depends on good leadership.”
Wong said the revision would see his benchmark annual salary rise from Sg$2.2 million to Sg$3.6 million ( ₹27.05 crore).
Even before the raise, the Singaporean prime minister's paycheck vastly outstripped the wages of many other leaders, including those in the United States and other G7 nations.
However, Wong announced that he plans to donate the entire increase to “suitable good causes” during his term.
Lawrence Wong is the fourth Prime Minister of Singapore and leads the long-ruling People's Action Party (PAP). Under his leadership, the party dominates Singapore's parliament and steers its 21-member cabinet.
An economist by training, Wong holds degrees from the University of Wisconsin–Madison, the University of Michigan, and Harvard University. Before being elected to Parliament in 2011, he served as a civil servant across multiple ministries and as Principal Private Secretary to Lee Hsien Loong.
He previously held portfolios in Culture, Community and Youth, National Development, and Education. He gained widespread prominence co-chairing Singapore’s COVID-19 pandemic task force, later becoming Deputy Prime Minister in 2022 before succeeding to the premiership.
Wong said the pay raises were recommended by an independent committee.
Under the revised framework, according to AFP, the benchmark salary for the Deputy Prime Minister will rise from Sg$1.87 million to Sg$3.06 million. Cabinet Ministers will receive between Sg$1.80 million and Sg$2.88 million, depending on seniority and the weight of their portfolios.
Existing office holders will not be moved immediately to the new benchmarks. Instead, the report said, they will receive a one-off adjustment of up to 9 per cent starting from October 15, depending on individual circumstances, including performance.
“Any subsequent changes will be based on individual performance and responsibilities,” said Wong.
(With AFP inputs)

Is 15-year-old Gabriel set to become Man Utd's youngest ever player?
- Published
When Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick was asked about 15-year-old JJ Gabriel last month, he navigated the narrow path between high praise for a young player of immense talent and the knowledge he will ultimately be the one who decides when it is time for first-team exposure.
"JJ is one of the boys," he said. "He's obviously got a really big talent. He's trained with us quite a bit and is getting experience all the time.
"He's physically adapting to each step, and we're just continuing his development."
Carrick was at Leigh Sports Village four days earlier when Gabriel, making his Premier League 2 debut against Ipswich, ran on to Jack Fletcher's through ball and after taking the pace off the pass with his left foot, scooped the ball over an advancing keeper from the edge of the area with his right.
It was an audacious finish, one that highlighted Gabriel's thought process given the most obvious route to goal was either a low shot or sprinting round the keeper.
Seven days later, Gabriel followed up with a completely different, but even better effort.
Taking Tynan Thompson's short pass in a central position, with his back to goal just inside the area, Gabriel's first touch was a drag back with his left foot that allowed him to spin round so he was facing the right way.
Then, showing strength to keep his balance after being nudged by an opponent, he nicked the ball to his left with his right foot, gliding past a second defender.
He took another touch to steady himself before rifling a low shot into the net from just inside the six-yard box.
From start to finish the manoeuvre took less than five seconds.
It was impossible not to be impressed. The goal itself has been viewed on various social media accounts millions of times.
'Sometimes it gets to a point where you can't not pick him'
Ryan Giggs, United's record appearance holder, was 17 when he made his United debut in 1991.
Like Carrick with Gabriel, Sir Alex Ferguson saw Giggs playing youth football in the flesh, initially in a trial game at the Cliff training ground.
In his first autobiography, Managing My Life, he recounts the experience like this:
"A gold miner who has searched every part of the river or mountain and then suddenly finds himself staring at a nugget could not feel more exhilaration than I did watching Giggs that day.
"I shall always remember my first sight of him, floating over the pitch so effortlessly you would have sworn his feet weren't touching the ground. He carried his head high and looked as relaxed and natural on the park as a dog chasing a piece of silver paper in the wind."
Giggs can't assess what he looked like. But he knows what it felt like and in an insightful chat with his former United team-mate on Rio Ferdinand Presents: The Debrief,, external Giggs offered this assessment:
"Sometimes you have to be patient. Sometimes it gets to a point where you can't not pick him and not have him train in the first team; that might be in a month, might be six months, might be a year.
"It's that in-between time where he thinks he should be in the first team. He thinks he should be in the squad every week when Michael sees it a different way, that, actually, no, you need to play games because it's not really going to do you any good travelling here, there and everywhere and you're getting five minutes here, 10 minutes there."
Plotting the right path
It feels as though Gabriel is at that 'in-between' point Giggs mentions just now.
Aside from the first game in Helsinki, Gabriel was a feature of all United's pre-season trips this summer.
Yet he played just once, as a late substitute against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm when his first involvement led to him being clattered from behind by Uruguay skipper Jose Maria Gimenez, who, at 31, is twice Gabriel's age.
United have posted plenty of footage of Gabriel training with the first team this season and having a joke with fellow forward Benjamin Sesko. As Carrick says, the youngster is "one of the boys".
There was a view Gabriel may be given his first-team debut in the EFL Cup third round, which would make him Manchester United's youngest ever player, beating goalkeeper David Gaskell, who was 16 years and 19 days when he made his senior bow. Gabriel is not 16 until 6 October.
However, as United have had a tricky start to the season results wise, and play Premier League opposition in Brighton at Old Trafford on 16 September, is that practical?
Champions League games offer 11 substitute places, rather than nine in domestic competition. Does that mean he could be involved against Sabah FK on Thursday? Given he did not train with the first team on Wednesday, possibly not.
Is the Under-19 Uefa Youth League - a competition United's academy is prioritising after pulling out of the EFL Trophy and National League Cup this season, and for which last season's FA Youth Cup final squad are eligible - a more appropriate stage?
Gabriel would have been looking to a Premier League 2 Manchester derby at City on Saturday evening, but that game has been postponed because of United's various Thursday European commitments.
Thirty-five years ago, Giggs was content when Ferguson blocked media from talking to him.
There was no social media or digital forums. Expectation, discussion and demands now are huge and cannot be silenced.
Those close to Gabriel clearly have their own idea of what his future should look like.
United's last Premier League 2 game before the international break is against Brentford at Leigh on 18 September. After that, England's various age group teams have their matches to play.
Gabriel's own abilities are creating the pathway. The big question is, where does it lead?

The data center backlash has entered the midterms conversation.
Data centers are bringing Americans together
And politicians can’t run away fast enough.
Politicians from across the spectrum have changed their minds — or at least their policy positions — about data centers in the past few months as public resistance to their construction has skyrocketed. A major example is Texas, where just about one year ago, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott was proclaiming that his state was the “epicenter of AI development.”
Now, after months of grassroots organizing and community outcry, Abbott is pushing to slow the roll of new data centers in Texas. He’s imposed a statewide moratorium on new construction pending an audit over the new connections to Texas’s power grid. While he hasn’t explicitly said the change is tied to his reelection campaign this November, the pause is expected to last through the election.
As dramatic as Abbott’s about-face has been, he’s not alone: Democrats and Republicans alike are following suit.
Jeremy Merrill, a data reporter at the Washington Post, analyzed thousands of social media posts and newsletters to see what elected officials on both sides of the aisle are saying about data centers. He spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about his findings, what they say going into midterm elections, and how the backlash might change the way we think about what politicians owe to their constituents.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
What did you find?
Data centers didn’t used to be a big deal. And now, almost all of a sudden, they’re a big issue. Candidates are falling over themselves to sound tough about data centers. And data centers are overwhelmingly portrayed as a problem rather than an opportunity or a benefit.
A great example is Sen. Jon Husted, who’s a Republican senator from Ohio, who’s up for election this November. He used to praise data center projects that were coming to Ohio when he was lieutenant governor because it would help establish Ohio as “an important tech hub in America.”
He said that data centers are essential to our digital lives. And now he’s saying he’s trying to “protect Americans from having to foot the bill for data centers.”
He’s really emblematic of a shift that happened all across the Republican Party in about February of this year. That’s when the bulk of messages from Republicans about data centers flipped from focusing on them as bringing benefits to their states and communities, to talking about their downsides.
This is really a case of the anger and unhappiness bubbling up from everyday people up to political elites. And that grassroots anger was all across the political spectrum over a whole range of issues: power bills, claims about how much water data centers may use, air pollution, eminent domain, taxes, subsidies, and a generalized, physical manifestation of the anxiety that people feel about what AI is going to do to our society, to our brains, to our kids and to our jobs.
We know that it’s not just one single candidate, maybe even not just a handful, because you reported that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that, “Data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”
That’s pretty strong language. Is the National Republican Senatorial Committee admitting that the wrong position on data centers is enough to lose a candidate a race at this point?
I think it’s something that they’re certainly worried about. He’s in a tough race. It’s a tossup. And presumably you’re looking for an edge, or to prevent your opponent from getting an edge over you.
What about President Donald Trump’s messaging on data centers? He, initially at least, was very bullish on AI investment in the US. What has Trump been saying?
This is a story in two or three parts. As President Trump took office again last year, he was overall trying to portray his second term as president as “inaugurating a golden age for American manufacturing and technological dominance.”
As part of that, he issued an executive order trying to make it easier to build data centers in the United States. And I think that’s probably why last year most Republicans across the board were talking about data centers as a benefit to the country and to the communities where they were being built — talking about jobs, talking about investment.
But like I said, the tide turned. And so on the one hand, you have President Trump promoting this bill that would protect people from having data centers cause their power bills to go up. But on the other hand, he just wrote earlier this week on Truth Social, “If [communities] want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”
He’s saying if they don’t want data centers, they’re going to “end up being backwards and poor.” So he’s still very pro-data center, which is fascinating.
Let’s talk about the Democrats. Which Democrats in particular are we seeing change their minds?
There are a lot of governors who used to be very positive on data centers in their states because these bring jobs. These bring construction investments, some amount of permanent jobs, some amount of construction jobs. Examples of folks who are now limiting data centers in their states include Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania and [Gov.] J.B. Pritzker of Illinois.
The most striking case of a Democrat whose rhetoric has shifted so much is Rep. Ro Khanna of California, whose district actually includes Silicon Valley. In 2025, he was calling for building more data centers in the United States versus overseas. When the Trump administration did an AI deal with the United Arab Emirates, he said, “Why are we putting data centers and research hubs in Dubai?”
But now he’s more critical, calling for an end to data center extraction, taking communities’ water and jacking up their bills, sucking all the money into the hands of a few tech billionaires.
Is anyone in either party still coming out strong for data centers?
My favorite example of this is Rep. Eric Burlison, who’s a Republican from Missouri. He’s really focused on the need to build data centers in order to compete with China. In June, he wrote, “Ask yourself who benefits when Americans turn against data centers? China does.”
He’s making the point that I think a lot of people in tech are making, which is, “This is coming whether you like it or not.” And part of politics is dealing with reality.
In this day and age, it seems constituents don’t want to deal with that reality, but clearly there are people who hold office, or who hope to hold office, who are going to maintain the line that this is something we’ve just got to do.
This is a classic political science dispute about what a politician’s job is supposed to be. If you accept the premise that we need data centers to build a wonderful technological future or keep pace with China or whatever the argument is, is the job of a politician to just do what their constituents want, to be their tribune in Washington? Or is it to be the wise, thoughtful leader who’s willing to push back when constituents are missing something important?
This is one thing I keep in mind when analyzing — particularly some of these governors who shifted more recently — is that they’re talking about the downsides of data centers. They’re talking about mitigating those downsides. They’re saying, “Oh, we need to get data centers to pay their fair share. We need to make sure that data centers don’t screw up our water. We need to make sure they don’t raise your power bills. We need to make sure they give back.”
But then it’s so that we can build them and still reap the benefits while mitigating the costs.
What is it about this issue, do you think, that has got us to this place? We’re polarized, but we’re not polarized in the same way that we’re often polarized.
One possibility is that this is coming from the grassroots so much and bubbling up to politicians and political elites, that everybody got the signal at the same time that this was something that they ought to oppose.
The other possibility is people have for a while been saying, “Are we living through a generational political realignment in the United States where a lot of things are up for grabs?”
You don’t see a lot of the libertarian-adjacent pro-business, free markets, free trade Republican Party. And so when all these issues are up for grabs, politicians see opportunity in being innovative rather than sticking with the same traditional views of their party.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

N Korea has built two-storey uranium enrichment facility, says watchdog
- Published
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) says North Korea has built a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex.
The new building is said to be capable of housing up to twenty-eight centrifuge cascades, which are used to enrich uranium.
The nuclear watchdog's director, Rafael Grossi, called the continuing production of weapons-grade material a cause for "serious concern".
The IAEA also reported that Pyongyang has started operating an expanded annex at another enrichment site. These findings, drawn from satellite imagery, point to a steady expansion of North Korea's nuclear infrastructure.
In a statement published earlier this week, Grossi said that there was a new building in Yongbyon. The agency, which was expelled by Pyongyang in 2009, does not have inspectors in North Korea but relies on satellite imagery to carry out assessments.
The IAEA had first reported on the existence of the building in June this year, according to a report released on 28 August. The report said that leader Kim Jong Un had on 3 June reportedly visited a "newly inagurated nuclear materials production factory", which it identified as the Yongbyon enrichment facility.
Kim had then praised the country's "greatly expanded production capacity", adding that this would "offer the possibility of carrying out larger plans", according to the IAEA report.
The IAEA also said there were indications that operations had started at another encirhment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, in January this year. An annex had first been constructed in Kangson in 2024, it detailed.
The report relied on satellite imagery, open-source information, and photographs in state media.
"The continuation and further development of the DPRK's nuclear programme are clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and are deeply regrettable," said Grossi in a statement released earlier this week.
The IAEA had said in April this year that North Korea appeared to be stepping up its ability to make nuclear bombs, saying they were monitoring the apparent expansion of Yongbyon.
In August, South Korea's president, Lee Jae Myung, proposed talks with North Korea on officially ending the war between the two countries, adding that this could serve as a forum for discussing "effective ways to halt the advancement of the North's nuclear capabilities".
North Korea has yet to respond to the proposal.
North Korea declared itself a nuclear power in 2022 and vowed never to relinquish its weapons, of which it is estimated to possess dozens.
Lee previously said Pyongyang was producing 15 to 20 more warheads annually, telling the BBC last year he would back a deal between US President Donald Trump and Kim to freeze production.

The US on Tuesday (September 8) struck multiple Iranian oil tankers after further attempted missile attacks targeted a US Navy warship, escalating an already tense confrontation between Washington and Tehran. The strikes, reported by The Associated Press citing a US official who spoke anonymously, came as Iran warned tanker crews in the Gulf that their vessels could be targeted in retaliation.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy warned crews aboard oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels.
The Revolutionary Guard told tanker crews to abandon their vessels whether they were anchored or docked, warning that the ships “will be targeted.”
Iranian media separately reported that a US missile struck a small tanker near Kharg Island, a key hub for Iran’s oil exports.
Tasnim news agency said the tanker was hit by a US projectile about four miles from the island. It reported no casualties.
The reports could not be independently verified.
Several blasts were also reportedly heard on Kharg Island, where most of Iran’s oil exports are handled. Iranian media also reported two explosions in the southern port of Jask.
Iranian Armed Forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi warned that Tehran would target US military bases across the region if Iranian oil tankers were attacked.
He said any attack on Iranian oil tankers would trigger strikes against US bases by Iran’s armed forces.
The warning came after what Iranian officials described as an evacuation notice issued to Iranian tanker crews ahead of possible US attacks.
The Revolutionary Guard also said it intercepted and destroyed an MQ-1 drone over the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC said the drone was brought down by what it described as a new advanced Iranian defence system operating under the country’s integrated air defence network.
Iran did not identify who was operating the drone. The MQ-1 is used by only a small number of countries, including the United States.
The latest military escalation comes as both Washington and Tehran seek greater control over the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global energy chokepoint through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war.
Oil prices surged amid the latest developments, with international benchmark Brent crude briefly reaching $99.46 a barrel on Tuesday, adding to political pressure on the Trump administration ahead of the November midterm elections.
Alongside the military strikes, Washington intensified economic pressure on Tehran.
The US Treasury announced sanctions targeting all remaining Iranian airlines that had not previously been subjected to such penalties.
The department said the latest measures target 36 entities for supporting Iran’s aviation sector, which Washington accused of being used to transport weapons, personnel and illicit cargo.
Despite the military escalation, Iran said diplomatic efforts over the Strait of Hormuz were making progress.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said talks with Oman on managing the strategic waterway had achieved “significant progress.”
Iran’s Foreign Ministry said Araghchi briefed his Japanese counterpart on the latest status of the Iran-Oman discussions during a phone call.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio meanwhile said Iran was behind attacks launched by Yemen’s Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia.
Rubio described the Houthis as Iranian agents and proxies and said there was “clearly” an Iranian hand behind some of the attacks.
The Houthis have launched a fresh offensive near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a crucial gateway to the Red Sea, as Yemen’s civil war has intensified after a four-year ceasefire.
The wider regional tensions also spilled into Lebanon.
Israel carried out a wave of airstrikes in southern Lebanon on Monday, killing 13 people, including women and children, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry.
The strikes marked an escalation following several weeks of relative calm. No new Israeli strikes were reported in Lebanon as of early Tuesday evening.

The Cost Of India’s Convenience Economy Fuelled by massive capital and discounting wars, India’s instant service platforms are preparing for a mega festive season. But the gig workers are facing rigid targets and uncertain earnings. The Invisible Cost: For an instant help worker, a booking is only one part of their shift. The rest can involve waiting near high-demand communities, staying logged in to remain eligible for assignments and finding an affordable way to reach the next home. While the platforms depend on this proximity to promise quick service, workers claim that the time spent being idle often produces no income. Pay Promise Evolves: The instant help platforms initially marketed domestic work as a route to assured earnings. But gig workers now claim that compensation is increasingly linked to logged-in hours and tier-based performance. The issue is not merely linked to pay. Missed shifts, emergencies and a lack of bookings can make take-home income far less certain. Algorithmic Control: Ratings, availability and allocation systems also shape who gets the next booking. This pressures workers to accept jobs to avoid account suspensions or reduced payouts. Furthermore, workers also claim limited access to toilets, shaded waiting areas and secure resting places near customer clusters. Safety Question: For women workers, rapid order allocation can mean accepting jobs in unfamiliar locations with little room to assess safety concerns. With ratings, incentives and account access tied to responsiveness, declining a booking may carry a cost. There is also a complete absence of welfare benefits like paid period leave or emergency medical support. The Litmus Test: This festive season will test whether instant help platforms can build a business that values the workforce as much as customer convenience. Discounts may bring bookings, but retention will depend on fair pay and safety support. But as demand accelerates, will these platforms invest enough in the workers who make convenience possible? Even if you’re a casual consumer of MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, you know the names: anchors like Chris Hayes, Stephanie Ruhl, and yes, the one and only Rachel Maddow. The network has built a stable of talent who’ve amassed a massive number of casual viewers, plenty of fans … and more than a few obsessives.
Now, the network’s president, Rebecca Kutler, is looking to build that entire audience into something more akin to a fandom—turning casual viewers and fanatics alike, whether on TV or online, into paying members of an MS NOW media universe.
To do it, she’s launching an ambitious subscription program, called Membership, designed to connect MS NOW consumers much more directly to the Hayeses and Maddows of the world. Sure, plenty of news providers now offer subscriptions, WIRED included (and by the way, you can subscribe here). But what struck me about Kutler and Co.’s efforts was both their methodical approach—they surveyed 18,000 people before landing on a final offering—and their resolute focus on MS NOW’s deep bench of talent as the locus of their paid program. In a world where influencers are the new newscasters, and linear TV is in an inevitable decline, MS NOW is diving directly into the breach: applying the influencer playbook to build a sustainable business that’s future-proofed … at least until the next great audience pivot.
I caught up with Kutler at WIRED’s New York studios, just days before MS NOW’s subscription launch. We talked about turning TV talent into fandom magnets, beating Fox, and whether media consolidation is actually good news for the network.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: Rebecca, thank you so much for being here today. Start by telling me when you joined MSNBC. What’s the timeline?
REBECCA KUTLER: I think it was right before the midterms in 2022. I had grown up at CNN. I spent more than 20 years there. I left earlier in 2022, and some folks that I knew and really respected reached out from then MSNBC, and they talked about one of those jobs that has a lot of running room and is a little ambiguous, but in the best way. I thought, “Yeah, let's check it out.” I started at MSNBC, now MS NOW, running their digital businesses, basically all their nonlinear businesses.
It gave me a real opportunity to learn the place, but also think about what are the missed opportunities that we could take advantage of in the next few years.
At some point in your tenure, you took on the whole thing.
Yes.
What were those big challenges that you identified when you looked at the whole portfolio and thought to yourself, “What are we going to do here?”
One of the things that immediately struck me when I came over was the fandom.
I had worked in other newsrooms. I have friends who work in other newsrooms. I love the news and love what we do, but I had never worked at a place where the audience really sees themselves as fans, with a deep connection to talent.
When I joined MS, it was also at the same time Jen Psaki joined, and we had known each other a little from a previous life. So we went out into the field together and did a few pretty straightforward field reporting pieces. And I've walked through airports over my career with a lot of different anchors and newspeople, but I’ve never had the experience of walking through with Jen and seeing the [attention she got]. That's why she was a great fit for MS. She’s someone people were behind and were rooting for, and had a deep connection with.
When you think about Rachel Maddow and how she lands. You’re very close to this industry. If you talk to anyone in publishing and ask them where they would ideally like to debut their book, I think most of them would say The Rachel Maddow Show. There’s a reason for that: The audience loyalty and engagement with Rachel has been proven over decades.
It’s funny, when she shares a WIRED story on social media, the traffic to that story and the engagement on her social media around WIRED is crazy. I can tell you firsthand looking at the analytics, you can feel it.
I want to ask you more about talent in a minute, but that brings me to this Membership program you're launching. I'm going to read from the press release, which I very rarely do. You will offer “new opportunities for members to interact directly with the brand’s trusted journalists, exclusive community features to engage with each other, a new roster of contributors and experts, original creator content, new verticals that explore how news and politics impacts everyday life, and 24/7 access to livestreams and television programming.”
In layman’s terms, if someone’s a MS NOW viewer, they watch it on TV sometimes, they see it on social media, what should they expect from this? What are they getting that they’re not already getting by having cable TV?
I want to answer your question directly, but I just don’t want to assume your audience is the MS NOW audience. So if you'll allow me 30 seconds …
Give us your best pitch.
We launched as a new brand about a year ago. People traditionally see us as this cable channel, and that's great. We have a huge cable audience. We're actually right now the number two most-watched basic cable channel.
Who's number one?
Fox.
I see. OK. We might talk more about that later.
But that’s just one piece of our business. We have, right now, a digital business before we even launch what we're launching this week, that has more uniques than places like Axios, Politico, The Atlantic. People spend more time with us digitally than places like the Washington Post and NPR.
And on YouTube, we have been quite efficient at building out our presence in that space. We get more clicks on YouTube than ABC News, NBC News, and CBS News combined.
I say all of that to say we are starting from a position of strength. What we are excited about, and why we're launching this product, is all those digital things I just mentioned, we don't have a way to catch all those people if they’re not going to be watching cable.
Got it.
It’s taking our current superfans who watch us on linear and giving them more. So what are they going to get? They're going to get direct access to our talent. Seven days a week at noon and at 6:00 pm, if you are a member of the MS NOW community, you can hop on and directly interact with one of our anchors or one of our reporters.
On Monday it’s going to be Rachel Maddow, and then you go through the week. You're going to hear from Michael Steele, you’re going to hear from Jen Psaki, you're going to hear from Reverend Al Sharpton. You’re going to hear from the people that you know and love from watching them on MS NOW and have the opportunity to ask them your question directly, and not just interact with our talent, but also interact with each other.
When we started this process around a year and a half ago, we didn’t just sit in a conference room and think, “Hmm, let’s make another commodity news app.” Because let's be honest, a lot of that already exists. What we did was actually start from a place of product research. We went out to 18,000 people. We did surveys, we did in-person interviews, and we spent time taking that research and getting to where we are this week.
What I most want people to know is, what you see this week will look vastly different six months from now and a year from now if we're doing our jobs right. What we need to do is build and learn and test and add investment and expand where we need to, but not really think that we’re going to get it all right on day one, but give ourselves that latitude.
Is the goal to pull linear viewers onto digital, or is it to better engage the digital audience, or both?
It's both. All those people consuming us on YouTube, on digital, on social, in audio, 90 percent of those people do not regularly consume us on linear television. So a big function of this product is to say, “Hey, you’re watching YouTube videos all the time of Lawrence O'Donnell. Maybe you’re not someone who's going to be a cable subscriber. But can you come join our community in another capacity? Can we create a product that entices you to be part of an MS NOW community, even if you're someone who's reluctant to become a cable customer?”
I would say that, for the average person, if you ask them, “Fox News, MS NOW, who do those networks reach?” I would say Fox News reaches Republicans, and that’s who has it on TV, that's who’s going to that website. I would say MS NOW reaches progressives, Democrats, left-leaning people. Is that a stated goal for you, or do you want that tent to be bigger?
Is the audience for MS NOW different from the audience for Fox? Of course it is. There's probably a small amount of overlap, but not a lot, and that's OK.
For example, when I think forward to election night, I gotta say, I think there’s nowhere I'd rather hang out on election night than at our table with Rachel and Nicolle [Wallace] and Lawrence and Chris [Hayes] and Michael [Steele] and everyone.
What we try to do is be smart, respect our audience, and be a fun place, and a place where, again, Michael Steele is a big part of our election night. He was chairman of the Republican National Committee.
Right.
We have a broad range of views, but I think they all fall under that pro-democracy banner.
Are you competitive? Do you want to beat Fox? Do you want to see that number one?
Look, I am a pretty competitive person. I just see who our competition is as wider than that typical cable landscape.
I want to build a great product right now and have a large membership community, and I want to make sure that we are competing on every battleground.
That is yes, absolutely on cable, yes on digital, yes on YouTube, yes in audio. I think that because of the life that this brand lived under previous ownership, there were times when our wings were clipped a little from a business perspective, and that wasn't—if I was sitting in the seats of the leadership team at NBC, I might have made the same decisions.
When you’re working for the very large, very successful companies that NBCUniversal and Comcast are, they need to look at the whole company and figure out where best to invest their dollars. So what they did makes sense for them. But now we're lucky to be a part of Versant, and Versant has several pieces of their portfolio that generate a lot of cash.
What is Versant, for those who may not know?
Versant is the spinoff, so a spinout, of NBCUniversal. For folks that weren't following along day by day, around a year ago, NBCUniversal spun out a series of businesses. Those include what is now MS NOW, CNBC, brands like E!—you know, Live from the Red Carpet—and then golf.
We are now part of a company that is incentivized to invest the money that we earn as MS NOW back into MS NOW. We're just no longer part of a company that has to invest in theme parks and other things that, for that company, made a lot of sense.
I don’t think it’s a secret that cable news audiences are declining, and I’m going to ask this in the bluntest possible way: That’s an older audience, so what do you do when they die?
I am not blind to the long-term challenges. That’s why we are investing in digital. But do I think the cable business right now for MS NOW is quite healthy? I do.
Our average viewer watches nine hours a week.
That is a lot of MS NOW.
Do I wake up in a panic in the middle of the night? No. Do I know there are long-term challenges? Yes.
What do you wake up at night worrying about? Working in media and journalism is hard. It's a hard business, and these are really difficult transformations to try to undertake, and to undertake successfully. What's the hardest part of this for you right now?
What I wake up angsty about sometimes is I know we have this guest or that guest coming up, but how can we upgrade? How can we make it better? What is the better question? What is the better way in?
I might be old-school when I say this, but I think content always wins. Every single race.
I want to ask more about talent. You do have some real fandom magnets. I think one of the biggest challenges in publishing today, especially on digital, is that it is so noisy. There is so much competition. It’s not just news, but it’s everything on someone's Instagram feed. How do you encourage your journalists, your talent, to break through that in a digital context?
I'll just pick on Chris Hayes for a minute here. Because there’s almost no time that I talk to Chris Hayes that I don’t then hang up the phone or walk out of his office and think to myself, “That guy’s brain is huge.”
I think that’s the answer to the question of how do you break through? Every brand and every place in the media has to figure out what their breakthrough is. Look, there's people who want to break through by showing cat videos all day. People want to break through by writing outrageous headlines that aren’t really based in facts.
Yes.
Where I want MS NOW to break through is being brainiacs, is coming to the table with something that is intellectually interesting, that is showing me something or teaching me something or adding value to a news story in a way I hadn’t thought about it before, of drawing on their experience, decades of experience working in the room, being in the room where it happened.
What has the experience been like of transitioning some of the more TV-comfortable talent that you have, who are accustomed to doing a cable news show, and saying to them, “Now you do these interactive sessions with our audience, now you do TikTok, now you participate in these other parts of the ecosystem”?
One of my rules is: don’t do anything that feels weird for you. What I mean by that is, if you in your own life don’t use TikTok, I don’t recommend trying to become a TikToker. It’s going to land weird. We’ve seen it. So what I have encouraged our shows, our hosts, everyone in the MS NOW family, to do is don’t try to be everywhere. Don’t try to be everything.
I mean, a great example, Symone Sanders [Townsend] is fantastic at TikTok and Instagram because she grew up in those spaces and knows those audiences. That might not be the same for Lawrence O’Donnell. Lawrence O’Donnell is a huge hit on YouTube.
What has Trump 2.0 been like over there? Have you seen an audience bump? Have you seen fatigue? The challenge with the story of Trump 2.0 is that there are a thousand stories a day. How are you thinking about reaching your audience in a way that can grab them and hold them?
What I want our audience to know is that we are who we are, and we’re proud of who we are, and you can come to us on any platform at any time and trust that you are getting our best reporting and our best analysis without fear.
We haven’t talked about it yet, but as part of the spinoff, we had to build our own newsroom. What we tried to do is build our newsroom knowing the moment. We’re not trying to be commodity news. We’re trying to build an absolutely kickass DC newsroom, and I think we’ve done that.
MS NOW is one of the very few media brands in growth mode right now. It's impressive.
I'm curious about your take on the possibility of a merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, which would place CNN and CBS News under one owner. Would that consolidation be good for you? Does this help you even if the broader implications can be troubling?
In a functioning healthy democracy, you need a very healthy free and fair press. So I am rooting for better, stronger newsrooms. I worked most of my career at CNN, and while they might be technically a competitor or rival now, the world is a better place with a stronger CNN.

Late last year, men in parts of Congo’s Tshopo province began whispering about something strange that was happening in nearby villages. At first, the stories sounded too absurd to travel far. A man in a market claimed his genitals had suddenly shrunk after brushing against a stranger. Someone else said it happened inside a taxi. In another village, people spoke about a man who returned from town convinced that the part of his body had disappeared altogether.
And then the videos started appearing, people gathered around phones watching clips of alleged victims speaking inside crowded churches while pastors stood beside them claiming they had been cured through prayer. Some videos spread through Facebook pages and TikTok accounts. Others moved from phone to phone through Bluetooth shares and WhatsApp groups, spreading across villages faster than official information ever could.
In many places, the rumours arrived before the authorities did. By the time officials in Tshopo publicly denied the existence of any mysterious illness, fear had already settled across parts of northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where rumours, churches, and social media had combined to create something more powerful than a simple falsehood. Men spoke cautiously around strangers. Communities became suspicious of outsiders. Stories changed slightly depending on who was telling them, but the central fear remained the same.
Something was stealing men’s bodies. In the month of October, the health workers travelling through the Isangi area of Tshopo province arrived in villages already consumed by weeks of panic. They carried tablet computers, questionnaires, and reflective jackets as part of vaccination-related field surveys, but in some communities those unfamiliar objects and routines were interpreted very differently by residents who had spent weeks hearing that outsiders were spreading a disease that caused men’s genitalia to shrink or disappear.
According to Reuters, at least four health workers were later killed after crowds accused them of spreading the supposed illness.
One of them was Dr. John Tangakeya. His wife later told Reuters that the family had spoken to him earlier that day because it was his birthday. The children were waiting for him to come home that evening so that they could celebrate together. Instead, news arrived that the health team he was part of had been attacked by mobs even as they tried to explain that their surveys had nothing to do with the rumours spreading in the province.
The World Health Organization(WHO)-backed Africa Infodemic Response Alliance, which monitors dangerous health misinformation across Africa, later linked at least 17 killings to the rumours, though some incidents could not be independently verified.
Long before social media existed, versions of this panic had already travelled across parts of Africa.
Researchers have documented similar episodes for decades in Ghana, Nigeria, Cameroon, Benin, and Congo itself, where rumours of “penis theft” or genital shrinking periodically triggered mob attacks against people accused of witchcraft or supernatural powers. In Ghana, during the 1990s, several people accused of “penis snatching” were beaten to death by mobs. In Kinshasa, in 2008, police detained more than a dozen suspected “sorcerers” after panic spread through the capital and led to attempted lynchings.
Anthropologists who study such incidents have often argued that the panic is not simply about superstition. In many places, fears around genital theft became tied to larger anxieties about masculinity, illness, vulnerability, power, and social instability, particularly in societies where spiritual explanations for misfortune remain deeply embedded in everyday life.
But something about the Congo episode felt different. Earlier, panic spread through markets, crowded taxis, churches, and radio broadcasts. This time, much of the fear moved online first, where videos featuring alleged victims and miracle cures circulated rapidly through algorithm-driven feeds before local officials fully understood what was unfolding on the ground.
Several churches in Kisangani hosted testimonies from supposed victims while Facebook pages and TikTok accounts reposted clips that gathered hundreds of thousands of views. Some videos remained online even after authorities publicly dismissed the claims as false.
Health officials later said the violence exposed a deeper crisis facing public health systems in parts of Africa, where distrust toward authorities has been shaped by years of political instability, misinformation, and memories of earlier health emergencies, including Ebola and COVID-19 outbreaks, during which some communities viewed outside medical teams with suspicion.
In villages where people had already spent weeks discussing the rumours among themselves, the arrival of unfamiliar health workers carrying devices and asking questions appeared, for some residents, to confirm the fears they already believed were true.
Months later, the rumours have still not completely disappeared.
Officials continue running radio campaigns and public awareness programmes aimed at stopping the spread of misinformation. Arrests have been made in some areas. But many of the original videos are still circulating online, resurfacing again and again across different parts of Congo, long after authorities declared that the illness itself never existed.
