Brands have a proposition for influencers: What if you didn't make those pesky #ad disclosures?
The Utah-based wellness influencer Sharon Johnson, who describes herself in her Instagram bio as a "Reformed Tradwife," said a supplement company recently asked her not to include an #ad disclosure in posts showing her receiving and opening the company's product.
Johnson said she labeled the posts anyway, wary of losing her audience's trust and of a potential penalty from the Federal Trade Commission, which mandates clear labeling. The brand's request also rubbed her the wrong way.
"It almost feels like these companies are taking advantage of us because we are doing this for our livelihood," she said.
That request from the supplement brand was part of a broader trend. A survey of 365 creators conducted for Business Insider by the influencer marketing company SheSpeaks found nearly one in five (18%) said a brand had explicitly requested that they not disclose a partnership in the past year.
It's not just brands that are flouting the FTC rules. In the survey, 14% of creators said they didn't always disclose partnerships, up from 2% when SheSpeaks conducted a similar survey a decade ago. Eighty-four percent said they "always or almost always" made their brand partnerships clear, down from 95% in the prior survey.
"The fact that disclosure went down was very surprising — we expected everyone to say, or at least know to say, yes," said Aliza Freud, CEO of SheSpeaks.
"Paradoxically, it's a little bit more like the Wild West" now than a decade ago, Freud added.
The FTC states that influencers should ensure people see and understand ad disclosures using "simple and clear language," such as by thanking the brand for sending a free product or by using terms like "advertisement," "ad," or "sponsored." The FTC doesn't mandate specific wording, but says the relationship must be displayed "clearly and conspicuously" to the viewer.
Several creators and talent reps said requests to forgo disclosures were rare and tended to come from smaller brands rather than from big public companies.
Leila Marsh, chief talent officer of The Drive Agency, said brands have occasionally asked that posts not include disclosures, saying they wanted the post to look "organic."
"We always do our best to push back," Marsh said. "The entire reason people have these audiences is that they're honest and authentic. The second they start saying it's not a paid partnership, the viewers can see right through it."
One reason brands may want to hide sponsorships: a widespread belief that it hampers engagement and reach on social platforms.
"I work with celebrities, we send them the captions with #ad in front of them, and they say, 'Do we have to? It hurts engagement,'" said Shelby Currie, a director at the media agency Moroch. "We push back."
Some platforms are taking matters into their own hands: YouTube said earlier this month that it's introducing automated detection technology to label brand deals that haven't been disclosed in creator videos. TikTok and Meta have similar systems.
Creators seek clarity
AJ Eckstein, founder of Creator Match, a creator marketing agency that works with tech brands, said influencers feel under increased pressure to perform and grow at a rapid pace.
"Speed is everything right now, and disclosures get treated like something that slows you down or leads to lower performance," Eckstein said.
Eckstein said that in the past six months, two brands had asked his agency not to disclose, and that he no longer works with them.
"We've walked away from six-figure contracts over this," he said. "The audience's trust is the entire asset you're renting. If you hide the deal, you're spending down the exact thing you paid for."
Even if brands do want creators to disclose partnerships, the SheSpeaks survey found gaps in the process. Just over half of those polled (57%) said the agency or brand provided clear disclosure instructions in the past year, while 36% said the agency or brand reviewed their content for disclosure compliance.
Some influencer marketing insiders say more education is needed for brands and creators. In April, the Institute for Responsible Influence, part of the Center for Industry Self-Regulation, launched the Responsible Influence Certification Program. The program trains creators on advertising rules and standards and helps brands and agencies work with creators responsibly. It is supported by TikTok and a coalition of advertising industry groups.
A lack of regular enforcement actions by the FTC has created an environment in which creators and brands may feel there's little risk in breaking the rules, according to Lauren Wolfe, counsel at Travelers United, a nonprofit representing travelers that has brought actions against influencers for failing to disclose advertising.
Rob Freund, an advertising and e-commerce lawyer, said consumers are entitled to know whether an endorsement is genuine or paid because that information can influence purchasing decisions.
"Even if it doesn't have a lasting financial impact, we shouldn't want to live in a society, in my opinion, when it's OK to lie about who likes what product," Freund said.

Maharashtra is working to establish India’s first state-level legal framework for blockchain-based tokenisation of land and other immovable assets, chief minister Devendra Fadnavis said. Speaking at the Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 in Mumbai, Fadnavis said the state is developing the architecture for the proposed Maharashtra Digitisation and Exchange of Land Token Asset (DELTA) Act. This comes after Fadnavis directed state officials in July to draft the legislation and constitute an expert committee comprising representatives from SEBI, BSE, and NSE, along with academics and experts from the technology and legal sectors. At the GFF, Fadnavis said the government has moved beyond discussing the idea and is bringing together the expertise required to develop the framework. He estimated that unlocking the value embedded in land and real estate could represent an opportunity of around ₹50 Lakh Cr. Tokenisation involves digitally representing rights or value associated with a physical asset on a blockchain. In the case of property, the proposed framework is intended to make it easier for owners to access capital against their assets and facilitate more transparent transactions. “For generations, land has represented wealth in India, but very often it is wealth without liquidity. A family may own an asset of significant value and yet struggle to access capital against it efficiently. An entrepreneur may have an asset but may not be able to unlock its economic potential quickly,” Fadnavis said. He added that the state’s proposal is not intended to encourage speculation but to improve liquidity and transparency and convert dormant wealth into economic opportunities. Guardrails For Emerging Tech Besides asset tokenisation, Fadnavis spoke about the potential role of agentic AI and quantum technology in financial services. He said agentic AI can give individuals greater control over financial services, while quantum technology can strengthen the security infrastructure underpinning digital finance. However, the chief minister cautioned that fintech products built using emerging technologies would require safeguards around accountability, consent, security, and human oversight. “UPI democratised transactions. The next generation of fintech must democratise credit, intelligence, ownership, and opportunity. Agentic AI must give people greater agency, tokenisation must unlock productive capital, quantum must strengthen trust, and technology must ultimately serve one purpose: to expand human opportunity,” Fadnavis said. His remarks come a day after Prime Minister Narendra Modi called on fintech companies to strengthen cybersecurity and consumer protection as technologies such as agentic AI, tokenisation, and quantum computing reshape financial services. Addressing the inauguration of GFF 2026, Modi outlined four priorities for the sector — stronger cybersecurity, ethical data protection, better consumer protection, and closer collaboration between the industry and regulators. He also urged fintech companies to move beyond payments and develop products across credit, insurance, pensions, fraud prevention, and automated decision-making.

On 06 September 2026, a nearly 30-year-old five-storey building housing a boys’ PG collapsed in Delhi’s Satya Niketan area near Delhi University’s South Campus, killing seven people, including five students, while 12 people were rescued. The building was reportedly undergoing renovation work in the basement, where water had accumulated, and authorities are investigating whether this contributed to the collapse. Police arrested the building owner, Hariram, his wife, Urmila, and son, Mahesh, while the MCD suspended five South Zone officials over alleged lapses. The Delhi High Court has also ordered an audit of PGs and hostels following the incident (here, here, and here).
In the aftermath of this incident, several videos (here, here) are being shared on social media, claiming to show the PG building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The video shows the PG building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan.
Fact: To sum up, none of the videos show the PG building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan. The first video shows the demolition of an unauthorised building in Jasola, Delhi, while the second shows a building collapse in Moradabad, Uttar Pradesh. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
In our investigation, we found (here, here, and here) that the video is not related to the PG building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan. The video shows the MCD demolishing an unauthorised four-storey residential building in Jasola, southeast Delhi, after it began tilting dangerously.
Video 2
In our investigation, we found (here, here) that the video is from Moradabad, Uttar Pradesh. The video shows the collapse of a severely dilapidated building on Jama Masjid Road, near Humsafar Marriage Hall in the Sadar tehsil area, amid incessant rainfall. According to the District Magistrate, the building had been inspected and found to be in an extremely dilapidated condition. The administration had sealed the building on 04 September 2026 and restricted movement around it as a precautionary measure. The building collapsed on 05 September 2026, but no casualties were reported as the premises had already been sealed.
To sum up, none of these visuals show the PG building collapse in Delhi’s Satya Niketan.

Five Miami plane crash victims identified after Amazon jet ran off runway and slammed into van
NTSB’s chairwoman warned that the agency’s recommendations must be implemented ‘or we’re going to be here again’
All five people who died when an Amazon cargo jet ran off the runway at Miami International Airport were inside a shuttle van used by an aircraft cleaning crew, authorities say.
The crash occurred during a landing attempt on Sunday when the aircraft hit the van on airport grounds, broke through a perimeter fence, and subsequently struck an SUV on a nearby city street.
Five other people were injured. Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said Tuesday that both the pilot and co-pilot have been released from the hospital, while two victims remain in critical condition and a third is in stable condition.
National Transportation Safety Board Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said at a press conference that the 55-year-old captain had 7,145 flight hours and the 37-year-old first officer had 2,655.
The NTSB is investigating the crash, with a primary focus expected to center on the absence of specialized systems designed to slow and stop overshooting aircraft at the end of runways.
Miami International Airport is not among the 120 airfields across the US equipped with lightweight, crushable materials that the Federal Aviation Administration says have saved around 500 lives.
Even without an engineered deceleration system, the airport appears to comply with federal rules because it maintains a 1,000-foot (305-meter) safety buffer beyond the end of its runways, according to aviation experts.
Homendy noted that while her agency aims to prevent such tragedies, runway overruns continue to occur despite previous safety recommendations.
"Our recommendations must be implemented or we’re going to be here again," she said during a news conference on Monday.
Investigators have recovered the flight data recorder and are reviewing its information. Official interviews with the pilot, co-pilot, air traffic controllers, and other witnesses are being scheduled, Homendy said.
Amazon released a statement expressing its full cooperation with the investigation, adding that its deepest sympathies are with the victims and their families.
Five people killed in a van used by plane cleaners
The five victims were traveling in a van owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., a company contracted to clean planes. The vendor stated it would refrain from commenting on the crash out of respect for the families of the victims.
"Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved. Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed," the company said in a statement Tuesday.
The sheriff identified the deceased as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.
The flight was finishing a two-hour journey from Puerto Rico as storms gathered near the Miami airport.
NTSB officials stated that the plane traveled approximately 1,300 feet (396 meters) past the end of the runway.
Homendy described the scene as "utter devastation," featuring scattered vehicle wreckage, deployed air bags, destroyed navigation equipment, and ruined fencing along the aircraft's path. She noted that safety precautions were necessary because jet fuel remained present 24 hours after the crash.
NTSB examining why pilots didn’t abort landing
Strong winds exceeding 25 knots were reported on Saturday afternoon. Experts reviewing footage of the landing suggested a powerful tailwind likely pushed the jet far down the runway past its intended touchdown point, with the aircraft remaining airborne without flaring its nose to force the wheels onto the ground.
It remains unclear why the flight crew did not abort the landing to make a second attempt.
Air traffic controllers had also not shifted the landing direction to allow the plane to approach into a headwind, an operational adjustment airports routinely make when winds change.
The flight was operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 originally flew as a passenger plane for several foreign airlines over more than two decades before being converted to carry freight in 2015, according to Flightradar24.
Two of the airport's four runways remained closed Tuesday. Homendy said they will not reopen until NTSB investigators gather all required evidence from the crash site.
More than 225 flights were canceled across Sunday and Monday, with hundreds more delayed, officials said.
Homendy said the NTSB will work to hand the runway back to airport management as quickly as possible after documenting the scene.

Another Apple event is almost here, though this one will likely feel a little different than the September events of lore. The event will be livestreamed on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern). You can watch the stream right here on this page, or on Apple’s website and YouTube channel. Apple will also stream the event on its Apple TV devices and Apple TV+ streaming service. Leaks and rumors have left just about everyone expecting news about Pro-level iPhones and a long-awaited Apple foldable device.

WIRED will also have a roundup of everything the company announces for your perusal right after the event.

There are three big players in the running for the best smart speaker: Amazon, Google, and Apple. Each voice-assistant-powered system has its own benefits and limitations, and you’ll have to consider several factors to pinpoint the right smart speaker for your needs.
You may already have a favorite ecosystem. Maybe it's the one that’s compatible with your phone, as an Apple or Android user. Or maybe it's Amazon's Alexa, if you already own one of the many speakers that the company launched following the 2014 arrival of the first Amazon Echo. Amazon's smart-speaker fleet, in particular, is expansive, often seeing multiple new models every year, while the offerings are much narrower for Google and Apple. That said, a few months ago, Google did launch a new smart speaker for the first time in years—the 2026 Google Home Speaker—and I share my thoughts on it in this guide.
After trying nearly every single smart speaker that's come out in the last decade, I have a sense of the best options available today to fit various needs. Also, check out my guides to the Best Alexa Speakers, Best Google Speakers, and Best Smart Displays if you want more insight into each category.
Updated September 2026: I've added details about Amazon’s increased prices and which speakers were affected, and noted that the Google Nest Hub Max is currently out of stock online.
The Best Smart Speakers
Best for Google Users
Google's latest smart speaker, the Google Home Speaker (8/10, WIRED Recommends), is an amalgamation of great features from other smart speakers. It shares its name with the original Google speaker from 2016, but its shape and size are reminiscent of an Apple HomePod Mini. It has the tap controls and fun colors I remember from the older Google Nest Mini. And it joins the rest of Google’s smart speakers (other than the Google Pixel Tablet with the charging dock) by using Google Gemini as the default assistant instead of Google Assistant.
Gemini does sound impressively human, offering answers that approximate an interaction with another person. Sometimes its answers get a little long-winded, so just be prepared for that. But Google Gemini is nonetheless a touch smarter than other assistants in its cohort; it’s able to answer questions about my own schedule and knows to check with me about my artist preference if a song I request has multiple covers.
Gemini for Home is free, but some features you might like to use are hidden behind paywalls. For instance, Google rebranded its video camera subscriptions to “Google Home Premium,” which bundles some smart-home assistant features and video storage into one price. There are two tiers: Standard ($10 per month or $100 per year), which includes 30 days of event-based video history, intelligent alerts for things like familiar faces and packages, Gemini Live, and an AI-based tool to help you create smart-home routines for your household. The Advanced tier ($20 per month or $200 per year) includes 60 days of event-based video history, 10 days of 24/7 video history, descriptive notifications, searchable video history, video event descriptions, and daily summaries of recorded events, plus everything in the cheaper plan.
Gemini Live is the main behind-the-paywall feature you might want; it lets you switch your smart speaker into a more conversational mode. Using this feature, I had a long, natural-feeling chat with my speaker that covered my 3-year-old’s sleep patterns, scalp sunburns, and the previous night’s Love Island episode. It worked well, but it's not a capability I imagine I’ll use when I'm not actively testing.
Gemini Live doesn't work on every Google speaker, but in addition to working on the Google Home Speaker, it also works on all three versions of its available smart displays, including two iterations of the Nest Hub. My favorite is the 10-inch Nest Hub Max; it doubles as a digital photo frame powered by Google Photos, which works much better than Amazon's clunky uploader and might even be a tool you're already using. Google accounts get up to 15 GB of free storage (that'll include any Gmail or Drive files, too), so there are a lot of photos you can store and display on this device.
The Nest Hub Max has a solid sound profile given its slim frame with two 10-watt tweeters and a 30-watt woofer. The 10-inch touchscreen is a great size for everything from controlling your smart home and streaming videos to pulling up recipes and enjoying your own photos. Many of these capabilities rely on the smart display, which means you couldn't access them with a screen-free smart speaker. It's not the only smart display option on the market, but it has a prettier interface than Amazon's Echo Show 11 (below), and unlike on the Show 11, you won't see any ads sliding onto the screen on this Nest. There's also a camera for video calls and gesture-based controls. While there’s no cover for the camera, you can disable it if you prefer.
However, the Nest Hub Max seems to be completely out of stock at all retailers. I'm hoping we see it return, or get news of a new version. But we'll have to wait and see.
Best for Amazon Users
Most of the smart speakers I spot in friends' homes come from the Amazon Echo line. Options abound, and many that I see are older models, like the puck-shaped Echo Dot. Such dated speakers are still fairly well-supported, though not all of them can gain access to Alexa+, Amazon's newer AI-powered voice assistant. But even if your smart speaker can use Alexa+, it's only worth the upgrade if you have Amazon Prime, which includes access to the assistant. Without a Prime subscription, you'd have to pay $20 a month for Alexa+ on its own. It's literally cheaper to get Amazon Prime ($15 a month for most plans), which comes with a wider range of benefits. This price model is surely intentional, as it may serve as a push to get you to sign up for Prime if you haven't already.
The Echo Dot Max is one of Amazon's newest models. It launched in late 2025, taking the small form from past Dot models and upgrading the device with impressive sound quality, a built-in smart-home hub, Alexa and Alexa+ access, and a slightly different look. It’s surprisingly loud without getting muddled, especially considering its small size. Impressively, it can still hear my requests even when the room is loud or it is playing loud music. I tested it against the latest Echo Studio last year and found the speakers were more similar in quality than I expected. The Dot Max is more expensive than older Dot models; if you don’t need next-level sound, the more affordable Echo Dot (fifth gen) might be a good fit for your needs.
Both the Echo Dot Max and the Echo Dot were hit by price increases at the end of August. Amazon raised prices across its product categories, including its Echo speakers. The Echo Dot Max got a $20 increase and a new $120 price tag, while the Echo Dot (5th Gen) went from $50 to $80. I'm most disappointed about the Echo Dot, since now its sale prices will likely only go down to the $50 range instead of landing between $25 and $30. It makes it a less appealing buy at its new price, and I recommend waiting for a sale for both of these models.
If you're looking for something with more capabilities, like being able to read recipes, stream shows, and even make video calls, you might want a smart display instead of a smart speaker. These devices can perform the same functions as any other smart speaker, but they add a screen and camera to unlock a variety of new abilities.
Amazon launched two new smart displays last fall: The Echo Show 11 ($250) is the pricier of the two, but I liked it better than the new Echo Show 8 ($200). The Show 11 has better sound, and its 11-inch screen was a nice size for both my desk and kitchen counter. The interface is updated for Alexa+, but I didn’t love some of the changes. For instance, when you ask Alexa+ questions, the Show 11 brings up a chat-like interface. Because of this, some answers don’t provide the same level of detail as I got with the original Alexa. The change that I like the least is how Alexa+ handles the weather; I loved seeing the pages of weather info for the day and week that original Alexa would show, and now I just get a small snippet in a sea of written words. If you want something similar but cheaper, I'd recommend the older third-generation Echo Show 8 ($150) over the newest one. That model had a better sound when I tested both Echo Show 8 versions side by side.
It's also important to note that Echo Show devices have a lot of screen clutter, and the devices also show ads. You might not see the ads right away, but eventually you'll start seeing prompts to buy things on Amazon. You can activate photo mode to hide the ads, but that will only last three hours before going back to regular mode. You can also remove clutter (like the multiple news, sports, and food-related topics it'll show by default) by going into the device's settings. An Echo Show device can technically double as a digital photo frame, but it's annoying to upload pictures and won't put vertical photos side-by-side.
Neither the Echo Show 11 nor the older Echo Show 8 increased in price like the Echo Dot Max, but the newer Echo Show 8 did and is now retailing for a base price of $200. It's on sale right now to match the price of the older model, though, so that's a pro for now. The new prices really just make my two preferred options an even better buy than before—just a $20 increase to get the Echo Show 11 over the new Show 8 is well worth the better sound and larger screen.
Best for Apple Users
Smart speaker options are the most limited for Apple users. My colleagues and I weren’t impressed by the sound quality of the larger HomePod when it relaunched in 2023. But the smaller HomePod Mini is a fine investment for the price, and you'll find it to be the most convenient option if you already use the Apple Home app and Siri.
It's about a third of the price and smaller than the full-size speaker; otherwise, it’s capable of just about everything the larger model can do. It doubles as a smart home hub to connect your Apple-compatible devices, so you don't need the larger speaker or Apple TV if you're mainly looking for smart-home control. It's still not my favorite smart speaker overall, and Apple HomeKit isn't my favorite ecosystem. It has serious limitations, and I find myself running into more issues adding my devices to the Home app than on any other platform. But if you're committed to your Apple ecosystem, this is the speaker to buy.
There's also no smart display option in Apple's ecosystem, so if you'd like one of those in your home, you'll have to go with Google or Apple. Notably, Apple's price hikes in June affected both the Apple HomePod Mini and the larger HomePod. The HomePod Mini used to be $99 but now retails for $129.

What’s Alexa+?
Amazon announced the new and improved Alexa, named Alexa+, in February 2025. This second generation of the Alexa voice assistant is more conversational than its predecessor, offering an experience similar to what you get with AI assistants like ChatGPT. This makes sense, given that Alexa+ was built on generative AI. Alexa+ does a better job at answering a variety of questions than first-gen Alexa and responds quickly to all kinds of requests. You can learn about my firsthand experience with Alexa+ here.
Alexa+ is free for Amazon Prime members. If you aren’t a member, you can get a free trial of the new assistant for 30 days, but after that, a subscription carries a $20 monthly fee. At that point, it’s cheaper to join Prime than it is to subscribe to Alexa+. This is likely by design to hook you into Amazon's larger ecosystem. Yes, the Prime subscription fee is a big jump from being free, but most people who choose to get an Amazon Alexa device in the first place are also likely Prime subscribers. If you aren't, though, this assistant isn't worth the cost of the subscription.
Alexa+ also requires that all voice recordings be sent to Amazon for processing, and Amazon has changed its policy for recordings with regular Alexa, too—those now also go to Amazon. There was previously a “Do Not Send Voice Recordings” privacy feature that you could select, which would process voice requests locally, but Amazon killed that functionality last year. The privacy change will affect all users, whether or not you sign up for Alexa+, regardless of whether you're using an Alexa+-compatible device or not.
What’s Gemini for Google Home?
Google announced late last year that Gemini for Home, the new version of its voice assistant, is rolling out to existing Google Home users. It's replaced the previous Google Assistant entirely and is currently slated to roll out to almost all of Google's devices. One of the notable exceptions is the Pixel Tablet; otherwise, Google's existing hardware properly reflects what Gemini for Home will reach.
Unlike Alexa+, this new assistant will always be free. However, Google is changing its camera subscription, Nest Aware, to become a new subscription named Google Home Premium. As I mentioned above in my pick for the best smart speaker for Google users, this subscription has two tiers, Standard ($10 a month) and Advanced ($20 a month). FAQs
How Should You Choose Between Alexa, Google, and Siri?
The easiest way to choose which smart assistant to add to your house is to consider which ecosystem you're already using in some capacity. If you're a big Google or Android user, for example, adding a Google Gemini–powered speaker to your home is a no-brainer. It's not always that simple, though. If you’re an Apple and iPhone user, you’ll find benefits in choosing HomeKit-powered devices. But because Apple's ecosystem is so limited, you might want to choose a different assistant for the devices you want. Amazon's Alexa has the widest range of offerings, but Google's seamless experience has me coming back again and again.
Here's what you should ask yourself to decide:
- What assistant are you already using, if any?
- What products do you want to use in your home, and which assistants are they compatible with?
- What features do you want in a smart speaker? Which ecosystem can offer you those features?
Why Do I Prefer Google Devices?
There are many reasons to love Amazon’s Alexa voice assistant, and it works pretty well. If you want to use your voice assistant to shop or use Amazon services like Prime Music or Prime Video, chances are an Alexa-powered speaker is best for you.
Google's smart speakers have fewer skills and are compatible with fewer smart-home devices than Alexa, but Google Gemini, like Google Assistant before it, can do enough to qualify as truly useful—plus, Google adds new skills fairly frequently. Speakers with Google Gemini continue to work better when you network them together, and they're compatible with a wide variety of Google apps and services. Google is better at answering random questions and telling you where to go out to eat, since it can access and send information to your phone through Google apps.
Spotify, Pandora, and YouTube Music are the main ways to play music with Google Gemini. The service can also send Netflix shows and movies to your TV if you have a Chromecast attached.
If you're using a smart display, I also prefer Google’s options to Amazon's, mainly because Alexa Show devices serve you sponsored content while Google's will not. Amazon's Show displays are already crowded with content by default that you'll likely want to remove. (To do so, go to Settings on the device, and then click Home Content. You'll currently find more than 40 options you can toggle on and off.) But you can't fully remove the sponsored content unless you're in Photo Frame mode. Meanwhile, Google's displays make for better photo frames, thanks to Google Photos. These displays also have a less crowded interface, with less content to distract you. I'd stick to a Nest Home Hub unless you definitely want an Alexa display and won't mind the occasional onscreen ad.
How Can I Get the Most Out of My Smart Speaker?
My biggest piece of advice for enjoying a smart speaker to its fullest potential is to make sure you put it somewhere you'll use it often. I love having a small speaker in my bedroom to ask about the weather while I'm getting ready for the day, and then I make sure there's a smart speaker somewhere near my desk and living area (usually multiple, but I'm an odd case since I test these for a living) so that I can call out requests as I work, cook, and watch TV.
The next biggest to-do for maximizing your smart speaker is to invest in other compatible smart-home gadgets. Smart speakers work best when they have other devices to control and speak to. Set up some smart lights, a smart lock or two, a video doorbell, a couple of security cameras—you name it! And then command your smart speaker to help you control them or otherwise check on your home.
Can I Use My Smart Speaker With My TV or Entertainment System?
Sometimes! This varies by TV model and what’s connected to your TV. You can find some TVs that have built-in voice control, though some might use voice control through the remote rather than with the smart speaker. Apple's smart speakers and Apple TV sync the best among single-system options I've tested. But otherwise, I haven't found it as painless as I would have hoped.
If you're looking for music entertainment, smart speakers are great. You can connect multiple smart speakers for a stereo system, or connect your smart speaker to existing systems. Depending on the system in question and what you already have, you might have to choose a smart speaker with a 3.5-mm wire-in option or a speaker that has built-in compatibility with Amazon Alexa and Google Gemini for Home.
Should I Be Concerned About My Privacy?
Adding microphones to your home (and sometimes cameras) is a valid point of concern. Smart speakers are technically always listening, though they're supposed to only listen for their wake word and otherwise ignore all other audio until asked a question. But there have been cases where police have requested audio recordings from smart speakers to use as evidence, including two separate murder cases in 2018 and 2019.
Most of the speakers I recommend have some method to shut down the speaker's listening tendencies, whether an off switch or a camera cover, but it's annoying to switch on and off if you want to use your speaker regularly. Alexa also no longer allows local processing, so everything you ask Alexa is now sent to the cloud to help Alexa+ run.
Ultimately, you should be concerned about your privacy, and it's worth considering whether you want a set of microphones in your house. In my years of testing, I haven't felt any of my smart speakers to be invasive, and they do a good job giving themselves away when activated (lighting up and asking “Hmm?” if they don't understand the question), so it's never felt like my speakers are sneakily listening to me. But it's certainly a personal choice.
Will Smart Speakers Become Bricks?
The smart speakers in this guide are primarily made by large brands—Amazon! Google! Sonos!—and it's unlikely any of them will suddenly vanish or become a useless brick speaker on your desk. There are even some first-generation Amazon Echos still working that are about a decade old (with mixed results, based on what users say online).
But a UK law passed in April 2024 adds more protection here. The law mandates three key points: more secure password procedures, more clarity on how to report bugs and security issues, and that manufacturers and retailers must inform customers how long these products will receive support and software updates.
The last point is the most relevant for smart speaker users, since the fear is that you'll buy a speaker that will suddenly stop getting updates and become unusable. I'll be watching to see how much information is really offered to shoppers as it takes effect, but so far, we haven't seen any changes. Nonetheless, it's a law we like. While there's not yet an equivalent law in the US, I'll watch for updates here as well.
How Does WIRED Test Smart Speakers?
I employ a variety of tests with smart speakers. I do microphone tests, gauging how far away a speaker will hear and respond to a question, both while music is playing and while music is off. I also play a variety of songs to see how well the speaker performs at playing everything from chill lo-fi to my favorite metal band and beyond. I also sync it with smart devices to see how well it connects and controls those devices, and what kind of capabilities it has. If there's a screen, I also test the included features. Finally, I also live with these speakers for at least a week (if not more like months!) to see how they fare in day-to-day use and long-term performance.
How Does WIRED Acquire Smart Speakers? What Does WIRED Do With Them After Testing Them?
Most of the smart speakers I test are press samples that brands send to me. I obtain these samples with the understanding that no coverage is promised, nor are there any agreements about what that possible coverage will look like. I also occasionally purchase my own speakers.
After testing, I keep most smart speakers for long-term testing or in storage for future comparison tests. If I deem a smart speaker redundant, I usually recycle the device locally, as it likely won't receive more updates or support from the company. If it's still a viable speaker, I'll donate it instead.

Out in rural India, a crisis casts a dark cloud over the seemingly tranquil vistas of wheat fields and soy farms. Over the past 20 years, more than 400,000 farmers have killed themselves, beset by mounting debts and low market prices for crops. Shot in Maharashtra, the state with the highest rate of farmer suicides in India, Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary sensitively captures another tragedy that lingers after death: left behind by their dead husbands, generations of grieving widows struggle to find their way in a society still burdened by patriarchal values.
Sanjivani, a woman in her 30s, is one such case. Eight years after her husband killed himself, she has taken over some of the farming responsibilities, along with other odd jobs, to provide for her two children. The camera rarely finds her at rest; Sanjivani not only works in the fields but also performs domestic labour for her extended family – cooking, cleaning and doing laundry. Her resilience is stunning to witness, but even more impressive is the emotional support provided by a tight-knit network of other widows. Together, the women gather for counselling sessions where they can freely discuss their emotional, physical and financial issues.
One widow, for example, laments her former status as a child bride; another talks defiantly of her decision to remarry, still a taboo act in this conservative village. Though each has their baggage, the women all share the pain and anger of being rendered invisible by their widowhood. On certain celebration days, they are not even allowed to go out, for fear of inflicting bad luck on others. Sanjivani’s transformation over the course of the film, however, inspires hope. As she continues her education and works at a local pharmacy, Sanjivani’s steps towards independence show that, with the support of the collective, life can – and must – go on for the marginalised and forgotten.

South Park creators rename show 'South America' in apparent dig at Trump
- Published
The creators of South Park, the animated TV show, have announced that its new series will be named South America, in an apparent reference to US President Donald Trump's attempts to rename a lake and a gulf.
"Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA," creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker wrote in a statement.
Trump signed an executive order in August to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and last year declared that the Gulf of Mexico be known as the Gulf of America.
The announcement from South Park, now in its 29th season, comes after the show won an Emmy for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday.
The official name change shared to the show's official social media account featured an image of the South Park sign with the word 'Park' replaced with 'America'.
"We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount - a Skydance Capitulation," its creators said in the post.
Paramount Skydance is the show's parent company. The Trump administration this year approved a $111bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery - one of the biggest media deals in history.
But the merger has since been paused until June 2027, after 12 US states filed lawsuits against the deal for fear of it harming competition and leading to higher prices for consumers.
A day before the show's announcement, Trump shared an AI-generated video of him placing the word 'America' over 'Mexico' on a "Welcome to New Mexico" sign.
In August, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, Trump ordered a similar change for Lake Ontario - renaming it Lake America.
Apple and Google subsequently changed the name in their respective Maps apps for US-based users.
And last year, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed as Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.
South Park, which has run since 1997, has regularly mocked the US president during his two presidency terms.
Both its creators, Stone and Parker, have repeatedly drawn criticism from Trump, the White House and MAGA supporters for its jabs at the president.
During its 27th season, the White House described South Park as a "fourth-rate" show that was "hanging on by a thread with uninspired ideas in a desperate attempt for attention", after an episode depicted Trump naked in bed with Satan.
After winning the award for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday, South Park also shared an image depicting a fictionalised Donald Trump with the words: "You finally got your Emmy."
The new season of South Park will premiere on 16 September.

Apple’s September 9th launch event could be one of its biggest in years. Apple’s expected to announce a new lineup of iPhones, which could include its first foldable phone.

Flights at major British airports were disrupted on Tuesday after a technical fault at air traffic control provider NATS affected its flight data processing system, leading to more than 1,000 cancellations and hundreds of delays.
According to Reuters, NATS said the issue was resolved at 1834 GMT and that "safety was not compromised". The provider said it was operating normally but warned that it would take time to clear the backlog created by the disruption.
NATS CEO Martin Rolfe told Sky News that the company had not "fully done the investigation" into the cause of the technical issue.
"We don't have an idea yet of exactly what went wrong," Rolfe said.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 said 1,300 flights to and from UK airports were cancelled on Tuesday, while another 177 flights had been cancelled for Wednesday, nearly all at Heathrow.
Heathrow said arrivals had been suspended for the remainder of Tuesday, while departures had resumed. The airport warned that disruption was expected to continue.
FlightAware data showed around 490 departures were delayed at six airports -- Heathrow, Gatwick, London City, Luton, Edinburgh and Bristol -- as of 1518 GMT. Another 525 arrivals at the six airports were either cancelled or delayed.
At Heathrow, 38 of 661 scheduled arrivals had been cancelled or were unable to operate, according to aviation analytics company Cirium. British Airways was the most affected carrier at the airport, cancelling 16 of 333 scheduled departures.
"The severity of the issue means there will be a significant knock-on impact for customers and colleagues," British Airways said in a statement.
The disruption has renewed questions about the resilience of Britain's aviation infrastructure, coming three years after a flight-plan processing failure at NATS caused widespread disruption.
Aviation analyst John Strickland said delays can quickly cascade through Europe's tightly scheduled aviation network.
"A few hours of outage may on the face of it sound limited but the impact is enormous when a substantial number of airports across the UK are affected," Strickland said, according to Reuters.
Ryanair said around 150,000 of its passengers had been affected by delays of up to eight hours and that it had cancelled more than 200 flights. The airline's Chief Operating Officer Neal McMahon called on NATS CEO Martin Rolfe to resign.
Wizz Air also called for urgent reform, saying airlines, passengers and airports should not continue to bear the consequences of recurring system failures.
"A critical national infrastructure provider should not repeatedly bring the aviation system to a standstill. NATS is simply not fit for purpose in its current form," Wizz Air said in a statement.
Air India flights operating to and from UK airports had also been impacted.
In a traffic advisory, the airline said it had been forced to divert, delay or cancel multiple flights scheduled to operate to and from UK airports.
Air India also warned that the disruption could affect some of its other services because its aircraft and crews had been left out of position following the incident.
The airline advised passengers to check the latest status of their flights before proceeding to the airport. Air India said it was closely monitoring the situation and making efforts to minimise disruptions.
"We regret the inconvenience caused by this unfortunate situation, which is entirely beyond our control, and thank our passengers for their patience and understanding," the airline said in a statement on X.
Britain's aviation regulator said it would expect NATS to share a full report of Tuesday's incident. The Civil Aviation Authority said it would then consider whether further steps were needed to secure the reliability of the UK's air traffic control system.
In 2024, the CAA had said NATS needed to review its contingency plans for outages after an automatic flight-plan processing malfunction the previous year caused disruption across Britain's airports.
In July last year, a radar-related technical issue in Britain's air traffic control system also disrupted flights for more than four hours at major airports in London and elsewhere, including Heathrow.

Prince George starts Eton College as Harry and Meghan grapple with 'brutal put-down'
Harry, Meghan surprised by King's confirmation they will remain non-working members of Royal Family
It was a day of ups and downs for the Royal Family as, on the one hand, Prince George started his first day at prestigious Eton College and, on the other, Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, grappled with their status as non-working members of the Royal Family.
The Prince and Princess of Wales were all smiles as Prince George started his first day at the 600-year-old school Tuesday morning, following in his father's footsteps. The trio appeared relaxed as they dropped off George, King Charles's 13-year-old grandson and second in line to the throne.
"Welcome, good luck and enjoy," said headteacher Simon Henderson, shaking hands with George before ushering everyone inside to the school where George will be boarding.
Later, George was photographed grinning in his new school uniform: a black tailcoat, waistcoat and a white collar.
Eton is the alma mater for many of the country's elite, including Prince William and Prince Harry, and has educated 20 British prime ministers, including Boris Johnson and David Cameron, as well as actors Hugh Laurie, Damian Lewis and Tom Hiddleston.
As BBC reports, George's time at Eton will likely see him somewhat shielded from media and public attention. Prince William has previously spoken about much he enjoyed being "just another student" at the school.
Harry and Meghan 'surprised' by letter
On the other hand, Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, experienced what some observers are calling a rude awakening back in the U.K. after Charles confirmed Monday they will remain non-working royals.
The news, which came in the form of a letter from Buckingham Palace sent to senior British officials, said that after Harry and Meghan stepped down from official royal duties in 2020, they "are no longer working members of the Royal Family."
"In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests," the letter stated.

On Tuesday, The Associated Press reported that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were surprised by the way Buckingham Palace released the letter. They were "a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance," their representative said in a statement on Tuesday, as reported by BBC.
The couple’s representatives received a copy of the letter just one hour and 12 minutes before it was released to news outlets, the person said. That left them with little time to respond because they were unable to reach Harry, who was in a meeting, until just two minutes before the letter was released, the person added.
The letter reiterates the palace's previous stance.
Harry and Meghan stepped back from royal duties in 2020 when they moved to North America to make their own living, turning to ventures such as deals with Netflix and Spotify. At the time, Queen Elizabeth made clear that the couple could not be part-time royals. Charles reiterated that position after he became King in 2022.

In an interview with GB News, royal historian Alexander Larman called Charles' move a "brutal put-down."
"I would call it a right royal knees-up, actually, because Harry's just been back a couple of weeks now and we're seeing how it's all going for him," Larman said.
"This is basically the King saying: 'You're back, I'm delighted on a paternal level that you're back. But, as head of a firm, I'm making it very, very clear that you are not back in the Royal Family."
As CBC's The Royal Fascinator reported over the weekend, Harry and Meghan's return to the U.K. set off shockwaves because it seems so counterintuitive and contradictory to everything that they have said since they left.
Royal expert Phil Dampier told The Sun the King's statement was a "warning shot" not to overshadow the Royal Family.
"It’s really sending out a message — a warning shot across their bows, you could say. What they’re [the palace] emphasizing is that nothing has changed as far as they’re concerned," Dampier said.
"Now that they’ve come back and might start turning up to various charity events or doing commercial activities, it’s got to be absolutely clear to everyone that they are doing it as private individuals and not as royals.”
On Monday, Meghan posted a photo on her As Ever Instagram account, in which she relaxes on a lawn with the couple's black lab, Pula. "Long weekend plans," notes the caption.

The story so far: India’s food regulator has proposed a red, hexagonal warning label on the front of packaged foods high in added sugar, saturated fat or salt, in a move aimed at giving consumers a simple, at-a-glance signal about unhealthy products.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), in an affidavit filed in the Supreme Court on August 28, has proposed that the warning initially apply to products high in two or more of the three “nutrients of concern” — added sugar, added saturated fat and salt — as well as specified highly sweetened beverages.
The proposal comes after years of debate over front-of-pack labelling and intervention by the Supreme Court. The Court is scheduled to consider the affidavit on September 10.
Also Read | FSSAI’s proposed warning labels could let unhealthy foods escape scrutiny, says expert
How the proposed system is expected to work?
FSSAI has proposed a two-phase rollout. In the first phase, products high in at least two of the three nutrients would carry the red hexagon, along with specified highly sweetened beverages.
In the second phase, the warning would extend to products high in any one of the three nutrients. However, FSSAI has not specified a firm timeline for moving to the second phase.
The thresholds are proposed to be based on the Indian Council of Medical Research–National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024. However, the FSSAI proposal refers to added sugar and added saturated fat, rather than total sugar and total fat.
Single-ingredient foods and products inherently rich in these nutrients, including ghee, edible oil, jaggery and honey, are also proposed to be exempt.

What do critics say about the proposed change?
Nutrition advocates say the biggest concern is the decision to initially require a product to be high in two nutrients before it attracts a warning. A product that is high in sugar but low in salt and fat, for instance, could escape a warning altogether.
“This defeats the purpose of a warning label,” Arun Gupta, convenor of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPI), told The Hindu. He has argued for a simpler principle: if a product is high in sugar, salt or saturated fat, it should carry a warning.
Also Read | Why the FSSAI is also putting liquor under the scanner
The distinction could matter particularly for products such as sugary beverages, which may be high in added sugar but contain little or no fat or salt and could therefore fall outside the warning requirement in Phase I.
Dr. Gupta has also raised concerns over the use of “added” rather than total sugar and fat, the size of the proposed warning and the absence of a firm deadline for Phase II. He has called for the warnings to be available in Hindi and English, arguing that language and visibility are essential if the labels are to reach consumers across the country.
He has urged the Court to examine the proposed nutrient thresholds, definition of high-fat/sugar/salt foods, warning size, language requirements and exemptions to ensure that the system remains visible and scientifically robust.
Also Read | From Bournvita to ‘100% Pure’: Why is FSSAI tightening the rules on food claims?
Why is this significant?
Front-of-pack warning labels have been under discussion in India since at least 2018. Draft regulations on high fat, sugar and salt (HFSS) foods were proposed in 2022, but did not become law.
The issue returned to the centre of the public-health debate in 2026 after the Supreme Court directed FSSAI to move towards interpretive warning labels for unhealthy packaged foods.
The regulator’s approach has also evolved rapidly in recent weeks. An earlier proposal placed before the Court in August relied on displaying nutritional information against recommended daily limits. Following the Court’s intervention, FSSAI returned with the red-hexagon warning framework in its August 28 affidavit.
Also Read | FSSAI proposes front-of-pack red pictorial warnings for foods high in fat, sugar, salt
For consumers, the proposed red hexagon is intended to make it harder for marketing claims such as “natural” or “multigrain” to obscure the nutritional profile of a product.
For the food industry, mandatory warnings could increase pressure to reformulate products by reducing sugar, salt and saturated fat. FSSAI has said the phased approach would give industry time to reformulate.
But the proposal is not yet a notified regulation. The immediate question before the Supreme Court is whether the framework provides a clear and meaningful warning or leaves products high in a single nutrient outside the net for an unspecified period.

The anger was impossible to miss.
As television reporters walked into Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and adjoining protest sites to cover the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, many were greeted with chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’. Several journalists carrying microphones or wearing lanyards bearing the logos of prominent television channels — including NDTV, News X, ABP News, and Times Now — found themselves surrounded by protesters questioning their coverage of the movement. In some instances, reporters were heckled. In some instances, the confrontation turned physical: Times Now reporter Dev Kotak was roughed up by the crowd at Jantar Mantar, and video of the aftermath circulated widely. A Zee News reporter was filmed in Mumbai standing in the rain as youth protesters around him jeered.
The mood was most poignantly captured, perhaps, by a banner at the protest site. It contained the mugshots of six senior mainstream media journalist-cum-anchors: Arnab Goswami of Republic, Sudhir Chaudhary of DD, Chitra Tripathi of ABP, Anjan Om Kashyap of Aaj Tak, Amish Devgan then of News 18, and Rubika Liyaquat of Times Now Navbharat. Above their photos, the banner said, “India’s worst enemies — More dangerous that terrorists or anti-nationals”.
Taken together, the scenes that unfolded in Delhi raise the important question: Why did a large section of young protesters reserve some of their sharpest criticism not for politicians or police, but for television news channels?
Television Crew Faces Public Anger
The protests that erupted in Delhi in June-July brought together thousands of students and young people from across the country, turning a satirical political collective called the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) into the nucleus of a wider youth-led movement. What began as a mobilisation around the NEET-UG paper leak and concerns over the examination system expanded into a broader expression of anger against the government, with protesters demanding accountability from those in charge. The demonstrations grew in scale over weeks, drawing sustained public and media attention and eventually contributing to Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation.
As the protests grew, major television networks deployed reporters to cover the events. Instead of the routine interactions that often accompany live reporting, many ground reporters encountered open hostility from sections of the crowd.
Slogans of “Godi Media” were raised during a gathering in the national capital Delhi. pic.twitter.com/oyZpCVz0EY
— The Nawakadal (@thenawakadal) July 20, 2026
Videos shared widely on social media show protesters chanting ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ — a phrase originally coined by journalist Ravish Kumar, roughly translating to ‘lapdog media’ — as reporters prepared to go live. In one video, a protester says he stopped a News18 vehicle from being damaged despite his own anger towards the channel. “I am a Muslim myself. I protected their vehicle from being damaged. Though I know this evening, they will again do a Hindu-Muslim debate,” he said.
GODI MEDIA IS DEAD!
Yesterday’s Massive Student Protest Delivered The Final Verdict:
Traditional Mainstream Media has COMPLETELY LOST Gen Z’s Trust!
Lakhs of Students who hit the streets got EVERY piece of Real Information from Social Media — not your Biased Propaganda Boxes.… pic.twitter.com/zLIOM5GXP1
— তন্ময় l T͞anmoy l (@tanmoyofc) July 21, 2026
As reporters started being identified by the brands they represented, some began using unbranded microphones instead. NDTV’s Shiv Aroor and Vishnu Som, and India Today’s Preeti Choudhry were among those.
The outbursts were not confined to a handful of isolated incidents. Numerous videos from different locations captured similar confrontations, while comments beneath those videos echoed the protesters’ criticism of mainstream television news. Smaller outlets perceived as pro-government were heckled as well, suggesting the hostility was directed at a type of coverage rather than at legacy television alone.
At the same time, several incidents crossed the line from protest into intimidation. Videos also emerged showing journalists being pushed, chased or physically heckled by sections of the crowd.
This andhbhakti of CJP is now crossing all limits. You can tell godi media to walk away, raise slogans, but you can’t physically push, grope or beat them.
Wonder whether these are genuine protestors or lumpen elements.https://t.co/Xo4bTJ1DgX
— 🍉 (@DelhiIsNotFar) July 21, 2026
In Kolkata as well, reporters of mainstream media outlets were allegedly pushed and shoved after a march on July 24 in solidarity with the Jantar Mantar protest.
Why Were Protesters Angry?
The central allegation against sections of legacy media seemed to be that they had stopped acting as the voice of the people and had instead become the voice of the establishment.
For many of the demonstrators, the resentment did not begin with the July protests.
Television news channels have failed, over the years, to hold the Union government to account over a wide range of issues that affect ordinary citizens’ lives — from examination paper leaks and irregularities in recruitment exams to unemployment, price rise, public health etc. This is precisely the role the media is expected to play as democracy’s fourth pillar. Most television news channels that have ample airtime for communal debates and polarising studio confrontations show far less urgency when the failures of the government directly affect the lives and futures of citizens.
The dissatisfaction was not simply about what television channels were reporting during the protests, but what they had consistently chosen not to report. For a generation facing an increasingly precarious education and employment landscape, the perceived reluctance of mainstream television to question those in power became a source of deep distrust.
Explaining the reasons for the anger against the mainstream media, AISA leader and student face of the Delhi protests Neha Bora said, “The hate that the government peddles comes to our drawing rooms, our WhatsApp groups and our very personal lives, within the four walls of our homes, through the Godi media. The Godi media and the IT cell are single-handedly responsible for the venom that runs through the veins of this country presently. Through systematic targeting and organised campaigns, they have made enemies out of citizens, neighbours and friends.”
Elaborating on how they had failed in their duty, she added, “The government is not a God-like figure. They are there to do a job; they have been elected to serve us. They will have to be questioned. The Godi media has systematically dismantled this idea. We are told not to question the government, criticise its policies or talk about the problems we face. If I say that the answer sheet in the Class 12 examination is not mine, the Godi media and the IT cell are going to call me a Pakistani.”
In May, Doordarshan anchor Ashok Srivastav called Class XII student from Delhi Vedant Srivastava a Pakistani. After receiving unexpectedly low marks in Physics, Vedant had applied for photocopies of his answer sheets through CBSE’s reevaluation process. When the copies arrived, he discovered that the Physics answer sheet uploaded by the Board was not his. He made an X account to post about his grievances.
“The disrespect that the youth has for Godi media stems from this — the recognition that this Godi media and its anchors, who scream at the top of their voices on TV screens, have fractured the democratic, secular fabric of this country,” Neha added.
Asked for her response to ground reporters being heckled, Neha said, “We recognise that there are ground reporters in Godi media who do honest work, and that is why we urged our people not to disrespect them. Our differences need not be expressed through violence. We don’t believe in mobs. But there is no denying that the mainstream media has become a BJP propaganda cell, it seems.”
The protesters’ criticism was also shaped by how they believed the movement itself was being portrayed.
Arnab Goswami, for example, in an apparent bid to discredit the protest and question its legitimacy, mentioned China, US, Bangladesh, Pakistan, BitChat, the deep state, Greta Thunberg, Jeremy Corbyn, and even John Cusack as conspirators behind the CJP protest.
In a podcast hosted by Navika Kumar, lyricist and screenwriter Manoj Muntashir Shukla called protesters anti-nationals.
As clashes broke out between protesters and police on July 20, ANI did not post a single news update throughout the day which mentioned injury to protesters.
In Kolkata, Zee reporter Ayan Ghoshal said while interviewing BJP leader Dilip Ghosh, “For the last 3 days efforts are on in Delhi to break India. PM has shown restraint. We know how Pak or Indonesia curbed students’ protest. Dead bodies were strewn on sreets. But no tough action here. They’re getting encouraged.”
The mainstream media drew criticism on social media for what protesters described as coverage that closely mirrored the official version put forward by the Delhi Police and the government. The channels, on the other hand, maintained that they were reporting developments on the ground.
You are the most vile, most pathetic, most disgusting person @sudhirchaudhary
I always agree to disagree, never hate anyone but you are really a bad person.
You are now labelling innocent students for your propaganda.
Shame on you! pic.twitter.com/lYj5cNlURk
— Arpit Sharma (@iArpitSpeaks) July 21, 2026
Rahul Shivshankar, editorial director of CNN News 18, amplified a video where RSS leader Atul Limaye called the CJP protest anti-national and “a weapon against the Constitution”.
It is worth noting that coverage of this kind carries risks beyond the newsroom. Framing a protest movement as anti-national, foreign-funded or a security threat can shape how the protesters are treated on the ground, by the state and by ordinary citizens alike. The Zee reporter’s on-air remarks, for example, were arguably not only biased, but amounted to incitement. Seen against this backdrop, at least some of the heckling and intimidation directed at reporters on the ground could be a reaction to this pattern of coverage.
A Widening Trust Deficit
The outpouring of anger at journalists points to a broader crisis of credibility confronting sections of India’s television news industry.
Alt News’s years of fact-checking work and media-watchdog journalism point to a pattern rather than isolated lapses: In the recent past, large sections of mainstream television media have functioned as an echo chamber for the government. The clearest symptom is the collapse of verification standards and rampant amplification of misinformation. During the India-Pakistan military escalation following the Pahalgam attack, several major channels aired unverified and outright false claims — old and unrelated videos and fabricated visuals presented as live combat coverage.
ALSO READ: Op Sindoor: As Indian media made false, outrageous claims, PIB looked the other way
Further in the past, we documented instances of mainstream media broadcasting misinformation targeting protesters and protest movements. During the 2024 farmers’ movement, Republic, News 18, India TV, Zee News, India Today, Navbharat Times — all ran a doctored video of farmer leader Jagjit Singh Dallewal without any context and amplified the misleading claim that he said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s popularity graph had skyrocketed after the Ram Mandir inauguration and reached an all-time high.
More examples of such misreporting related the farmers’ protest can be found here and here.
It is worth noting that during the farmers’ movement of 2020–21, too, several mainstream television channels faced sustained criticism over their coverage, including banners at protest sites slamming Godi Media. Farmers accused sections of the media of portraying the agitation as foreign-funded or sympathetic to Khalistani groups rather than engaging with their demands. However, the scale and frequency of confrontations witnessed during the CJP-led protests appear significantly greater than what was seen during the farmers’ movement.
ALSO READ: The fictional strikes on the Karachi port and what it says about Indian media
A second, related failure is the normalization of communal debates on prime-time shows. On almost a daily basis, senior journalists anchor panel debates that are structured for conflict, with the hosts allowing and sometimes encouraging inflammatory rhetoric against minorities, because it drives engagement.
Check the thumbnails in the compilations from 2022 below. Each and every bulletin represented by these thumbnails was on communal issues. All on News 18:
Hosted by Aman Chopra:
Shows hosted by Amish Devgan:
The cumulative effect is to cloak hate-mongering as news content night after night. Several prominent channels have faced punitive action in the last few years for peddling communal propaganda on shows hosted by ‘star’ anchors. Related reports by Alt News can be found here, here, here, here and here.
After Operation Sindoor, when several mainstream channels aired unverified and absurd claims, including reports that India had attacked Karachi, the BJP’s official X handle shared a monologue by anchor Sushant Sinha defending the media’s coverage as part of a broader “information war” in national interest.
पाकिस्तान कभी नहीं सुधरेगा और हो सकता है कि युद्ध भी हो, लेकिन क्या ऐसे लड़ेगा भारत?
ऐसे भारत विरोधी तत्वों को पहचानिए, जिन्होंने #OperationSindoor के समय अपने देश, देश की मीडिया और देश की सेना का मजाक बनाया था…
हमारे जवान तो जंग के लिए तैयार हैं, लेकिन क्या आप मन से तैयार… pic.twitter.com/spQrwxqbTm
— BJP (@BJP4India) May 14, 2025
There could be no clearer indicator of the alignment of the mainstream media with the BJP government.
In a functional democracy, the public square is a space that should be open to everyone, equally, without fear, intimidation or violence. Whether that principle still holds in India is increasingly open to question. If sections of society — minorities, independent journalists and critics of the government — cannot live and function without fear of harassment, vilification or even incarceration, the mainstream media has played a significant role in creating and reinforcing that climate. And there appear to be few meaningful avenues for holding these media organisations accountable.
Structural Questions: The Nexus among Media, Corporate Power & the BJP Government
Structural factors help explain this pattern. Both the ownership and revenue models of India’s mainstream media organisations constrain their capacity for critical journalism. Several major outlets — including NDTV, IANS and News18 — are owned by large business conglomerates such as the Adani and Ambani groups, which have close ties to the Union Government.
The journalism produced by these organisations reflects those ties, more often than not. Television news, being capital-intensive, is also heavily dependent on government advertising and large corporate advertisers, who are often reluctant to fund critical journalism.
The incentive to toe the government line shows up not always as an explicit directive but more as a pattern of editorial choices: Aggressive coverage of opposition-ruled states, muted coverage of the same failures under the Union government or in BJP-ruled states; extensive coverage of minor opposition controversies, minimal coverage of major stories embarrassing to the ruling party. See here, here and here.
The closeness between media and corporate power was captured vividly when India Today anchor Rahul Kanwal was filmed tasting food meant for elephants at the Ambanis’ Vantara animal sanctuary, alongside Anant Ambani. For many viewers, the spectacle reinforced the perception of a media establishment more comfortable warming up to power than challenging it.
This was in March 2024. Exactly one year later, Vantara was in the news again. This time, after a South African wildlife coalition urged its government to investigate the transfer of wild animals to the Reliance-owned facility. A handful of Indian outlets reported the concerns, but within days, many of them took down their reports, leaving readers with ‘Error 404’ or ‘Page Not Found’ messages. The reasons for the removals remained unexplained. At least three media houses told Alt News that they had received threatening calls or emails.
In 2018, ABP News managing editor Milind Khandekar and anchor Punya Prasun Bajpai resigned after Bajpai’s show ‘Masterstroke’ fact-checked a claim made during a public interaction involving Prime Minister Modi. Chandramani Kaushik, a farmer from Chhattisgarh, had told Modi her income had doubled after she switched from paddy cultivation to processing custard apple. When ABP interviewed her, she said she had been coached by officials to make the claim. Senior anchor Abhisar Sharma was taken off air days later after e juxtaposed a Modi speech in Lucknow praising Uttar Pradesh’s improved law-and-order record with a shootout in the state on the same day.
Efforts to counter this nexus have had limited success. The Independent and Public-Spirited Media Foundation (IPSMF), set up with funding from Azim Premji and Nandan Nilekani to support independent journalism, has faced funding constraints in recent years and has been the subject of income tax investigations.
These dynamics are reflected in India’s global press freedom rankings, which have declined in the last two decades.
Reporters, like people in every other field of work, must be able to do their job without harassment or fear of violence. And physical retaliation can not become an acceptable response to disliked coverage. Once it is, it can easily be turned against any journalist doing legitimate reporting — not only those seen as compromised. But condemning those attacks should not foreclose an examination of the reasons behind the hostility.
The chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ were directed not merely at individual reporters standing in front of television cameras, but at institutions that many protesters believe have repeatedly failed to hold those in power accountable. Whether or not that perception is fair, the scenes from Delhi point to a widening gap between a section of India’s youth and parts of the country’s mainstream television news industry — a gap that did not emerge overnight, and is unlikely to close soon.

A landmark petition is to be handed to King Charles by Jamaican over slavery reparations, aiming to confront historical crimes that still disadvantage former British colonies, the Caribbean nation’s culture minister has said.
The petition will be lodged with Charles, Jamaica’s head of state, on Monday.
“We’re a resilient people. We were able to bounce back from [Hurricane] Melissa, for example,” said Olivia Grange, who arrived in London at the weekend with members of Jamaica’s National Council on Reparations.
“But we still have a lot of work to do, and you can imagine if we did not have those inherited problems, the legacy that came out of slavery, how much better we would have been able to do so.”
First announced in June last year, the petition asks the monarch to use his authority to request legal advice from the judicial committee of the London-based privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.
It wants Charles to ask whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful, if it constituted a crime against humanity, and whether Britain is under obligation to provide restitution to Jamaica for slavery and its enduring consequences.
Grange said that these questions and a privy council response were critical to progressing the country’s reparations claims.
Between the 15th and 19th centuries, more than 12.5 million Africans were kidnapped, forcibly transported to the Americas and sold into slavery.
Grange said that Jamaica had been the first Caribbean nation to create a national reparations mechanism, establishing it in 2009. She said the aim was to address the enduring impacts of slavery, that put countries such as Jamaica at a grave economic disadvantage and affected its ability to respond to modern-day challenges in the Caribbean, such as the climate crisis.
“We have inherited systems that continue to deprive our country and our people. The legacy in education, even in health, the way we eat, our diet because of what we were fed, our ancestors were fed,” she said.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines who was instrumental in setting up the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, echoed Grange’s sentiments.
“The present is very much the past, because what we are dealing with is the legacies of underdevelopment which you can source, and we do source, to native genocide and enslavement of African bodies,” he said on Sunday.
“People must remember this: that European nations were enriched because of the enslavement of African bodies.” Gonsalves is an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice.
He said Jamaica’s visit was a critical milestone among a number of upcoming events, including a Caribbean reparations conference in Barbados later this month, and planned advocacy at the upcoming UN general assembly in late September and the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua in November, which King Charles is scheduled to attend.
There are growing global calls for Britain and other former colonial powers to recognise hundreds of years of transatlantic slavery that treated African people as chattel as a crime, and to engage in a process of reparatory justice.
In March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity. In June, the Caribbean launched a manifesto outlining the “moral, ethical and legal case for reparations”. And last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other measures to address the enduring legacy of racial discrimination.
The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the March UN resolution, and in October 2024, the former British prime minister Keir Starmer resisted pressure from member states to include reparations in the Commonwealth heads of government meeting agenda.
Grange said she hoped the visit would facilitate a unifying response to the complicated history.
On Sunday, the delegation will host a remembrance church service in Brixton, and later in the week they are due to meet UK members of parliament. Grange said there would also be a visit to the British Museum, to discuss repatriation of Jamaican artefacts.
She said: “We may have different history, different heritage, different skin colour, but it’s about humanity. It’s about, as a people, being able to live together, to work together, and to respect each other.
“And in our efforts to seek reparatory justice, we will use the opportunity to also promote and encourage what Jamaica is known for, One Love, because we have the song of the century through Bob Marley.”

Chelsea agree £47.1m move for Monaco's Camara
