What’s the Matter With Moderation?
Hoping to break a 94-year losing streak, Kansas Democrats have turned to Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor whose mood may not match his party’s.
One simple rule shapes Kansas politics: Republicans win statewide. In U.S. Senate races, the GOP has prevailed without interruption for more than 90 years. But the rule has a corollary, which accounts for the occasional Democratic governor. A Republican thought to be too extreme, too ideological, or too big for their britches can be beaten by a centrist Democrat when the wind blows just right.
And so, on the same August Tuesday that saw Michigan Democrats choose Abdul El-Sayed, Kansas Republicans realized their safe seat might not be so safe. Kansas Democrats had picked a man who extols moderation as a matter of faith—literally. Adam Hamilton, the founding pastor of America’s largest mainline Protestant congregation, will challenge the first-term incumbent Senator Roger Marshall in November. In the handful of months since he announced his candidacy, Hamilton has defeated 10 garden-variety Democrats in the primary while setting new records for Kansas fundraising, pulling in $1 million in his first week and nearly $3.7 million in his first quarter.
Political analysts continue to rate Hamilton a long shot; admittedly, they have nine decades of justification. But Marshall ticks every box that can mean trouble for otherwise-invulnerable Kansas Republicans. Full of himself even by senatorial standards (one Republican Senate colleague described him to me as a “know-it-all”), Marshall is leery of public forums where he might hear from protesters and tends to speak before thinking—a hazard of his appetite for cable-TV appearances. In nearly six years as a constituent of the senator, I have traveled from one end of Kansas to the other, and I have concluded that passionate supporters of Roger Marshall are the electoral equivalent of jackalopes: If they exist, I have never found one.
Should Hamilton break the Senate’s longest GOP win streak, he would score more than an enormous off-year upset; his influence on 2028—a free-for-all to define post–Donald Trump politics—could be even larger. Because Hamilton seeks to vindicate the belief, beleaguered in today’s culture, that moderation is a good thing, not just as an electoral strategy, but as an approach to life.
In Texas, James Talarico’s Christianity seems, at times, to dovetail with uncanny precision with the agenda of secular progressivism. Hamilton’s rhetoric suggests that his Democratic revival tent would be roomier, but at the same time he has so far faced relatively little pressure to translate his disposition into details. He is motivated by “compassion, a belief in safety nets for vulnerable people,” he told me, and also by “fiscal responsibility, limited government, and strong defense.”
Such inoffensive straddling may be out of step with today’s politics. “People are really pissing mad, really, really pissing mad,” El-Sayed explained to Michelle Goldberg of The New York Times. A roiling left has risen to match Trump’s raging right. To win, Hamilton must not only persuade independents and Republicans to vote for him—he must also motivate angry progressives in this time of throat-cutting.
If El-Sayed and others like him are the furious faces of the Democratic future, perhaps Hamilton is a DINO. When I asked him if Democrats should seek to impeach Trump a third time, he ventured his belief that “the impeachments in the first term did not accomplish anything”—a claim that dismisses the expression of righteous anger as a political imperative in itself. Hamilton likes to talk about the good that he could accomplish in partnership with the well-liked Senator Jerry Moran, the senior Republican from Kansas. But maybe that’s not what the people, who truly are pissing mad, really want.
Emporia is the seat of Lyon County, which in 2024 gave 56 percent of its votes to Donald Trump and 41 percent to Kamala Harris. Yet Hamilton was not in hostile territory when he visited one late-August morning. Gravel City Roasters is a combination coffee shop and art gallery located directly across Emporia’s main drag from the county Democratic headquarters. There is a Pride flag on the wall with Refugees welcome superimposed on its rainbow stripes. The chai, served in mismatched mugs, is excellent.
But the comfort zone is narrow here for a 21st-century Democrat. The little city with its college campus is surrounded by farmland that has historically bred beasts, grains, and discontent. In its heyday—the era of William McKinley and Theodore Roosevelt—Emporia was home to the journalist William Allen White, whose Gazette newspaper was a sort of proto-Substack. Readers around the world vibed to his grumbling, which often had to do with the eternal sense of Kansas as undervalued and overlooked. “Go east and you hear them laugh at Kansas; go west and they sneer at her; go south and they cuss her; go north and they have forgotten her,” White wrote in his career-launching screed, dated 1896 and titled “What’s the Matter With Kansas?”
Thirteen decades later, an Emporia pharmacist, John Schmidt, picked up the theme, telling me at the coffee shop of the town’s beef processing plant (closed), its Michelin rubber-track factory (downsized), its maker of plastic ice scrapers (victim of a bankrupt holding company), and the nearby drugstore (battered by low reimbursements). The area’s future, too, feels festooned with pink slips.
A few dozen people awaited Hamilton, who arrived in a blue blazer and an open-collared white shirt. He immediately went to work shaking hands and nodding thoughtfully. After watching Hamilton campaign half a dozen or so times, the best description I can manage is “pastoral.” Fair enough, I suppose, for a 62-year-old pastor. Hamilton has a soft voice, and his gaze is gentle, intent, and framed by horn-rimmed glasses. His head moves constantly in tiny yeses and no’s, like a seismograph needle registering each quick conversation.
After working his way to the rear of the shop—pausing to autograph a woman’s copy of his book on the Holy Spirit—Hamilton used a wireless microphone to tell a joke about hypocritical politicians pretending to know the Lord’s Prayer. “I am a Democrat who actually knows the Lord’s Prayer,” he said. “When it says, ‘give us this day our daily bread,’ it’s reminding us to make sure that people have enough to eat.”
A sturdy little stump speech rolled out from there, befitting a man who has been crafting sermons since Seinfeld was new. He said he is a fifth-generation Kansan who married his sweetheart a week after high-school graduation and wants to give his granddaughter “a better country.” He said he built a church from nothing to 24,000 members. He said he prayed a year and a half ago that Trump would govern “with wisdom, grace, and compassion,” but found himself watching something quite different. Somebody’s got to do something became Maybe I should do something.
Rather than take on Trump directly, however, he aimed the balance of his fire at Marshall, who, Hamilton noted, “has voted for nearly everything the president has done.” Hamilton said he is against tariffs because they hurt farmers, against the Iran war because it drives up fuel prices, against Medicaid reductions because they threaten rural hospitals, and against cuts to food aid because more than 14,000 Kansas children need that support. “Since when did it become woke to care about your neighbor?” he asked rhetorically, aware that his audience was already seeing attack ads trying to tie him to left-wing ideas, and that Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas used an X post to denounce one of Hamilton’s sermons as “heretical.”
Don Duncan was part of that audience, having driven to town from nearby Chase County to have a look at the candidate. In the primary, a local Democrat, Christy Davis, drew 113 votes in Chase County, leaving Hamilton with eight; on the Republican side, Marshall got 479. Duncan, a self-described “Democrat who leans independent,” told me he did not think things are as bleak for Hamilton as that would suggest.
“It’s just a matter of people getting to know him,” said the retired school administrator and coach. “We need someone to get us back together.”
Could that be Marshall? I asked. “I can’t say we ever talk about him,” Duncan answered.
About 100 miles north and east, amid the big houses and busy shops of Kansas City’s southern suburbs, stands Hamilton’s monument to open minds, the “church for thinking people” that he founded in 1990. The main sanctuary of Leawood’s United Methodist Church of the Resurrection is visible from all directions, an elliptical edifice clad in glass and stainless steel, vaguely reminiscent of Disney’s Space Mountain. Rising 100 feet above a 77-acre campus of auxiliary buildings and parking lots, it features the largest fused-stained-glass window in the world, a work roughly the size of a basketball court. Nine satellite churches in greater Kansas City—four in Kansas; five in Missouri—carry the COR brand to sites around the area and beyond.
If the words megachurch pastor conjure images of hellfire oratory and $400 haircuts, Hamilton comes as a surprise, as mild as Jake from State Farm. Yet his success stands in contrast to the decline of mainstream Christianity in his lifetime.
Born in 1964 and raised by divorced parents in Prairie Village, one of those same southern suburbs, Hamilton came of age in a time of Protestant crisis. Perplexed by the social upheaval of the 1960s, Hamilton’s United Methodist denomination lost more than 10 percent of its membership in the 1970s and a further 5 percent in the 1980s. What energy there was in American Christianity came from conservative movements energized by opposition to abortion, homosexuality, scientific modernism, and a grab bag of philosophical attitudes derided by evangelicals as “secular humanism.”
Even as a teen, Hamilton found this alienating. Drawn to church for its social possibilities—“I didn’t believe in God, but I believed in girls,” he likes to say—the God he eventually embraced was one who delighted in discovery and gloried in progress. God gave us a brain for a reason, he thought, taking to heart the biblical admonition to worship with all of one’s “heart and soul and mind.”
In college at Oral Roberts University in Tulsa, Oklahoma, Hamilton “grew more and more interested in the parts of the Gospel that evangelical churches were leaving behind,” he told me during a July interview at a barbecue joint across the state line in Kansas City, Missouri. “I began focusing on scriptures dealing with social justice, ‘rolling down like waters,’ as Amos has it; the caring for widows and orphans; the story of the Good Samaritan. And I noticed that our churches were great at helping the people who came to church, but not so much with the people who were outside.”
Trained as a pastor at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, Hamilton returned with his young family to Kansas City in the late Reagan years. He soon persuaded his regional bishop to let him start a new congregation for people turned off by what Christianity had become. Though United Methodism suffered a further 29 percent drop in membership from 1990 to 2020, Hamilton’s congregation grew from fewer than a dozen people meeting in a funeral-home chapel to the largest mainline Protestant congregation in America.
He credits an idea known to theologians as the via media, the “middle way,” which has roots in ancient philosophy and scholastic Christianity, but had its flowering in Elizabethan England. At its core the idea involves a belief that truth is not to be found on the extremes and that compromise in pursuit of worthy aims is a virtue. Society as Hamilton envisions it is a sort of Newton’s cradle, the toy that is composed of a line of metal balls suspended by threads. When the ball on one end is lifted and released, it swings into contact with the pack, where its energy is conducted to the ball on the other extreme, which swings away in reaction. Energy might come from extremism, but stability lies with the center.
COR is that stable center, Hamilton maintains, “roughly equal parts Democrat, Republican, and independent,” where inevitable conflicts among freethinking people can be respected and accommodated in pursuit of shared missions. “I am wired to see both sides,” he told me, “which is not the same as saying that all issues are 50–50. I believe cutting Medicaid and closing rural hospitals is just wrong. Making it harder for public schools to serve special-needs students is wrong, and I am willing to talk with anyone to explain why I think so. But I don’t expect everyone to agree with me all the time.”
Hamilton hasn’t shied from hard issues as a pastor. When a faction of American Methodists joined forces with culturally conservative congregations in Africa to try to pass anti-LGBTQ ordinances for the denomination, he led the opposition. Criticizing what he saw as a misguided focus on a few biblical verses over a larger Gospel of inclusion and acceptance, Hamilton ultimately concluded that a schism was inevitable, and he was instrumental in negotiating the many details of separation.
The thing to notice about that story, as Hamilton tries to turn from pastor to lawmaker, is that the via media was the road not taken by Hamilton and the Methodists when the chips were down. There was no middle ground, and now there are two denominations where there used to be one.
Hamilton would likely run into an even more challenging divide in Washington, where the two factions cannot go their separate ways. Can moderation really be an agenda? In the biblical story of King Solomon, when confronted with a seemingly unresolvable impasse, the wise solution was not to split the baby, but for one combatant to surrender for the greater good. That’s not the Washington way.
Electoral politics is, in some ways, just second-grade math: addition and subtraction. Candidates seek to add votes in Column A while subtracting votes from Column B. All of the money, overt or dark; all of the advertisements; all of the pandering and polarizing; all of the door-knocking, the text messages, the awkward TikToks, the yard signs, the stilted visits by candidates to factories, diners, fairgrounds, living rooms, nursing homes, colleges—it’s all about addition and subtraction.
For Hamilton, the problem pencils out at around 80,000 votes. Any combination of addition and subtraction that hits this target, whether raising the Democratic vote share or reducing Marshall’s compared with his 2020 victory, will get the job done. That’s a big number in a state the size of Kansas, where about 1.3 million people voted in 2024, but so is the number of people who cram the pews of Hamilton’s sanctuaries each Christmas and Easter: around 100,000 per holiday.
As shown by the August 4 results, his stronghold is in Johnson County, home to his church and to about a quarter of the state’s voters. Once a bastion of chamber-of-commerce Republicanism, the county turned purple during its explosive growth in the Baby Boom years and has, in the Trump era, become a relatively safe base for Democratic Representative Sharice Davids.
Driving up turnout in Johnson County and other metro centers—working-class Wyandotte County (Kansas City, Kansas), liberal Douglas County (Lawrence, home to the University of Kansas), booming Sedgwick County (Wichita, still the state’s largest city)—will be the keys to Hamilton’s addition problem.
As for subtraction, meet Marshall. A retired ob-gyn who calls himself “Doc”—a nickname that hasn’t caught on with Kansas voters—he has distinguished himself as one of Trump’s most obsequious acolytes, though not always the most on-message. Marshall’s ready-fire-aim approach to public speaking has left his candidacy riddled with self-inflicted wounds. Asked whether he’s okay with Iran having ballistic missiles (the program Trump was promising to destroy), Marshall said, “I would prefer they didn’t. But I don’t think that’s the key issue here. I think that they have to be able to defend themselves.” Of rising gas prices triggered by the war: “Freedom is not free. Americans are going to have to make some sacrifices.” When Kansans died on a plane that collided with an Army helicopter over Washington, Marshall blithely blamed their deaths on DEI, a theory unsupported by crash investigators.
Having sold his house in central Kansas shortly after being elected to the Senate, Marshall is dogged by allegations that his status as a Kansas resident is largely fictitious. He lists as his residence a roughly 1,200-square-foot cabin on a family ranch property, but for several years his congressionally paid travel plans included frequent stops at his “vacation” home in Florida, which he says has been uninhabitable since suffering severe hurricane damage in 2024. Marshall’s campaign did not respond to my requests to discuss the race for this article, but in a recent social-media post he wrote, “Over the last six years, I’ve averaged 185 days per year in D.C. doing the work you sent me to do, 130 days per year in Kansas with over 300 stops per year across the state, about 35 days of official travel, and 20 holiday/personal days.”
When he does visit Kansas, Marshall has avoided open meetings with the public ever since a crowd in a rural community jeered him in March 2025 during Elon Musk’s DOGE fiasco. “The town halls just became non-productive and dangerous,” Marshall told a newspaper in Hays, Kansas.
The odor of weakness around the incumbent helped inspire the GOP-dominated legislature this year to spitball easing Marshall out of office in favor of an appointed successor whose term they would extend through 2028. Voilà! No election needed. The scheme died amid criticism that the Constitution doesn’t allow states to change the length of a Senate term, no matter how lame their senator might be.
With no choice but to defend Marshall, the GOP is probing for Hamilton’s vulnerabilities. A Massachusetts-based super PAC spent a reported $600,000 on a TV ad that pieces together phrases from sermons to portray Hamilton as “mega-woke.” “Black Lives Matter,” Hamilton says in the ad, “marching for righteousness.” In another moment, marked with an ellipsis on-screen, he says, “By virtue of being white … I have to repent.” The Kansas City Star dug up the June 2020 sermon from which the clip is taken and found Hamilton saying “I have certain benefits by virtue of being educated, white, and male, right?” adding, almost a minute later, “Before I can do anything to help anyone else, I have to have a conversion. I have to repent.”
Ted Cruz’s X post avowing that Hamilton held “heretical” views relied on a sermon in which Hamilton says that non-Christians might enter heaven. Marshall thanked Cruz in his own post and added, “Wait until you hear about the ‘hundreds of mistakes in the Bible’ my opponent claims to have found.” In response, the Hamilton campaign shared a quote from Joshua Leu, a pastor of a church in Great Bend, Kansas, where Marshall once served on the board. HuffPost had asked Leu about Hamilton. “I would say that he’s a middle-of-the-road pastor who is willing to listen to all sides, and then based on his understanding of the gospel, try to make the best decision,” Leu said.
Attacking Hamilton as a fellow traveler of the progressive left, a democratic socialist in gossamer disguise, might work in Kansas. But there are reasons why even Kansans who reject that portrait as grossly inaccurate might still say no to his candidacy. The party of Lincoln still has deep resonance in a state where people were battling years before Fort Sumter. Bob Dole’s success at amassing power in Washington and using it to funnel money to the state taught lessons in the value of seniority that are still remembered. Western Kansas is not only overwhelmingly Republican, but it is also suspicious of what it regards as the citified East, where Hamilton is from. And not even all of his Johnson County congregation’s members are Hamilton supporters, by the candidate’s own assessment. As the church has grown, some members have griped that Hamilton has become less accessible—an issue that his Senate campaign is likely to exacerbate, to say nothing of actually serving in the Senate. He’s taken a leave from sermonizing for now, but would stay on as senior pastor and preach at least a dozen times a year if elected.
A Kansas Democrat starts out in such a deep hole in a Senate race that Hamilton considered running as an independent, but the recent example of the failed independent Greg Orman (who lost a race for Senate in 2014 and governor in 2018) convinced the pastor and his advisers that only a Democrat could unseat Marshall. When voters ask, as they frequently do, how Hamilton would deal with pressure from party leaders, he told me his answer is: “I won’t work for Chuck Schumer; I’ll work for the people of Kansas.”
But other candidates in the region—Dan Osborn in Nebraska, Brian Bengs in South Dakota—have chosen the middlest of ways by running as independents. Perhaps Hamilton’s decision to step off the via media by allying himself with one of our nation’s two political parties is a concession to the reality of politics. Before Hamilton can be as nettlesome for Schumer as, say, West Virginia’s Joe Manchin was during the administration of Joe Biden, he first must win in November. Well-intentioned concessions, however, are the beginning of another, much more famous, road.
With money continuing to pour in from more than 16,000 donors, Hamilton can answer the attacks. And he has another shield in his armory. A prolific author of books on scripture, prayer, and Seeing Gray in a World of Black and White, Hamilton has created texts and instructional videos that are staples at Bible studies and Sunday-school classes in at least 500 Kansas churches, he told me. This makes him something of a known commodity in rural communities that might otherwise be leery of a big-city candidate.
As he calculates, 500 churches averaging 50 people each represents a small army of 25,000 people at least partly inoculated against anti-Hamilton attack ads. He doesn’t expect to win them all in counties where Democrats sometimes number in single digits, and he doesn’t need to. Maybe a handful in each precinct, in the secrecy of the voting booth, stung by the price of tractor fuel and fertilizer, will mark his name, or simply skip Marshall’s.
Hamilton is not a dynamic political performer; he doesn’t suck the oxygen from the room. The son of a service-station manager, a husband and father by the end of his teens, Hamilton instead relies on approachability, on his feeling for life as ordinary people live it: sometimes messy; sometimes painful. He seems to genuinely believe that what people have in common matters more than their differences. You can build a church on that. But can you build a campaign?
Jim Hightower, the former Texas agriculture commissioner turned liberal pundit, used to say, “There is nothing in the middle of the road but yellow stripes and dead armadillos.” But Kansas has—or had—something of a tradition of moderate Republican senators in the not-so-distant past. Nancy Kassebaum, the daughter of former Governor Alf Landon, the Republican Party’s 1936 presidential nominee (even Kansas went for Franklin D. Roosevelt that year), died last month. She served three terms in the Senate, from 1978 to 1997. She was a Republican who worked on health care, voted to ban assault weapons, and opposed, for nearly all of her career, a constitutional amendment to balance the budget. “We should be wary of the seemingly simple solution,” she said. Hamilton might anger partisans on the left and right—in his pews and beyond—by adhering to the middle way. He will need to make compromises in order to win, or, should he win, in order to govern. Politics inevitably sullies religion. But Jesus, in the Gospel of Matthew, also recommends the narrow road instead of the wide and easy one.
As a student of the via media, Hamilton surely knows what came for Queen Elizabeth’s moderate vision. The elegant span she championed connecting Catholic structures and rituals to Protestant individualism proved a bridge to nowhere. The decades after her death belonged to the extremists. Rivers of blood flowed across Europe as Catholics and Protestants waged their Thirty Years’ War. In England, sectarian Puritans staged a regicidal revolution. Refugees from religious violence poured into the Americas.
Some eras in history are like that, obstreperous and irreconcilable. Hamilton likes to point out that Kansas contains the geographical center of the lower 48 states, and he hopes to find America’s political midpoint too. The risk is that, like so much of the Farm Belt, the center has been hollowed out.

Police arrest suspect in Germany power grid attacks after dayslong search
Police have arrested a suspect in connection with a series of attacks on power distribution systems across Germany
BERLIN -- Police arrested a suspect Tuesday in connection with a series of attacks on power distribution systems across Germany which had led to a massive, dayslong search.
A 48-year-old man was arrested near a power plant in Weisweiler, in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
The man, whose name and nationality were not given in line with German privacy rules but has been widely identified by local media as Daniel V., was in possession of explosives and offered no resistance at the time of his arrest, Cologne police said in a statement.
When the first acts of sabotage took place early last week at a substation near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg in northeastern Germany, and then hours later, a short circuit knocked power lines out of service at the Bergheim power substation near Cologne, top security officials in both states raised alarm and said they couldn't exclude that the attacks were committed by foreign powers.
The incidents took place as the country was on high alert after the government blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 using a drone laden with explosives.
However, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Friday that the acts were believed to have been committed by a single activist in connection with climate extremism.
In addition to the first sabotage attacks near Jänschwalde and Bergheim, the man is alleged to have attempted, at several locations in North Rhine-Westphalia, and the eastern states of Brandenburg and Saxony, to use homemade rockets to shoot a thin wire across high-voltage power lines, thereby causing a short circuit.
Most recently on Monday police discovered several launch devices on a high-voltage power line near the Weisweiler plant — very close to the spot where police were able to arrest the man. Investigators also found a letter there claiming responsibility — in addition to several other letters they had found at other locations before, German news agency dpa reported.
In the letters, the man justified the attacks on the power grid as part of the fight against fossil fuels. Lignite is still being mined and used to generate electricity in all three of the states where the man allegedly committed or tried to commit attacks on power plants.
Police said Tuesday that near the place where they arrested the man, they also found a tent set up in the underbrush nearby, which contained additional explosive charges.
The items are currently being examined by a bomb disposal expert from the North Rhine-Westphalia State Criminal Police Office.
An arrest warrant had been issued earlier for the 48-year-old by the Cottbus Public Prosecutor’s Office.
Officers were at the scene in Weisweiler Tuesday to secure evidence and check whether any additional, as yet undiscovered, detonation devices have been set up in the surrounding area, police said.

Deaths in India due to second hand smoke increased nearly 50% in 2023, compared to 1990, even as death rates improved by about 30%, according to a global analysis published in The Lancet Public Health journal.
The estimates also suggest that while the population exposed to second hand smoke increased from 375 million in 1990 to 444 million in 2026 -- up by 18.4% -- age-standardised prevalence dropped from 43.2 per cent in 1990 to 30.6 per cent in 2023 in India.
Age-standardised prevalence is a statistical adjustment made to data to allow a fair comparison of prevalence across age groups.
An international team of researchers forming the 'Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 Second-hand smoke Collaborators' estimated prevalence of exposure to passive smoking and the disease burden it contributes to across 204 countries and territories.
"In 2023, an estimated 2.71 billion people worldwide were exposed to SHS (second hand smoke), including 767 million children aged 0-14 years," the authors wrote.
Globally, exposure prevalence was 33.9 per cent in 2023. China, India, and Indonesia accounted for nearly half of the world's exposed population, with 664 million, 444 million, and 142 million people exposed, respectively, in 2023, they found.
However, "age-standardised prevalence was highest in southeast Asia, east Asia, and Oceania (48.4 per cent), with female individuals in some countries experiencing nearly 1.8 times the exposure prevalence of male individuals," the team said.
In India, absolute deaths in 1990 due to passive smoking were 2,17,700, while those in 2023 were 3,25,600 -- death rates or deaths per hundred thousand population, however, fell from 46.1 in 1990 to 30 in 2023, down by 35%, the findings show.
"The numbers mean that despite a fall in the adjusted rates, the absolute number of people exposed to passive smoking is still increasing. This can have long-lasting effects across multiple organ systems, not just the respiratory system," Neetu Jain, pulmonologist and senior consultant at Pushpawati Singhania Hospital and Research Institute, New Delhi, told PTI.
"Second-hand smoke exposure is associated with an increased risk of several diseases, including cardiovascular and respiratory conditions. The effects of passive smoking can also be particularly concerning in people with conditions such as coronary artery disease," she said.
Children were found to account for more than 12% of the world's health burden from second hand smoke, with lower respiratory infections causing the greatest burden, according to the study.
"Passive smoking is avoidable if smokers take steps to prevent exposing others to tobacco smoke. Smoking outside the home and away from enclosed spaces can reduce exposure to second-hand smoke, particularly among family members and children. Children are especially vulnerable because their lungs are still developing, and exposure to tobacco smoke can adversely affect their respiratory health," Dr Jain said.
"The effects tend to be greatest among those who are least aware of what passive smoking is and the health risks associated with it," the pulmonologist said.
"However, we should encourage smokers to quit and focus on bringing down smoking across the country through effective tobacco-control measures, including higher tobacco prices and taxes," she said.

- U.S. businesses and the U.S. government have accused Canadian companies of acting as a "backdoor" funneling Chinese steel into the United States. President Donald Trump's administration also has accused Canada of being one of China's "biggest enablers" in efforts to avoid tariffs in general.
- In May, the Department of Justice reached a settlement with two Canadian companies accused of falsely labeling Chinese steel as Canadian to avoid customs duties. However, the companies did not admit fault as part of the settlement.

We reached out to the U.S. trade representative's office and will update this story if we hear back.
In the fall and summer of 2026, social media users claimed that Canada resold Chinese steel as Canadian to help China avoid U.S. tariffs.
The rumor spread on Facebook and X (screenshot, screenshot). Snopes readers also contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
It is true that American businesses have accused Canadian companies — not the country's government — of skirting tariffs by selling Chinese goods, including steel, as Canadian. In an August report, Trump's administration also accused Canada of being one of "China's biggest enablers" in helping evade tariffs in general through "transshipment," or the shipment of goods from one country to another via a stop in yet another country.
In May, the Department of Justice reached a $19 million settlement with two Canadian companies over allegations that they "knowingly and improperly" failed to pay duties owed on steel manufactured in European and Asian countries, including China. The defendants denied the allegations and the settlement is not an admission of fault, but it also does not mean the United States' allegations were unfounded, according to the court documents (Page 2).
Snopes relies on independent verification and primary evidence for all of our conclusions. As of this writing, the courts have not determined that any Canadian company or government official has attempted to evade tariffs or help China avoid tariffs through this supposed scheme. Furthermore, there is not enough publicly available evidence that such a scheme has happened or is happening. As such, we have not rated this claim.
In an emailed statement, a Canada Department of Finance spokesperson said that Canada "takes concerns related to transshipment and the circumvention of trade measures very seriously."
"Canada is not a source of foreign steel or aluminum transshipment into the U.S. market and has implemented some of the world's most robust measures to prevent these practices," the statement said. "Canada remains committed to working with its partners to protect the integrity of North American supply chains and to address unfair trade practices."
We reached out to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer for more information and await a response.
It is also worth noting that the claims connected these allegations to the breakdown in U.S.-Canada trade talks in late summer 2026. That may be because Greer reportedly raised concerns to Canadian officials about the transshipment of Chinese steel through countries Canada is seeking new free-trade deals with.
Here's what we know about the allegations:
US businesses accuse Canadian firms of avoiding tariffs
In December 2025, American industry leaders accused Canadian and Mexican firms of using cheap Chinese materials in ways that undercut U.S. businesses during a public hearing on the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade 
For example, here's what Brandon Farris, vice president of the Steel Manufacturers Association, said, according to Page 135 of the official transcript for the Dec. 4, 2025 hearing:
Some producers of steel-intensive goods in both countries continue to rely on steel sourced from non-market, excess capacity nations such as China. From 2020 to 2024, Mexico's steel imports from China rose by 59 percent, while Canada's increased by nearly 75 percent. Just as Canada and Mexico have experienced rising imports from countries with chronic excess steel capacity, the U.S. has faced its own surge of steel products from both neighbors.
Michael Salmon, CEO of Specialty Steel Works in Indiana, said that "China in particular continues to use Mexico as back door access to key U.S. markets, including steel" (Page 139). And Bob Wahlin, CEO of Stoughton Trailers, an American trailer manufacturer, said the United States must "close loopholes in the agreement" allowing "highly subsidized" Chinese steel to "enter the U.S. market from Canada and Mexico" (Page 244).
DOJ, US government accusations against Canada
The best publicly available evidence that at least some Canadian firms may be skirting tariffs on Chinese steel appears to be the previously mentioned Department of Justice settlement with two Canadian companies, Farjess and Royal Canadian Steel.
According to the Justice Department's complaint, the same people oversee Royal Canadian Steel and Farjess. Royal Canadian Steel imported steel into Canada and supplied that steel to Farjess (PDF pages 4 and 5).
The DOJ alleged that Farjess and/or Royal Canadian Steel personnel removed labels on steel referencing a Chinese company in order to conceal the origin of the steel from customs officials (PDF pages 13 to 15). Allegedly, the companies replaced the Chinese labels with their own. Evidence submitted in court included scans of those labels (see Exhibits 7 and 8).
While this scheme may have helped Chinese companies avoid tariffs, the Justice Department's allegations focused on the benefits to the two Canadian firms — specifically, that they experienced "windfall profits" from the allegedly fraudulent activity (PDF Page 22).
Skepticism of US claims and Canada's response
CBC reported in 2025 that Eric Miller, an expert on Canada-U.S. trade policy with the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, said Canada is "nowhere near as much of a back door for Chinese steel as the American companies make it out to be."
Miller reportedly said Canada is "quite militant" about prevention of Chinese transshipment because it wants to protect its own access to the U.S. market.
"Any objective look at Canada's track record would say that repeatedly over the last decade, Canada has seriously put in place measures to try to control imports of Chinese steel," the CBC quoted Miller as saying.
Indeed, in July 2025, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced measures to restrict and reduce foreign steel from entering the Canadian market amid fears from Canada's steel industry that it would be overwhelmed by an influx of Chinese steel newly subject to U.S. tariffs.
Canada's Department of Finance, in its statement, said Canada operates steel and aluminum import monitoring programs and requires importers to report "the country of melt and pour for steel imports" for transparency, among other measures.
The spokesperson also noted, accurately, that according to U.S. data, more than 95% of steel imported into the United States from Canada was melted and poured in either Canada or the United States.

England to extend head coach Borthwick's contract

England head coach Steve Borthwick will have his contract extended past the 2028 Six Nations in a bid to avoid uncertainty over his future before and during next year's Rugby World Cup.
As it did with Red Roses boss John Mitchell before the 2025 World Cup, the Rugby Football Union has moved to ensure Borthwick and his staff have some clarity over their positions going into the global showpiece.
According to RFU performance director Conor O'Shea, extending Borthwick's deal into the middle of 2028 will allow time to decide who leads the team in the longer-term.
"You don't want them looking for a job going into [a World Cup]," O'Shea explained.
"Everyone knows it will be judged on the World Cup, but you can't have a group of coaches going in with that uncertainty, especially when you look at the timing.
"So we will give that certainty, and that will give us time to look properly."
England '100% can win the World Cup'
Following a review into England's "horrendous" Six Nations earlier this year, Borthwick has been backed to lead the team through to the World Cup, with O'Shea adding he can't see a scenario where Borthwick isn't in charge in Australia.
In the July leg of the Nations Championship, England recovered from a bruising defeat by South Africa in Johannesburg to vanquish Fiji in Liverpool and edge out Argentina to finish the campaign with two wins from three.
However at this stage the RFU has stopped short of committing to Borthwick on a long-term basis, unlike Ireland, who have signed their head coach Andy Farrell up to 2031.
"I see in Steve someone who bleeds England, and wants England to succeed more than anything you can imagine," O'Shea said.
"This England team is unequivocally one of probably five teams who can win the World Cup next year. I believe this team can win a World Cup.
"Is the talent there? 100%," he added.
"If over this next 12 months this England team shows the best version of itself, I know it can beat anyone in the world."
Selection rules 'best for English rugby'
As was the case for a number of his predecessors, Borthwick is only able to select players based in the English Prem, meaning the likes of Toulouse flanker Jack Willis – one of the outstanding performers in the French Top 14 – is ineligible for his country.
Cap centurion Courtney Lawes, who has returned to English rugby with Sale after two seasons at Brive, believes the RFU should review the policy to ensure the best players are available.
But O'Shea is adamant the ruling is what works for English rugby as a whole, and has warned against the impact of loosening the policy.
"It is something done not just for England, but for English rugby," O'Shea said.
"As of now, if all the best players were picked by England and went abroad, and we had less of the top players in our league, the unintended consequence towards investment into that from some of our owners… why would you invest in the pathways if the best players are going to be taken away?
"I get it completely, the life experiences are great. But for the English game, it is absolutely the right thing."

9/11 unleashed two decades of war. Now Putin is exploiting the damage
The horror of the attacks 25 years ago and their aftermath has seen the Cold War replaced by endless conflict between competing cultures and religions, explains world affairs editor Sam Kiley
It’s unlikely that Osama bin Laden picked up the idea of a clash of civilizations from a Harvard professor’s essay in a 1993 edition of Foreign Affairs, but when Al Qaeda terrorists slammed two aircraft into New York’s Twin Towers and attacked the Pentagon eight minutes later - that’s what he got.
The conflicts between cultures and religions that would replace the Cold War, as Prof Samuel Huntingdon predicted, have defined the last two decades and will dominate the world for the rest of this century.
Ironically, this new chapter in history started as a war between east and west in the form of Islam vs the Christian world.
But now, the West is again under attack from a Cold War enemy that watched the US and its allies waste lakes of blood and trillions in treasure enfeebling themselves after 9/11.
In the immediate aftermath, cooler heads in Washington might have been able to more deliberately and surgically exact revenge for the murder of 2,977 people on that day when, live on television, the world watched in horror as the towers came down.
Amid an act of war that turned out to have been launched, not by a state, but a fanatical group of mostly Saudi extremists led by the scion of a billionaire family hiding in Afghanistan, President George W Bush reacted as Osama bin Laden would have hoped.
The pain and the outrage, the fear and the amazement that the heart of the US government had been the target of mass murder, were so visceral that the US president invoked article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s charter for the first, and so far, only time in history.
An attack on one Nato nation was met by almost all the others, plus additional allies, joining a war to wipe out al Qaeda and topple the Taliban, Afghanistan’s ruling deeply conservative Islamists.
The Taliban had no interest in global terror then. They have none today either. But they had given bin Laden a safe haven for his plot against America and were guilty by association at least, if not actual accomplices.
By the end of that year, the Taliban had been felled. Bin Laden had been seen fleeing the caves of Tora Bora close to the borders with Pakistan, and a new military doctrine was being used by America and its allies.
This allowed for the killing of members of terrorist organizations in pre-emptive attacks. They didn’t need to be ticking bombs; they just had to be part of a movement that made them.
The massive reaction of the US and its allies to 9/11 created a new world disorder. Pre-emptive strikes were launched in Pakistan and elsewhere. Many civilians died in extrajudicial executions under the new doctrine.
But al Qaeda groupies and Islamists around the world were led to believe that America - an abomination in the eyes of bin Laden - could be humiliated and humbled.
From the sophisticated madrassas of Pakistan - with a Deobandi and Wahhabi version of Islam which argued for a seventh century literal and xenophobic interpretation of Islam - to north London mosques and online brain washing forums, young men were tempted to flock to al Qaeda’s black flag.
Reporting from Tora Bora at the end of 2001, I watched “daisy cutter” thermobaric bombs turn the sky magenta and felt the whomp of American explosive power like a chest punch five miles from detonation. It looked then that the al Qaeda brand had been obliterated.
But when the US invaded Iraq along with UK under Tony Blair, the black al Qaeda flag became a magnet.
The US and UK had lied the west to war. First, they said that Iraq was developing a nuclear weapon and, second, that Saddam Hussein was part of al Qaeda’s global agenda. Saddam’s regime had no nuclear programme and a scant understanding of Middle Eastern politics would have revealed that as a bloody and secular dictator, he was always an enemy of Islamic radicalism.
International law had long been seen as imperfect and usually employed by the strong to punish the weak. But there was a sense that the West, with the United Nations headquartered in New York, had been key in establishing global mechanisms designed to avoid war.
That went out of the window in Iraq where there was no mandate for an international military intervention.
Instead, people around the world saw Iraqis getting shot at road blocks by occupying American troops, US companies hoovering up contacts in Iraq funded by Iraqi oil revenues, and a system of near impunity for occupying forces to kill and maim as they fought against “insurgents” there.
These insurgents were old Baathist thugs left over from Saddam’s regime. Shi’a militia backed by Iran - and al Qaeda.
The clash of civilizations was now in full swing, fulled by western hypocrisy as well as growing systems to radicalize and terrorize Muslims.
During my time in Falluja, Iraq, I was abducted along with three colleagues in the early stages of that clash and taken away to be murdered. We were chased the wrong way up a motorway, cut off by armed men in a saloon car and escorted to their vehicle. Taken into the desert we were forced to our knees and prepared to die.
We survived by a fluke but had al Qaeda been in action, as it soon was, we could have suffered the televised fate of other hostages and been slaughtered on camera - dressed in orange overalls of the kind that Muslim prisoners were being made to wear in American prisons - without trial.
The so-called Islamic State emerged as a hybrid of Baathist tactics and radical ideology, employing ultra-violence to terrify a vast area of northern Iraq and Syria into submission.
The west, other allies in the Arab world and the new Iraqi government fought back after Isis formed a “caliphate” and had become a magnet for thousands of youth who now flocked to its banners to join the mass murder gangs and fantasies of a new world run on fundamentalist principles.
By the end of 2017, Iraq’s Mosul, where the Isis had claimed its caliphate, and then Raqqa were recaptured by Syrians, Iraqis, Kurds and Special Forces teams from the West. Isis was over.
But these wars of choice in Iraq and Afghanistan that had been seen by many in the west - as the late Sir Alex Younger put it - as “away games of football” entrenched the truth that in the west the lives of dark skinned people, especially Muslims, were less valued in the clash of civilizations that bin Laden ignited.
Islamic rage may yet return - partly driven by the actions of Israel in Gaza and the inactions of Israel’s allies to stop the slaughter there.
But another civilization identified by Prof Huntingdon has been plotting and planning. Vladimir Putin stayed away from Middle East conflicts, except to back Bashar al Assad in Syria in 2017.
But enraged by the expansion of Western democracy into eastern Europe, where states - once vassals of Moscow - have embraced freedom and the European Union, Putin invaded Ukraine in 2022, convinced that “the West” was plotting to annihilate Russia’s soul.
He would have done so anyway, but it helped that Iraq had been invaded without UN sanction and on baseless whims too.
The clash of civilizations that he has joined lately has already cost the US dearly. Brown University’s Costs of War project estimates that the US spent $4.37 trillion on its wars in Iraq, Afghanistan and Syria.
Hundreds of thousands of human lives have also been squandered - leaving the west spiritually and politically impoverished, deeply indebted and unable to meet new defence needs, and therefore vulnerable.
Putin has bin Laden to thank for that.

What's going on with OpenAI and the Navier-Stokes controversy?
Artificial intelligence has solved a major mathematics problem, but credit for the accomplishment is murky.
OpenAI announced today that it has found a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the longest-standing puzzles in mathematics. It's a major accomplishment, but the news has been marred by a debate over whether the company acted based on unpublished research from other parties. Additionally, OpenAI has been accused of attempting to influence who will receive credit for the achievement in publication.
The Navier-Stokes problem
First, some background. The Millennium Prize Problems are a group of seven complex questions established by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. The organization is offering a reward of $1 million for solutions to each of these questions, all of which have stymied mathematicians for decades, if not centuries. Since the prize's creation, only one of the other problems from the collection had previously been solved.
The Navier-Stokes problem centers on fluid dynamics, the rules for analyzing the behavior of both liquids and gasses. The angle that had been posed to mathematicians, in extreme layperson terms, is whether there are any edge cases where the original set of Navier-Stokes equations lead to results that cannot happen in reality.
Having a solution to a second Millennium Prize Problem is a massive accomplishment when it comes to applying artificial intelligence and large language models to solving some of the most perplexing quandaries in mathematics. However, the use of tools made by rival AI businesses in developing those solutions has created friction in the field regarding who gets to claim responsibility for the work and how.
The allegations
Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, and Levent Alpöge, a researcher employed at Anthropic but working in a personal capacity, had been developing their own solution and made use of multiple different LLMs in their efforts, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI's Codex tool and its Astra frontier model. According to a statement by Buckmaster, OpenAI may have doubled down on its efforts regarding Navier-Stokes after learning that a team including rival Anthropic was close to a solution. He questioned whether OpenAI had leveraged the work he and his colleague had done with Codex to obtain its own breakthrough.
"I asked whether the model had been trained on, or had access to, our sessions in Codex, into which we had been putting all our drafts for the whole of this project. I was told the model did not look up user data. I asked again, about training, and I did not get an answer," the statement reads.
Buckmaster then said he spoke with Sebastien Bubeck, a mathematician and AI researcher at OpenAI, and another unnamed party and was offered two options for claiming credit for the work. One was to publish a partial development, with OpenAI to publish its Navier-Stokes solution the following day. The other was to write a solo paper that credited the use of an OpenAI LLM in the Navier-Stokes solution without the inclusion of Alpöge's name. Buckmaster said he declined both proposals.
Both Bubeck and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have posted their versions of events to social media in response, with Bubeck specifically refuting the claim that he asked for Alpöge's name to be removed from a paper. The announcement from OpenAI also stated that the company did not plan to claim the $1 million prize for its solution.

Ezekiel J. Emanuel and Abe Butler-Baker have been debating the proper place for AI in medicine with American Medical Association CEO John Whyte. Now, they are taking their discussion to STAT’s First Opinion. Read Whyte’s essay below and read Emanuel and Butler‘s essay here.
Would you want artificial intelligence to tell you that you have cancer?
Not help a physician identify the cancer. Not analyze the scan, synthesize your medical history, or recommend the treatment most likely to work.
Would you want AI, on its own, to tell you that you have cancer? Or guide you through what comes next?
These questions get at something missing from much of the debate about AI and medicine. As AI becomes more capable, we will have to decide not only which parts of medicine can be automated, but which parts we want to automate.
Those are not the same question.
I recently debated this issue with oncologist and bioethicist Ezekiel Emanuel, who has argued that AI will eventually perform many of the functions physicians perform today, and in some cases do them better.
He may well be right about many of those functions. AI can already interpret images, summarize medical records, suggest diagnoses, and answer health questions with a fluency that seemed impossible just a few years ago.
But there is a leap in logic from “AI can do many things physicians do” to “AI can replace physicians.” That leap rests on an imprecise view of what practicing medicine actually is.
I am optimistic about what augmented intelligence can do for medicine. I believe physicians should play a leading role in shaping and adopting these technologies. But I profoundly disagree with the conclusion that increasingly capable AI makes the physician expendable.
That conclusion reduces medicine to a collection of tasks: reading an X-ray, identifying a diagnosis, renewing a prescription, selecting a treatment. If AI can perform each task as well as, or better than, a physician, the logic goes, why do we need the physician?
Because medicine has never simply been the completion of tasks.
Medicine is recognizing when the diagnosis does not quite fit. It is understanding why the treatment supported by the evidence may not be right for the person sitting in front of you. It is helping a patient choose among imperfect options. It is delivering life-changing news. It is knowing when to push and when to listen. It is the art and the science of medicine.
Too much of the debate over AI in health care asks a deceptively simple question: Can AI outperform physicians?
Studies comparing AI and physicians on diagnostic questions, image interpretation, and other clinical tasks are important. We need rigorous benchmarks to understand where AI performs well and where it does not.
But passing a benchmark is not the same as practicing medicine.
Patients do not arrive as carefully constructed clinical vignettes. They describe symptoms imperfectly. Their medical records contain gaps and contradictions. The decisions they make are influenced by their preferences, fears, family circumstances, and tolerance for risk.
And medicine requires something benchmarks rarely measure: responsibility.
Physicians are licensed. They operate within professional and ethical standards. Their decisions can be scrutinized, challenged, and reviewed. Responsibility can ultimately be assigned.
As AI assumes more consequential roles in care, those questions become more important. Who is responsible when an autonomous system makes the wrong diagnosis? What happens when it confidently reassures a patient who needed immediate care? Who recognizes when an algorithm’s recommendation may be statistically sound but wrong for the person in front of it?
As AI advances, the companies that create it must be willing to bear the responsibility, and take on higher levels of liability, when decisions are wrong.
These are not arguments against AI. They are arguments against confusing technical capability with clinical responsibility.
AI tools and advanced digital devices are already changing medicine. Patients increasingly begin the medical encounter before they enter an exam room. They search symptoms, review laboratory results, and ask chatbots what a diagnosis might mean. Used well, these tools can help people understand complicated information and formulate better questions.
For physicians, the opportunities are even greater. AI can help gastroenterologists identify polyps they might otherwise miss. It can help radiologists detect cancers earlier. It can synthesize years of medical records and reduce administrative work that consumes time physicians would rather spend with patients.
Most exciting, AI could democratize access to medical expertise.
Consider cancer care. A patient’s options can still depend partly on whether they live near a leading academic medical center or hours away from one. Imagine instead that every person diagnosed with cancer could receive an AI-assisted second opinion incorporating the latest evidence, their complete clinical history, and the characteristics of their individual cancer — with a physician interpreting those recommendations and helping the patient decide what comes next.
That is not a lesser vision for AI because a physician remains involved. It is a more ambitious one.
The goal should not be to reproduce today’s health care system with fewer humans. It should be to use AI to give every physician and every patient capabilities that today are available only in the best-resourced settings.
There is another reason technological capability should not determine the future of medicine: Patients must have a say in what that future looks like.
Some moments in medicine require something other than information.
When a biopsy comes back positive, the patient’s first question may not be, “What does the evidence recommend?” It may be, “Am I going to die?”
When a patient must choose between a treatment that may extend life and one that may preserve quality of life, there may be no algorithmically correct answer. The decision depends on values, relationships, uncertainty, and an understanding of what matters most to that person.
AI can inform those conversations. It may make them better. But it should not conduct them on its own.
The role of physicians will change. It should. Some tasks physicians perform today will be automated. AI may allow doctors to spend less time searching for information, documenting encounters, and completing administrative work, and more time exercising judgment and caring for patients.
That would be progress. But we should not confuse the automation of medical tasks with the automation of medicine itself.
Someday, an AI system may be perfectly capable of telling you that you have cancer.
That doesn’t mean it should be the one sitting across from you when you hear the news.
John Whyte, M.D., M.P.H., is CEO of the American Medical Association.

Dozens feared trapped in collapsed building in Delhi

A residential building in the Indian capital Delhi has collapsed with dozens of students feared trapped inside.
Eyewitnesses told local media that as many as 50 people were inside the five-storey building in the Satya Niketan neighbourhood of south-west Delhi when it came down around 13:30 local time (08:00 GMT) on Sunday.
At least one person was killed and two others are in a critical condition, NDTV reports, citing local police. Six people were said to have been rescued so far.
There had been construction work going on in the basement of the building, Hostel Daze, which sits a short distance from the Delhi University campus.
Many of the students staying there were thought to be in their rooms at the time of the collapse as there were no lessons on Sunday.
A legislative assembly member said at the scene that some of the trapped students had been making calls from under the rubble.
Eyewitnesses told local media that another building beside the hostel had also collapsed.
Chief Minister of Delhi Rekha Gupta said an adjacent building had been evacuated "as a precautionary measure".
"Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped," she added.

British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years
- Published
A 78-year-old British widow has told the BBC she is struggling to eat or sleep as the Swedish government threatens to deport her over a late post-Brexit residence application.
Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse, moved to Sweden 22 years ago with her husband, who passed away from cancer three years ago.
This came after they were informed by the Swedish authorities that they should have made a formal application to stay in the country after Brexit.
Thomas has since had numerous applications and appeals rejected, and Tuesday marks the latest deadline for her to leave voluntarily.
"This is absolute hell," she said from her home in Sweden.
"I can't sleep, I can't eat. You get up in the morning, you don't know what's going to happen."
The Swedish migration minister told the BBC that the government will "examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected" by some consequences of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement.
When the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, British citizens stopped being EU citizens, which meant they could no longer stay in Sweden with right of residence status.
During a transitional period, British citizens could apply for residence status under the withdrawal agreement between the UK and the EU - which ended on 31 December 2021.
Thomas said she and her husband were unaware that they needed to submit an application and she was only informed of the rule once she attempted to re-enter the country in 2023.
After years of appeals, the Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, told her last month that her voluntary departure deadline was 8 September.
Her lawyers are arguing against the deportation, but she is still waiting to hear from the government.
Thomas said the possibility of having to leave her son, grandchildren, friends and husband's grave has become too much to bear.
"I'm tired, I really am tired and I'm not young anymore," she said.
"Where is the empathy? I've lived here for more than 20 years - I've got friends, I've got family."
According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025, 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. This is almost a third of more than 7,500 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU Member States over this time period.
The Migrationsverket said it could not comment on Thomas's case without her consent and did not respond to a question about how many British nationals are at risk of deportation.
However, it told the Guardian last week that 458 British citizens had been deported or forcibly removed since Brexit.
Last month, a family told the BBC how their father, who has dementia and vascular parkinsonism and is living in full-time care in Sweden, was also threatened with removal after more than two decades in the country.
Swedish minister for migration, Johan Forssell, told the BBC that the current framework was implemented by a previous government and that it "will therefore look closely at the situation and examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected".
He did not address Thomas's case directly but said "the government believes the rules should be applied generously".
"The UK is a very important partner for Sweden, and we want British citizens who live and work in Sweden to be able to remain here," he said.
"We are currently in dialogue with the relevant Swedish authorities to get a clearer picture of what measures may be possible," he added.
A spokesperson from the the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said: "We welcome the statement from the Swedish authorities that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so."

Audio-Technica's new wireless ATH-AL5NC completes its open-back headphone lineup
The new $279 wireless headphones offer more natural sound, but not noise isolation.
After introducing open-back versions of its wired headphones, Audio-Technica is doing the same for wireless. The $279 ATH-AL5NC Open-Back Wireless Headphones combine the more natural sound presentation of an open-back design with the convenience of a wireless Bluetooth connection, trading some noise isolation for a more comfortable fit.
The ATH-AL5NC features 53mm drivers and supports high-resolution 24-bit/96kHz wireless audio through LDAC, along with codecs like AAC and SBC. Multipoint Bluetooth pairing allows the headphones to stay connected to two Bluetooth devices at the same time, and Audio-Technica claims they'll offer up to 75 hours of continuous playback and the ability to give you an extra eight hours of listening from a 15-minute charge. Through the headphones' CONNECT app you can also tweak things like presets, codecs and EQ, and switch between discrete modes for low-latency gaming, noise reduction and sound leakage reduction.
The design of the new headphones has pros and cons. Using an open-back design means air can flow from outside the ATH-AL5NC's ear cups past its drivers to "reduce heat buildup," Audio-Technica says, while presenting any audio you play in a more natural way than closed-back headphones. The headphones are also supposed to have "minimal clamping pressure," which should make them more comfortable to wear. The drawback of all that open airflow is that the ATH-AL5NC will naturally leak more audio than other headphones and can't offer true noise cancellation to block outside noise, hence Audio-Technica's attempts to tweak things with its various software modes.
For true audiophiles (or anyone working from home) a little sound leakage won't be a major problem, and while Audio-Technica's open-back headphones come at a premium in comparison to something like the $150 HyperX Cloud Alpha Air, adding wireless Bluetooth is genuinely convenient. Audio-Technica's ATH-AL5NC Open-Back Wireless Headphones are available today for $279, and come with a 1.2m (3.9-foot) cable and a carrying pouch.
