On the intervening night of June 18 and 19, Jalil Akhtar, an elderly Muslim man, from West Bengal’s Bagroi village in Karandighi block of Uttar Dinajpur district, was woken up from sleep and picked up by Dalkhola police from his home, his family alleged. Other members of his household, sleeping in the same home, came to know of his arrest only the next morning.
The 66-year-old man, whose name appeared in both the 2002 and 2026 Special Intensive Revision (SIR) lists, was allegedly arrested on grounds of “being a Bangladeshi”, his family told Alt News. After spending nearly three months in various holding centres and judicial custody, when Akhtar was produced before additional chief judicial magistrate (ACJM) of Islampur court on Wednesday, September 2, the investigating officer of the case gave a written declaration that identity documents submitted by Akhtar were valid. However, Akhtar has not yet been granted bail, the court is expected to hear the matter next on September 10.
During his nearly three-month-long incarceration, Akhtar was kept in two holding centres, and then lodged in Islampur jail, until, his family claimed they were told he would be deported to Bangladesh. They further alleged that during the entire duration, police failed to prove that Akhtar’s citizenship and legal documents were fake, raising questions over why the arrest was made in the first place when his name appeared in the latest SIR list.
“My brother is an Indian, we have all the documents and he has never even seen the Bangladesh border. Yet, he was arrested, kept in holding centres and jailed on a mere suspicion of being a Bangladeshi, which the police could not even prove. Was he held for so long just because we are Muslims and live in a border district with significant Muslim population?” asked Motiur Rahaman, Akhtar’s cousin.
‘Picked up at Night without Family Being Informed’
According to his family and locals, Akhtar slept on a cot in front of his single-room home. His wife, Taufa Bibi, woke at dawn on June 19 to find him gone. She initially assumed that he might have gone to offer ‘Fazr Namaz’, but began to panic when she found his kurta hanging from the family closet.
Motiur was first to launch a hunt for his cousin, a landless villager who was entirely dependent on his two migrant worker sons. Describing the long fight in detail to Alt News, Motiur said he assembled a crew of fellow villagers and they scoured through the entire neighbourhood including forest areas through the day. They were eventually informed by a local that a police vehicle had entered the village the previous night.
Upon calling one of his sources at the recently established Bazargaon police camp, which falls under Dalkhola police station, Motiur learned that the police had picked up a man from his village the previous night, allegedly identifying him as an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant. The group then reached the police outpost, and found Akhtar sitting on the floor of the lock-up, bare bodied, as the police, Motiur claimed, did not even allow him to wear his kurta while nabbing him.
Motiur further alleged that, as per Akhtar’s recollection of the arrest to his family, the police held him at gunpoint, apparently to keep him silent while taking him into custody from the densely populated area.
The Family’s Fight To Prove His Citizenship
“In the police camp we tried to reason with the officer in charge that Jalil Akhtar’s name was not only in the 2026 SIR list, but was also in the 2002 list, so he should be released. The police retorted saying ‘don’t you people dare to threaten me, those days of threatning are over…now the government has changed,” claimed Motiur.
Another officer of the outpost reportedly told Motiur to give them some time to verify the documents and if everything came out clean, his cousin would be released. However, the same morning, Akhtar was moved to a holding centre in Nizampur near Chakulia.
To establish his Indian citizenship, Akhtar’s family began gathering every document they could find. According to his family, they obtained the 1995 voter list and the 2002 SIR list, both of which included Akhtar’s name. They also collected land deeds linking Akhtar to his father, Rousan Ali, as well as a residence certificate issued by the Bazragaon-2 panchayat, stating that Akhtar was a permanent resident of the panchayat area.
On July 9, they visited Dalkhola police station and submitted the documents for verification. Before that, they had also approached the district superintendent of police’s (SP) office. On both occasions, the police asked them to allow time for the documents to be verified and assured them that no harm would come to Akhtar if he was indeed an Indian citizen. According to his family, the police also said they were under “considerable pressure from higher-ups to identify and deport those deemed to be illegal Bangladeshi migrants”, and that they were only acting as per orders.
‘An Attempt To Send Him To Bangladesh’
However, as days went by, Akhtar remained under police custody and shifting between holding centres. Dulal Rajbanshi, organiser of the Votadhikar Surakkha Samanway Samity, an organisation formed to help those whose names were deleted in the 2026 SIR, helped Akhtar’s family. “We were able to prevent the police from sending Jalil Akhtar into Bangladesh twice. When they failed to send him into ‘no man’s land’, the police eventually filed a false FIR and produced him before the court,” Rajbanshi alleged.
According to Rajbanshi, Akhtar was moved to another holding centre near Phulbari border crossing near Siliguri, allegedly to send him to Bangladesh. The state police keeps the detainees at temporary holding centres, before handing them over to the BSF for deportation into Bangladesh, Rajbanshi claimed. He said that in Akhtar’s case, first the police handed him over to the BSF, who took him towards Phulbari to apparently deport him.
“We were informed by local sources that Akhtar was moved from the Nizampur holding centre and taken towards Phulbari on July 6. The next day, we reached Uttar Dinajpur district magistrate’s office in Raiganj, who asked us to immediately contact the SP in Islampur,” he said.
“We travelled a 110-kilometre distance from Raiganj to Islampur, where again, the SP said that he needs time to investigate, as there is “immense pressure from above to deport illegal Bangladeshis”. However, we were later told that Akhtar was brought back to the Chakulia holding centre. It was unclear what happened after this, and which border they took him to in order to attempt deportation the second time.”
However, acting on the SP’s direction, the group then met Dalkhola police station’s inspector-in-charge (IC) in the following days. “The IC asked us whether we could bring any relatives of Akhtar to the police station for verification. By that evening, we had brought even his 90-year-old aunts and all other relatives to the station. But the police did not meet them, instead, they collected the death certificate of one of Akhtar’s brothers,” Rajbanshi alleged.
According to Rajbanshi, the BSF often selects a favourable point along the border to ‘pushback’ alleged Bangladeshis, sometimes at gunpoint. “Currently, the Border Guard Bangladesh and Bangladeshi villagers are on high alert to prevent any pushback from India. As a result, many people are getting stranded in no man’s land, as neither country is willing to take them in. Akhtar’s family was wary of this exact fate,” he claimed.
According to Motiur, the IC also mentioned “immense pressure”, stating that the police were already “holding a list of 500 names whom they have to deport and 50 more were recently added”.
‘It Is Better If They Kill Me’
In the meantime, Akhtar’s family visited him at the detention centre. According to Motiur, Akhtar broke down completely. “My brother kept saying, what will I do if I am sent to Bangladesh? I don’t know anybody there. I have never been to that country. I can’t even beg there. It is better if they kill me than push me into Bangladesh,” Motiur said.
According to the family, a Border Security Force (BSF) team also visited their home to investigate the matter. “The BSF team came and spoke with us. They were infuriated by the state police’s actions — or lack of investigation — and told us that they would not deport an Indian citizen. At least the BSF came to the village to investigate. Nobody from the state police even cared to do that,” Motiur claimed.
On July 20, villagers organised a protest against Akhtar’s arrest in the nearby Rasakhowa Haat. However, before the programme could start, police intervened and dispersed them, they alleged. The next day, Rajbanshi alleged, the administration again attempted to send Akhtar into Bangladesh.
“On July 21, we received information that he had once again been moved from the Nizampur holding centre. We got the news around 2 pm and, by 4 pm, had organised a press conference at the Uttar Dinajpur Press Club in Raiganj. We shared information about the press conference across social media. We were worried that police might announce that he has gone missing. The next day, on July 22, police informed the family that they would produce Akhtar before the Islampur court,” claimed Rajbanshi.
Discrepancies between FIR and Police Submission
As per the FIR lodged against Akhtar by Dalkhola police, he was picked up from Nizampur around 1:05 am on June 20. Nizampur is also where, according to his family, he was subsequently held at a holding centre — the location is around 35 km from Akhtar’s home.
Motiur alleged that upon prodding the police on who lodged a complaint against Akhtar, police refused to reveal the name of the complainant. According to the FIR, Akhtar was detained at the Nizampur centre along with two other “illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators”. The FIR states that all three detainees are from “AndhaRahamatpur village of Thakurgaon district of Bangladesh”. It is claimed that this was revealed by Akhtar himself during interrogation.
The FIR further states that Akhtar crossed the Hili-Malda border and entered India around 24 years ago. However, the documents submitted by his family before the court show that his name appears in both the 1995 voter list and the 2002 SIR list. In both documents, his father’s name is the same. If the police account is accurate and Akhtar entered India only around 23-24 years ago, it would be impossible for his name to have appeared in the 1995 voter list, nearly three decades ago, and subsequently in the 2002 SIR list.
Alt News has seen the case diary submitted by police in court on August 5. It says Akhtar voted in 1982 elections as well, although it does not clarify which elections and where. The submission also mentions that during investigation, police had been told by locals that coming to Uttar Dinajpur in 1982, Akhtar worked as a rikshaw puller in Delhi and does not speak proper Bengali. These statements directly contradict the FIR claim that he entered India around 24 years ago and does not establish any link between Akhtar and Bangladesh.
According to the police’s submission, Akhtar was born in either 1959 or 1960 and first appears in official records in 1982. No records relating to him from before 1982 could be found, the police said. They also claim that he failed to establish a credible link with Raushan Ali, whom he identifies as his father, through land records or other documentary evidence.
However, Rajbanshi claimed that Akhtar was not required to produce his parents’ birth records to establish his Indian citizenship. “Under the Indian Citizenship Act, a person born before 1987 does not need to show the birth records of their parents to prove their Indian citizenship. The 2002 and 2026 SIR exercises were also meant to identify and remove illegal entries from the electoral rolls. Akhtar’s name appears in both lists. Yet he continues to be detained, merely to serve what appears to be the BJP’s political agenda,” he said.
The September 2 Hearing
As per legal records, the police postponed the bail hearing four times stating that they need more time to verify the documents. During the hearing on September 2, the additional chief judicial magistrate and the defence counsel asked the police to testify whether the documents provided by Akhtar were valid. The police ultimately confirmed the documents were legitimate.
According to Akhtar’s lawyer, Firoz Ahmed, the police deliberately avoided telling the court whether the former’s documents were genuine. “The ACJM pressed the investigating to state whether Akhtar’s documents are genuine before carrying on with the investigation. Even then, the IO remained silent,” he said.
Later, however, the police stated in a report submitted in the late afternoon that Akhtar’s voter ID and PAN card were genuine Indian documents, and that his records in the 1995 voter list and 2002 SIR list were also genuine. “They are awaiting an email response to verify the authenticity of his Aadhaar card, so they could not say anything about it,” Ahmed added.
“As his birthplace and his current residence are different, and fall under different police stations, the police are now harping on that, as if relocating to another place is a crime,” Ahmed alleged.
“The police had been given a target to identify and round up Bangladeshis, and they are targeting any vulnerable person they can find. Since Akhtar was born in another village, around four to five kilometres from ours, and is extremely poor and owns barely any land, it is easy for the administration to portray him as a Bangladeshi, citing a lack of evidence,” Motiur alleged.
Dalkhola Police’s Response
Alt News spoke to Sankha Chatterjee, IC of Dalkhola police station. Upon being asked whether Akhtar was arrested at gunpoint as alleged by his family, he said, “A lathi is enough for us to arrest a 66-year old. We don’t need a gun for it. As for the family’s allegation, tell them that we used a Bofors cannon to take Jalil Akhtar in custody.”
He further said that police had submitted their findings before the court. “Now it up to the court to decide whether Jalil Akhtar is an Indian or a Bangladeshi or a Pakistani or a Cuban citizen. According to our investigation, we couldn’t find any documents of Jalil Akhtar till the age of 21. All his documents are from the age of 22 till 66,” said the officer.
Alt News asked about the discrepancies between the FIR and the case diary submitted by the police before the court, however, the officer’s response did not clarify the aforementioned loopholes. Chatterjee simply said: “I don’t want to get political, but if you come to Uttar Dinajpur, I can show you people who have voter cards and other documents of both India and Bangladesh. It’s better not to get into how they were able to cross over to this side.”
Motiur, Rajbanshi and Akhtar’s family claim their efforts have helped prevent Akhtar’s ‘pushback’ till now. But the family’s ordeal is far from over. They still do not know when, or whether, he will be freed from detention and his name will be cleared in this ‘test of citizenship’. For the family, what began as an effort to establish his identity has become a prolonged battle against an administrative process that they believe is inherently designed against them.

Maharashtra Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Bill (CEB) has no provision to regulate treatment rates charged by private hospitals to patients, highlighted Jan Arogya Abhiyan (JAA), a coalition of NGOs and health professionals, on Friday while launching a statewide campaign appealing public to send objections to Joint Legislative Committee (JLC).
JLC is a committee comprising 21 MLAs, who have been reviewing the objections and suggestions on the Bill. The campaign also includes meetings with all 21 MLAs who are members of the JLC, demanding Health Minister convene a statewide consultation with organisations and networks working in the health sector to discuss the Bill.
JAA pointed out that the Bill must include fixed treatment charges for common procedures, different categories of beds, investigations, ICU services and doctors’ consultations; hospitals violating these rates should face penalties, a refund provision, a mandatory estimated bill by hospital detailing the treatment cost to be given to the patient, and the prescribed limit should not exceed estimated limit more than 5–10%.
The other suggested provision includes, ban withholding of patients or dead bodies over payment issues, establish accessible grievance-redressal system, establish an independent, well staffed regulatory authority, and ensure participation of all stakeholders in the State Council.
CEB was introduced in state Assembly on July 3, advocating compulsory registration of hospitals, clinics, and diagnostic centres transparency in treatment prices, and no deposit mandate for emergency cases. The new bill replaces the 77-years-old Maharashtra Nursing Homes Registration Act, 1949.
According to Arogya Abhiyan representatives, the analysis of hospital data from five major private hospitals in Mumbai, Pune and Nagpur shows that the average treatment charges faced by patients in these hospitals range from ₹24,000 to ₹62,000 per day. “This means just one day’s treatment in a large private hospital can cost as much as the average monthly per-capita income of a person in state,” said Abhay Shukla, the public health expert.
The latest NSS 80th Round data for Maharashtra shows as many as 77% of all hospitalisations in Maharashtra take place in private hospitals, highest among all states in India, average out-of-pocket expenditure on hospitalisation is ₹40,500, and on average rural hospitalisation costs have increased by 87%. 40 lakh people in Maharashtra are estimated to be pushed into poverty because of healthcare expenses.
Jan Arogya Abhiyan appealed to the Joint Legislative Committee to substantially strengthen this Bill in public interest as Section 11-Q of the Maharashtra Nursing Home Registration Act Rules, 2021 states that treatments rates should not exceed rates determined by the government.

A senior Anthropic safety researcher has said there is more than a 10 percent chance artificial intelligence “could kill all humans” by the end of the decade, just hours after a colleague resigned over fears the AI lab and its rivals are carelessly racing to build “superhuman systems” they cannot control.
Worried Anthropic researchers warn that AI ‘could kill all humans’
A departing researcher says AI companies are ‘gambling with our lives’ by racing to develop self-improving AI.
In a post on X announcing his departure, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who has trained AI systems at Anthropic, said he had quit the company over its lax approach to safety. Coxon, who previously trained systems for OpenAI, accused the two AI companies of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” even though “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Industry insiders have long expressed concerns about the potential dangers of self-improving AI systems, which they warn could spiral out of human control in a runaway loop often described as recursive self-improvement. While not yet realized, companies are actively pursuing this goal and much of today’s AI code is written with the help of AI.
In a direct response, Evan Hubinger, who leads one of Anthropic’s AI safety teams, said he worries about self-improving AI, adding that it “is happening faster than we thought.” He also agreed with Coxon’s characterization. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” he said, personally estimating the chances to be greater than one in 10 “within the next decade.”
Despite this, Hubinger said Anthropic does “not yet have a plan” for ensuring advanced AI remains safe and aligned with human values and “are not clearly on track to” develop one either. Coxon says the companies are “locked in a race” to develop advanced systems first so are pushing ahead “despite the risk.”
Coxon’s departure marks one of the most high-profile examples of an employee leaving Anthropic, a company founded by former OpenAI members following concerns over safety at the company. In recent years, multiple researchers have cited safety concerns as motivating their decision to leave OpenAI.
The exchange illustrates mounting concerns within the industry about the dangers of increasingly sophisticated AI models and the speed at which systems are being developed, particularly as the companies prepare for anticipated IPOs. It also comes as the companies manage the fallout from numerous rogue agent incidents and high-profile safety warnings about the monitorability of frontier models.

US strikes Iranian oil tankers as Tehran targets American base in Jordan
- Published
US forces struck five Iranian tankers on Tuesday, sinking one, in response to Tehran twice targeting an American warship, US Central Command (Centcom) said.
Four Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) were targeted, as well as another near Kharg Island, a major oil terminal off Iran's coast, Centcom added.
Tehran responded by launching missiles at a US base in Jordan - most of which were shot down - and said it attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tit-for-tat strikes between the two countries have escalated in the past week, more than six months after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February.
Oil prices rose in Asia trading. Benchmark Brent crude was up by 1.5% at $99.35 (£73.35) a barrel, while US-traded oil was 1.3% higher at $94.23.
Jordan said it had shot down 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, while two of them fell in unpopulated areas, an official spokesperson for the Jordanian Armed Forces said.
After warning of further retaliatory strikes, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they had attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers and 10 "non-compliant vessels" trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported.
The latest round of escalation comes after Iran targeted a US warship with ballistic missiles, which Centcom said were "successfully evaded". It added that no American troops were harmed during the attacks.
In response, the US said that the five Iranian oil tankers it targeted were "part of a multi-billion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies".
One of the ships it had struck, the M/T Riesco, sunk in the Gulf of Oman, Centcom later said, posting a video on X of the damaged vessel.
Kharg Island - where one Iranian tanker was attacked in the latest round of US strikes - hosts Iran's main terminal for exporting oil.
Some 90% of the country's crude oil passes through the island in the Gulf, transported through pipes from the mainland.
Pressure on oil prices has been exacerbated by wider regional instability.
Also on Tuesday, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement attacked energy facilities and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 people, according to Saudi authorities.
The drone and missile attack caused fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry said.
When asked by reporters about the latest tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the situation was "pretty straightforward".
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And, for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters during a trip in Colombia.
The US strikes on Tuesday came hours after Iran's navy claimed it had seized an uncrewed US submarine in the Strait of Hormuz.
US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, said that the "underwater drone operated by US forces malfunctioned more than a day ago" and was used to survey regional waters "in support of ongoing operations".
The defective drone was "an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment", he said, adding that US operations in regional waters were ongoing.

Paul Adams: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades
- Published
Israel's furious response to the British government's decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank testifies to just how important this moment is.
Britain took the brunt of Israel's anger, but the fact that 12 countries chose to move together clearly sharpened the sense of outrage.
Officials in London always knew that such a dramatic shift in policy towards Israel-Palestine was going to elicit a hostile response, but seemed taken aback by the speed and ferocity of Israel's reaction.
The closure of the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem, which serves the West Bank and deals directly with the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, and the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre, the body set up last year to co-ordinate stabilisation and relief efforts in the Gaza Strip, are very hostile moves.
They tell you that Israel is deeply troubled by Tuesday's action by the UK and 11 other countries, which include France, Spain and Canada.
Products manufactured in settlements may not represent a significant proportion of Israel's exports, but the political symbolism of singling these out for special treatment is powerful.
For decades, the British and other governments have regarded settlements in occupied Palestinian territory as illegal but stopped short of banning products grown or manufactured there.
Now, having announced that Britain agrees with the 2024 International Court of Justice ruling that the occupation as a whole - including Israel's military presence - is unlawful, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says the government's economic relationships must reflect that.
Hence the ban, not just on products but also on companies that provide construction, infrastructure or finance to settlements. The measures, which also include restrictions on arms sales that "materially contribute to the occupation", go further than many expected.
And it's not just the actions - it's the language of the foreign secretary's heartfelt, sometimes deeply personal statement that is so striking.
As a "proud British Jew... unwavering in my support for the state of Israel," Miliband spoke more directly and starkly than practically any of his predecessors.
That a British foreign secretary should say that "settler terrorism is rampant" and was responsible for the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians in parts of the West Bank, while the Israeli government "turned a blind eye to this" is truly remarkable.
Miliband calls this a "reset" in British policy. At times today, it felt like a radical rethink, and it leaves British-Israeli relations at their lowest ebb for decades.
Yes, the heated, febrile atmosphere that invariably accompanies an impending Israeli election may have contributed to Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar's brutal response, but most Israelis will have shared his sense of outrage.
Many Israelis find the violent, messianic ideology of some settlers deeply problematic. Some see them as a national embarrassment.
But that's not the same as saying they agree that settlements, built on land captured during the 1967 Six Day War, are illegal.
Most would disagree violently with the former prime minister, Ehud Olmert, who last year accused his successor Benjamin Netanyahu of turning Israel into an international pariah.
But they can feel the walls of international opprobrium closing in - from protests at Eurovision or sporting events, to international arrest warrants being issued against their leaders and now to bans on settlement products - and that makes them anxious and defensive.
For the Palestinians, on the other hand, this feels like progress.
The Palestinian foreign ministry commended the countries adopting sanctions but called for "urgent, concrete measures" to stop Israel's "illegal settlement enterprise".
In London, the Palestinian ambassador Dr Husam Zomlot called the government's decision "a turning point in the UK-Palestine relationship".
Britain's "courageous steps", he said, would help pave the way for the independence of the State of Palestine on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
But Zomlot knows that the reality of Israel's 59-year occupation has not ended, or even substantially changed.
The prospects for a viable Palestinian state remain vanishingly small, and there's little immediate sign that concerted action by 12 countries will reverse Israel's seemingly inexorable takeover of the West Bank.
Only the United States has that kind of influence, should it choose to wield it.
In 1991, President George HW Bush and his steely Secretary of State James Baker threatened to withhold $10bn (£7.4bn) in loan guarantees from the government of Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, when the famously tough Shamir refused to promise that it wouldn't be used to finance settlement activity in the occupied territories.
But Donald Trump has so far shown no desire to curb Benjamin Netanyahu's settlement plans.
Some parts of Trump's MAGA movement have turned against Israel in recent years, but the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, is a fervent Christian Zionist who shares Israel's view that the West Bank was promised to the Jews by God.
So Tuesday's action by the UK and its partners pits them not just against Israel but also against Israel's backer-in-chief in Washington.

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

Delhi Court dismisses YouTuber Ajeet Bharti’s anticipatory bail plea in caste remarks case
Bharti has been accused of publicly issuing statements which were casteist, derogatory and humiliating towards a member of the Scheduled Caste community.
A Delhi court has dismissed the anticipatory bail plea of social media influencer and YouTuber Ajeet Bharti in a case concerning alleged caste-related remarks, observing that the ingredients of an offence under Section 3(1)(r) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 were prima facie disclosed from the material placed on record.
The court held that, in view of the prima facie case under the SC/ST Act, the statutory bar under Section 18 of the Act applied and precluded the grant of anticipatory bail to the applicant.
“For the foregoing reasons, this Court finds that the ingredients of an offence under Section 3(1)(r) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 are prima facie disclosed on the material on record, and that the bar under Section 18 of the Act, 1989 accordingly precludes the grant of anticipatory bail to the applicant,” the court observed.
Additional Sessions Judge Saurabh Partap Singh Laler of Patiala House Courts passed the order on September 7 while dismissing Bharti’s application for anticipatory bail in connection with an FIR registered at North Avenue police station.
The case arises from allegations concerning statements made during a programme on social media. According to the FIR, the alleged incident took place on social media through the applicant’s verified account on X and a programme published on YouTube.
The complainant alleged that certain statements made during the programme were casteist, derogatory and humiliating towards a member of the Scheduled Caste community.
Bharti had sought anticipatory bail, arguing that no offence under the SC/ST Act was made out from the allegations. It was submitted that the statements in question needed to be considered in their complete context and that the complainant was not personally present when the alleged remarks were made.
The applicant had also argued that custodial interrogation was not required as the material relied upon in the case was already available in the public domain and there was no question of its recovery or discovery.
The State and counsel appearing for the complainant opposed the anticipatory bail application.
The court examined the FIR, the transcript and other material placed before it, along with the legal requirements for attracting Section 3(1)(r) of the SC/ST Act.
After considering the rival submissions and material on record, the court concluded that the ingredients of the alleged offence were prima facie disclosed and that the bar under Section 18 of the SC/ST Act was applicable.
The court accordingly dismissed the anticipatory bail application.
At the same time, the court clarified that the observations made in the order were confined to deciding the present bail application and should not be construed as an expression of opinion on the merits of the case.
It further clarified that the trial court would not be influenced by any observation made in the order.
The court also said that nothing contained in the order would prevent the applicant from renewing his prayer for relief or seeking any other remedy available under law if circumstances change.

In Summary
- As concerns around smart glasses and privacy grow, Meta has ensured that users cannot use the cameras on its smart glasses if they cover or tamper with the LED that lights up during recording.
- While Meta’s move is a step in the right direction, it still does not go far enough to address the privacy issues posed by smart glasses.
- Smart glasses brands need to do more to prevent misuse. This includes informing and educating not just users, but also the public, who could unknowingly end up in footage shot on these devices.
Smart glasses have existed for a while but have attained a whole new dimension of popularity since Meta invested in them. For those of you who might not be aware (welcome to high-tech planet, folks), smart glasses look like regular glasses but come with a number of tech add-ons, such as displays, speakers, and most notably, cameras. These smart glasses can take photos, record videos, handle phone calls, play music, let you speak to an AI assistant, figure out your way around town, get recommendations, and more.
Table of Contents
Smart glasses? Pervert glasses, more like!
Sound uber cool, cutting-edge and futuristic, don’t they? Unfortunately, this tech rose comes with a stack of thorns that would make a cactus turn even more green with envy. While the tech world and content creators may be going gaga over all these smart glasses can do, more and more people are beginning to refer to them as “pervert glasses.” There is a sound reason for this – these glasses are increasingly being used to record people (often women) without their consent and knowledge, resulting in a massive breach of a person’s privacy. There have been a number of incidents in which people have been recorded without their knowledge and the footage shared in public or private groups, causing severe trauma to those who appeared unknowingly in the footage.
What’s worse, the onus of figuring out that they are being recorded fell on the person being recorded. Being vigilant, actively looking for signs of someone wearing smart glasses, and catching up on tech cues were all part of the package – we also did a story on ways one could find out if they are being recorded as smart glasses moved from being content creators to destroyers of privacy. As incidents of “secret recordings” through these glasses increase, pressure has finally started building on the brands making these devices to make them safer not just for their users, but also for those in their vicinity.
Meta finally moves, but is it enough?
Recently, Meta finally fixed a flaw that was making it easier for users to covertly record others. In a post made on Threads (https://www.threads.com/@ahimel/post/DcjTatTGyn-), Alex Himel, Vice President of Wearables and Vice President of Augmented Reality at Meta, said that the camera on the glasses would stop working if the LED on the glasses was covered.
He was referring to a small LED indicator on the glasses that lights up when the glasses are recording. While the cameras on the glasses would not allow users to record if the LED was covered, many users found ways around this. One method was as simple as covering the LED light after starting to record the video. Following Himel’s announcement, an update will ensure that if the LED is covered at any stage (before or after starting a video recording), the glasses will automatically stop recording the video or taking photos. What’s more, if users tamper with the LED light and destroy or disable it, the glasses will now disable the camera feature permanently.
While this is definitely a step in the right direction, it does not really solve the biggest issue around these glasses. We have seen Meta’s glasses in public, and it is very difficult to spot when they are recording, especially in daylight or if the person is some distance away. The LED light is bright, but can easily be missed if one is not looking for it. What’s more, one can place a hand in front of it to stop others from seeing it, without actually covering it. We really think more needs to be done to safeguard the privacy of users in the vicinity of these devices. Brands need to come up with stronger measures that can help people spot those who may be wearing smart glasses and steer clear of their line of vision, if they so wish.
Making smart glasses safer: five more things brands can do
Given how limited the LED indicator can be, here are five measures that tech brands can take to make smart glasses safer for those in front of them:
Just make them look different…VERY different
One of the reasons why it is extremely difficult to find out if a person is wearing smart glasses is because they look exactly like usual glasses. Clear, tinted, or even running smart glasses all come with designs/frames that make them look like “normal” glasses. This makes them difficult to spot and enables users to record footage without being noticed.
We think that, given the privacy nightmares they can potentially pose, smart glasses need to look fundamentally different from everyday glasses. Visible badging, colors, even frame size or design should make them easy to spot. Who knows, this might even catch on as a style statement, but at least it will alert those in the vicinity that the person is walking around with a camera literally on their eyes!
Better, brighter (and maybe even more) LED lights
An LED light blinking while recording or taking photos is currently the only way to find out if someone is recording video or taking photographs from their smart glasses. As we have said before, a single light can be missed or even discreetly covered. The solution? Brands could perhaps use multiple LEDs of different colors, and which are of larger size, to pretty much advertise that a smart glasses’ camera is in use. Something like Nothing’s Glyph UI would be very handy!
Pump up the volume
Smart glasses should also give clear audio signals when their cameras are functioning. It should not be possible to take photographs without a loud camera shutter sound, and adding low but constant beep sounds when video is being recorded would also alert people to the presence of a camera in their vicinity.
Mandatory identifying apps
There are already apps like Zuckoff in the market that notify users if they are around someone wearing smart glasses. But these are unofficial and a little hit and miss. We think it would be wonderful if smart glass manufacturers took the initiative to come up with an app that can alert people in a small radius (say, 10 meters if based on Bluetooth), letting them know that they are in the presence of someone wearing smart glasses. Yes, it does violate the privacy of the person wearing smart glasses, as it is likely to make people in their vicinity notice them, but then that’s the price one pays for wearing such a device.
Better marketing and awareness
Brands have been pouring sackfuls of money into normalizing and promoting smart glasses. It would be great if they could allocate some of these funds to also highlight the dangers they can pose, and how they can be misused. Some might think this is counterproductive, but we feel this is the socially responsible thing to do – to make people aware that the device has its dark side too. And it is best that the brands do it themselves before they are forced to do it by Governments around the world.
The Government needs to step in as well. While new tech does make lives easier, there are always people who can find ways to misuse it. It happened with the Internet, it happened with smartphones, it is happening with AI, and it is happening with smart glasses too. To make sure that technology is not misused, there need to be strict privacy laws that are implemented effectively and come with stringent punishments. Perhaps statutory warnings on devices, advising consumers not to misuse them, might be an option worth considering. People need to realize that with great tech comes great responsibility.
Smart glasses need a Meta-morphosis, pun intended. They do not need to blend in, but to stand out and make people realize that they are present in a room. People need to know that they could be on camera. And the onus for this lies not just on those doing the recording, but on the brands who facilitate this.

The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) on Wednesday (September 9, 2026) began conducting raids on the residences and other premises linked to Karnataka Public Works Department Minister Satish Jarkiholi and his daughter Priyanka Jarkiholi, who is a Congress MP from Chikkodi Lok Sabha constituency.
The ED has said they have registered a case against Satish Jarkiholi.
The raids are on at the residences of the Jarkiholis in Bengaluru, Belagavi and Gokak, apart from other locations. A total of 18 locations, including residences of his family members, associates and businesses linked to the Jarkiholi family, are also being searched.

Manjunath, the brother-in-law of Mr. Jarkiholi — who was raided by the ED in June this year in relation to a money laundering case pertaining to alleged corruption in the Excise Department — is also being searched on Wednesday (September 9, 2026).

Case against Satish Jarkiholi

Here's a novel idea for countering the painful side effects of chemotherapy: beforehand, take the hallucinogenic drug found in magic mushrooms.
The study published Thursday in the journal Science involved tests on rats and certain human tissues as researchers looked at using psilocybin to fight a condition called peripheral neuropathy, which affects millions of people around the world.
It is a nerve ailment that hits about three quarters of all people who undergo chemo and commonly causes numbness and tingling, Patrick Dougherty, a co-author of the study, said in a call with reporters.
But a third of that group will develop non-stop, burning pain, said Dougherty, a pain treatment specialist at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.
The symptoms can lead to trouble walking and other debilitating complications that can last after a person finishes chemotherapy, and even remain with them for life.
And it is not just a quality-of-life issue. This complication also affects a cancer patient's chances of survival because sometimes the side effects are so bad they force doctors to cut back on chemo or stop it altogether.
Protecting nerves
It was almost by accident that these researchers found that psilocybin can help cancer patients.
The team was initially studying how the disease manages to hijack nerve cells in order to grow.
And the researchers were surprised to see the mushroom ingredient -- it was being used to study a brain pathway regeneration concept called neuroplasticity -- actually prevented the emergence of peripheral neuropathy.
Later experiments highlighted psilocybin's role in protecting nerve cells and stimulating inside them the transport of mitochondria, often referred to as a cell's powerhouse.
This is key because chemo destroys the microscopic railroads that allow mitochondria to send energy all the way to the tips of people's hands and feet, killing off nerve endings there.
Psilocybin also seems to act on the brain, preserving electrical activity that chemotherapy thwarts.
In rodents, taking two doses of psilocybin before chemo was enough to prevent the appearance of painful hypersensitivity during as many as six rounds of treatment. And it did this without affecting the animal's immune system or hindering the cancer-fighting action.
Careful with self-medicating
"This is a highly promising finding," said Kristy Townsend, a professor of neurobiology at The Ohio State University who was not involved in the study.
And psilocybin's nerve-protecting quality does not seem to be linked to its hallucinogenic effects because a non-hallucinogenic analogue had the same effect in a lab test, she added.
Before the treatment can be made standard for people, testing will be needed to see if it is safe and effective, said Townsend.
This will be a long, slow process though it should be eased by a boom in medical research on psychedelic substances and a Trump administration executive order in April to speed up research and regulatory reviews, these scientists say.
The MD Anderson Cancer Center plans to launch clinical tests with psilocybin on cancer patients later this year.
Meanwhile it is important for cancer patients to avoid using magic mushrooms on their own as treatment, the researchers warned.
Psilocybin is legal in a few U.S. states.
The drug has an "amplifier" effect and cancer patients who take it without supervision could feel more stressed and anxious than they already are because of their cancer diagnosis, said Gregory Jones, a psychiatrist who took part in the study released Thursday.
"If you put somebody in adversity under these psychedelic substances, you can get much worse," Jones said.

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

Leading chipmakers Samsung Electronics and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. announced plans to adopt ASML’s latest chipmaking machines in the next several years—and they also joined Intel in agreeing to a crucial technology change that could boost chip production on the new machines by 40 percent.
This signifies the semiconductor industry’s broader embrace of high NA EUV photolithography technology that can cost up to $400 million per machine and is only provided by the Dutch technology company ASML, Bloomberg reports. The technology would allow chip designers to implement even smaller features in potentially more powerful and efficient next-generation chips produced for AI data centers and consumer electronics such as smartphones, tablets, and laptops.
ASML’s EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machines enable chipmakers to use powerful laser light to imprint patterns in silicon wafers, layer by layer, and gradually form the computer circuitry that makes silicon chips work. Compared to older deep ultraviolet lithography, EUV technology harnesses a more powerful source of light with a shorter wavelength to create even smaller features on silicon wafers.
This has necessitated development of an incredibly complex system of lasers that is continually zapping molten tin into plasma with temperatures around 200,000° C, along with mirrors collecting light from the plasma and redirecting it into a “bus-size” lithography tool for projecting the intricate circuitry patterns onto the silicon wafers, ASML researchers wrote for IEEE Spectrum. ASML’s newest high-numerical-aperture (high NA) EUV machines use bigger mirrors and an improved optical system to more precisely collect and focus light.
South Korea’s Samsung plans to use ASML’s high NA EUV machines in producing memory chips by 2028. Meanwhile, Taiwan’s TSMC aims to use the technology for manufacturing the most advanced chips for its customers—including companies like AMD, Apple, Nvidia, and Qualcomm—starting in 2030.

South Park isn't holding back any punches — it just took a dig at Apple and Google.
The satirical comedy show shared an announcement from its creators, Trey Parker and Matt Stone, on Instagram on Tuesday, ahead of the release of its 29th season on September 16.
"Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA," the creators wrote in the statement.
The post was accompanied by a picture of the South Park logo, with a license plate spelling out "AMERICA" pinned over the word "Park." A glowing US flag was added in the corner for extra flourish.
Parker and Stone's reference to Apple and Google was a barely veiled mockery of the companies for changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America on their map platforms.
On August 27, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename the water body that straddles the US and Canadian border. The order instructed the US government to change the name of the lake in federal maps, contracts, and documents. It came amid rising trade tensions between the two neighbors.
Days after Trump's order, Google said it had updated Google Maps such that US users would see "Lake America," Canadian users would see "Lake Ontario," and users outside these two countries would see "Lake Ontario (Lake America)."
The tech giant said it updates Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which in the US is the US Geographic Names Information System. It made similar changes last year with the Gulf of Mexico, which Trump renamed the Gulf of America.
Apple Maps followed suit the week after, renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America for US users.
South Park, which debuted on Comedy Central in 1997, is a satirical animated comedy about four elementary school kids living in the fictional town of South Park, Colorado. Over its nearly three-decade run, it has a history of trolling the bigwigs of politics, tech, and media, including Trump, CBS, and Tim Cook.
In their Instagram statement, Parker and Stone also took a quick swipe at South Park's parent company, Paramount Skydance, which was created after David Ellison of Skydance Media bought out Paramount in 2025.
"We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount — a Skydance Capitulation," they wrote.

Srinagar, Sep 09: Renowned Bollywood actor and filmmaker Akbar Khan has hailed the first-ever film festival in Srinagar, saying the event has the potential to grow into an international cultural landmark and eventually compete with the Cannes Film Festival.
Addressing a press conference in Srinagar, Khan congratulated Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah and the organisers for what he described as a “spectacular opening festival”.
“The show was mesmerising, soulful and captured the rhythm and the purpose of this first-ever film festival in Srinagar,” Khan said, praising the musical performances at the opening ceremony.
He particularly recalled the performances of Dr Janas-e-R Akhtar, Rani and Falak, saying they “captured the mood of the festival” and “the heart of the beginning of such a beautiful initiative”.
Khan also praised Chief Minister Omar Abdullah's speech at the inaugural event, describing it as “very heart-rendering”.
“He was so prolific, recollecting the nostalgia of the Indian film industry, the Bollywood film industry, capturing chapter by chapter, moment by moment, how the people of Jammu and Kashmir love the units and the film stars and the directors and the producers who come and make the films here,” he said.
Recalling Bollywood's long association with Kashmir, Khan referred to films that helped establish the Valley as one of Indian cinema's most evocative locations.
He specifically mentioned Junglee, saying the famous “Yahoo” call by Shammi Kapoor
“had become a kind of a call of the Valley for every filmmaker to come and shoot”.
Khan said the festival had been organised in a location uniquely suited to bringing filmmakers and cultures together.
“I would say that there could not have been a better place than Srinagar to be the chosen city for such a grand first-ever film festival,” he said.
He predicted that the event would rapidly acquire an international profile.
“I feel from year to year this festival will grow from strength to strength and very soon would be in competition with the Cannes Film Festival and maybe even get better,” Khan said.
He argued that Kashmir's landscape itself could become one of the festival's greatest attractions.
“Because Cannes does not offer such an environment. Such a beautiful landscape,” he said. “It becomes a source of all filmmakers when they visit such a place.”
According to Khan, filmmakers attending the festival would not merely watch films from different countries but would also be inspired by Kashmir itself.
“Besides watching films of each other countries and different great directors, they also get inspired by the soul of Kashmir,” he said.
‘Cinema is the most powerful medium’
Khan placed particular emphasis on cinema's ability to build bridges across communities and countries.
“I would like to mention that cinema is the most powerful medium that makes bridges between nations and civilisations,” he said.
“It carries across borders, stories, civilisations, culture, people from different parts of the world who interact and meet and bring out, above all, their souls to understand each other.”
He said film festivals should therefore be judged primarily on artistic and cinematic merit.
“The greatest part of a film festival is that it should be judged on merits,” Khan said.
“Every film that is being chosen should be judged on merits, on its cinematic excellence, free of prejudice, free from the changing winds of ideology.”
He said filmmakers, actors, producers and singers should be allowed to present their artistic work without ideological interference.
“Actors, directors, producers, singers come on to a platform and present their artistic cinema, music, art, culture,” he said.
Khan also spoke at length about the responsibility of filmmakers when dealing with India's history and communal relations.
“I am very vocal. I respect every filmmaker. Every filmmaker has the right to present his film, his ideas, but never distort history. Never distort history to serve a purpose of creating disturbance, hatred [against] one another,” he said.
He added: “Cinema which spreads hatred should be discouraged in every nook and corner of the world, especially when it is designed for a specific propaganda.”
Khan said filmmakers could portray historical figures as heroes or villains, but should not manipulate history for a predetermined narrative.
“There are people who make films on villains and heroes and give the correct perspective as it is without dabbling it, without the historians and filmmakers diverting [it],” he said.
‘Kashmir has a very distinctive identity’
Khan also spoke about Kashmir's cultural identity, describing it as deeply rooted in Sufi traditions and communal coexistence.
“Jammu Kashmir is a very, very beautiful concept and identity. Kashmir has a very distinctive identity,” he said.
“Like every state has its lovely identity in different ways. But Kashmir has the Sufism involvement where people of all caste and creed are one.”
Describing Kashmir as “a secular centre which is mixed with warmth, love, affection”, Khan referred to Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs living together through its history.
He said India's civilisational diversity should be preserved and reflected responsibly through cinema.
“India is one of the greatest countries, a 5,000-year-old civilisation,” he said, before invoking the historical reigns of Ashoka and Akbar.
Khan recalled his own work on historical television productions, including The Sword of Tipu Sultan and Akbar the Great, saying his intention had always been nation-building.
“I first directed the first 22 episodes of The Sword of Tipu Sultan when my brother was struck by an unfortunate hand of destiny,” he said, adding that he later made Akbar the Great.
“At that time, Sulh-e-Kul was the religion of Emperor Akbar, where every religion comes under one umbrella. Peace for all, submission to all,” Khan said.
“I made that serial Akbar the Great again for nation-building. It brought harmony amongst the Hindus, the Muslims.”
Plans to bring Taj Mahal to Kashmir
Khan also announced plans to bring his film Taj Mahal: An Eternal Love Story to Kashmir for a premiere.
“My film Taj Mahal: An Eternal Love Story, inshallah, I will bring it to Kashmir to have a premiere of the film shortly and release it all over India again,” he said.
He said the film had already begun its international journey and recalled its screening in Malaysia.
“My film Taj Mahal has already started to take its first international journey on 6th February, 2006, where the Prime Minister of Malaysia had watched the film and he wrote a review, the same with the Minister of Culture,” Khan said.
He described the Taj Mahal as a symbol of love and said he wanted that message to reach audiences across the world.
“I want that this symbol of love, Taj Mahal, should sink into the minds and heart and soul of the people of the world,” he said. “It is the greatest message and Taj Mahal is one of our greatest monuments of pride before all the country.”
Khan concluded by thanking the organisers and praising Omar Abdullah and National Conference leader Farooq Abdullah for what he described as their commitment to an inclusive society.
“I have enjoyed every moment of my stay here with the warm hospitality of every officer, bureaucrat,” he said.
He described Farooq Abdullah as “one of the tallest leaders of a country” who believes in “the inclusive society, the love and harmony of a Brahman, of a Muslim, of a Christian, and a Jain”.
Khan said the presence of both father and son in Jammu and Kashmir's political leadership offered hope for the future.
“It is an amazing combination of a father and son and I am sure there will be great amount of peace, harmony, success and the people of Jammu Kashmir will soon be seeing a golden period,” he said.

The National Medical Commission’s plan to create a National Medical Register (NMR), is running into rough weather again as doctors are questioning why medical practitioners are being made to pay a fee and register again for entry into the NMR when their database is already available with respective State Medical Councils.
The question assumes significance as the Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB) of the National Medical Commission (NMC) is moving to amend the Registration of Medical Practitioners and Licence to Practice Medicine Regulations, 2026.
The NMR is envisaged as a single, reliable national database that would make it easier to verify doctors’ qualifications and registration status and facilitate their practice across State boundaries. The system envisages a unique NMR identification number linked to every doctor’s State registration number.
The dispute now is over how this national database would be created -- is it the task of the State Medical Councils to provide the data for the creation of the NMR or should individual doctors have to put in application afresh, pay a fee and then await EMRB’s verification of credentials?
What the law says
Doctors point out that the NMC Act, 2019, already settles this. In Sections 31(1) , 31 (6) and 31 (7), the NMC Act says that the EMRB “shall maintain a National Register” of all licensed medical practitioners.; the State Medical Councils will maintain and update respective State Registers with the EMRB and that it will be the task of EMRB to maintain the National Register and ensure the electronic synchronisation with the State Registers.
“Nowhere in the NMC Act is it stated that it is the responsibility of registered medical practitioners to apply for NMR registration,” points out the Kannur-based doctor and RTI activist, K.V. Babu. Also, in a written reply in the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2025, the Union Health Ministry, quoting the NMC, had said that applying for NMR registration was voluntary.
Doctors therefore argue that the NMR should be populated from the verified data already held by State Medical Councils. “Our data is already with the State Medical Council and it just needs to be handed over to the EMRB. We fail to understand why the NMR database creation should be so complicated and why doctors are being put through the registration and verification formalities all over again,” says the State President of Indian Medical Association, Kerala, M.N. Menon
A registration backlog
The concern raised by doctors is genuine. Applications submitted by several doctors for NMR registration have remained pending before the EMRB for years, raising questions about the practicality of requiring every State-registered doctor to individually apply for national registration. According to the minutes of the NMC’s 17th meeting, fewer than 32,000 registered medical practitioners had applied for NMR registration by December 2025.
The cost angle
The issue also has a financial dimension. Doctors point out that they are already paying a substantial amount as registration and licensing-related charges to State Medical Councils. The registration fee that will be charged in the name of NMR will be another burden on doctors, Dr. Babu says.
Doctors have demanded that the NMC withdraw the proposed draft amendment and ask State Medical Councils to send its database to the EMRB for creating the NMR as well as the unique ID for doctors

Brazil Supreme Court removes federal police chief, deepening crisis at the top court
Brazilian Supreme Court Justice André Mendonca has removed the head of the federal police and the intelligence chief from their posts
SAO PAULO -- Brazilian Supreme Court Justice André Mendonca on Tuesday removed the head of the country’s federal police and its intelligence chief from their posts, deepening a crisis at the top court and drawing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's government into the turmoil ahead of October national elections.
Mendonca, an appointee of former President Jair Bolsonaro, said in his ruling that federal police Director-General Andrei Rodrigues, a Lula nominee, and the intelligence director of the force, Leandro Almada, headed an organization that allegedly produced six illegal reports on the justice's activities through the end of August.
Mendonca currently chairs two politically sensitive investigations: one into the collapse of Banco Master, which has ensnared several politicians, and another into alleged frauds in Brazil's pension system. The first has hit mostly figures of the country's opposition, while the latter has raised questions of wrongdoing by one of Lula's sons.
Brazil’s government did not immediately respond to a request from The Associated Press on whether it will appeal.
William Marcel Murad, the federal police's executive director, said in a statement that the director-general has the force's “full confidence” and that agents “will not be shaken by attacks.”
Lula is bidding for reelection in October against Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president who is currently serving his 27-year prison sentence at home for an attempted coup.
Mendonca’s decision to remove the federal police chief comes amid a major clash between him and fellow justice Alexandre de Moraes, who sentenced Bolsonaro to prison last year. Last week, Mendonca unsealed federal police documents that showed that Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro frequently sought de Moraes' legal advice before his arrest.
De Moraes had previously denied wrongdoing involving Vorcaro, though his wife provided legal services to Banco Master as part of a 130 million reais ($25 million) contract. Since Mendonca's decision to unseal documents last week, de Moraes is under pressure from politicians, the media and legal experts to resign. He is yet to make public comments about the case.
Brazil's main media reported last week that Mendonca was seeking a suspension for de Moraes from the court until it decides whether he should be investigated in the potential graft case. De Moraes, in turn, said in another ruling that Mendonca should be investigated by the court and potentially impeached by the Senate for interviewing Vorcaro in August without the presence of federal police agents or prosecutors.
On Monday, Brazil's Independence Day, tens of thousands of supporters of opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro filled Sao Paulo's key artery, with many calling for de Moraes' removal. Demonstrators held a giant inflatable figure of Mendonca and wore shirts in support of the Supreme Court justice.
