Iran says captured US underwater drone in Strait of Hormuz
Pentagon plays down the seizure, saying it was an older unmanned vehicle that had malfunctioned
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday it had captured a US uncrewed submarine at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, offering a rare glimpse into how underwater drones are being used in military operations.
Iranian state media said the vessel was a Dive-LD, a large autonomous underwater vehicle built by California defence firm Anduril. The 5.8-metre (19-foot) submersible can carry out missions including mine countermeasures, seabed mapping, intelligence gathering and the inspection of underwater infrastructure such as cables and pipelines, the company has said.
“We trapped one of the most modern, intelligent and unmanned submarines of the terrorist American army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. This submersible is equipped with the latest technologies,” the Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by Iranian state media.
In response, a Pentagon spokesperson said an underwater drone had “malfunctioned more than a day ago”.
“It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,” the spokesperson said.
Anduril confirmed the loss of one of its vessels, but played down the significance of the incident.

‘Now Naraz Fufaji will start shouting’: PM Modi's jibe after unveiling ₹35,000-crore projects in Gujarat
Prime Minister Narendra Modi slammed the previous Congress-led regime over what he called a slow pace of development.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday slammed those who question his government's development record, once again calling them "Naraz Fufa" (angry uncle), as he inaugurated and laid foundation stones for ₹35,000 crore-worth development projects.
Addressing the 'NaMo for Viksit Bharat' programme at Vadodara in Gujarat, he also took a swipe at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' initiative, stating that youngsters would not be misled by "Jhooth ki Goonj" (echo of lies).
India is scripting a new saga of manufacturing, spanning "chips to ships", with components, final products and the supply chain for self-reliance being set up in the country, he said.
Deep Dive
The projects the PM inaugurated included a 2,800-km dedicated freight corridor, which he called a "historic achievement for the 21st century" and a testament to how the country's work culture has transformed over the past 12 years.
He also slammed the previous Congress-led regime for the slow pace of development.
A double-stack container freight train recently transported cargo equivalent to that carried by over 250 trucks from Jawaharlal Nehru Port in Mumbai to Vadodara in a single trip, Modi said.
Targeting those who would question the utility of the corridor project, he said, "Now Naraz Fufa ji will start shouting: what would happen to truck drivers and the trucks they had purchased?
"This Fufa ji has found something new to complain about," Modi said, without naming Rahul Gandhi. The PM, notably, had recently used the folksy term at an event in Delhi to target naysayers.
"After 2014, India built 50,000 modern rail coaches, but the previous (Congress) regime could not build even 50,000 toilets in 10 years," Modi said.
He inaugurated three key sections of the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor, connecting Jawaharlal Nehru Port in Navi Mumbai with Dadri in Uttar Pradesh, marking the project's completion.
"Dedicated freight corridors are the lifeline of a fast-developing India. India's transformation is accelerating because of this modern freight network," Modi said.
Earlier, passenger and goods trains had to run on the same tracks, slowing down both passenger travel and freight movement, but the Dedicated Freight Corridor has changed this, he said.
"After 2014, with your blessings, when I reached Delhi, and as soon as we arrived there, we began accelerating this project. Work on the 2,800 km dedicated freight corridors has been completed today," he said.
"Today, the Eastern and Western Freight Corridors are becoming the main backbone of the country's trade and business," Modi said. More than 430 freight trains operate daily on the two corridors, he added.
"The idea for the Dedicated Freight Corridor began in 2004. In 2006, a special company was established to carry out this work, and until 2014, files just kept shuffling from one place to another," he said.
"Unfortunately, even these files weren't fortunate enough to get a dedicated corridor. The files would get stuck, hang around and wander aimlessly," Modi said.
Referring to Rahul Gandhi's 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' youth outreach initiative, he said, "At every nook and corner, you will find people who will try to mislead you through 'Jhooth Ki Goonj', but today's youth will stand with the truth."
The prime minister said the youth could see how focused the government was on working across sectors, including solar, wind, hydro and nuclear energy.
"The youth of the country have to become experts in AI, and we want our youth to excel in the field," he added.
Modi flagged off freight train services from New Sanand, New Makarpura, New Umbergaon and New JNPT in Navi Mumbai. He also flagged off a passenger train service between Tanda Road and Vadodara.
He said India had emerged as a major manufacturer of railway coaches, metro coaches and locomotives in the last decade. Since 2014, India has manufactured about 50,000 modern rail coaches, and 2.5 lakh wagons were added to the railway fleet.
A 100-km journey that earlier took 6.5 hours for a freight train can now be covered in less than half the time, while a 30-hour journey by truck can be completed in 10-12 hours on the Dedicated Freight Corridor, the PM noted.
He said the corridors had reduced fuel consumption, lowered freight costs, saved time and benefited the environment.
The freight corridors were also enabling farmers from eastern and western India to transport flowers, vegetables and fruits to major markets more quickly, he said.
Rail connectivity was also reaching parts of the country where it had been absent for decades, with tribal areas in Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra being connected through these projects, he pointed out.
During the previous government, only one or two trains would be announced in the budget and take a long time to materialise, but now, new trains are being launched one after another, Modi said.
Infrastructure projects in roads, railways, metros, airports, gas pipelines and housing for the poor not only made life easier but also generated lakhs of employment opportunities, he added.
The railway budget this year stood at ₹2.75 lakh crore, several times higher than 12 years ago, and railway modernisation was creating thousands of new jobs, Modi said.
He further said India had developed a solar PV module manufacturing capacity exceeding 200 gigawatts, helping expand the PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana.
So far, 55 lakh families, including 11 lakh in Gujarat, have installed rooftop solar panels, creating employment opportunities, he said.
The future would depend on an electric ecosystem and industries like data centres and AI, which require large amounts of water and electricity, he said, adding that India was preparing the ecosystem needed to become a global superpower in AI and was signing international agreements regarding uranium and critical minerals.
Earlier, Modi walked on an elevated ramp to arrive on stage, and was greeted by the audience, mostly Gen Z youth. He reciprocated with folded hands and waved back.

From game show to Champions League - Sabah coach tells his incredible story
- Published
On Thursday, Valdas Dambrauskas will walk out at Old Trafford as manager of Sabah in the Champions League.
The Lithuanian's career will come full circle, some 20 years since he made his first steps into coaching with Manchester United Soccer Schools.
"This is beyond my imagination," Dambrauskas told BBC Sport. "To go through that tunnel on to that pitch.
"I've been many times to Old Trafford with the kids, and now I'm going to come as a coach."
This only scratches the surface of Dambrauskas' remarkable story.
It begins with an appearance on the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, Dambrauskas using his modest winnings to move to London and forge a career in football.
It is a tale of casual jobs, a determination to succeed and a nomadic coaching career across Europe - which now brings the 49-year-old back to England in the Champions League with the Azerbaijani club.
How a gameshow gave Dambrauskas his break
As Sabah's players and staff celebrated reaching the Champions League two weeks ago, unbeknownst to Dambrauskas he was becoming a social media star.
It all related to that appearance on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? in 2002.
Not because he was on the show, but how he spent the money he won.
"This is so long ago," said Dambrauskas with a wry smile. "A back-in-the-year story that really was forgotten.
"And now suddenly everybody is speaking about this."
Dambrauskas walked away with 4,000 litas (about £725). That might not sound like much, but it was six months' wages to the average Lithuanian.
For Dambrauskas, the real story should be his career and not a gameshow.
"Everybody now takes only this part, you know, about the money," Dambrauskas said. "But yes, it is a true story.
"My idea was somehow I will try to go on these [coaching] courses to gain the coaching badge, maybe go back one day to Lithuania and start to work as a football coach."
What began with Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? would map out his whole career.
'I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs'
Dambrauskas says he had known since the age of 12 he would not make it as a player, but coaching would keep him close to football.
He arrived in London in August 2002 aged 25 on a student visa with limited English.
What followed would be eight years of hard work where he would coach for community projects, at a semi-professional club, within professional youth programmes - and hold down multiple jobs while raising two children.
In 2004 he enrolled on a course in sports science and coaching at London Metropolitan University, the first real step in his career.
Then he started out coaching by volunteering with the Access to Sports Project for deprived children in Finsbury Park.
He went on to work with London Tigers, a charitable community organisation which runs teams from junior level right through to semi-professional.
Starting out as a volunteer, across five years he progressed to manage the first team in non-league football in the Spartan South Midlands League, FA Cup and FA Vase.
Dambrauskas became the first Lithuanian to achieve a Uefa coaching licence through the London Football Association.
"I went on every possible course, every possible conference, London Football Coaches Association meetings," Dambrauskas said.
"Everywhere I could go just to gain some information, some knowledge, some extra diploma, extra course.
"That was very important for me and I took my chances."
He got his first break at a professional club when Manchester United Soccer Schools took a chance on him in 2004.
Dambrauskas spent five years coaching on residential courses in the UK and in Europe.
"That was the best thing that could happen in my life," Dambrauskas said.
"I went through three or four interviews. I will be forever grateful to [Foundation chief executive] John Shiels, the way he gave me this chance, because I didn't have experience.
"I'd never been in a place with so many great personalities as I got in the Manchester United Soccer Schools."
After a short spell with Fulham, Dambrauskas moved to Brentford. He credits academy director Ose Aibangee as one of the biggest influences on his career, pushing his limits.
All the while he was juggling home life and working multiple jobs to make ends meet.
"I was a gardener, a handyman, doing newspaper rounds at the beginning, also polishing floors in a pub," Dambrauskas said.
"So many jobs. Working in retail, and then as a sports development officer, then a sports development manager, and the central YMCA.
"I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs."
As well as the trip to Manchester United this week, Sabah will complete their Champions League group games at Arsenal in January.
This also feels like fate for Dambrauskas - one of the buildings at London Metropolitan University on Holloway Road overlooked Emirates Stadium.
When asked about his time in England, Dambrauskas' face lights up.
"When I hear this word 'England', it for me sounds like opportunities," Dambrauskas said.
"It was really amazing. England gave me all this and I'll forever be grateful."
From England to 13 trophies in five countries
Dambrauskas was working three jobs - at Brentford, London Tigers and as a sports development manager - when the opportunity arose to coach full-time.
It meant leaving England to return to Lithuania, champions Ekranas appointing him assistant first-team and reserve-team coach at the end of 2010.
After four years at Ekranas he was named manager of Zalgiris Vilnius, Lithuania's biggest club, where his career really took off.
Dambrauskas won two league titles, three Lithuanian Cups and two Lithuanian Super Cups across three seasons - including a treble in 2016.
Then came a series of moves in which Dambrauskas took charge of eight teams over nine years in seven countries.
First RFS, with whom he won the Latvian Cup, and then Gorica in Croatia.
A third league title came with Bulgarian side Ludogorets Razgrad, along with another Super Cup and Europa League qualification.
Dambrauskas then returned to Croatia with Hajduk Split, a time which he described as "absolutely amazing" as the club won the Croatian Cup - their first trophy for 10 years.
Next up was a spell in Greece with OFI Crete, then Omonia in Cyprus - who qualified for the Conference League - and Diosgyori in Hungary.
Finally, in the summer of 2025, he arrived at Sabah, the 10th club of his career.
Dambrauskas completed the league and cup double in his first season, as the club won the title for the first time.
It took his trophy tally to 13 across five countries.
Next stop, the Champions League.
Champions League 'beyond imagination'
Dambrauskas had to navigate four knockout ties to get Sabah to the Champions League, and they are the only club to make it all the way through from the first qualifying round.
Welsh club TNS, Finland's KuPS, Danish side Aarhus and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were all knocked out.
The final qualifying game was as dramatic as Dambrauskas' own story.
Sabah were going out, then a goal by Tellur Mutallimov in the fourth minute of stoppage time sent the tie into extra time. They went on to win 5-2 on the night and 6-4 on aggregate.
"To go to the Champions League is something beyond imagination," Dambrauskas said.
"We have never qualified for the Conference League, we have never qualified for the Europa League. We have never passed more than two rounds in a row in one competition, and now suddenly we are here."
Sabah are based in the town of Masazir - 30 miles north of the Azerbaijan capital Baku - with a population of just 19,000.
Known as the Owls, Sabah were only formed in 2017 and on Tuesday will celebrate their ninth birthday.
Like many small clubs, their Bank Respublika Arena home, with a capacity of less than 9,000, does not meet Uefa regulations. Instead, the club are expected to play their matches at the Olympic Stadium in Baku.
Sabah will host Borussia Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli, and face a trip to Villarreal - as well as the visits to England.
"It can be a very hard draw, and it can be a Sabah draw," said Dambrauskas, clearly excited by the prospect.
"You dream for this, to play in this competition, to play against those teams.
"So now is the time to show that you can handle it, to find a way to compete and we will try to do this.
"We have a good team, we have an ambitious team, we have hungry players who are really keen to show themselves."
Sabah president Magsud Adigozalov last week was full of praise for Dambrauskas' impact.
"His influence goes beyond tactics," Adigozalov told Report. "He has instilled a mindset and winning mentality in the team.
"Even in the most difficult moments, the team never abandons its game or fighting spirit, which is the result of the coach's work."
Twenty years ago, Dambrauskas looked out over the pitch at Old Trafford during one of his job interviews, dreaming that one day he would stand in one of the dugouts.
Now his coaching career will return to where it started.
"I lived in England when the battle between Manchester United and Arsenal was the biggest rivalry. Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger," Dambrauskas said.
"Now I'm going to come back as a coach in the Champions League and hear that anthem. It's really amazing."

CBS News accused of photoshopping image of new 60 Minutes lineup ahead of nerve-wracking launch
According to CBS, the promotional shoot took place in Grand Central Station’s Oyster Bar as a deliberate homage to network pioneers Edward R. Murrow and Walter Cronkite
CBS News is pushing back against online claims that a promotional photograph for the upcoming 59th season of “60 Minutes” was digitally altered or artificially generated.
The image, captured by photographer Mark Seliger at Grand Central Station’s Oyster Bar, features the program’s new lineup.
Following its publication, social media users highlighted several visual anomalies, drawing particular attention to reporter Lesley Stahl appearing to lean against empty space, overlapping feet that critics argued would compromise balance and an unclenched left hand gripping nothing.
“There’s a table behind her,” Jeremy Adler, the senior vice president of communications for CBS News, told The Daily Beast.
Seliger defended the portrait, noting the difficulty of getting a large group into a single frame.
“Bringing ten people together in one frame can be a challenge, but with this team there was an immediate chemistry and a real sense of connection,” Seliger said, according to CBS News. “You could feel the history of 60 Minutes, but also the energy of where it’s going. That’s what I hoped would come through in the photograph.”
The shoot location was intended as a tribute to network pioneers Edward R. Murrow, Walter Cronkite and Douglas Edwards, who broadcast from Grand Central when CBS maintained studios in the terminal between 1939 and 1964. According to the network, the historic studio was situated directly above the Oyster Bar, though “60 Minutes” did not premiere until 1968.
The backlash comes as the program prepares for its first full season under the leadership of Bari Weiss, whose appointment following the May departure of longtime executive producer Tanya Simon has drawn continuous controversy.
Critics have accused Weiss of censorship and shifting the program’s editorial stance, while the upcoming season launch features an interview with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Many users on X tied the picture's apparent glitches directly to ongoing frustrations with the broadcast's direction, with one calling it a “fake or poorly AI’d photo.”
User Darin Yates labeled the program “Liberal Propaganda and Fake News,” adding that “even your photo is fake.”
Other accounts questioned the staging entirely.
X user David Andersen asked, “Do they dislike each other so much they won't take a group photo?”
Commenters also zeroed in on specific physical awkwardness in the portrait.
“Is that a fake photo?” one user asked. “Lesley Stahl don't look right. Why on Earth would you use a fake photo ever and especially why for this?”
The Independent has contacted CBS News for comment.

The US military says it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday, local time, in response to the latest attacks on its warships.
Tehran says it hit back at American targets in Jordan and attacked 10 ships in the Strait of Hormuz, including two US vessels.
Jordan's military says its air defence systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it has fired ballistic missiles at a base in Jordan used by the US military and attacked 10 ships trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz in a sharp escalation of the six-month-old war.
The Americans said they destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday.
The US military's Central Command has posted video of the strikes, which it called a response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeting a US Navy warship twice with ballistic missiles over the previous two days.
No Americans were harmed, the US said.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that they're going to lose tankers," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia.
Iran then carried out a ballistic missile attack on a base used by US forces near Al Azraq in Jordan, according to an IRGC statement on state media.
Although Iran said its missiles inflicted heavy damage, Jordan said its air defences intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, with two falling in unpopulated areas with no casualties.
A US official said Iran's strikes in Jordan were ineffective and all American troops were accounted for.
The IRGC said on Wednesday, local time, it also attacked 10 ships, including two US vessels and eight oil tankers, attempting to cross a "prohibited and unsafe" area of the Strait of Hormuz.
Both the US and Iran are seeking to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war began.
Iran has targeted US assets and allies in the region throughout the war, including in Jordan several times, killing at least two US military personnel during one strike in July.
Iran has also threatened oil tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, according to a statement carried by state media.
A maritime security source has reported a liquefied natural gas tanker was damaged in the Emirati port of Khor Fakkan, though it was unclear who was responsible.
Oil prices extended gains in early trade on Wednesday with Brent crude nearing $US100 a barrel on market concerns over the disruption of oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
Recent attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on top energy producer Saudi Arabia have added to supply concerns.
The US strikes on Tuesday came as Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it had captured a US uncrewed submarine at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
In response, a Pentagon spokesperson said an underwater drone had "malfunctioned more than a day ago".
"It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment," the spokesperson said.

The Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.
City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.
Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.
In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.
Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.
“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.
“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, We offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.
BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.
The public-owned Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE) acknowledged that BAPS had requested that “interactions with women” be limited, and said it should not have accepted these conditions. “They are not in keeping with SETE’s values or the principles of equality between women and men and the neutrality that must guide the organisation of visits to the monument,” it said.
Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, has promised an investigation to “get to the bottom of this as soon as possible”.
He said moving female staff out of sight was unacceptable.
“These are not my values nor those the Eiffel Tower must represent,” he wrote on X.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the Paris Centre district and president of SETE, said he was unaware of the “shocking and unacceptable” conditions afforded the visiting group.
“I confirm again the Eiffel Tower’s commitment to republican values and gender equality,” he said.

Srinagar, Sep 9: The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has set aside the discharge of an accused in a UAPA case stating that secessionist sloganeering in a mob in the presence of the head of a banned separatist organisation prima facie falls under the definition of unlawful activity.
A division bench headed by acting Chief Justice Sanjeev Kumar set aside the discharge of Mohammad Yousuf Lone in a 2013 UAPA case by the Additional District and Sessions Judge (Designated Special Court under NIA Act) Kupwara.
"The sloganeering for secession, raised by an accused leading a mob in the company of the head of a proscribed separatist organisation, coupled with incitement of the public and violence against security forces, is capable, on a prima facie appreciation, of falling squarely within this definition," the bench observed in its order.
According to the case, a mob headed by Mohammad Yousuf Lone and Late Syed Ali Shah Geelani, chairman of the banned Hurriyat Conference, came out of Jamia Masjid in Kupwara on November 8, 2013, raised anti-national slogans against the Government of India, and pelted stones at police and security forces.
The separatist leaders also allegedly instigated the general public against the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Union of India, according to the chargesheet.
"The trial court has recorded, in a single sentence in paragraph 6 of the order impugned, that the facts 'do not fulfil the ingredients of Sections 2(o) of ULA(P) Act' without setting out the reasoning by which the specific statements or conduct attributed to the respondent in the chargesheet were tested against the statutory definition. This amounts to a bare conclusion rather than a reasoned finding," the high court said.
It said the material with chargesheet -- including the recorded slogans, the leadership role attributed to the respondent, and the resultant violence -- discloses a strong suspicion sufficient to put the respondent on trial, leaving the question of whether the charges are ultimately proved to be examined at trial and not foreclosed at the threshold.
"It is trite that an order of discharge must reflect application of judicial mind to the material on record, and that the findings at the charge stage, though summary, cannot be conclusory. However, it is abundantly clear from perusal of the order impugned that the same does not indicate that the specific contents of the chargesheet, the statements of the witnesses to the procession, the site plan, and the material, alleged to link the respondent to the incitement and the resultant violence, were tested against the ingredients of Section 13 read with Section 2(o) of the UAPA before the conclusion of non-applicability was recorded. On this ground, the order impugned is unsustainable and calls for interference," it added.
The court said it is neither making any definitive finding on the guilt or innocence of the respondent, nor expressing any opinion on the ultimate merits of the case.
"However, when specific material is brought on record that, on the face of it, discloses the commission of an offence and the complicity of the respondent, the trial court cannot act as a mute spectator and shut the doors of trial without assigning valid legal reasons," it added.
Allowing the criminal appeal filed by the state, the high court directed that the chargesheet be restored and the trial court proceed with the framing of charge against the respondent afresh after considering the material placed on record by the appellant.

Eye donation is said to be one of the most meaningful forms of donation, as a single donor can potentially restore sight to two individuals through corneal transplantation. India has made considerable progress in eye banking; the country currently has 396 functional eye banks, and corneal collections increased from 62,370 in 2022–23 to 69,848 in 2024–25. However, the need for donor tissue substantially exceeds its availability. There are approximately 2 million corneally blind people in our country, but only 40,000 corneal transplants performed per year.
Role of stakeholders
The government has a crucial role in strengthening the eye donation ecosystem through the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI). Government support includes funding for eye bank infrastructure and equipment, training of ophthalmologists and eye bank technicians, promotion of eye donation, and provision of corneal storage media. Government hospitals can further improve donation rates by establishing Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes (HCRP) and integrating eye donation into routine end-of-life counselling.
Non-governmental organisations and service organisations have an equally important role in creating awareness, dispelling myths, encouraging pledges and, most importantly, counselling families at the time of death. Organisations such as eye bank networks, Lions Clubs and other community-based groups can take the message of eye donation to schools, colleges, workplaces and rural communities.
Private eye hospitals and institutions can complement these efforts by establishing or strengthening eye banks, developing efficient corneal retrieval networks, maintaining high standards of tissue evaluation and preservation, and providing advanced corneal transplantation. Recent initiatives such as the expansion of the National Eye Bank at AIIMS, Delhi through partnerships with additional hospitals demonstrate the value of collaborative retrieval networks.
Building strong PPPs
Ultimately, the future of eye donation in India lies in a strong public–private–NGO partnership. Awareness must translate into timely family consent, consent into retrieval, and retrieved tissue into high-quality transplantation. Strengthening this entire chain will be essential to bring down the burden of corneal blindness and make the gift of sight a reality for many more Indians.
The goal is clear: to transform the gift of eye donation into the gift of sight. Every donated cornea carries a legacy of compassion—allowing one person’s life to bring light into another’s.
(Dr. Mohan Rajan is chairman and medical director and Dr. Sujatha Mohan is executive medical director, of Rajan Eye Care Hospital. drmohanrajan@gmail.com)

Norway to bid farewell to King Harald V with funeral attended by royalty, dignitaries
Norway will bid its final farewell to King Harald V with a funeral paying tribute to the 35-year reign of the popular monarch who died on Aug. 28, aged 89
OSLO, Norway -- Norway will bid its final farewell to King Harald V on Wednesday with a funeral attended by royalty and leaders from across Europe and beyond, who will pay tribute to the popular monarch's 35-year reign.
Harald, who died on Aug. 28 aged 89, was Europe’s oldest monarch and had modernized the royal house, but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who have abdicated in recent times. His son immediately became King Haakon VIII and last week pledged an oath of allegiance to Norway's constitution in parliament.
On Wednesday, the coffin will be taken from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral in a procession, followed by Haakon, other senior Norwegian royals, foreign guests and representatives of Norway’s parliament and others.
Ahead of the funeral, Norwegians have waited patiently to file past Harald's coffin as it lay in state in the chapel of the royal palace in Oslo. The queue was seven hours long at one point over the weekend.
Large crowds are expected in the capital for the funeral. The downtown area will be closed to vehicles and electric scooters, and police have instructed people not to bring bicycles, umbrellas or sharp objects. Large screens have been set up for people to watch the ceremony.
Among the guests expected to attend are the monarchs of Sweden, Denmark, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium and Jordan. The heir to the British throne, Prince William, is also expected, as is Crown Prince Akishino of Japan. Presidents from a range of European countries will join them.
A minute's silence will be held across Norway at the start of the funeral ceremony. Eulogies will be delivered by Norway's parliament speaker and prime minister, and there will be a candle-lighting ceremony with representatives of different faiths.
After the funeral, Harald's coffin will be taken in a procession to the palace chapel at Akershus Castle, where the late king's ancestors are buried. After a private ceremony for the Norwegian royals, who will be joined by some of the foreign guests and senior Norwegian officials, it will be lowered into the crypt.
Norway’s monarchy traces its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy.
Today, the throne's role is largely symbolic and power lies with the elected government and parliament, but the Norwegian royal family retains a role in promoting the wealthy Scandinavian nation around the world.

ANI moves Delhi high court division bench in OpenAI case
The agency argued OpenAI had scraped, stored and commercially exploited its work, infringing its exclusive rights under copyright law.
News agency ANI has moved a division bench of the Delhi high court against a single judge’s order dismissing its plea to restrain OpenAI from using its content to train ChatGPT.
ANI’s appeal against the July 24 verdict was listed before a bench of justices V Kameshwar Rao and Manmeet PS Arora. However, it was adjourned to September 14 as the bench did not assemble.
ANI challenges Delhi HC ruling on OpenAI’s use of news content
On July 24, Justice Amit Bansal dismissed ANI’s plea, holding that OpenAI’s use of the news agency’s material for training its large language model (LLM) fell within the statutory exception of “fair dealing” under Indian copyright law.
The judge said the use qualified as “private use” under Section 52(1)(a) of the Copyright Act, 1957. The provision permits fair dealing of copyrighted material for private or personal use, including research, criticism, review and reporting of current events.
Also read: Delhi HC's OpenAI-ANI ruling: What it means for AI, copyright and publishers in India — so far
Justice Bansal, in his 135-page verdict, reasoned that the training data was accessible only to the AI model during the learning process and was not made available to the public for viewing or downloading.
ANI, in its appeal, argued that the injunction was denied without adequately considering OpenAI’s alleged admission that it had scraped, stored and commercially exploited the agency’s work. The agency contended that such acts infringed its exclusive rights under the Copyright Act, including the rights to store, reproduce, adapt and translate its original works.

Matthew Brennan emerged victorious in the 16th stage of the Vuelta a Espana to claim his fourth stage win of this year's race.
The British Visma Lease-a-bike rider sprinted to victory ahead of Bryan Coquard and Vito Braet in Palos de la Frontera.
Brennan, 21, held up four fingers to celebrate each of his four stage wins in his first Grand Tour.
"It's unbelievable, four victories here and the plan was for one," Brennan said after the 181km stage.
Stage 16 was expected to be another chance for the sprinters.
A five-man breakaway got up the road early on, but with 100km remaining the peloton started to reel them in. The break was caught with around 23km remaining, setting up the bunch sprint finale.
Spanish rider Enric Mas of Team Movistar maintained his 2min 6sec general classification lead on Felix Gall, with Primoz Roglic a further four seconds behind.
The next stage takes place on Wednesday, consisting of 185km from Dos Hermanas to Seville, offering another sprint finale.

Rivian’s futuristic e-bike is delayed, and customers are not happy.
Rivian’s Also apologizes for delays in shipping futuristic e-bikes
The TM-B from Rivian’s micromobility spinoff Also was supposed to reach customers by spring 2026. But after months of delays, the company is opening up about the challenges it’s facing.
Last year, Rivian’s micromobility spinoff Also unveiled a new, software-controlled electric bike called the TM-B that immediately set the e-bike world ablaze. With USB-C chargeable battery, removable seat post, and software-controlled pedal-by-wire system, the TM-B set itself apart with a totally unique approach to electric bicycle design. It’s not an exaggeration to say that nothing else looked like this bike.
But that list of high-tech features is creating unexpected bottlenecks for Also’s product team. The company had originally said customer deliveries would start in spring 2026, and then later summer. But now, with fall approaching, the TM-B has yet to reach any customers — and several reservation holders are making their frustrations with the delays known on Reddit.
This past weekend, Also went the unique route of responding to those criticisms on Reddit. Saul Leiken, Also’s product manager, posted a 661-word letter apologizing to customers for the delays, attributing the hold-up to strict quality standards rather than rushing an unfinished product.
Leiken attributes the delay to “significant supply chain challenges” as a result of the AI boom. Specifically, the company has struggled to find enough printed circuit board (PCB) and integrated circuit (IC) materials for its software-powered e-bike. In some cases, Also’s team has had to find new materials that deviate from the original design, which requires more engineering and testing work to make sure its the right fit.
TM-B’s battery has also presented some hurdles. The batteries, which are available in either 538Wh or 808Wh packs, are supposed to offer up 100 miles of range. But the 240W power delivery exceeds current regulatory guidelines, which is forcing Also to work with standards groups to establish “new safety and testing protocols,” Leiken says.
Lastly, Also may have bitten off more than it can chew with the DreamRide drivetrain system. It’s a pedal-by-wire system, which means there’s no mechanical connection between the pedaling and the movement of the bike. Instead, the rider pedals a generator motor on the crank, which replenishes the battery; a separate traction motor at the rear wheel is software-driven via a Gates Carbon belt drive. But the system requires “high-precision manufacturing,” Leiken admits, which has led to “a slower production ramp-up to ensure quality.”
Rivian’s Also set out to build one of the most high-tech, complex e-bikes ever made. So it shouldn’t necessarily come as a shock to anyone that it’s taking a while to get the manufacturing and production process just right. You could certainly argue that Rivian should have been more clear-eyed about the challenges it would likely face given the complexity of the bike. And to his credit, Leiken does admit they could have done a better job at communicating those delays to customers, and for that he apologizes.
“With any complex and technology-laden product, we have a choice,” he said. “As we ramp production we can relax standards against an original timeline or we can hold to a high standard and face potential delays. We believe our decision to hold that standard was, and is, the right one. And, at the same time, we agree that we should have been more communicative along the way.”

Watch: Pupils return to West Bank school behind barbed wire to protect against settlers
A school in the occupied West Bank has been surrounded by barbed-wire fencing as Palestinian parents fear for their children's safety due to the rise of Israeli settler attacks in the area.
The isolated village of al-Mughayyir, north-east of Ramallah, has been increasingly surrounded by Jewish settler outposts, and regularly blocked by Israeli forces who frequently operate an ad-hoc checkpoint at the entrance.
Six people, including three pupils at the school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of settler-related violence against Palestinians. One of them, 14-year-old Aws al-Naasan, was shot dead by a settler outside the school gates in April.
All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law. Many of the small ad-hoc settler outposts that have mushroomed around al-Mughayyir are illegal under Israeli law too.

Washington, Sep 09: The US military said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to the latest attacks on its warships and Tehran hit back at American targets in Jordan, the latest burst of back-and-forth strikes that have lurched the sides back toward open hostilities in a more than six-month-old war.
Following the American strikes, Iran launched missiles toward US targets in Jordan, Iranian state-run media said.
Jordan's military said its air defence systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and two others fell in places where no one lives.
It said it has no reports of casualties. Jordan is a staunch US ally that hosts American forces, making the kingdom's military bases a target of repeated Iranian strikes. US Central Command said it had no information to offer.
The latest strikes are part of a dual economic and military approach by President Donald Trump as he struggles to bring an end to the war.
The Trump administration on Tuesday also imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran's aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers, in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.
Both the US and Iran are seeking to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war began. Rising energy prices are posing political problems for Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections. A barrel of international standard Brent crude briefly climbed as high as $99.46 on Tuesday.
The US forces also destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday after Iran's Revolutionary Guards tried to attack a US aircraft carrier and destroyer with ballistic missiles, warning that it would, “if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet”.
Iran later said it planned to announce a new “exclusion zone” near the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels intending to transit.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US will not allow Iran's attacks to go unanswered.
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today,” Rubio told reporters on Tuesday when asked about the latest attacks in Iran while on a trip to Colombia.
Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran expert at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, warned that such back-and-forth strikes can only risk more retaliation and further impact on the global economy.
“There is no kinetic solution to the Strait of Hormuz problem,” he said on social media. “Every attempt to impose one only brings Washington and Tehran closer to an escalation that may become increasingly difficult to control.”
US Central Command said the military struck the tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards targeted a Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days.
“The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” it said in a statement.
It said the Iranian tankers destroyed on Tuesday were the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1 and the Riesco in the Gulf of Oman. The US military also destroyed the vessel Derya, which was located near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The statement said the crews of the five vessels were told to abandon ship before the attacks.
Iranian state television also reported the US strikes, saying US forces attacked Iranian oil tankers near the southern port of Jask and near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. It said the crews were evacuated.
An Iranian state TV reporter in Jask said an Iranian tanker was struck near the coast of Yekbeni. State TV later reported that the US military attacked a second tanker near waters off Jask. Separately, state television reported that another Iranian tanker was attacked in the Kharg Island anchorage area.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy on Tuesday had warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for US attacks on Iranian tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting US forces and assisting in the attacks.
A US blockade of Iranian ports has squeezed the country's economy by limiting its oil exports, while the American military has been helping a limited number of ships transit on a route through the Strait of Hormuz off Oman. Tehran wants ships to follow a route that it chooses through the strait, which was considered an international waterway before the war.

- A rumor circulating in late August 2026 claimed crews cut down dozens of cherry trees to pave the way for U.S. President Donald Trump's plans to renovate a Washington, D.C., golf course.
- As of this writing on Sept. 1, we've found no evidence to support the claim dozens of cherry trees had been removed as part of the project.
- The golf course makeover, which Trump said would begin on Sept. 1, aims to create a championship-style site by overhauling the East Potomac Golf Links property inside East Potomac Park.
- The rumor about cherry trees appeared to have originated with readers misunderstanding or misrepresenting an Aug. 28 Washington Post article reporting that an informal count found roughly 60 trees had been removed. Out of those 60, only one was a cherry tree.
- An Interior Department spokesperson told Snopes arborists recommend the removal of dying, declining or hazardous trees as a part of routine maintenance. For example, during the Biden administration, the National Park Service reportedly removed 300 trees (including 140 cherry trees) from the Tidal Basin area north of East Potomac Park as part of a three-year project capped off by the replanting of 277 cherry trees.
In late August 2026, Snopes received emails and searches asking if it was true crews cut down dozens of cherry trees to pave the way for U.S. President Donald Trump's Washington, D.C., golf course renovations, specifically the East Potomac Golf Links property inside East Potomac Park, the site of the nation's first cherry blossom planting.
Earlier in the year, the Trump administration revealed visual plans to overhaul the property into a championship-style golf course. Then, Trump announced on Truth Social that work on the golf course would begin Sept. 1. Earlier in the year, the DC Preservation League filed a lawsuit challenging the project, including citing crews dumping White House East Wing debris at the site.
Readers specifically asked if a rumor that between 60 and 158 cherry trees were chopped down was true, and whether the administration violated a court order by doing so. They also wanted to know if the alleged tree removal impacted the cherry tree collections gifted to the U.S. by Japan in 1910 and 1912.
For example, one reader emailed, "Despite court orders, Trump is moving forward with plans to remove 158 iconic cherry trees near the Tidal Basin and 60 have already been cut down."
Another email read, "Has Trump ordered the removal of dozens of cherry trees in DC that were a gift from Japan?"
Social media users shared variants of this claim on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived), among other platforms.
(X user @adamemedia1)
In sum, as of this writing on Sept. 1, we have found no evidence to support the claim, nor any examples of news media outlets reporting that dozens of cherry trees were removed from East Potomac Park, including any that arrived from Japan in 1910 or 1912.
Regarding court orders, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes reportedly said on May 4 the court must be told if the renovation plans called for the removal of more than 10 trees.
We haven't given this multipart claim a true or false rating given the lack of conclusive evidence either way and the fact that it remains an ongoing situation.
One popular Facebook post (archived) indicated the rumor stems at least in part from people misrepresenting an Aug. 28 Washington Post report. That story, headlined "Trees are coming down by the dozen as Trump's D.C. golf makeover nears," tells of "newly cut stumps and bare patches of dirt [marking] the places where dozens of trees recently stood" and says an informal count found that 60 trees "appeared to have been removed in recent weeks." The Post mentions noticing at least one removed cherry tree near the 14th green of the blue course, as well as two large sycamores removed around another area.
An Interior Department spokesperson provided the same statement the Post published, saying arborists recommended recent removals of dying, declining or hazardous trees as a part of routine maintenance:
Arborists are doing routine maintenance at East Potomac Park with selective removal of hazard trees, non-native invasive trees and declining and dying trees that cannot be brought back to good health through any degree of intervention. Trees throughout the park are regularly monitored for potential safety impacts to visitors, and when a tree is determined to be dying, declining or hazardous our arborists may make the decision to remove it.
In response to the department's statement, we requested numbers of removed trees from previous years for comparison.
For example, in March 2024, when former President Joe Biden was in office, the NPS reportedly announced a $133 million project to rebuild and reinforce the sea wall of the Tidal Basin, an area located north of East Potomac Park. The work, scheduled at the time to last three years, featured the removal of 140 cherry trees out of 300 total trees, as well as the replanting of 277 cherry trees at the project's conclusion. Those removals included a beloved tree named "Stumpy."
According to an NPS article last updated in 2019, fewer than 100 of the cherry trees Japan gave the U.S. in the early 1900s remain to this day and are planted along the Tidal Basin and around the park and the city. Those few remaining trees make up only a small portion of "the nearly 4,000 cherry trees growing in West and East Potomac Parks, on the Washington Monument grounds, and in several other park locations."
Officials reportedly burned most of Japan's 1910 cherry-tree shipment after arrival upon finding they were infested with insects and disease, with the 1912 shipment proving more successful. In 2009, the Post, citing century-old reporting, told of some of the 1910 trees possibly being saved and planted in an "experimental plot" — a group possibly remaining to this day.
We reached out to the White House, which referred us to the Interior Department, as well as the DC Preservation League and the National Park Service for further comment, and will update this article if we receive further information. We also contacted Post writer Rick Maese, who posted on X, "It doesn't seem like any cherry trees from the historic grove have been impacted thus far." Another journalist responded to the post, bringing up the 2009 Post article about officials possibly planting a small number of Japan's 1910 shipment.
An online booking search for East Potomac Golf Links tee times showed availability continuing into the first days of September, with no sign of any potential closures.
Tree care company denies axing cherry trees
During the Post's Aug. 27 visit to the property — a site Snopes has not visited firsthand — the writer reported seeing a company named RTEC Treecare cutting trees, including a large tree that showed "clear signs of decay." The writer also mentioned noticing white dots and yellow ribbons on some trees, marked for purposes not known to the Post.
The RTEC Treecare website displays a message addressing the cherry tree rumor, reading in part as follows (bolded emphasis theirs):
RTEC Treecare is currently performing hazard tree pruning and removal services for the National Park Service at East Potomac Park Golf Course. The trees assigned for treatment have been evaluated and selected by National Park Service arborists based on established hazard assessment criteria.
We want to be clear: RTEC Treecare has not removed any cherry trees at East Potomac Park Golf Course. Our work has been limited to trees identified by the National Park Service as hazardous, non-native, or invasive.
We contacted RTEC Treecare to ask if they were aware of who chopped down the cherry tree the Post reported about and will update this story if we receive more details.
DC eyewitness reports from East Potomac Park
On Aug. 31, Threads user @drybrarian, whose bio identifies him as "Kennedy Center Bike Guy," posted (archived) photos purporting to show the current state of East Potomac Park, including one displaying a newspaper with the day's date as evidence of when he captured the images. The thread of posts, featuring more than the post embedded below, reported that the user witnessed some trees being cut down, adding, "there has NOT been a wholesale Cherry Blossom Massacre," as well as that "the VAST majority of the trees are still there."
We messaged the user to ask for further information and will update this story accordingly.
For further reading, we previously reported in July about similar rumors of the Trump administration planning to chop down cherry trees.

Russell hindered or just Antonelli brilliance? - F1 Q&A
- Published
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli climbed from 19th on the grid to win the Italian Grand Prix - his home race - in one of the great Formula 1 drives.
Antonelli extended his lead at the top of the drivers' standings to 66 points over team-mate George Russell.
Max Verstappen, in the Red Bull, finished third to complete the podium at Monza.
BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before round 14 of the 2026 season in Madrid, Spain.
- Antonelli 'walks over water' for win that will go down in F1 folklore 
  - Published1 day ago
Why wasn't George Russell given the opportunity by Mercedes to pit under the virtual safety car in the Italian Grand Prix? I know he had the hard tyres on, but as the lead driver on track should he not have been at least given the choice? - Tom
In hindsight, it would be easy to think there would be some controversy around the decisions that were taken when the virtual safety car was called mid-race at the Italian Grand Prix.
In reality, though, there was not any.
At the time, George Russell was leading the race on the hard tyre and Kimi Antonelli was second on the medium, a few laps after the Mercedes drivers had been advised to call off their 'yo-yo' scrapping to allow them to optimise their pace and build a gap to Max Verstappen's Red Bull.
Without a VSC, the question was whether the mediums on Antonelli's car would last to the end - probably not - and what Mercedes would do about that.
With or without the VSC, the race result was up in the air.
The VSC changed the complexion of the race, but Russell, who had fitted hards at the red flag with the express intention of going to the end, said he had given no thought to changing tyres at the time.
"I didn't," he said. "I actually thought the guys behind me were going to stay out as well. But I'm sure the team were quite nervous on the pit wall watching our battle and were probably quite happy to send us on different strategies.
"And of course, when we had Max in the mix as well, from a team perspective, you're covering off both scenarios.
"If either of us were to pit, it was going to be Kimi. And that's why I was just a little bit annoyed with the timing of that VSC because I think it would have been tough for those guys on the medium to have competed with anybody on the hard tyre. But it takes nothing away from Kimi's drive."
At the time, Mercedes' strategy computers were saying staying out was the best option.
Team principal Toto Wolff said: "We didn't know what was the better strategy. At that stage, the system said that the one-stop comes out ahead. That two-stop was coming close to the end, but didn't catch it. That's what the software said."
All of which goes to underline the main takeaway - the sublime quality of Antonelli's drive.
He made remarkable progress up through the field from 19th on the grid, wasting no time in picking off cars in front, minimising any loss from overtaking to his overall race time.
He made this look easy, but as many other drivers proved at Monza on Sunday, overtaking another car of similar performance and immediately pulling away was anything but.
This was a performance for the ages - like Lewis Hamilton in Brazil in 2021, Max Verstappen in Brazil in 2024 or 2025, or Fernando Alonso in Valencia in 2012.
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella, who knows a thing or two about this sort of performance having worked with Michael Schumacher and Alonso, said: "While he had a very competitive car, we have to say that he beat a team-mate starting second on the grid.
"It's a very special day, very important for his championship. But for his career and for the fans, motorsport in general, this will be an iconic day. This will be remembered in the years to come."
Is Charles Leclerc's tendency to crash out of races starting to become a problem both for him and Ferrari? - Nathan
Charles Leclerc certainly did not have his best day in Monza on Sunday.
He was arguably too aggressive with Lewis Hamilton at the first chicane on the first lap, forcing his team-mate into the gravel and dropping him to 10th, and crashed out a lap later.
By then, he had also been passed by Max Verstappen, and his accident at Parabolica seemed to be influenced by the fact he was slightly wide into, through and out of the corner because he was defending an attack from McLaren's Oscar Piastri, although Leclerc himself said he thought that was not the cause of his crash.
"I wouldn't say that this is the issue," he said. "From lap one to lap two, I had a bit of a difference in power delivery. We'll look into it, but I don't want to comment too much before checking the data and confirming it 100%."
Having said that, does the allegation that Leclerc has a "tendency to crash out of races" stand up?
He has done it twice so far this year - the previous time was in Monaco, when he lost control at a restart on the broken track surface at Anthony Noghes.
But, unless I've missed something, you have to go back nearly three years to the one before that, when he retired with car damage after an incident-packed race at Zandvoort in 2023.
In that period, for comparison, Hamilton has done the same thing four times - Brazil and Netherlands last year, Austin in 2024 and Qatar in 2023.
Ferrari clearly have some things to sort out, however, in terms of their operations and general approach.
Hamilton is not happy about the way the team have effectively disregarded his - albeit slim - title hopes this year in favour of driver equality, and he said after dropping more points to Antonelli on Sunday that it was "far too late for those decisions to come".
The incident between Leclerc and Hamilton on lap one took place in the context of Hamilton saying after qualifying they had to "work as a team to try and topple" Mercedes.
Leclerc said of the first-corner incident: "I don't really know who is forcing that narrative that we are one against the other. I mean, honestly, Zandvoort there was way too many talks already.
"Here it's true, though, that we went too far. Lewis in Turn One, then Turn Two, I tried to do the tightest corner possible, but that was just not enough and doing it here is not good."
Hamilton was not impressed by the suggestion he had done anything wrong at Turn One.
When those remarks were put to Hamilton, he said: "He said what? I was ahead in Turn Two. By the ethics, I was ahead. There was no 'we' in it."
He added: "I don't race dirty. I've always raced clean and fairly and always left space."
Team boss Frederic Vasseur, who said he would talk to the drivers before discussing this in the media, has some smoothing out to do before this weekend's race in Madrid.
Aston Martin have had their major upgrades but were right at the back of the grid again in Monza. Have the upgrades just failed? - Colin
Aston Martin had a major car upgrade in Hungary two races ago, and a "spec two" Honda engine at the race before Italy in Zandvoort, on either side of the summer break.
There is no question the car upgrade worked. What was effectively an all-new car, apart from the rear suspension and gearbox, cut lap times by about two seconds.
Fernando Alonso made it into the second part of qualifying for the first time all year in Hungary, and drove an outstanding race to finish ninth on merit in the Netherlands, on a one-stop strategy, holding at arm's length the faster Alpine of Pierre Gasly and Racing Bull of Yuki Tsunoda in the final stint.
More upgrades are expected, in the form of a weight reduction around the gearbox, for either Madrid this weekend or Azerbaijan.
The Honda engine upgrade that made its debut in Zandvoort has been less impressive, which is why Aston Martin found themselves at the back again on the power-sensitive Monza track.
Trackside general manager and chief engineer Shintaro Orihara says Honda "observed a step forward in terms of performance from our metrics".
But if there has been one, it is small. Drivability of the spec two in Zandvoort was noticeably worse, too, although it had made a step forward in Italy.
The Aston Martin car seems to be a midfield-level chassis now, somewhere around the borderline of getting into the final part of qualifying, depending on circuit layout, if it had a competitive engine.
And on the chassis side, the team have a sense of direction that gives them confidence they can make another step next season.
With Honda, which still has comfortably the worst engine in F1, the upgrade has been less reassuring.
What is the new Madring circuit in Spain like in terms of power compared to all the previously visited circuits? Who is it expected to suit most of all? - Andrew
The Madrid circuit which makes its debut this weekend has been built from scratch.
The circuit layout has lots of corners, and it is expected to have a low power sensitivity, around the level of Zandvoort.
Medium-speed corners predominate. And overtaking is expected to be difficult - again, like Zandvoort, or even Hungary.
Given Lando Norris took dominant wins in the Netherlands and Hungary, some teams believe McLaren might be favourites heading into this weekend, but McLaren themselves are not so sure.
Hungary and Zandvoort have long-duration corners, where the McLaren excels. But the Madring corners are generally short duration, the exception being the long, banked Monumental, which is expected to be flat out.
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said after the race in Monza on Sunday: "We still think that tracks like Baku and Madrid, where you have to be very precise with the trajectory, short corners, maybe they don't play to the best of our car.
"Yet, we have to say that in Zandvoort and Hungary we were in position to win races and here, while we were not, we know that it's a special race.
"Drag will be less important in Madrid. There is a much higher density of corners. We will definitely give it a go."
New tracks always throw up surprises. So, in short, while one can speculate about car and circuit characteristics all one wants, no one will actually know until qualifying on Saturday.
