Eat more fatty fish.
That dietary advice has changed the way the world consumes salmon, pushing consumer demand ever upward and production to higher and higher levels. Most of that demand is being met with farmed salmon: Today, nearly 70 percent of the salmon consumed on the planet are raised in pens and cages.
The US Department of Agriculture’s Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend eating at least 8 ounces of fish a week and urges people to choose salmon or other species that are similarly high in “heart-healthy” Omega-3 fatty acids. But new research led by USDA scientists finds that levels of these fatty acids in farmed salmon have dropped considerably, potentially making the agency’s own advice, and similar recommendations, including from the American Heart Association, outdated and insufficient.
“These old figures are what are still used in their national dietary guidance,” said Laura Lee Cascada, director of the Aquaculture Accountability Project, a watchdog group. “So in the meantime, it’s going to stay the same and people will have this wrong idea of how much Omegas they’re getting.”
The report’s authors note in their research that the sample they examined was not large enough to require changing the government’s advice and that “a broader and more representative study is warranted.” The agency declined requests for an interview and did not answer questions via email.
The reason for the decline of the Omega-3s, the new study says, is a major shift in the diets of the naturally carnivorous salmon, from smaller fish species—which were over-exploited to feed farmed fish—to a mix that includes land-based oils and crops, including soy and canola. A 2016 study noted similar declines, also attributable to the shift toward a crop-intensive diet.

Mumbai: The Indian rupee came under sharp pressure on Wednesday, falling 34 paise to close provisionally at 95.08 against the US dollar, as Brent crude crossed the $100-per-barrel mark amid escalating US-Iran tensions.
Concerns over higher inflation, foreign fund outflows and weakness in domestic equity markets also weighed on the Indian currency.
Rupee Touches 95.22 During Trade
At the interbank foreign exchange market, the rupee opened at 94.80 against the US dollar, which was also its intraday high.
As crude oil prices climbed, the currency weakened to an intraday low of 95.22 before recovering some losses and settling at 95.08. It had closed at 94.74 in the previous session.
The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against six major currencies, edged 0.05% higher to 98.84.
Brent Crude Crosses $100
Brent crude futures climbed 2.94% to $100.73 per barrel, crossing $100 for the first time in almost six weeks.
Oil prices surged after attacks on energy infrastructure and ships in West Asia intensified concerns over already strained global supplies amid the US-Iran conflict.
Higher crude prices are particularly significant for India because the country depends heavily on imported oil. A prolonged increase can raise the import bill and add pressure on inflation and the rupee.
FII Selling Adds Pressure
Foreign institutional investor outflows also weighed on the USD-INR exchange rate. FIIs sold Indian equities worth a net ₹123.19 crore on Tuesday, exchange data showed.
Domestic markets witnessed another sharp sell-off. The Sensex plunged 813.35 points to 74,764.23, while the Nifty dropped 203.60 points to 23,431.50.
The rupee could continue to face pressure if crude prices remain elevated and geopolitical tensions intensify, though movements in the US dollar may influence its near-term direction.

A video (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that it shows a group of people reciting the Quran on a hilltop in Nepal during rescue operations amid the recent flash floods that occurred on 26 August 2026. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing a group of people reciting the Quran in Nepal during August 2026 Nepal flood rescue operations.
Fact: The video is unrelated to the 2026 Nepal flood rescue operations. It shows local villagers reciting the Quran during a massive search effort in Kyrgyzstan for a 6-year-old boy who was swept away by a river following a tragic car accident. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of the keyframes extracted from the viral video led to the same video (archive) uploaded on 25 June 2026 by a Kyrgyzstan-based Instagram page, two months prior to the Nepal tragedy. Additional footage posted by the same account indicates that the viral video is related to a rescue operation in Kyrgyzstan.
According to the media reports (here, here & here), on 23 June 2026, a passenger car fell off a cliff into a river in the Kegety Gorge in Kyrgyzstan’s Chuy region. While the adults and three children managed to escape, two children remained trapped. Rescuers initially recovered the body of a 12-year-old girl, while a 6-year-old boy was swept away by the strong current. The Ministry of Emergency Situations (MES) conducted an active, round-the-clock search operation.
The effort lasted for nearly four days and was joined by local and international volunteers. Reports indicated that local Muslim leaders recited the Quran and prayed for the safe return of the child. The operation concluded on 26 June 2026, when the boy’s body was recovered. Moreover, the viral video shows one of the rescue personnel wearing a chest badge belonging to the Ministry of Emergency Situations (MES) of Kyrgyzstan.
To sum it up, an unrelated video from Kyrgyzstan is being falsely shared as visuals of people reciting the Quran during rescue operations for the August 2026 Nepal floods.

Sony isn’t backing away from its decision to kill the video game disc in January 2028. But Sony isn’t shutting down production as quickly as we thought, either. Two months after reports that Sony’s last discmaking plant was already being repurposed, the company’s discmaking division now says that one widely reported detail was wrong.
Sony isn’t phasing out discs quite as quickly as we thought
Sony’s last discmaking plant is reportedly decreasing production by 10 percent, not 90.
Originally, it sounded like the division’s president said the Thalgau plant would produce 90 percent fewer discs in 2028 — but the reality is it will only produce 10 percent fewer discs in 2028, an unnamed Sony DADC spokesperson told Game journalist Brian Crecente.
“To clarify and avoid any misleading information: in that statement Dietmar anticipated an overall product volume decline by 10 percent, not a decline down to 10 percent,” the spokesperson said.
Sony DADC did not respond to The Verge’s fact-check request, including our question about whether the division is still restructuring and retraining every single one of the plant’s 300 employees to work on microlenses instead of discs, as ORF Austria reported in July. It wouldn’t tell Crecente any more details, either.
One reason that the discmaking plant might take longer to transition: Even if Sony won’t produce brand-new games on disc after the January 2028 cutoff, the company will continue to let publishers “place re-orders for existing PlayStation disc games.”
Even if PlayStation discs stick around longer than we thought, the future isn’t looking good for the concept of video game ownership. Several major game publishers are conspicuously missing from Microsoft’s disc-to-digital initiative, and Sony keeps giving gamers reason to believe it doesn’t respect the idea of ownership at all.
Most recently, Sony made the breathtakingly blunt legal argument that “reasonable consumers” couldn’t possibly believe they own a game after they buy it — because if they truly owned a game, how could multiple copies exist at a time?

The Charges Were Dropped, but the Damage Was Already Done
David Huerta was arrested while protesting ICE raids in L.A.
David Huerta sat on a steel bed too small for his burly frame in a Los Angeles jail last summer and looked out a small rectangular window at Dodger Stadium, where he’d once spent evenings with his two boys. He was the kid who’d made good, although it hadn’t been easy. His mother died from breast cancer when he was 4. He was raised in southeast L.A. by his dad, a veteran of the Korean War turned Teamster, who paid the bills by loading and unloading cargo—and, when he was out of work, took his sons with him to the hiring hall. Huerta steered clear of gangs and instead went to college, became a union organizer, and worked his way up to become president of the largest labor union in the state, the Service Employees International Union of California.
Yet here he was.
He was sure that he hadn’t done anything illegal. He had screamed at masked federal agents as they executed search warrants at a downtown apparel business that was suspected of hiring undocumented immigrants. He had been angry, no question—especially at President Trump. He had flipped his middle fingers at the masked federal officers. At one point, he sat down in front of the business’s gate; later, he encouraged other protesters to form a picket circle in front of it. When an officer warned him he might be arrested, he replied, “I can’t hear you through your fucking mask.” And when a police van tried to enter, he stood with his hands on his hips nearby. He considered all of that well within the bounds of his First Amendment rights. But he couldn’t stop second-guessing his decision to show up at such a volatile scene alone.
Huerta wondered how his wife and sons, his niece and nephew, and his other family members would react to seeing videos of his arrest. He wondered if he had somehow jeopardized the safety of his union’s hundreds of thousands of members by drawing unwanted headlines. He wondered if his arrest would make others more fearful of opposing this administration’s actions. He wondered when he would be released—or if he would be. He wondered if he could survive prison, should it come to that. And he wondered what his late dad would’ve thought of him sitting on a thin, stained mattress as his cellmate on the top bunk managed a comedown from drugs. Would he have been ashamed, or proud?
Trump’s top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles charged Huerta with conspiracy to impede a federal officer—a felony, under a Civil War–era statute that had rarely been used before last year. If convicted, Huerta faced up to six years in prison. But months later, prosecutors lessened the charges to a misdemeanor count of obstructing, resisting, or opposing a federal officer. This July, the Justice Department said it would drop the charges altogether, adding it to the growing list of federal prosecutions that have fallen apart before going to trial.
Although those dismissals have been celebrated as victories, the cases have taken a financial and psychological toll on the defendants. For Huerta, the past 15 months have been filled with anxiety. He has endured sleepless nights and grown emotionally distant from his wife of 30 years. The public attention continues to make it more difficult to do his job. And despite his pride in standing for what he believed in, he struggles with the shame of being jailed and appearing in court in shackles—an image he worries that his two sons and niece and nephew (whom he has raised as his own) will never forget. As we spoke inside a coffee shop in his neighborhood of Highland Park one recent afternoon, Huerta’s voice rose in anger and indignation while he recounted and, at times, reenacted the minutes before he was shoved to the ground by a federal officer. He teared up.
“The president of the union just got fucking arrested,” he said. “If they can do this to me, imagine what they’re doing to other people.”
On the morning of June 6, 2025, the phones at the SEIU office were ringing with reported sightings of immigration-enforcement operations in and around downtown L.A. Huerta and his team—along with other labor leaders, Democrats, and social-justice groups—had been preparing for a moment like this ever since Trump was elected to a second term. The administration was trying to detain and deport as many immigrants as possible. Workplaces were being targeted, and even American-born Latinos were getting caught up in immigration dragnets. Huerta and his team would later learn that this day was the opening of a monthslong operation in the L.A. area overseen by then–Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino. It aimed to not just increase arrest numbers but also intimidate immigrant communities.
The union’s rapid-response network was designed to help employees during moments like this. “Shit’s happening,” Huerta recalled thinking that morning, “and we’re now in the fight.” He heard a report of an immigration raid in the apparel district, so he scrapped his plans and headed there.
Federal agents were swarming an industrial complex. A woman stood outside the facility’s gate, prosecutors later claimed in charging documents, filming officers and telling someone by phone what was happening. A federal agent later said that Huerta seemed to be communicating with that woman and other protesters “in a concerted effort to disrupt” the operation.
As the crowd grew, people screamed expletives at the officers, and someone yelled, “I want you to kill yourself,” according to the accounts of federal agents contained in court filings. The agents described Huerta joining in the taunting, urging protesters to “walk in circles and picket,” and pacing in front of the gate, “effectively preventing law enforcement vehicles from entering or exiting.”
Huerta told me that he had never acted quite like this at a protest, but that he had snapped when he saw how the officers were treating a young girl who was crying about her dad, who she said was inside the building. “They were so dismissive of her,” he said. He screamed at the agents, asking how targeting workers was making the city safer, and telling them that they were “taking orders from a fucking monster.”
When a federal agent ordered Huerta to move away from the gate, he remained in place, confident that the vehicles had plenty of room. An officer then began to move Huerta out of the way. He recalls not fighting back and keeping his hands on his hips—just as he was trained. But he was still pushed to the ground. A video shows Huerta falling on his back, his head hitting the curb. He told me that he was rolled onto his stomach, sprayed with a chemical irritant, cuffed, and taken to the hospital, where he spent several hours before being transferred to a federal detention center.
His wife, Lucía Aguayo-Huerta, learned of his arrest while at the doctor. His oldest son, Ismael, heard from a cousin, who was crying hysterically. He jumped on Instagram and typed in his father’s name. Huerta had a bum shoulder from an old skiing injury. His other son, Camilo, watched as Huerta’s arm was pulled behind his back in one of the videos. “I was almost on the verge of tears,” he told me. “Almost screaming at my phone, like, You’re fucking with his shoulder!”
Huerta didn’t sleep that first night in jail, and when he arrived at breakfast, he squirreled away packaged food in case it would become valuable in the days ahead. He’d been fingerprinted for detention on a Friday night but had not been fully processed and so had no way to call his family, although he’d briefly called his wife, Lucía, while he was at the hospital.
Protests had erupted in parts of downtown Los Angeles as word of the raids spread. Outside the detention facility, people were showing up in large numbers, clashing at times with police. Inside, news of those protests streamed on a TV. At one point, an inmate looked back and forth from the TV to Huerta, and asked Huerta if that was him on-screen. “That’s me, bro,” Huerta replied. He said the man asked, You’re the fucking union president? What the fuck are you doing here? His title, and years spent helping workers, made his life over the next 48 hours easier. Another inmate gave him toilet paper, a cup, and toothpaste, the holy trinity of jail provisions. Word spread, Huerta told me, and soon 100 or so men had gathered to applaud him.
It was a demonstration of support that Huerta hadn’t realized he needed. The sense of community he felt in that moment reminded him of his own union and the solidarity shown by his dad’s old Teamster buddies, who’d rallied around their family after his mom died, bringing them money and bags of food. He spent the rest of that day learning about the other men and the circumstances that had landed them in jail, in hopes of helping them after his release.
The hardest part of all, Huerta said, was when his wife and kids showed up for his arraignment and bail hearing and he had to look them in the eye. He wore a black T-shirt, black jeans, cuffs, and shackles. From his perspective, it was humiliating. From theirs, it was honorable. His sons told me that their dad had held his head high, his shoulders back, and his chest straight.
Dozens of other union leaders and workers packed the courtroom to support Huerta, along with Democratic Senator Adam Schiff. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass wrote a letter to the judge, urging her to take into account his ties and contributions to the community as she decided bail. Huerta was charged with conspiracy, released on $50,000 bond, and dropped outside without his shoes. Facing a throng of supporters, he defended his actions and spoke of the men he had met who were still stuck inside. “We will have our time for justice,” he told the crowd, “but we must do it in a way that we demonstrate the power of working people.” That night, though, after a long shower and dinner from his favorite taco truck, Huerta lay awake in his bed thinking about a new, terrifying phrase: “conspiracy to impede.”
The psychological stress was, Huerta later realized, his worst punishment. He wanted to get back to work, but he didn’t want his presence at the office to draw negative attention to the union. For a time, he worked remotely. Lucía and the boys worried about his health. He had grown moody and snippy, often wanting to be left alone after work. Other family members worried that Huerta’s critics might try to physically harm him.
Three attorneys and their teams from Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., represented him pro bono, and nonprofits helped pay other expenses. But Huerta was still stressed about the many hundreds of hours that his case was consuming. All of the time he was spending on his legal fight was time lost organizing laborers, he said. Senator Alex Padilla of California, a Democrat, told me he figured that the federal government’s case against Huerta, a friend, would fail, but he knew it had to be taken seriously. “It was clear to me that it was weighing on him,” Padilla said. But Huerta also understood, the senator said, that his members were “looking to him for how to handle the chaos that was going on and the pain that was being inflicted.”
“Free David Huerta” rallies popped up around the state; supporters carried posters featuring his stenciled portrait and wore T-shirts emblazoned with his name. “An injury to one,” the AFL-CIO wrote on Facebook, “is an injury to all.” Huerta attended two rallies to protest Trump’s immigration policies, but kept his appearances short, he told me. He left one as people marched toward a detention facility; he didn’t want to violate the terms of his bond that required he stay at least 100 yards away from federal-law-enforcement agents or operations. One day, while at home with Lucía, he paced the house and imagined how much worse things could get, feeling out of control. “Hey, calm down, you’re okay,” his wife told him. He later realized that he had suffered an anxiety attack. He was raised in a culture in which seeking treatment for mental health carries a stigma, but he knew he needed help. He began to see a therapist for the first time.
In October, his charge was downgraded to a misdemeanor. Prosecutors needed to establish that he had planned to interfere with federal officers that day—but his actions were unplanned, his attorneys said. His team tried to get prosecutors to dismiss the case entirely.
The lesser charges brought some relief, but his character and reputation were still under attack. “Those anxieties of uncertainty,” he said, “they kept creeping up.” The case continued to weigh heavily on his marriage. Then, in July, prosecutors gave up. Late last month, the charge was dismissed with prejudice. He got back his passport and phone, two items that symbolize his freedom and his work. He did not celebrate. “I was detained—and fortunately, that’s all that happened,” he told me. Others—in Minneapolis, Houston, Maine—had been shot dead while interacting with immigration officers. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said on X that Huerta, since his arrest, had complied with conditions to not interfere with federal agents and operations, but “should he unlawfully interfere with any federal agent engaged in their duties, we will not hesitate to arrest and charge him again.” His office declined further comment.
If the point was to try to make an example out of him, a conviction wasn’t necessary. The case against Huerta signaled to the labor and immigrant communities that no one could protest immigration raids without real risk, he and other labor leaders told me. Some union members grew afraid of speaking out, they said. But many others were moved to show their disapproval of the immigration crackdown by protesting peacefully because of how they saw officers treat Huerta, Arnulfo De La Cruz, who took over in April as president of SEIU California, told me. “In a lot of ways, he was the embodiment of a transition from fear to We’re not gonna back down.”
Huerta doesn’t know when—or even if—he will show up at another immigration-enforcement protest, he said. His experience has made him think hard about how he tries to achieve his goals. “I’m not leaving the work,” he told me. “But I would be a liar to say that it’s not in the back of my head that I could find myself in the same situation.” On the day I saw him, he had just pulled into town from Big Bear, a rare escape. He spoke not of the views or the lake, but of the workers powering the restaurants and hotels.

'Between entities concerned': MEA reacts to BAPS-Eiffel Tower row
This came a day after the Eiffel Tower shut down following staff allegations that female workers were asked to leave due to a BAPS group visit.
The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday responded to reports that women employees at the Eiffel Tower were asked to avoid certain areas during a BAPS delegation’s visit, saying it was a matter was “between the entities concerned.”
This came a day after the Eiffel Tower shut down following staff allegations that female workers were asked to leave due to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visit. The tower reopened on Tuesday. MEA official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India was “aware of the opening of a temple by the BAPS Sanstha in the Paris area.”
What did MEA say?
MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, “We are aware of the opening of a temple by the BAPS Sanstha in the Paris area. As to the particular issue pertaining to the Tower, this is a matter purely between the entities concerned.”
On a reporter's query regarding Prime Minister Narendra Modi speaking at the inauguration of the BAPS temple, Jaiswal said it was a “common practice” for the PM to do so. “It is a common practice for the Prime Minister to convey his good wishes on such occasions. In this case, it was done virtually. There is no cause for any comment in this regard,” the MEA spokesperson added.
How did the controversy erupt? BAPS' response
The controversy erupted owing to a visit by the BAPS spiritual movement to the Eiffel Tower. "During the visit of this delegation, women were asked to leave their places of work in order to place men there," staff union representative Diane Davoine told Reuters news agency.
The representative said the female workers “felt humiliated”. “Some were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts, they were replaced by men. And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present,” Davoine said. She added that following tensions over the weekend, the staff had opened a dialogue with the company management on Monday “to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again.”
The company which operates the monument, Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), said the delegation had asked to “limit interactions with women”, while stating that this should not have been accepted in the first place. “I restate the Eiffel Tower's commitment to republican values and to the equality of men and women,” SETE president Ariel Weil told AFP.
In a statement on X, the BAPS Hindu temple in Paris said their visit was coordinated in advance with the teams at the Eiffel Tower during the opening hours of the monument.
"To our knowledge, at no time was access to the Eiffel Tower denied to anyone. Nevertheless, we wish to offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or inconvenienced by this situation. We are deeply committed to the universal values of mutual respect and service to others," the BAPS statement said.

Renewed U.S.-Iran exchanges send oil price back over $100 US for first time in several weeks
In addition to attacks on the war, Iran fired missiles at base used by U.S. in Jordan
Iran said Wednesday it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers, in the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the six-month-old war.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had responded with a ballistic missile attack on a base used by U.S. forces near Al Azraq, in eastern Jordan, and had fired on two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers attempting to cross an area of the Strait of Hormuz that it has declared off limits.
The attacks in and around the vital waterway sent the price of oil surging, with the international Brent crude benchmark breaching $100 US a barrel for the first time since July. Since the war began, oil prices have been as low as $70, reflecting since-scuppered hopes that the U.S. and Iran would agree on a plan that would allow stranded tankers to move oil out of the Persian Gulf safely.
Escalating combat between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthis that control most populated parts of Yemen has created additional uncertainty for energy markets. On Tuesday, the Houthis launched an attack on four cities in Saudi Arabia, causing huge fires at oil installations that were visible from space. Saudi authorities said 73 people were wounded.
American consumers have felt the pinch at the gas pumps, a politically sensitive issue with less than two months before November midterm elections that threaten Republican control of the Senate and House of Representatives.
A gallon of regular gasoline averaged $4.15 in the U.S. on Tuesday, up 26 per cent from a year ago, according to motor club AAA. Diesel, at $5.90 a gallon, cost 59 per cent more than the same day a year earlier.
"In our view, reaching a durable deal before the U.S. midterm elections is increasingly unlikely, and it could remain elusive even beyond that," Bank of America analysts said in a Tuesday research note.
Average gas prices across Canada have also climbed since the start of the war, with increases between 25 and 40 per cent in most locations. The federal government announced an extension of the gas tax holiday as a result, until the end of January.
Iran reveals area of restricted maritime zone
The Americans said they destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, releasing video of ships ablaze before they sank. The U.S. military's Central Command called its attacks a response to the IRGC targeting a U.S. Navy warship twice with ballistic missiles over the previous two days.
"Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia.
Iran says it is imposing a wider off-limits zone around the strait and using new, more capable missiles to attack U.S. ships.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Wednesday a maritime restricted area would extend from Chabahar in Iran into parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, with its precise co-ordinates to be announced. The announcement follows comments Sunday by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, who was quoted by state media as saying Iran would soon establish a restricted zone outside the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, a tanker carrying about two million barrels of Iraqi fuel oil was struck by a drone in Iraqi territorial waters on Wednesday, two Iraqi port officials told Reuters. It caused a fire aboard the Panama-flagged oil tanker New Andros, the port officials said, but there were no reports of casualties among the 22 crew members.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency had said earlier that vessels in the northern Gulf and Gulf of Oman were hit by disabling fire during military activity in the region overnight.
Iran has also threatened oil tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, according to a statement carried by state media.
Iran has largely choked off transit through the Strait of Hormuz that carried one-fifth of global oil before the war, as well as significant amounts of natural gas, fertilizer and other resources.
Washington has responded with a military blockade of Iranian ports, and says it has been able to guide many tankers through the strait, although independent monitors say the extent to which oil is escaping has become increasingly difficult to assess.

Preliminary data showed just six ships crossing with transponders over the last 24 hours.
Iran also said it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by U.S. forces in Jordan.
Iran said that its missiles fired inflicted heavy damage, while Jordan said its air defences had intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, with two falling in unpopulated areas and no casualties.
Video filmed in Ash-Shajarah, in northern Jordan, and verified by Reuters showed flashes lighting up the night sky.
Iran has targeted U.S. bases in the region throughout the war and killed at least two U.S. military personnel in a strike on Jordan in July.

The Indian Junior Women’s hockey team continued its dominant run at the Women’s Junior Asia Cup 2026, cruising to a commanding 7-0 victory over Japan in its third Elite Pool encounter in Moqi, China, on Tuesday.
The win saw India maintain its perfect record in the tournament and secure its place in the quarterfinals.
Having opened its campaign with a 4-1 win over Korea before registering an 11-1 victory against Malaysia, India carried its attacking momentum into the clash against Japan and took control of proceedings right from the start.
India’s early pressure was rewarded in the fifth minute when Krishna Sharma found the back of the net to give the Indian side a 1-0 lead. The advantage was doubled in the ninth minute after a foul by a Japanese defender inside the circle resulted in a penalty stroke. Supriya stepped up and made no mistake from the spot to put India 2-0 ahead.
Purnima Yadav scored a field goal in the 14th minute as India finished the first quarter with a commanding 3-0 lead.
India then scored three goals in the space of five minutes in the third quarter. Geeta Yadav smashed a field goal in the 41st minute to make it 4-0 before completing her brace in the 45th minute, further strengthening India’s commanding position.

Purnima found the back of the net in the 46th minute to complete her brace and take India’s lead to 6-0 at the end of the third quarter. The rout was completed in the 50th minute when Sanika Chandrakant Mane scored her first goal of the match.
India will next face China on September 9 in their final pool match, with the encounter set to determine the top position in the pool.

Rahul Gandhi's Delhi-Lucknow flight makes go-around due to weather, lands safely later: Report
Rahul Gandhi was on his way to Lucknow to proceed to his parliamentary constituency, Raebareli, for a two-day visit.
Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi's flight from Delhi made a go-around before landing at Lucknow airport on Tuesday due to weather conditions, aviation sources said.
Gandhi was on his way to Lucknow to proceed to his parliamentary constituency, Raebareli, for a two-day visit.
The Air India-operated Airbus A320 flight had a scheduled arrival at 3.30 pm but landed at Chaudhary Charan Singh International Airport at around 3.55 pm, the sources said.
"The flight had departed Delhi around 20-25 minutes behind schedule. On its first approach, the aircraft did not land due to light rain and low atmospheric pressure conditions and made a go-around," the source said, adding it's a "normal practice in such weather conditions."
"The aircraft landed safely around seven minutes after the go-around, following which passengers disembarked and proceeded to their respective destinations," the person added.
Upon landing, the Congress leader was welcomed at the airport by party workers and local leaders, including Uttar Pradesh Congress president Ajay Rai and Akhand Pratap Singh.
He then left for Raebareli by road.
Gandhi, who represents Raebareli in the Lok Sabha, reached the constituency towards evening. He was scheduled to meet party workers and locals, and a few groups.
On Wednesday, he will attend a district development coordination and monitoring committee (DISHA) meeting and review development works.

Riot, after 17 years, finally adds team voice chat to League of Legends
“Voice skins” are also on the way.
When League of Legends launched, Barack Obama was in his first year as president, the Black Eyed Peas dominated the airwaves and the iPhone 3GS was cementing Apple's status as a smartphone leader. Through all the years since, the game went without team-wide voice chat. Now, after 17 years, Riot Games is finally adding it.
League of Legends is a game where split-second coordination can make all the difference. But up to this point, its built-in voice chat was limited to premade groups: those that queued up together before a match. Starting with Patch 26.20, players in North America and Oceania can talk with everyone matched onto their team. The company says other regions, including Korea, Latin America and Brazil, may follow if the early rollout goes well. (Brazil and Latin America are separate regions on LoL's servers.)
How well it goes will largely depend on how Riot handles moderation. Will this truly lead to better planning, or just more venom? The company's first safeguard against the latter is an Honor requirement. Players will need to be Honor level 3 or higher to speak; everyone else is limited to listening. For those unfamiliar, Honor is League's behavior rating for players: it changes based on conduct and post-match voting. The company says it will keep refining the system to "better reflect in-game behavior."
Also on the way are "voice skins," which let you modify how you sound in chat. The company claims the voice effects will remain understandable during chaotic fights. Riot hasn't specified which skins will be available, but the game's cast of characters would be a logical assumption. Riot says the patch also brings better noise cancellation, faster connections and improved stability.
And how did the announcement go over with League of Legends' famously critical community? Let's say cautiously optimistic. "I'm glad they are giving voice chat a try," one user posted in the LoL subeddit. "It might not work out, but at least there was an attempt." Another added, "I'm optimistic voice chat will remind people your teammates are human and lighten the mood."

The story so far: A rabies vaccine, that could be critical in preventing a fatal infection, has failed a mandatory potency test, after vials bearing the batch number of a genuine Abhayrab consignment were seized from an unlicensed premises in Delhi. The Central Drugs Laboratory (CDL), Kasauli, has declared the samples in question as “Not of Standard Quality” and “misbranded”, setting off an investigation into whether counterfeit vaccine was being manufactured or distributed.
Rabies is almost invariably fatal once clinical symptoms appear, while timely and quality-assured post-exposure vaccination can prevent complications and death. The immediate concern for investigators, therefore, is not only how the questioned vials came to bear the details of a genuine vaccine batch, but whether any person bitten by a potentially rabid animal received a product that lacked the required potency.
The samples, bearing batch number KE25012, were seized on April 22, 2026, during a joint enforcement operation by the Delhi Police Crime Branch and officials of the Delhi Drugs Control Department at an unlicensed residential premises in Mukherjee Nagar, Delhi. Four persons have been arrested in connection with the case, according to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).
The laboratory found that the questioned vials failed the prescribed potency test and differed from genuine reference samples in several respects. These included packaging, labelling, artwork, QR-code verification, cap colour and licence details.
Genuine batch or counterfeit? Where is the investigation going?
Indian Immunologicals Ltd. (IIL), which manufactures Abhayrab through its Human Biologicals Institute (HBI), has denied manufacturing the seized vials.
In a statement issued on September 4, the company said the genuine KE25012 batch comprised 83,370 vials, underwent the required testing and was released on November 7, 2025, through its authorised distribution network.
More significantly, IIL said the CDL identified 17 differences between the questioned vials and the genuine retention samples of the same batch submitted by HBI for batch release.
The company has submitted its manufacturing, quality-control, reconciliation and distribution records to CDSCO and has asked authorities to trace the source of the questioned vials and take action against those responsible. The CDL finding establishes that the seized samples were NSQ and misbranded. It does not establish that the genuine KE25012 batch manufactured by IIL was defective. IIL’s position is that its legitimate batch passed the prescribed testing and that the batch number may have been reproduced on unauthorised material.
What are authorities investigating?
Investigators now have to establish who manufactured the questioned vials, where they were stored, how they entered circulation and whether they reached patients through any part of the legitimate or informal medicine supply chain.
A particularly important question is whether anyone was administered the suspect vaccine. If so, authorities may have to determine the nature of the exposure, the treatment received and whether additional medical intervention is required.
The Drugs Controller General of India has asked State and Union Territory drug controllers to maintain strict vigilance over the movement, distribution and availability of Abhayrab bearing batch number KE25012 and to take appropriate regulatory action.
CDSCO has also stated that no part of the concerned genuine batch was exported to another country.
International counterfeit rabies products
The case follows a suspected counterfeit Abhayrab episode involving batch KA24014 in 2025. IIL had reported suspected counterfeit vials to authorities, following which health warnings were issued in some countries over the possibility that travellers to India could have received counterfeit rabies vaccine.
That episode highlighted the international dimension of counterfeit rabies products. Travellers exposed to rabies may begin treatment in one country and complete their vaccination schedule elsewhere. A falsified vaccine can therefore create a public-health concern beyond the country in which it was obtained.
In the present case, however, CDSCO has said no part of the genuine KE25012 batch was exported. The investigation will have to establish whether the questioned vials were entirely domestic and, crucially, whether they entered patient use.
Why rabies vaccine matters?
Rabies is a viral disease that affects the central nervous system and is transmitted mainly through the saliva of infected animals, usually through bites or scratches. Dogs account for up to 99% of human rabies transmission globally. Once clinical symptoms appear, the disease is virtually 100% fatal.
Yet rabies is preventable. Prompt post-exposure prophylaxis involves thorough wound washing, vaccination and, for appropriate severe exposures, rabies immunoglobulin or other recommended biologicals. Quality-assured PEP can prevent the virus from progressing to the nervous system.
This makes the quality of a rabies vaccine particularly consequential. For a person exposed to a potentially rabid animal, the vaccine is not routine preventive medicine; it is a time-sensitive intervention intended to prevent a disease that, once symptomatic, offers virtually no chance of survival.
India’s rabies burden
India continues to bear a substantial share of the global rabies burden. A recent ICMR-National Institute of Epidemiology estimate cited by WHO puts annual human rabies deaths in India at 5,726, alongside an estimated 9.1 million animal bites each year.
Globally, WHO estimates about 59,000 people die of rabies each year, with more than 95% of deaths occurring in Asia and Africa.
The suspected circulation of a misbranded rabies vaccine therefore raises a question that goes beyond counterfeit packaging or regulatory compliance: whether a person who believes they have received life-saving protection has actually received a vaccine capable of providing it.
What happens next?
The Union Health Ministry maintained that the immediate task is to establish the origin and distribution of the questioned KE25012 vials and determine whether any patient received them. Authorities will also have to establish the scale of any unauthorised manufacturing or distribution network.
For IIL, the laboratory comparison, together with its manufacturing and distribution records, will help determine whether the episode concerns a manufacturing-quality failure or the unauthorised use of its product identity and batch details.
For patients and healthcare providers, the case reinforces the importance of obtaining rabies vaccines through licensed hospitals, clinics and pharmacies and reporting suspicious products to drug-control authorities.
With rabies, the margin for error is exceptionally small. A genuine, potent vaccine administered promptly can prevent a fatal disease; a counterfeit product can create the dangerous illusion that protection has been provided.

Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
- Published
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.
When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to thousands of prospectors arrived in Cheporor.
And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.
It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.
People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.
Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.
"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.
Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.
"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.
Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.
Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.
Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.
Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.
Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.
Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.
"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.
Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.
But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.
Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.
Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.
While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.
"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.
Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).
West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.
Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.
He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.
However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.
"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.
So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.
"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.
For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.
More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.
Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.
"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.
But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.
"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."
For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."
Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.
Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.
The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.
Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.
Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.
Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.
Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.
Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.
For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.
He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.
"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.
He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.
"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

Anthony Albanese has claimed he did not know he was a member of his local golf club when his government gave it $6m for renovations, accusing the ABC of inappropriate reporting.
The money came from an opaque $560m invitation-only grants scheme to fund projects Labor promised at the 2025 election, largely for Labor-held seats, prompting calls to make grant rules more transparent.
The prime minister had not declared he was an honorary member of the Marrickville Golf Club, which falls in his inner-west Sydney electorate of Grayndler. Albanese told ABC TV on Wednesday the membership was issued by the club 15 years ago without his knowledge.
“I haven’t been in there for years,” Albanese said. “I used to walk my dog along the path, as lots of people do, because it’s a community club.”
The ABC, which first reported the story on Wednesday, said that Albanese’s office had not answered its questions about his membership, or the process by which the Marrickville Golf Club was identified and recommended for the grant. Albanese accused the broadcaster of failing to report the facts.
“The ABC were told information they chose not to publish appropriately,” he said. “The ABC should do better.”
Albanese said the club’s funding was meant to fix issues caused by raw sewerage flowing into the adjacent Cooks River.
“I make no apologies for my electorate being serviced by me as a good local member,” Albanese said
In opposition, Labor claimed the Coalition government unfairly favoured its seats. That controversy, which became known as “sports rorts”, led to then sports minister Bridget McKenzie resigning from cabinet after she failed to disclose membership of a gun club that received funding. An inquiry by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet found she had breached ministerial standards. 
  Albanese’s electorate received two more grants, for a women’s health centre and a domestic violence shelter.
Eden-Monaro, a New South Wales marginal electorate held by a Labor minister, received eight grants totalling $26.4m, according to analysis of the $560m program by the Centre for Public Integrity (CPI).
Kristy McBain, the minister, told ABC Radio she had listened to local councils’ priorities for new infrastructure then put those forward as potential election commitments that Labor could make.
Crossbench MPs complained that councils in their electorates were not given the opportunity to seek funding from the program. McBain said in response: “I mean, obviously that’s how election commitments work.”
While Albanese and McBain’s electorates received millions of dollars, NSW over all received disproportionately less funding from the program in terms of its population, the CPI found. Queensland also received a disproportionately small amount while Victoria and Tasmania received disproportionately more.
The infrastructure minister, Catherine King, said she had signed off on applications under the program after they had been assessed to show they met value for money.
“That is what happens after every single election,” King said.
The justifications for the grants have not been made public. Thirteen crossbenchers have called for the government reform its grants rules to be transparent about how and why it chose to allocate public money.
The Tasmanian senator Jacqui Lambie said the existing rules permitting funding for “pet projects” were undermining Australia’s democracy.
“I don’t care how the government spins it,” Lambie said. “Using taxpayer money to buy votes or benefit party followers should be seen as corruption because that’s what it is.”

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”

Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.
Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.

Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”

Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

Tanzanian President Samia's husband dies in hospital
- Published
The husband of Tanzania's President Samia Suluhu Hassan, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, has died while receiving treatment at a hospital in Zanzibar.
Vice-president Deogratius Ndejembi - who made the official announcement of Ameir's death - said he had been suffering from a heart condition.
He was buried at his family's residence in Kizimkazi, a village on the country's semi-autonomous island of Zanzibar, on Monday evening.
Ameir was an agricultural academic who largely kept a low public profile. He became Tanzania's first First Gentleman after President Samia took office in 2021.
In his announcement, Ndejembi said Ameir died at 08:00 local time (06:00 GMT) on Monday at the Emilio Mzena Memorial Hospital.
The vice-president led tributes as he conveyed his condolences to Samia, as well as Ameir's family and friends.
Kenyan President William Ruto said he received the news of his passing with "deep sorrow".
"President Samia has lost a lifelong companion, her children a beloved father, and Tanzania a distinguished son," he wrote on social media.
Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema also shared his condolences, saying that they "stand side by side" with the first family, and all of Tanzania during "this difficult time".
Similarly, Burundi's President Évariste Ndayishimiye paid his respects and prayed for Samia and her family to have "comfort and strength in this difficult moment".
"May he [God] grant eternal rest to the soul of Hafidh Ameir Hassan," he added.
The First Gentleman rarely appeared in public alongside the president. He was only occasionally seen with her at official events.
He married Samia in 1978, before she entered national politics. The couple had four children - three sons and a daughter - together.
Their daughter, Wanu Hafidh Ameir, is also a politician who currently serves in Zanzibar's House of Representatives in the National Assembly.

A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
- Published
The images are hard to ignore.
Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.
One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.
They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.
At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.
Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.
His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.
"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.
The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.
Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.
But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.
An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.
"I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.
Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.
In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.
"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.
But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.
The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.
Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.
And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.
By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.
Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.
"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".
Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.
The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.
However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.
Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".
Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.
"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.
Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.
His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.
In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.
The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".
The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?
Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.
For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.
"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.
He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.
"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."
The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.
Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.
Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.
But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.
"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.
The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.
For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.
Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.
"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

Messi agrees to buy second Spanish club
- Published
Spanish second-division side Eldense say Argentina great Lionel Messi has reached a "preliminary agreement" to become the club's majority shareholder.
Eldense will become the second Spanish club Messi has invested in, having bought Catalan side Cornella in April.
The 39-year-old former Barcelona forward currently plays for Inter Miami and recently retired from international football after Argentina were beaten 1-0 by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final.
Eldense said: "A preliminary agreement has been reached with Lionel Messi for the acquisition of the shares currently owned by Grupo TH Soluciones, which would make him the club's majority shareholder.
"The transaction is currently subject to the completion of the remaining legal and contractual procedures, including the due diligence process, as well as the required authorisation from the Spanish National Sports Council (CSD)."
The club, based in Alicante, have two points from four games this season and, sitting 20th in La Liga 2, parted ways with head coach Claudio Barragan earlier this week.
Cornella are in the fifth tier of Spanish football and in April said Messi's ownership "reinforces his close ties to Barcelona and his commitment to the development of sport and local talent in Catalonia".
BBC Sport has approached Messi for comment.
He left Argentina for Spain when he was 13 and made his first-team debut for Barcelona aged 17 in October 2004.
He went on to score a club record 672 goals in 778 games before he left for French club Paris St-Germain in 2021 prior to joining Major League Soccer side Inter Miami in the United States in 2023.
Messi's former Real Madrid rival Cristiano Ronaldo, who plays for Saudi Pro League side Al-Nassr, bought a 25% stake in Spanish side Almeria in February.
