Trump banning import of Canadian booze, motorcycles, other goods into U.S.
Canadian retaliatory tariffs came into force earlier Tuesday
U.S. President Donald Trump is banning the import of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and various other products into the U.S.
Trump signed five proclamations on Tuesday night, which will ban those Canadian imports as of Sept. 29, and slap 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products starting next week.
Whey products and molasses are also included in the new ban, while certain dairy products, paper and wood products, aluminum products, furniture and mattresses will be subject to 50 per cent levies.
This is the latest move in an escalating trade war between Canada and the U.S. and comes after Canadian retaliatory tariffs, promised after trade talks fell apart last month, came into force on Tuesday.
A senior Trump administration official told reporters on background that Washington opted for outright bans instead of tariffs because some Canadian provinces banned the sale of American alcohol in provincially run stores.
"These are things that we are doing in order to level the playing field, defend American production and take action against one of the only countries on the planet to retaliate against the United States," the official said.
"Canada set this precedent of banning things."
The official said that they estimate the import ban would impact "single-digit billions" of dollars worth of Canadian goods.
Trump to bar Canada from purchasing contracts
Trump is using Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act, or the Smoot-Hawley Act, to implement the import bans. The same section was used to tariff a swath of Canadian imports last month, on top of sectoral tariffs that have been in place for over a year.
The proclamations say the U.S. will also remove tariffs from a series of products, including salt, toilet paper, refined lead and fishing rods.
Earlier, Trump moved to bar Canadian-made products from eligibility for certain U.S. government purchasing contracts.
In a post to his Truth Social platform on Tuesday afternoon, Trump said he is directing the General Services Administration — the independent agency that oversees federal government procurement — to remove Canadian-origin products from its "multiple award schedules."
While the General Services Administration's preferential purchase program accounts for roughly $50 billion US worth of procurement per year, only 58 Canadian companies were granted contracts through the program in 2024-25, the most recent fiscal year with details available, according to information extracted from a GSA database by CBC News.
LeBlanc calls U.S. response 'unjustified'
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said in a statement on social media Tuesday night that the government is assessing the latest moves.
"Our first priority remains on protecting and supporting Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses from these unjustified actions," he wrote, adding that he is in contact with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
"When the U.S. is ready to engage, our government will work in good faith and constructively towards a more secure mutually beneficial trading relationship that fully respects Canadian sovereignty," LeBlanc said.
Prime Minister Mark Carney released a video Tuesday morning warning Canadians that the country's pivot away from the United States will come at a cost — but insists the alternative would be far worse.
The prime minister reiterated Canada's plan to respond to the U.S. trade war by striking new trade deals with other countries to become less reliant on the U.S.
"We have everything we need to pivot and prosper," Carney said. "That pivot will come at a cost. There's always a cost to action. But it doesn't come close to the cost of standing still."
Canadian and American negotiators were working toward a trade agreement that would have given Canada some tariff relief in key sectors. But the Carney government ultimately decided to walk away, with the prime minister calling what the U.S. was offering "uneconomic."

Instagram uses icons for likes, comments, reposts, saves, messages, Reels, Stories, calls, profile tools, notifications, active status, and more. This guide explains what every major Instagram symbol means and what happens when you tap it.
Instagram is the most popular app with billions of users around the world. The platform has lately been getting plenty of new features and fixes.
Instagram is also one of the few platforms that are known for experimentation. Meta often changes their layout very often, which can sometimes confuse users. If you are new to Instagram, or even an existing user, the new features and some icons you never use can be confusing.
Some of the features on Instagram don’t have an undo option, so it is better to know what they do before pressing them. In this guide, you will learn everything about Instagram icons, their meanings, and what they are used for. To make it easy for you, we have included each and every icon on every page of Instagram and explained what it does.
Table of Contents
What Do Instagram Symbols and Icons Mean?
Instagram Post Symbols Meaning
Instagram posts are what we see and interact with most on a daily basis while using the app.
They come with several engaging elements. Most of them are easy to understand, but if you are confused, here is what they mean:
- Like: Wherever you see this heart symbol on Instagram, it represents a like for posts, comments, and all
- Comment: This represents a comment on the post. Tapping on it reveals all the comments, and you can also add a comment.
- Repost: Instagram has recently introduced the ability to repost. The reposted post also appears on your feed.
- Save: The save feature lets you save posts; in other words, it works like a bookmark.
Instagram Home Screen and Bottom Navigation Bar Icons Meaning
Now let’s look at what the icons mean on the home screen and on the bottom navigation bar.
You won’t find many icons on the home screen, except for the ability to create a new post and to view all your notifications.
If there is one area that Instagram constantly experiments with, it is the bottom navigation. Meta keeps changing the positions of the icons and also changes their designs frequently.
Here is what they mean:
- Notifications: The heart symbol here represents notifications. Here, you can see all the notifications you receive inside the Instagram app.
- Create: The plus symbol here represents “create,” which you can use to create a post or a story and more.
- Home: Tapping on the home icon takes you to the home screen. It is part of the main bottom navigation. Tapping on it also takes you to the latest posts.
- Reels: Instagram has added a dedicated Reels tab, where you can tap on it to go to the Reels section.
- Messages: Tapping on this icon takes you to the Instagram Messages screen, previously known as DMs.
- Search: Tapping on the search icon takes you to the Explore page.
- Profile: This is a profile icon, which takes you to your profile page.
Instagram Reels Tab Icons Meaning
Instagram offers a dedicated Reels tab where you can see all the latest Instagram Reels. It also comes with several interactive elements, some of which are already used for posts.
Here is what each and every icon means in the Instagram Reels tab:
- Create: You can also add new posts directly from the Reels page. You can tap on the Plus icon.
- Like: It lets you like the Reel you are watching. You can like it, and tapping on it removes your like.
- Comments: Lets you add a comment and see comments for the Reel you are currently watching.
- Repost: It lets you repost the Reel you are currently watching.
- Share: It lets you share the Reel with your friends. You can also copy the Reel link using this option.

Millwall 0-1 Newcastle: Joe Willock's late finish helps Matthias Jaissle's side to Carabao Cup victory at The Den
Report and free match highlights from the Carabao Cup third round tie between Millwall and Newcastle at The Den; Joe Willock scored a late winner after Millwall's Tairyk Arconte had hit the post just moments before
Tuesday 8 September 2026 22:48, UK
Joe Willock's late goal sent a relieved Newcastle into the fourth round of the Carabao Cup as the Premier League side scraped to a 1-0 victory at Sky Bet Championship outfit Millwall.
Just before going ahead, the Magpies had been given a fright when a shot from Tairyk Arconte hit a post, with the hosts at that point threatening to upset the competition's winners of two seasons ago.
The Lions brought on 15-year-old midfielder Regan Anderson, who became Millwall's second youngest player, in the time that remained, but Newcastle held firm in what was a hard-fought tie.

Jacob Murphy bent a shot harmlessly over in the early exchanges in what was the first meeting between the two teams since 1993.
The first time Millwall's debutant goalkeeper Filip Marschall was called into action was in the 15th minute when he parried Willock's strike into the air, with the ball dropping to left-back Elkan Baggott rather than the lurking Yoane Wissa.
The visitors dominated the early proceedings and came close again when Sven Botman headed Murphy's corner narrowly over at the far post.
A rare foray out of their own half by the hosts led to their first half-chance as Lyndon Dykes' hooked effort from Baggott's cross was gathered easily by Lukas Hornicek.
The Lions were providing a threat from set-pieces, with a good delivery from a free-kick by Camiel Neghli being met by a flying header from Caleb Taylor that went just wide.
Newcastle then almost had a stroke of luck at the other end as Fabian Schar's long-range effort took a big deflection and ruffled the side-netting, with Marschall stranded.
It remained deadlocked at the break and Millwall began the second half brightly with Jenson Metcalfe smashing a long-range effort just over within two minutes of the restart.
A Metcalfe free-kick then led to another warning for the away side as a header from Lions captain Jake Cooper drifted wide.
The Magpies had struggled to impose themselves since half-time, although Harvey Barnes had just their second shot on target after 65 minutes when his tame effort was easily saved by Marschall.
Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle sent on Anthony Elanga and deadline day signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo in an effort to finally force a breakthrough, but the Millwall centre-back pairing of Cooper and Caleb Taylor were repelling everything coming their way.
Millwall substitute Arconte was the closest to opening the scoring in the 79th minute when he got away from Tino Livramento before his shot came back off the near post.
Having survived that scare, the visitors snatched victory with nine minutes left when Lewis Hall's ball across the six-yard box was flicked in by Willock.
Hall hails Jaissle for lifting Newcastle negativity after cup win
Newcastle defender Lewis Hall speaking to Sky Sports:
"There was a lot of negativity before everything happened and as soon as the gaffer came in, he's been top, as well as all of the coaching staff.
"The way he's got us playing is amazing and I can speak on behalf of everyone - we're really enjoying playing under him.
"We knew it was going to be tough. Whenever you come away in the cup, anything can happen, so we're really proud of the win and to keep a clean sheet as well."
Willock: The Carabao Cup is important for us
Newcastle midfielder Joe Willock speaking to Sky Sports:
"We had a lot of chances in the first half, but we said at half-time that we needed to take our chances. Thankfully, in the second half we did, we got a goal and won the game.
"We won this competition before so it's very important to us. We've got a new coach and a lot of new players and we wanted to start the season well.
"I feel like we started it really well. We need to continue, and this was a big game in keeping that momentum."
Jaissle: It was all about patience
Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle speaking to Sky Sports:
"We're really happy. Job done. It's never going to be easy here at Millwall in a cup match, so we knew about that challenge and we faced it.
"It was about patience, but also being passionate, being tough, collecting the second balls and being efficient in front of their goal. We used the chance and therefore I'm really proud.
"We matched the physical challenge quite well and made a step in the right direction compared to the first half against Bournemouth. We brought the fundamentals onto the pitch, therefore I'm pleased.
"Joe [Willock] is doing an excellent job. Since we joined, already in pre-season, you saw that there is potential.
"I'm really happy with the start so far. I think we show unity on the pitch and off the pitch already after such a short amount of time. But again, we are realistic. We're happy, we're grateful for that start and now the focus is already towards Leeds.
"I love it [English football]. Honestly, I love it. Coming out for an evening match and knowing that atmosphere is something you dream about. It's a privilege."

A magnitude 5.3 earthquake struck Tibet on 8 September at a depth of 35 km (21.75 miles), according to the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC). Reuters reported the development. The earthquake struck the Mustang district in northwestern Nepal, according to PTI. Its epicentre was Lomanthang, 375 kilometres northwest of Kathmandu, according to Nepal’s earthquake monitoring centre. No damage was immediately reported. Tremors were also felt in neighbouring Manang, Dolpa and Myagdi districts. Mustang lies around 250 kilometres from areas hit by major flash floods. An ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border triggered those floods on 26 August. The swollen Bhotekoshi River swept away homes, vehicles, roads, and bridges, and damaged hydropower projects. The supplied report puts flood deaths at 1,357, with over 5,326 people missing. Separately, a landslide blocked the Kimrung River in Parbat district, raising concerns about downstream flooding. Authorities issued a flood alert at 8 pm Tuesday. Residents in Nayapul, Birethanti, and nearby residential settlements were urged to move to a safer location. Communities downstream towards the Kaligandaki confluence were also advised to remain on high alert. On 3 September, a magnitude 5 earthquake struck Tibet. For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

Uttar Pradesh Police took preventive action against six youths after a video showing a Muslim elderly man allegedly being subjected to indecent behaviour and having his skullcap pulled off during a procession in Etah district went viral, officials said.
The incident took place during a procession organised to mark the birth anniversary of Rani Veerangana Avanti Bai Lodhi in the Marhara police station area last week, the police said.
The members of the Lodhi community later apologised to the man and honoured him with a cap and garland.
The viral video that has surfaced now purportedly shows some youths pulling the cap off the elderly man's head, leaving him visibly distressed. A police officer can also be seen taking the man away from the spot, news agency PTI said.
Skull caps have religious significance in Islam. While wearing the cap is not wajib (obligatory) under Islamic law, it holds immense spiritual value as a Sunnah—a highly recommended tradition based on the practices of the Prophet Muhammad.
Taking suo motu cognisance of the video, police examined the footage and detained six youths, initiating preventive proceedings against them under Sections 170 (disobedience of an order promulgated by a public servant), 126 (wrongful restraint) and 135 (assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), police said.
A video subsequently circulated on social media showed the youths at the Marhara police station with their hands folded, apparently apologising.
However, Circle Officer Sadar Sankalp Deep Kushwaha said he was not aware of any accused having formally apologised at the police station.
"I have no information about any accused apologising at the police station," Kushwaha said.
The incident triggered resentment among members of the Muslim community, after which a meeting was held on September 3 at Chaudhary Matinuzzama Public School in the town, which is associated with Samajwadi Party district president Parvez Zuberi.
Around 60 to 70 prominent members of the two communities attended the meeting, including Chaman Prakash, vice-president of the Lodhi Kalyan Mahasabha's fair committee, and other office-bearers.
During the meeting, prominent members of the Lodhi community apologised to the elderly man over the incident and honoured him by presenting him with a cap and garland. Members of the Lodhi Mahasabha also expressed regret over the episode.
Zuberi said Chaman Prakash played an important role in resolving the matter.
"The decision was taken with mutual consent to maintain communal harmony, and both sides are now satisfied," Zuberi said.
He also alleged that the elderly man was subjected to indecent behaviour and that police personnel at the spot also behaved indecently with him.
Zuberi said the six youths against whom police had initiated action did not attend the meeting.
The participants also discussed the role of loud DJs in such incidents, with some suggesting that loud music and songs during processions could cause people to become agitated. They discussed avoiding DJs during future programmes organised on roads.
The procession was organised by the All India Lodhi Kalyan Mahasabha.
Former Uttar Pradesh chief minister Kalyan Singh's son Rajveer Singh alias Raju Bhaiya, Marhara MLA Virendra Lodhi, Farrukhabad MP Mukesh Rajput and several other Lodhi community legislators and leaders were among those reported to have attended the event.

NTSB investigators to interview pilots of crashed Amazon cargo jet Wednesday
Investigators say they will release contents of the voice data recorder info after speaking to pilots
The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) says it will interview the two pilots who survived the crash Sunday of their Amazon cargo jet in Miami. The NTSB says its has already obtained data from the voice recorder that was recovered from the aircraft Monday, but will not release it yet.
"The cockpit voice recorder contained more than two hours of good quality audio," said NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy at a briefing Tuesday evening. "We're interviewing the pilots tomorrow, and we want to hear their account of the accident before we release a readout of the cockpit voice recorder."
NTSB investigator Chihoon Shin told reporters at the same briefing that 30 seconds before the end of the flight data recording, the nose landing gear and right main landing gear touched down, while 19 seconds before the end, the left main landing gear touched down.
A few seconds later, he said, the brakes were released and the throttles were increased to values consistent with go-around thrust.
Shin added there was "no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed."
5 killed on the ground
The jet overran the runway while landing Sunday. It slammed into a van on airport property, careened through a fence and then smashed an SUV on a city street.
The five people killed were all in a van owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., a company that cleans planes. The company said it wouldn't comment on the crash out of respect for the families who lost loved ones.
"Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved. Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed," it said in a statement Tuesday.

The Miami-Dade sheriff identified the deceased as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.
Five other people were injured. Two people remain in critical condition, while a third is in stable condition, she said.
Both the mangled white van, its entire front end crushed, and the SUV — so badly damaged it was nearly unrecognizable — remained at the crash site Tuesday, along with the jet, which sat nose-down with a large soot mark near the P in "Prime Air."
The Amazon jet was landing after a two-hour flight from Puerto Rico as storms brewed around the Miami airport.
The NTSB said the plane barrelled roughly 396 metres past the end of the runway.
Miami's airport does not have a runway excursion system — the lightweight, crushable material that the Federal Aviation Administration says has saved around 500 lives.
Even without it, Miami's airport appears to be compliant with federal rules because it has a 305-metre safety buffer at the end of its runways, experts said.
The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines in foreign countries for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
Two of the four runways at the Miami airport remained closed Tuesday, and Homendy said they will not be reopened until NTSB investigators gather all the information they need from the crash scene.

After U.S. President Donald Trump announced in August 2026 that he would rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America," social media users spread a screenshot appearing to show a Truth Social post from the president that announced the construction of the "Melania Canal" that would 
The screenshot circulated across Facebook (screenshot) and Threads. Here's what Trump allegedly said:
The FAKE NEWS is saying we need the Canadian canals that connect to LAKE AMERICA. Total lie! We don't need their small, low-energy Welland Canal! America built the Panama Canal, we built the Suez Canal — incredible, beautiful, high-IQ canals! I have officially instructed the Army Corps of Engineers to build a much BIGGER, DEEPER, WIDER, and far more powerful canal bypass connecting straight into Lake America! It is going to be magnificent! And we are naming it after my stunning, beautiful wife: THE MELANIA CANAL. Every American will be able to EASILY enter the Melania Canal from BOTH the front end and the back side for a very minimal fee! Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Some users seemed to interpret the rumor as true, and Snopes readers contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
A closer look at the screenshot indicated that this post was labeled as satire, both under the usual spot for "Likes" on a Truth Social post and as a watermark across the image.
According to the watermark, this post originated with a Facebook account called Mrs. Putin, which identifies itself as "Satire/Parody" in its description. Mrs. Putin first shared the post (screenshot) on Aug. 29.
As Mrs. Putin pointed out in a Facebook message conversation with Snopes in 2025, the account's posts often include several indicators that they are satire, including misspelled names. In this case, aside from the "satire" label, other indicators that the post is fake include that Mrs. Putin changed "Likes" to "disLikes" and misspelled Trump's social media tag, "@realDonaldTrump," as "@realDotardTurmp" and his last name as Turmp.
(Mrs. Putin)
A search of Trump's social media accounts using the databases Trump's Truth and Factbase also determined that, as of this writing, the president has not declared the construction of a "Melania Canal." He did, however, float renaming the Strait of Hormuz to "Trump Strait" in a Sept. 2 Truth Social post.
For more on Lake Ontario and its renaming, Snopes previously debunked a claim that Canadian officials were refusing passage to ships with "Lake America" in their documentation and confirmed that Lake Ontario was not named after the Canadian province.
Snopes also has previously written about numerous satirical Mrs. Putin posts.
Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia ignite fires at oil facilities and wound 73 people
CAIRO — A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia Tuesday wounded more than 70 people and ignited fires at several oil facilities and utilities in the kingdom's southern region, authorities said, a major escalation in the renewed conflict between an important U.S. ally and the Iranian-backed rebels in Yemen.
The attacks come after weeks of escalating clashes between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen, which shattered a four-year truce in the country's civil war.
The flare-up delivered a new jolt to a region already destabilized by nearly three years of wars and brings more uncertainty for the global economy. The fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis threatens to squeeze shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical route of the Arabian Peninsula for oil and global trade. It also comes at a time when the Iran war has nearly halted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway that moved about one-fifth of the world's oil before the war.
Fighting has raged on multiple fronts including Yemen's west coast, with government forces saying they have made territorial gains in the provinces of Hodeida, Taiz and Baydah. The Houthis have also launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
Houthi attacks hit oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia
The attacks early Tuesday hit "civilian and economic facilities" in the Saudi cities of Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait, said Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen.
Al-Malki said the attacks wounded 73 people, including women and children. He didn't provide further details.
The attacks ignited fires at several oil facilities and utilities in Saudi Arabia's southern region, the kingdom's Energy Ministry said in a statement. Operations at the oil facilities and utilities were temporarily suspended, it said.
The southern region houses major oil facilities, including a 400,000-barrel-per-day oil refinery in Jazan, which is one of Saudi Arabia's largest. The Houthis had previously attacked the Abha airport.
The ministry said firefighters were battling the fires Tuesday morning.
Al-Malki called the attacks a "serious escalation" and a "flagrant violation of the kingdom's sovereignty, and a direct threat to the security and safety of its citizens and residents."
He vowed retaliation, saying that the Saudi-led coalition "will take all necessary operational measures to deter the terrorist Houthi militia with utmost resolve."
The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying they were in response to recent Saudi attacks on the rebels across Yemen.
In a prerecorded video statement, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the rebels' military spokesman, said they fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at oil and economic facilities, as well as an air base in southern Saudi Arabia.
He said they attacked Jazan City for Primary and Downstream Industries, a major industrial and logistics hub on Saudi Arabia's southwestern Red Sea coast. The rebels also attacked Aramco facilities in Najran and Abha, as well as King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait.
Saree blamed Saudi Arabia for the escalation, warning that "every aggression against our country and people will be met with a firm response."
Nasruddin Amer, deputy head of the Houthi media office overseeing the Saba news agency run by the rebels, took to social media to laud the attacks.
"The Saudi enemy has to understand that the time for committing crimes and massacres against the Yemeni people without response, deterrence or paying a price has ended," he said.
The attacks came hours after the rebels blamed Saudi Arabia for an airstrike that hit a prison in Yemen's northern province of Jawf. At least seven people, including a child, were killed and seven others were wounded in the strike in the Yemeni city of Hazem, the Houthis said.
Fighting forces about 18,500 people to flee their homes in Yemen
The latest escalation stemmed from a Houthi attempt to fly a plane from Tehran to Yemen's capital, Sanaa, challenging a decade-long air and naval blockade by the Saudi-led coalition. A coalition airstrike struck the runway of the Sanaa airport, preventing the landing of the flight.
The Houthis responded with missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, and a blockade of Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, ending a 2022 truce that had largely halted fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition.
The rebels also launched attacks on Saudi-allied forces inside Yemen, prompting government forces to respond with attacks on the Houthis across Yemen's west coast and elsewhere in the country.
Government forces reclaimed territory from the Houthis in the provinces of Hodeida and Taiz, and attacked the rebels in the northern province of Jawf as well as the central provinces of Marib and Bayda.
The flare-up displaced about 18,500 people in Taiz and Hodeida in southwestern Yemen, further pressuring communities in southern Taiz and the West Coast, according to the International Organization for Migration.
"Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," said Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen's Chief of Mission. "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before."
Yemen's civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and much of northern Yemen and forced the government into exile. A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year to try to restore the government to power.
The civil war has killed at least 150,000 people, according to U.N. estimates, and at times pushed the country to the brink of famine.

The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia.
Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey.
Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has Africa’s longest coastline. Thousands of crew members were taken hostage, netting $400m (£296m) in ransom payments for the piracy network’s financiers, the low-level “foot-soldier” pirates and the communities who provided them with goods and services. The attacks only petered out after a multinational anti-piracy force was deployed.
The hijacking of the Lutuf was the most high-profile of the recent incidents. Turkey has been expanding its influence in Somalia after an agreement signed in 2024 to build up its navy, and the Lutuf’s release two weeks after its capture involved a joint Turkish-Somali operation that resulted in the destruction of four pirate vessels.
However, local officials including Mohamed Mubarak, the head of the Puntland security coordination office, have said that a $2.5m (£1.85m) ransom was also paid, prompting warnings that such payments risked encouraging similar incidents.
In a comment for the Center for Maritime Security in July, Matthew Reisener, the thinktank’s national security adviser, warned that naval campaigns by Iran in the strait of Hormuz and Iran’s Houthi proxies in the Red Sea – launched in response to the US-Israel war on Iran – are allowing regional piracy “to once again thrive”.
He wrote: “Not only have the global navies that once combatted piracy off the Horn of Africa diverted their resources to counter the threats against ships in these critical waterways, but these conflicts have also drawn maritime traffic closer to Somalia’s coastline, creating openings for opportunistic pirates to target commercial ships.”
According to Reisener, about 70% of maritime traffic that passed through the Red Sea prior to the Houthis’ targeting of ships there is now being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.
A report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in May reached a similar conclusion: “The recent deterioration of maritime security followed a prolonged period of relative calm in the waters off the Somali coast, which resulted in the redeployment of international anti-piracy fleets and the relaxation of commercial risk-management practices. These factors – alongside the distraction posed by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea – have converged to create an opening that Somali pirates have been quick to exploit.”
Analysts also note that rising oil prices driven by the war have made oil cargoes a more valuable target.
Among the least developed countries in the world, Somalia has endured conflict and clan battles with no strong central government since the autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre fell in 1991. Insufficient patrol vessels and an inability to regularly pay salaries to those involved in coastal patrols are among the reasons why Somalia has long-struggled to secure its coastline.
Piracy has historically thrived during periods of increasing instability and political, factional and regional competition. Observers say the recent rise in incidents has been exacerbated by a domestic and international focus on arms smuggling to Yemen by networks acting on behalf of Iran. Analysts suggest some of these networks have become increasingly associated with Somalia’s Islamist al-Shabaab group as it once again expands its territorial control in central and southern Somalia and seeks to build ties with the Houthis in Yemen.
Local officials interviewed by the Guardian described how in the recent spate of incidents, pirate groups have been using vessels they had already seized to attack and capture other vessels.
According to the officials, the Lutuf was approached as it sailed three nautical miles from Somali shores near the fishing town of Maraya by a previously hijacked cement carrier, the MV Sward, which had been repurposed as a pirate mothership. Eight gunmen from the Sward then boarded the Lutuf and were able to overpower the ship’s armed guards.
Officials say the recent attacks have also been marked by increased technological sophistication on the part of pirate groups, including the use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service to facilitate the tracking of potential targets and for high-speed communications between pirates.
That reflects what Lloyd’s List has described as an increasingly “more capable and adaptive Somali piracy threat” that is already exposing vulnerabilities in carriers’ existing anti-piracy security measures.
In the weeks since the Lutuf ransom was paid, residents of Galkayo, a commercial hub in the north-central Mudug region, said money had started circulating through the local economy to a much greater degree than before. Consumption of the stimulant khat has reportedly increased, and greater numbers of expensive sports utility vehicles have been seen on the roads.
During the previous piracy boom, increased flows of money through the economies of coastal communities and places like Galkayo had profound societal impacts, including an expansion of alcohol and drug use and prostitution.
Perhaps foreshadowing the regime of tougher measures that may be required to counter the growing piracy threat, the Lutuf was only released after a series of drone attacks on the pirate groups involved in the seizure, both at sea and on land. The dead included nine armed men who were killed by a missile fired from a Turkish drone as they prepared boats to join the gunmen onboard the Lutuf.
The question now is whether the growing threat can be countered.
Writing in The Conversation in May, the UK-based academics Anja Shortland and Federico Varese, who studied Somalia’s piracy problem in 2014, were uncertain whether there was an international appetite or the capacity for the same sort of anti-piracy force deployed more than a decade ago.
“What happens next will depend on how the current hijacks proceed. Pirates rely on ransoms for reinvestment and to attract young men into their no-win-no-fee contracts. Fast and generous payments … may free the captive ships. But they will lead to escalating risks for everyone else.
“No state or alliance also currently has the will or capacity to run a naval mission on the scale seen in 2011 and 2012, when navies worldwide spent more than US$1bn annually on counter-piracy operations off Somalia.
“Although piracy manifests as a sea-based problem, it can only be solved on land.”

When Seher Hashmi speaks about mental health, her words do not stem from textbook theories or clinical observations. They carry the raw truth of a survivor. Having battled severe clinical depression and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), and having survived multiple suicide attempts and self-harm, Seher knows the darkest corners of anguish. Today, she is converting her trauma into a movement, traversing thousands of kilometres across India on her Royal Enfield motorcycle to shatter the silence surrounding mental illness.
Her ongoing nationwide campaign, titled ‘Beyond the Horizon – A Ride for Resilience,’ has reached Keralam after completing its north Indian leg. Together with a group of fellow riders, Seher is engaging with youth to transform societal attitudes towards mental health.
Seher’s life began under difficult circumstances. Abandoned by her biological parents at just nine months simply for being their third girl child, she was adopted by renowned social activist Shabnam Hashmi and scientist-writer Gauhar Raza. She is the niece of Safdar Hashmi, the iconic street-theatre activist who was murdered in 1989. Growing up alongside deeply committed parents whose demanding public lives sometimes left little room to process her childhood anxieties, Seher’s struggles gradually worsened into severe mental health challenges.
Path to recovery
Her path to recovery was forged through personal determination, medical intervention, and the empathy of her loved ones. Emerging from that dark space, Seher rebuilt her life as a motivational speaker, fashion stylist, and mental health advocate.
For Seher, every kilometre ridden is a step towards dismantling social stigma. By sharing her own story of survival, she offers young people across the country something far more powerful than advice—proof that resilience is possible, and that no struggle has to be faced alone.
Second journey
This motorcycle odyssey marks her second major awareness journey. Her first expedition took place in 2025, covering over 3,000 kilometres from Delhi to Kashmir and back, reaching thousands of students across 20 cities. Her current campaign—the south Indian leg—was flagged off on August 20, 2026, at the Constitution Club of India in New Delhi by veteran actor Sharmila Tagore. Spanning 55 days, 11 States, and over 7,000 km, the initiative aims at covering 100 venues across schools, colleges, and rural community spaces.
Entering Keralam on September 9, 2026 through Kasaragod, the team will cover nine districts—Kasaragod, Kannur, Kozhikode, Malappuram, Thrissur, Ernakulam, Alappuzha, Kollam, and Thiruvananthapuram—before heading to Kanyakumari on September 18. In Keralam, the campaign is supported by the Yuva Samithi of the Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP). Parishad volunteers are accompanying the team on motorbikes throughout the State, organising mental health awareness sessions and interactive discussions in educational institutions.

Man wanted over killings of wife and daughters in UK pleads guilty to gun offenses in South Africa
A man wanted by British police over the killings of his wife and two daughters has pleaded guilty to firearms offenses in South Africa
JOHANNESBURG -- A man wanted by British police over the killings of his wife and two daughters pleaded guilty Tuesday to firearms offenses in South Africa, where he was arrested in July while on the run.
Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma's guilty pleas to charges of illegal possession of a firearm and illegal possession of ammunition were part of a plea deal, South African prosecutors said. Tshuma also pleaded guilty to an immigration offense for entering South Africa while he was a fugitive.
South African authorities say they will move to extradite him to the U.K. after his local court case is concluded. Prosecutors in the U.K. say he will be charged with three counts of murder.
Tshuma's wife, Nothabo Zandile Tshuma, and their daughters, Natalie, 15, and Nala, 5, were found dead at their home near the town of Bedford, north of London, on July 6. They had all suffered head injuries.
British police say they believe Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma left the U.K. on July 4 and traveled to Zimbabwe and then arrived in South Africa before the bodies were discovered.
Tshuma, who was identified as a British citizen of Zimbabwean heritage, was arrested in Johannesburg on July 10 while in possession of a gun and ammunition after Interpol issued a notice for him to be apprehended.
South African police have said that they suspect he was going to use the gun to kill himself.

LAPD officers shoot dead man who approached them with a tree trimmer
Zimran Canas was shot outside his Boyle Heights home after approaching an officer with the blade of the tree trimmer
Los Angeles police have fatally shot a man who allegedly threatened them with a tree trimmer.
Officers with the Los Angeles Police Department were called to Zimran Canas’ home in the Boyle Heights neighborhood on Monday at around 10 a.m. local time.
The department said in a news release that they were told the man had a mental illness and was armed with a “metal pipe.”
When officers arrived at the home — located east of downtown Los Angeles — a family member came outside and directed them to Canas, “who exited a front gate armed with an approximate 8-foot pole with an approximate 12-inch serrated blade attached to the end,” according to the cops.
Police said they demanded that Canas drop the tree trimmer, but he refused and approached one of the officers “with the blade pointed toward the officer, resulting in an Officer-Involved Shooting.”
“They gave him commands to drop the item, but he advanced towards the officers,” LAPD Captain Mike Bland told local outlet KABC. “The officers did attempt to redeploy their position, but he continued to advance and not comply with their directives to drop the item and submit to arrest.”
Canas collapsed to the ground and officers provided first aid until paramedics arrived. He was taken to a local hospital, where he died.
No one else, including any officer, was injured during the incident.
It’s unclear how many officers drew their weapons and how many shots were fired. The Independent has reached out to the LAPD for comment.
Police recovered the metal pipe and pole with a serrated blade and booked them as evidence.
The LAPD’s Force Investigation Division is investigating the incident.
“Part of that process would include interviews with the involved officers, any body-worn video that they would have, any other video in the area, as well as interviews with any of the involved persons that were here at scene,” Bland said.

India's cleanest city Indore loses top spot in clean air survey by 1 point; mayor blames PM10 for slip
The rankings were announced at the fifth edition of the Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan Awards on Monday.
Indore, India's cleanest city, failed to retain the top spot and took the second place in the 2026 Clean Air Survey, with local authorities citing an increase in PM10 for the slip.
Following the survey, the city administration announced enhanced measures to tackle air pollution. Indore scored one point lower than Lucknow “due to (the city) lagging behind in PM10 particle standards”, mayor Pushyamitra Bhargava told PTI news agency.
PM10 (Particulate Matter-10) are ultra-fine particles in the air, which have a diameter of 10 micrometers or less, produced by vehicle exhaust, road dust, and industrial emissions. These enter the human respiratory system through breathing.
Also Read | Noida improves to 8th in clean air survey among mid-sized cities
The rankings were announced at the fifth edition of the Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan Awards on Monday. Cities and towns across the country were ranked on the basis of the Swachh Vayu Survekshan Framework released in 2022-23. The framework had laid down measures to tackle road dust, vehicular emissions, and industrial pollution, among others.
Lucknow ranks first with 198 points, Jabalpur occupies third spot
In the survey, Lucknow ranked first with 198 points out of 200, while Indore came second with 197 points in the category of cities with a population of over 1 million.
Jabalpur occupied the third spot, having scored 195 points, while Bhopal and Agra tied for the fourth place with 192 points each. Indore had topped the survey in last year, having scored a perfect 200.
In the list of cities with population between 3 to 10 lakh, Odisha's Rourkela emerged as the top performer with198.5 points, followed by UP's Firozabad and Guntur in Andhra Pradesh. Lucknow, Rourkela and Kalinga Nagar were honoured for their efforts by the Union environment ministry under the National Clean Air Programme, according to the PTI report.

Indore mayor announces measures to tackle PM10 levels
Mayor Bhargava promised that steps would be taken throughout the year to reduce pollution from traffic and industries in the city, including PM10 particles, PTI reported. The city current has the highest vehicle density in Madhya Pradesh.
Bhargava said public awareness initiatives, including "Red Light On, Engine Off" at traffic signals, promotions of electric vehicles, and the operation of e-buses, would be stepped up to curb vehicular pollution.
However, officials stated that Indore's overall air quality record remains robust, with the city recording a decline of more than 15 per cent in PM10 levels in comparison to previous years, according to Indore Municipal Corporation data.
According to the data, the Air Quality Index (AQI) in Indore was below 200 on average on more than 98 per cent of the days during the evaluation period for the Clean Air Survey.

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods struck parts of Nepal and Tibet, causing widespread destruction (here, here, and here). In this context, a video is being shared on social media with the claim that it shows 41 Nepali citizens converting to Islam following the August 2026 flash floods. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows 41 Nepali citizens converting to Islam following the August 2026 flash floods.
Fact: The video has been available online since at least 11 June 2023 and predates the August 2026 flash floods in Nepal. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google keyword search but found no credible reports stating that Nepali citizens converted to Islam following the August 2026 flash floods.
We then conducted a reverse image search of key frames from the viral video, which led us to multiple social media posts featuring the same visuals (here, here, and here). The earliest post we found dates back to 11 June 2023 and claims to show 41 Nepalis converting to Islam at a mosque in Saudi Arabia, confirming that the viral video is unrelated to the August 2026 flash floods in Nepal and has been available online since at least June 2023.
We also found a set of photos showing the same venue and a similar event. The caption identified the location as the Al-Da’wah Association in Badi’ah, Saudi Arabia, and stated that 44 Nepalese people converted to Islam.
A subsequent Google Maps search led us to Masjid Ghazwa Al-Mutairi in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia. Photos of the mosque’s interior available on Google Maps matched the visuals in the viral video, confirming that the footage was filmed in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
However, we could not independently verify the identities or nationalities of the people seen in the footage or the other details surrounding the incident. Based on the available evidence, it can be concluded that the video has been available on the internet since at least June 2023 and is therefore unrelated to the August 2026 flash floods in Nepal.
To sum up, this viral video does not show 41 Nepali citizens converting to Islam after the 2026 Nepal floods; it has been online since 2023.

- Players can tame boars, wolves, loxes, and askvins in Valheim.
- To tame them, players must feed the creatures while staying away from them.
- Once the animals are tamed in Valheim, they will become friendly with the player.
Taming is one of the strongest mechanics to create a powerful army or to farm specific materials easily in Valheim. Not all animals can be tamed in Valheim, but the ones you can provide a ton of value. Here is a complete guide on how to tame animals in Valheim, along with steps for individual animals.
List of All Tameable Animals in Valheim
Valheim has a huge variety of creatures, but not all of them are tameable. Here is a list of all the tameable animals in Valheim. If you are having trouble finding them, you can spawn them using Valheim console commands.
- Boars
- Wolves
- Lox
- Askvins
Want to know how to tame them in Valheim and what benefits you can receive from them? Check the individual how-to-tame sections below.
How to Tame Boars in Valheim
Taming boars is the easiest thing to do in Valheim, and it also solves your hide and meat requirements in the early game. Here is how to tame boars in Valheim:
- Make any boar follow you by appearing in front of it.
- Keep its aggro until you enter a secured pen. Close the door of the pen after the boar enters it.
- Now, drop berries inside the pen and get away.
- Make sure the boar is not frightened, which is indicated by the red exclamation mark. It will only happen when you are near the boar, so stay away. Also, avoid having torches or campfires nearby.
- Refill the berries in the pen if they are all eaten, until the boar is fully tamed. When the boar is tamed, a green health bar will appear above it. You can now give it a nickname and pet it.
How to Tame Wolves in Valheim
Now, taming wolves is a whole other ordeal and requires a ton of work. Wolves deal a ton of damage, so you need proper gear to do it. Here is how you can tame wolves in Valheim:
- Head to the mountains with proper gear to safeguard yourself from the cold. Make a closed stone structure, or a strong wooden structure that is not easily broken.
- Look for a wolf and aggro it onto yourself. Lure the wolf into the closed enclosure and drop some meat onto the ground. Leave the wolf inside and close the enclosure so that it cannot leave.
- Stay away from the enclosure to avoid frightening it. However, make sure to return from time to time to drop new meat and to repair the enclosure.
- Wait long enough, and the wolf will be tamed.
- You can now have the wolves follow you and make them defeat enemies.
How to Tame Lox in Valheim
Lox are found in the Plains, and they are quite friendly compared to their size and vicious looks. They can be tamed to be mounts in Valheim. Here is how you can tame Lox in Valheim:
- Dig a massive pit that can fit a Lox and lure one in by dropping Cloud Berries, Flax, or Barley before it to make it chase you.
- Lead it inside the pit and keep dropping food to keep it fed.
- Make sure to stay away to not make the Lox frightened.
- Wait for the Lox to become tamed. When you have tamed the Lox, you can ride it.
- Dig your way out to bring the Lox out of the pit.
How to Tame Askvins in Valheim
Askvins are the hardest creatures to tame in Valheim due to their aggressive nature and serious damage. They can be found in Mistlands, which in itself is one of the harder locations to survive. You can tame Askvins in Valheim to have them lay eggs. Here is how you can tame these animals in Valheim:
- Dig a massive pit and create a partial platform above it. Make sure to dig the pit in an area rich with Askvins.
- Drop Smoke Puffs, Vineberry Clusters, or Fiddleheads inside the pit. Lure the Askvins inside and leave the pit using a ramp or any other method.
- Stay away from the pit and make sure they are being properly fed.
- They will eventually get tamed in the pit. Once they are tamed, you can simply collect their eggs and hatch them elsewhere to get a new army of Askvins.
So, that’s it. Now you know how to tame animals in Valheim. Have any questions regarding the taming process? Tell us in the comments section below.

For those who see the world as a dark place, the universe seems to offer little solace. According to current estimates, approximately 70 percent of the stuff that makes up the cosmos consists of dark energy, an unknown force that pushes space to expand. And another 25 percent consists of dark matter, a mysterious material that holds galaxies together.
But semantically speaking, dark energy and dark matter are not so much “dark” as they are invisible. They do not emit, reflect, nor absorb light, and they have so far proven impossible to observe directly.
Generally, dark energy and dark matter are regarded as separate entities, their elusiveness their primary link. But recent astronomical observations have spurred scientists to look further into a less popular idea—that the two are in fact physically intertwined.
In 2024, the research team known as DESI, for Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, found evidence that the strength of dark energy, sometimes referred to as the “cosmological constant,” had lost its presumed constancy. A 2025 study based on more than twice as much data also concluded that dark energy was changing over time.
These results indicate that after attaining a maximum value about 2 billion years ago, dark energy may have begun to weaken. But the results also suggested that in an earlier era, dark energy could have grown stronger, in seeming defiance of the law of energy conservation.
Researchers describe this as dark energy entering the “phantom regime.” They liken the situation to a ball rolling uphill. It’s certainly possible, but only if the ball is under the influence of something other than gravity.
A growing number of theorists are looking into the possibility that what’s influencing dark energy are its ties to dark matter.
Even though scientists have assumed that dark energy and dark matter “don’t have anything to do with each other,” said Tim Tait, a particle physicist at the University of California, Irvine, “you can imagine a case where one influences the other. And it would not be surprising if [they] were manifestations of a kind of unified theory of the dark universe.”
Dark Interactions
The idea that dark energy and dark matter interact is not new. For example, Justin Khoury, a physicist at the University of Pennsylvania, investigated the prospect in 2005.
Khoury explained that in that study, he and two coauthors posed a hypothetical question: Could there be a form of dark energy whose energy density increased over time? He and his collaborators found that if dark energy and dark matter could affect one another, they could produce what looked like (but was not) phantom behavior. “It is the most natural, simplest way of achieving this,” Khoury said.
Two decades later came the DESI finding that dark energy might actually be changing over time. The result spurred Khoury and two Pennsylvania colleagues, Meng-Xiang Lin and Mark Trodden, to construct a model of dark interactions based on a dark-sector analogue of quantum chromodynamics, a cornerstone theory of particle physics. In the new model, both the energy density of dark energy and the mass of dark matter change in concert.
Another recent study imagines something similar. According to this model, which was published in January in the journal Physical Review D, dark matter could have transferred a small fraction of its energy to dark energy during a previous era of cosmic history. “Dark matter is the main brake on [the universe’s] expansion,” said one of the authors, Elsa Teixeira, a cosmologist at the University of Montpellier in France, so easing up on that brake would have caused the expansion of the universe to accelerate.
The appearance of phantom behavior is basically the result of bookkeeping, said David Andriot, a physicist at CNRS, the French National Center for Scientific Research. “Any change or evolution of the mass of dark matter has been put into the box of dark energy,” said Andriot, who presented his own coupled dark energy-dark matter model in May 2025.
Cumrun Vafa, a physicist at Harvard University, agreed. “The notion that you can compute dark energy independently of dark matter is wrong,” he said. “That assumption, often made by cosmologists and also followed by the DESI team, led to the physically unacceptable phantom behavior.”
The DESI findings are not the only reason to consider an association between dark energy and dark matter. Teixeira and colleagues’ recent study shows how allowing the two to interact can, at least in some scenarios, ameliorate one of the most persistent problems in cosmology: the Hubble tension.
At issue is the current expansion rate of the universe, known as the Hubble constant. Its value can be measured by using light from the early universe, which provides a view of how the cosmos was growing in its earliest days. It can also be measured by drawing upon more recent phenomena, such as exploding stars called supernovas, which reveal how the universe is growing now.
According to the standard model of cosmology, that expansion rate should be the same no matter how you measure it. But in recent years, scientists have found that the expansion rate of the early universe and that of the more recent universe vary by approximately 9 percent.
That discrepancy, or tension, “has provoked heated debates in the cosmology community about whether this difference could be due to systematic errors or whether it is a signal of new physics,” Teixeira and her co-authors wrote. Their model posits that in a world where dark energy and dark matter interact, what seemed to be a crisis caused by disparate expansion rates instead becomes something to be expected.
A Dark Dimension
If dark energy and dark matter do interact, it could mean that they have a common origin, Khoury said.
Ongoing work in string theory—the idea that our universe, at its smallest, most fundamental level, is made up of vibrating strings—suggests a way these concepts might be connected. In 2019, building on the idea in string theory that dark energy is naturally varying, Vafa and two collaborators concluded that the mass of dark matter particles may also vary over time. This led them to propose in 2022 that dark matter and dark energy could share a link with a so-called dark dimension.
String theory posits the existence of six or seven extra dimensions in addition to our familiar three dimensions of space and one of time. All of these dimensions are thought to be as small as physically possible—close to the Planck scale (10-35 meters)—but the researchers proposed that the dark dimension could be significantly bigger than the others—on the order of a micron (10-6 meters).
Gravitons, theoretical particles that impart the force of gravity, could leak into this enlarged dark dimension. If they did, they would pick up mass and become what are called dark gravitons. These massive gravitons would reside in the dark dimension, but their gravitational effects could be felt in other dimensions, allowing them to fulfill the role that is normally ascribed to dark matter.
In this scenario, “there is a very natural coupling between dark energy and dark matter,” said Georges Obied, a physicist at the University of Chicago. Changes in the size of the dark dimension would affect both dark energy and dark matter.
In a July 2025 paper, Obied and Vafa, along with Alek Bedroya of Princeton and David Wu of Harvard, found that the scenario proposed in 2019 was consistent with the DESI data. Their model predicts that the strength of dark energy and the mass of dark matter will decrease over time and that the rate at which dark energy changes will be proportional to its energy density. Because astrophysical measurements tell us that the energy density of dark energy is extraordinarily small, “it won’t change fast,” Vafa said.
“It’s not surprising that we didn’t see it until now,” he said, because the rate of change is so tiny. “We had to wait the entire age of the universe to detect something that small.”
If dark matter is coupled to dark energy, dark matter particles could interact with one another through a new, long-range force that is separate from gravity. The good news, Obied said, is that “there could be astrophysical ways of testing this.”
Coincidentally, two physicists—Marc Kamionkowski, now at Johns Hopkins University, and Michael Kesden, now at the University of Texas at Dallas—have already looked into one such test. In a paper published in 2006, they imagined a sequence of events in which two galaxies come close to each other and the gravity of one galaxy tugs at the other. If dark matter has a stronger gravitational attraction to other dark matter than it does to ordinary matter, a special kind of “tidal tail”—an extended stream of stars, gas, and dust—would form behind one of the galaxies.
Kesden and Kamionkowski looked for this effect and didn’t find it, which enabled them to set an upper bound on the possible strength of the extra attractive force. The upper bound was about 20 times bigger than the number Vafa’s team proposed, so the predicted value fell well within the observational bound. “It is interesting that we are now finding connections between that fairly abstract work and observational and experimental work,” Kamionkowski said.
The fact that a prediction based on calculations from string theory roughly agreed with the astrophysical evidence does not confirm the validity of these “stringy” models. But any correspondence between string theory and experiment is gratifying to Vafa, who has spent the past four decades trying to wrest the theory from the purely conceptual realm to the point of generating testable predictions.
Obied, one of Vafa’s former Ph.D. students, is driven by the same goal. Understanding dark energy and dark matter and the relationship they may share is a daunting problem, he said. “And I think it’s very beneficial to come at this in different ways”—be it from observational cosmology, from particle physics, or from string theory.
“This is how people should do science,” Obied said. “I mean, it’s the job of theoretical physicists to explore everything that’s possible, to get all the possibilities on the table. And eventually, the data will help us decide.

Welcome to Sportstar’s LIVE coverage from Day 4 of the Duleep Trophy Final between East Zone and South Zone being played at the MA Chidambaram Stadium in Chennai.
Mohammed Shami and Mukesh Kumar produced metronomic spells on the third day to further corner South Zone in its pursuit of 708 runs. Tilak Varma and Devdutt Padikkal notched up centuries and the former is still unbeaten, but South Zone is reeling at 242 for six.
Despite two days of play left, there’s little doubt over who is lifting the coveted trophy on Thursday. But for South Zone it is now about putting up a fight and denying East a march to an outright win.
This is Abhishek Saini bringing you the blog updates. We have our correspondent Aditya Padinjat at the ground to provide us with the latest developments.
East Zone loses a review. Milind tries to defend a delivery from Shikhar Mohan, misses the line and sees it crash into his back pad. It’s the impact that saves him.
With not much going right for the pacers, on comes Quraishi for East Zone.
Milind picks a boundary off the final ball, drills it right back past the bowler.
Milind not holding back at all. He gets a hint of width from Mukesh and he slaps this through point. He has been good with picking the singles too, he gets one off the third ball to deep square leg.
Tilak dabs the fourth delivery through the on-side and picks another run. Milind with a run through point.
Milind with a punched boundary through covers off Shami, plays it on the up and finds the gap through the three fielders on the off side.
Four more! This one was a more carefree loft over the in-field through the off side, was almost a six.
Four for Milind. Shami angles a short ball into the left-hander’s body but he’s ready for it, pummels it and finds the boundary through the gap between square leg and fine leg in the deep.
Umpire Virender Sharma has a word with Shami about his follow through, he’s straying perilously close to the danger area.
A single on the fifth ball for Milind, gets Tilak to face the final delivery.
Tilak drives the final ball through covers to pick a couple.
Tilak continues his rich vein of form.
Another overpitched delivery from Mukesh and Tilak transfers his weight onto his front foot with perfection to cream this wide of mid-off.
Shami to continue.
Milind is hit on his forearm off a short delivery from Shami. There’s a lengthy interruption as the physio comes out to check on him.
Just a single run off that over.
East Zone has taken the second new ball too to start the fourth day.
Four for Chama Milind now! Mukesh with the second over of the day, strays on the pads and Milind picks four leg byes through fine leg.
Four off the middle of the blade this time, overpitched and Milind drives through the air with a vacant cover region.
Shami to bowl the first over of the day.
Tilak is on strike. He gets an edge through towards gully on the third delivery but the ball does not carry to Shikhar Mohan.
A boundary for Tilak on the fifth ball, gets it on the pads and he flicks it away through square leg. A punch through long-on on the final delivery, the fielder at mid-on cannot cut it off.

A probe has been ordered by Bhopal Police Commissioner Sanjay Kumar, a day after at least four MBBS intern doctors suffered injuries due to water cannons that were used against them during their protest in the campus of government-run Gandhi Medical College (GMC) to demand a hike in their stipend.
On Monday (September 7, 2026), hundreds of interns of the GMC, Bhopal, protested at their campus over their longstanding demand that their stipend be increased from the current ₹14,437 to ₹30,000. However, as they planned a march to the Chief Minister’s residence, the police used water cannons on the protestors, visuals of which appeared on the internet.
The protestors also alleged that as they continued their march later in the day, the police also resorted to baton charge on them near the campus. The march was stopped less than 2 kilometres from the CM house, prompting them to launch a sit-in at the site.
The sit-in in Bhopal’s Kamla Park area continued through the night and on Tuesday (September 8) even as they boycotted the OPD and routine operation theatre (OT) services, while emergency services remained operational. Services were also interrupted at Gwalior’s Gajra Raja Medical College in support of the protest.
Four interns injured in the police action
Speaking to The Hindu, Siddhartha Kumar Rai, undergraduate student wing president of the Junior Doctors’ Association (JDA), Madhya Pradesh, said that at least four interns got seriously injured in the police action, including one person suffering a broken arm and another an eye injury.
“It was a completely peaceful protest inside the campus but still the interns who perform 36-hour-long duties and contribute the most in handling the heavy patient load at government hospitals were treated like goons by the police. They even targeted the girl interns who were standing on the side,” he said.
Meanwhile, various other doctors’ bodies in the State have also come out in support of the interns’ protest while condemning the police action.
Mr. Rai said that if a written assurance was not given by Tuesday night, the JDA and various other bodies will boycott medical services across the State from Wednesday (September 9).
Dr. Kavita N. Singh, Dean and CEO, GMC, Bhopal, also slammed the use of force in a letter to Commissioner Kumar while seeking an inquiry into the matter and action against responsible officers.
“Water cannon was used and lathicharge was done on the intern students at the emergency gate in which two students were injured.
Taking such action against intern students on the hospital campus without prior notice is completely inappropriate,” she wrote.
In an order, Mr. Kumar said that the matter was brought to attention by Deputy Chief Minister and Health Minister Rajendra Shukla and that Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP), Zone 2, Vikas Sahwal has been appointed to conduct an “impartial investigation of the whole incident”.
“It has been brought to the notice by Shri Rajendra Shukla, Deputy Chief Minister, that during the protest of intern doctors in Bhopal on September 7, 2026, the police sprayed water using water cannon near the gate of Hamidia Hospital, due to which some doctors were injured,” the order read.
Mr. Rai also claimed that Madhya Pradesh ranked 28th in the country in the amount of stipend given to MBBS interns, after the Uttar Pradesh increasing the amount from ₹12,000 to ₹25,000 in August.
“But in terms of MBBS fee at government colleges, we are at the third position with about ₹1.15 lakh. How is this fair,” he asked.
Meanwhile, Mr. Shukla also held a meeting with senior officials and the management of the GMC to discuss the issue and interns’ demand and said that a resolution will be reached soon.
“I am aware of the issue raised by intern doctors in Bhopal regarding an increase in stipends. The expectations and problems of young doctors in the state are being taken seriously. I am in constant touch with representatives of the intern doctors on this matter,” he wrote on X.
“Our effort is to engage in positive discussions with all parties and arrive at an appropriate and practical solution to this issue. Young doctors play a vital role in strengthening the health services of the state, and the government is sensitive to their rightful expectations. Following discussions and necessary deliberations, appropriate and necessary decisions will be taken in this regard,” he added.

Only the men's version is on sale.

The only real complaint I have with this jacket is that's it's on the noisier side, but at this price, I can deal with a little extra nylon crinkling.
The Rainier is our favorite budget rain jacket, especially when it's on sale. This particular deal, while limited in color options, is the lowest price I've seen in 5 years of covering REI sales. Unlike most rain jackets in this price range, the Rainier uses high-quality three-layer, seam-taped, laminate waterproofing that's non-fluorinated (meaning no PFAS). It has some other features rare in budget rain jackets, like pit zips or venting, a weatherproof center zip, and an adjustable, stowable hood.
Looking to avoid the sun? REI's Sahara Shade hoodie is a great alternative to sunscreen.
