I Tested the Best Water Leak Detectors for Your Home
Featured in this article
Water plays an essential role in our homes, but it can also wreak havoc. Burst pipes, leaky toilets, and misbehaving appliances can stop your day in its tracks. Water leak detectors help reduce the risk by alerting you to problems quickly so you can act to prevent severe damage. Around one in 60 insured homeowners file a claim related to water damage or freezing every year, according to the Insurance Information Institute, and the average cost of the property damage is about $15,000. The longer a leak goes undetected, the more damage it does, destroying furniture and decorations, spawning mold and fungi, and even threatening structural integrity.
I’ve tested many smart leak detectors over the past few years, and these are my favorites. Insurers love them, so before you go shopping, it’s worth checking with yours to see what they offer or recommend, and whether installing a leak sensor can reduce your premiums.
Updated September 2026: I added new water leak detectors from X-Sense, a mention of the Ikea Klippbok, updated my top pick with more info, and updated prices.
Other Leak Detectors We Like
Shelly Flood Gen 4 for $40: Shelly’s fourth-generation leak detector boasts support for the Matter smart home system and impressive connectivity via Zigbee, Bluetooth, and dual-band Wi-Fi. I had no issues setting it up in my Google Home app by scanning the Matter QR code, but you can also use the Shelly app or your smart home ecosystem of choice (Amazon Alexa, Apple HomeKit, Samsung SmartThings). Each IP44-rated unit requires four AA batteries (included), and you stick or screw it to the wall (so there's no risk of the unit being submerged), and plug the extendable 6.5-foot leak detection cable into the bottom to trail around the area you want to monitor. While I had some issues when I first tested, with it failing to alert in the Google Home app, these seem to have been resolved, and the detector correctly sounded an alarm when I dripped water on top and alerted me through the Home app.
Ikea Klippbok for $12: Super affordable, with a simple design, this Matter detector alerted reliably during testing. The Ikea Klippbok is a good choice if you already have an Ikea Dirigea hub ($140) to connect to for notifications on your phone. But it works out quite pricey if you don't, and it's not compatible with other hubs, such as the Ikea Tradfri. It does have an alert sound that goes as high as 80 decibels, but doesn’t carry far, and I wouldn’t rely on it alone. You must supply your own AAA batteries (it requires two), and this leak detector is only IP44 rated, so there’s a risk of malfunction if it gets immersed.
Phyn Smart Water Sensor for $37: With features very similar to our top pick, the Phyn Smart Water Sensor proved reliable, alerting me to water quickly with piercing beeps, a text message, and a push notification. Unfortunately, the setup was annoying; I had to reload and re-enter all my information because the app was flaky. The chunky disc design has three metal feet, and there’s an LED that flashes red when it detects a leak. You can add an Extension Node ($10) (a wired disc that plugs in) or a Water Sensor Cable ($27) (a 4-foot cable that can detect water along its length—you can daisy-chain up to three)—but neither comes in the box. This sensor also tracks temperature and humidity, with charts displayed in the app, and you can set alert triggers at certain thresholds. It wasn’t as swift as our top pick, but it was consistent in my testing. It takes two AA batteries (provided). Sadly, you have to press the button on the device to stop the alarm—there's no in-app option. It’s also relatively large (the size of a hockey puck) compared to other detectors I tested, limiting your placement options. And once again, there’s no real smart home integration. Phyn also offers a water monitor and automatic shutoff device ($540), but I haven't tried it.
TP-Link Tapo T300 Water Leak Detector for $20: What I like most about these water leak detectors is that they have four metal probes underneath and two above, so they swiftly detect water dripping on top or pooling beneath. Alerts came through reliably to my phone as push notifications within one to two seconds. The alarm is fairly loud (90 decibels), though you can reduce the volume in the app or even mute it. The TP-Link Tapo T300 requires a Tapo Smart Hub ($23) to function. Each hub can link up to 64 Tapo motion sensors, door or window sensors, switches, and other devices. The hub is a simple rectangular device that plugs directly into an outlet and connects to your Wi-Fi network. It doesn’t sound an alarm by default, but you can mirror the sensor’s alerts in the Tapo app. Another feature I like is the option to push the button on top of the sensor to have the hub confirm that it is within range. Each T300 sensor requires two AAA batteries (included) that TP-Link says can last for up to three years. There is a battery icon in the app to show the remaining power and warn when it is running low. As well as having the water leak alarm trigger your hub to sound, you can have it turn off devices in the vicinity if they are connected to Tapo smart plugs (I tested this, and it worked as expected). The T300 is a bit bulky, so it might not fit everywhere you’d like to place a sensor, and it continued to display as functioning normally in the app for several hours after I removed its batteries.
Eve Water Guard for $110: With HomeKit support, this is a good choice for iPhone owners with a home hub (an Apple TV or HomePod). HomeKit is also ideal if you have privacy concerns because you can be certain no data will be shared with third parties. There is an Eve app, but you can also view the Water Guard and set notifications directly through the Apple Home app. It plugs into an outlet and has a 6.5-foot cable that senses any water and immediately alerts you on your iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch, wherever you are, provided you have a working home hub. It also flashes red and has a 100-decibel siren. You can review alarm history, test or mute alarms, and update device firmware in the Eve app. The Eve Water Guard only detects water, but the sensing cable works well, triggering quick alerts and covering a large area. It needs a power outlet, which also limits your placement options, but you never need to worry about battery life. The obvious drawbacks are the complete lack of support for Android, the fact that you need a home hub for remote alerts and management, and the relatively high price. You can also add 6.5-foot sensing cable extensions ($20 each) up to a total length of 500 feet.
Govee Smart Water Leak Detectors (3-Pack) for $55: Quick and easy to install, Govee's sensors send alerts as push notifications and emails. They also boast one of the loudest sirens I tested (105 decibels). Mercifully, you can shut off the ear-splitting sound from the app. The sensors are quite small with metal feet, offering drip detection on top and leak detection underneath, but there’s no option to add a disc or cable. The Govee Wi-Fi Water Sensors only detect water, but they are effective. I found alerts triggered within a few seconds. The app is basic but works well and displays alert history. Unfortunately, these sensors require a Govee gateway (included in the box), which takes up a power outlet (and may block an adjacent outlet), and each sensor takes two AA batteries (also provided). These sensors care also IP67 rated, so can survive full immersion. One concern with these sensors is that I failed to receive alerts when my phone was connected to mobile data rather than Wi-Fi, though the email did come through. There’s also no smart home integration.
First Alert L1 Wi-Fi Water Leak and Freeze Detector for $65: This large flood sensor, branded First Alert, works with First Alert or Resideo apps and accessories. It sends push notifications and emails to alert you to any leak and sports a 100-decibel alarm that you can stop with the side button. The sensor was relatively slow to alert in all my tests, and the push notifications only came through when my phone was connected to Wi-Fi. The 5-foot water-sensing cable allows you to cover a much larger area, and I found it alerted faster. The detector connects directly to Wi-Fi, so you need a decent signal. This sensor can also track temperature and humidity, but not very accurately (it consistently overestimates temperature and underestimates humidity). The two AA batteries provided are supposed to last up to two years.
Eufy Security Water and Freeze Sensor for $35: If you have Eufy's security system, this could be the best water leak detector for you, but it requires connection to a HomeBase 2 or HomeBase 3 ($150). It proved quick and reliable to alert, offers long-range connectivity (up to 200 meters), and can warn you if the temperature drops below freezing. You receive alerts on your phone via the Eufy Security app, and you can configure the connected HomeBase to sound an alarm, but the detector doesn’t make any sound. A full battery lasts up to two years and the app tracks battery life. Sadly, it doesn’t show the temperature; it simply alerts below freezing.
SwitchBot Water Leak Detector for $17: This rectangular detector triggered swift alerts in all my tests with a 100-decibel alarm. With prongs on top and underneath, it's also quick to detect water. It connects directly to Wi-Fi, so you don’t need a hub, and can send push notifications and emails, though you must set them up in the app. Unfortunately, the push notifications did not come through when I was out of the house, connected to a cellular network instead of Wi-Fi. Smart home connectivity is good (Amazon Alexa, Google Assistant, and IFTTT), and you can set up automation in the SwitchBot app, which makes this a versatile option, particularly if you have other SwitchBot devices. SwitchBot says the two AAA batteries provided are good for up to two years.
AiDot Winees Water Leak Detector S1 Plus (3 Pack) for $50: Connect the plug-in hub to your 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi, place the three circular detectors in likely leak spots, and you are set. You can pair up to 10 with the hub and configure it to send emails and SMS messages on top of app notifications when there’s a leak. The probes on the underside of each detector are quite far apart, though, and it takes 2 millimeters of water before the alarm is triggered. It failed to go off with a steady drip on top, but the alarm sounded as soon as water pooled underneath. The alarm goes up to 100 decibels, and you can tweak its volume and duration. You can cancel alarms through the app or by pressing the buttons on the hub. These detectors take CR2 batteries that are good for up to a year, and there’s an indication in the app when they die. When I removed a battery from one of them, it took the app a few hours to update and show it as offline. One last downside is that the hub is circular, so it may block adjacent outlets. Support for IFTTT is a potentially handy extra that could trigger a water shut-off or a light to flash red when a leak is detected.
Aqara Water Leak Sensor for $19: This Zigbee sensor is best used with Apple’s HomeKit, and you need an Aqara hub (sold separately). The company makes a good security camera that doubles as a hub and offers a full range of smart home sensors. These small circular water leak sensors are very low to the ground, so just 0.5 mm of water underneath is enough to trigger an alarm. Dripping on top won’t set them off, but an iPhone notification is triggered as soon as water pools beneath the probes. You can also have your connected hub play an alarm and trigger automations through HomeKit. The sensors take CR2 batteries and can last up to two years.
Leak Detectors to Avoid
We did not have a great experience with every water leak detector we tested. These are not recommended.
Stitch by Monoprice Water Leak Sensor: This affordable water leak detector has a design that’s similar to our top pick. The main body is round, with metal feet to detect water pooling, and it slots into a bracket for wall mounting. It comes with a coin-sized plug-in extension that stretches up to 3.8 feet. Both the main detector and extension were quick to sound the alarm and send notifications to my phone when wet, but the on-device alarm is not very loud. It takes a single CR2 battery, displays the remaining power in the app, and alerts you when it’s time to change batteries. Unfortunately, the app is basic and poorly translated. You have to dry the detector to stop the alarm, and it took too long to warn me when it went offline (weirdly, the offline detector is toggled off by default in the app settings, so I had to switch it on).
Swann Leak Alert Sensor: While this battery-powered water detector (two AAAs) is affordable, I had a terrible time setting it up. Your phone must be on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi, but even then, it took me multiple attempts to connect. Frustratingly, you must remove the screw panel to reset it, because there’s no option in the app. Alerts came through to my phone around a minute after I soaked the sensor, and the Swann app is slow and clunky.
Know These Basics Before You Shop
Water leak detectors can detect water pooling, and some can also detect water dripping or even humidity rising. Premium water leak detectors monitor the flow of water in your pipes and may include an automatic water shutoff that kicks in when a leak is detected. All connect to a hub or directly to your Wi-Fi network to send alerts when they detect a problem.
Some water leak detectors have cables with sensors on the end, some have water-sensing cords, and others are self-contained with sensors on the top, bottom, or both. You have the option of extension nodes with some detectors. At the premium end of the market, you can get a water shutoff valve that must be fitted to your pipework to measure the flow of water and even automatically shut it off when a leak is detected. For the best protection you should combine both water leak detectors to perform spot checks around appliances, and flow monitoring systems to detect when a pipe bursts or a leak develops in any part of your plumbing system.
Unless you have a single problem spot or appliance you want to monitor, you will likely need several water leak detectors to safeguard your whole home. Think about the areas you want to cover when considering what kind of detector would work best for you and how many of them you need.
Place detectors anywhere you have concerns about a potential leak—for example, under the kitchen sink, behind toilets, next to washers, humidifiers, water heaters, and other water tanks. They can also be useful for monitoring basements, lofts, garages, and other outbuildings or vacation properties. Other spots worth considering include under the bath, behind the fridge if it has an ice or water dispenser (especially if it's plumbed in), your HVAC condensate pan, or next to your sump pump or pit. If you have a problem area where you have had a leak before or an aging appliance you are worried about, those are also good options.
Water Leak Detector FAQ
All the smart water leak detectors we tested send push notifications when there’s a leak, but some also send emails and texts. Most have some kind of built-in audible alarm sound, but some offer separate sirens or can be configured to send alerts through smart speakers or other devices. It’s worth checking whether your pick supports disconnection alerts to warn you when the connection is lost, which may happen if power or Wi-Fi goes out.
Most detectors are battery-powered, but you can get some that plug directly into outlets. You can set and forget plug-in detectors, but batteries give you more flexibility with placement, and the companion app will typically warn you when the batteries need to be changed.
Most smart water leak detectors connect directly to your Wi-Fi router or a hub, so make sure that you have a decent signal wherever you are installing them. Most of the devices we tested only connect to Wi-Fi on the 2.4-GHz band. Remember that they need internet access to alert you to any leaks or problems when you are away from home. If your internet goes down, they will simply act as local alarms.
While companion apps and mobile notifications are typical, some detectors support smart home standards, enabling you to access detectors in your chosen smart home app and set up triggers or automation. For example, you could set a water alert to flash your smart lights or select a temperature that triggers heating or air conditioning to turn on.
With some high-end systems, you can install a water-monitoring device with an automatic shutoff function, enabling any leak detection to shut off your water supply. But these systems are usually expensive and require professional installation.
Some smart water-leak detectors can also monitor the temperature and humidity, potentially alerting you to the danger of frozen pipes or damp environments that could indicate a leak nearby. You can generally review the temperature and humidity over time, so you can immediately spot any notable changes that need investigation. With smart home automation, you can also trigger heating or fans at certain levels to reduce the risk of damage.
How We Test
I test every smart water leak detector by dripping water on top, pooling water slowly beneath, and flooding rapidly to see how effective the water leak detection is and how quickly they alert. I install every app, check different alert options where applicable, and ensure alerts come through on my phone, whether I’m connected to Wi-Fi or the cellular network. I also remove the batteries or unplug each water leak detector to see if it shows as disconnected correctly in the app or sends any alert, then plug it back in or reinsert batteries to see if it recovers.
When detectors offer additional features, such as humidity or temperature tracking, I test and compare them with my SwitchBot Hub 3. Our top picks continue to be used over months, so we can be confident that the performance does not degrade.

Baby orangutans found in Indian forest spark trafficking inquiry
- Published
Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India's eastern state of Odisha, far from their natural habitat, prompting an investigation into how they got there.
Photographs and videos widely shared online show the young apes sitting together on the forest floor and eating bananas, thousands of kilometres from the tropical rainforests where they belong.
Orangutans are not native to India. The critically endangered apes are found in the wild only in Indonesia and Malaysia.
Odisha's forest minister has said investigators are examining whether the animals were trafficked into the country by an international smuggling network and abandoned near a highway.
The orangutans were rescued early on Tuesday in Balasore district after local people spotted them and alerted forest officials.
They were given first aid before being taken to Nandankanan Zoological Park in the state capital, Bhubaneswar, where they are in quarantine and being monitored.
Balasore District Forest Officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar told the BBC that the animals could not have reached Odisha naturally and may have been transported there by road.
"The five animals were found in Ranakata, a proposed reserve forest in Bhogarai block, near the West Bengal border," he said.
"The area is covered mainly by casuarina trees and is not a dense forest. It is also close to a state highway."
The Odisha government has also reportedly asked India's Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate. Police, forest officials and a special task force are involved in the inquiry.
Forest officials believe the orangutans had been in the area for only two or three days.
A search of the forest found no other orangutans or clues as to how the animals got there, Indalkar said.
Officials described them to the BBC as infants, although some local reports suggest they are between one and two years old.
Their young age makes their discovery particularly concerning, wildlife expert Biswajit Mohanty said.
Young orangutans typically remain with their mothers for several years, learning the skills they need to survive independently. Females also reproduce slowly, usually giving birth only once every eight years.
The discovery of five young orangutans together, thousands of kilometres from their natural habitat and with no adult animals nearby, has therefore raised concerns of how they came to be in Odisha.
There are three known living species of orangutan - Bornean, Sumatran and Tapanuli - all of which are classified as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN.
Over the years, their numbers have declined sharply because of deforestation, habitat loss and hunting.
International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites - the global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife. They are also protected under Indian wildlife laws.
Despite this, orangutans continue to be trafficked for sale as exotic pets and to private collectors.
This is not the first time young orangutans have been found in India.
In 2022, two baby orangutans were found abandoned at a checkpoint near the border between the states of Assam and Mizoram. Officials suspected they had been brought into India through neighbouring Myanmar.

The Biju Janata Dal (BJD) staged a massive protest demonstration demanding constitutional intervention for the reversal of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) (MMDR) Amendment Act, 2026 here on Wednesday (September 9, 2026).
On Wednesday morning (September 9, 2026), BJD leaders marched towards the Lok Bhavan to apprise Governor Hari Babu Kambhampati of the consequences for Odisha upon the implementation of the Act. They submitted a comprehensive memorandum addressed to President Droupadi Murmu through the Governor.
“Odisha is one of the most mineral-rich states in the country and has contributed immensely to India’s industrial and economic development through its reserves of iron ore, coal, bauxite, chromite, and other minerals. The mineral resources located within the territory of Odisha constitute an important component of the State’s natural wealth and have historically been a major source of revenue for the State government,” the BJD leaders said.
“Any legislative measure that substantially curtails the rights and financial interests of the State in relation to mines and mineral-bearing lands therefore has far-reaching consequences for Odisha and its people, and deserves careful constitutional and legal examination,” they said.
BJD leaders referred to the July 24, 2024 Supreme Court judgment, which recognised the power of State governments to impose taxes and levies on mines and mineral-bearing lands, and also dealt with the recovery of such dues from the period beginning April 1, 2005. “Odisha became entitled to receive substantial amounts towards arrears of mining-related taxes and levies. It was estimated that the State could receive more than ₹1 lakh crore towards arrears, apart from an additional annual revenue of approximately ₹12,000 crore,” the BJD leaders said. Following the amendment to the Act, Odisha stood to lose massive sums of the revenue, they said.
“These amounts are of immense significance to Odisha as they could substantially strengthen the State’s financial capacity to undertake development and welfare programmes, and to invest in infrastructure, education, healthcare, irrigation, rural development and other priorities, which, in our considered view, raise serious concerns regarding the constitutional rights, fiscal interests, and legitimate interests of the State of Odisha in its mineral resources,” the BJD said in its memorandum.
The party expressed its deep concern over different amendments to the legislation on mining and minerals. “By expanding Union control under Section 2 to include ‘mineral-bearing lands’; restricting State governments under Section 9D from levying taxes, cesses or similar charges on mineral rights or mineral-bearing lands; and empowering the Central government under Section 13 to frame rules limiting such State taxation, the amendment has significant implications for Odisha’s fiscal autonomy, and the constitutional balance between the Union and the States,” the memorandum said.
The BJD urged the Governor to exercise his power under Article 244(1) (Fifth Schedule) that provides a special constitutional framework for the administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.

Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to £65m Man City move
- Published
Iliman Ndiaye's journey to Manchester City has been something of a scenic route after he completed a move to Etihad Stadium from Everton in a deal worth up to £65m.
The deadline day move for the Senegal winger, 26, is worth £60m plus a further £5m in add-ons - a little over six years since he made his professional debut playing in the seventh tier of English football.
"I've worked my whole life for an opportunity like this," said Ndiaye, who has signed a five-year contract with the club.
"City are one of the best clubs in the world and I've seen them win everything as I've grown up. To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I'm determined to grab it with both hands."
Ndiaye had held talks with Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal earlier in the summer while Tottenham had agreed terms with Everton on Friday night for Ndiaye, when it looked as though Richarlison would move the other way in a separate transfer.
However, sources indicated Richarlison failed to agree personal terms with his former club and as a result, Spurs were unable to proceed with the Ndiaye transfer.
The move comes on the same day City agreed to pay a joint-British transfer record fee of £125m for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.
The Argentian international is set to become City's eighth summer arrival with Enzo Maresca's side having also signed Elliot Anderson, Geronimo Rulli, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Allan Elias, Jeremy Monga and Pierce Charles.
Ndiaye's journey from non-league football to City
As a 19-year-old living in London, Ndiaye was in the youth ranks of Boreham Wood and playing Sunday league football when he was invited for a one-week trial with Sheffield United.
Two trial games were enough for the then-Premier League club to sign the talented teenager, although it would be another 18 months until he made an appearance for the Blades.
Instead, he spent the second half of the 2019-20 campaign on loan at Hyde United in the Northern Premier Division, six levels below the top division.
He made six appearances in his very first taste of professional football, often risking missing the last train back to Sheffield to stay out on the training pitch.
"It's not always been easy in my career," said Ndiaye.
"But I always had the belief that I could play for a team challenging for the biggest prizes and now I'm here."
After returning to Bramall Lane, Ndiaye made his Premier League debut in March 2021 against Leicester City but it would be another three-and-a-half years until he became established at the highest level following the Blades' relegation.
Two seasons in the Championship culminated in Ndiaye spearheading their return to the top flight in 2023 with 14 goals in 43 starts but he was then sold to Marseille that summer.
Ndiaye struggled during a season in France before joining Everton for an initial £16m fee in July 2024.
A firm fan favourite on Merseyside, "Skiliman" scored 15 goals and provided four assists in 67 Premier League games for the Toffees before his City move.
Is £65m a fair price for Ndiaye?
In a summer of highly-inflated transfer fees, value has become increasingly hard to determine.
On one hand, the Senegal international is a player of superlative skill, evasive, quick and wonderfully entertaining with the ball at his feet.
Ndiaye was responsible for 73 of Everton's 250 completed dribbles last season, the highest share of any Premier League player.
Everton fans may also point to recent moves in the Premier League involving City, such as the sale of Savio to Tottenham for an initial £75m, as further evidence that the club should have demanded more for Ndiaye.
On the other hand, Everton are effectively quadrupling the initial £16m they paid Marseille to sign Ndiaye two years ago for a player whose underlying numbers, at this stage at least, are not truly elite.
In the Premier League last season, Ndiaye only ranked joint third at Everton alone for goal contributions (nine), with Beto (10) and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall (12) providing more.
It is reasonable to assume that those numbers for Ndiaye will improve in a more attacking team at City but his general creativity is also middling as things stand.
He created 36 chances in total in the Premier League last season, ranking him only fourth at Everton. Toffees midfielder James Garner created 26 more. Jack Grealish, whose season ended in January because of injury, created eight more.
Grealish has effectively replaced Ndiaye at Everton following his loan move from Enzo Maresca's side.
Casting the net a little wider, 45 Premier League players have recorded more goal contributions than Ndiaye's 19 since he made his Everton debut two years ago.
As a 26-year-old set to be surrounded by better players, it would be no surprise should his numbers flourish at the Etihad.
But even in today's money, £65m for Ndiaye's current output may not be as questionable a deal as it sounds.

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.
Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.
Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.
Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”
The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”
Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.
Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.
Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

Prime Minister (PM) Narendra Modi has directed Indian fintech startups to strengthen cybersecurity and consumer protection as the sector moves into its next phase of growth driven by agentic AI and quantum technologies. Addressing the inauguration of Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 in Mumbai today (September 8), PM Modi called for building stronger safeguards around India's rapidly expanding digital financial services and fintech sector. Modi added that the rapid adoption of new technologies must be matched by stronger security and trust mechanisms. He highlighted the need to build “top-notch cybersecurity” protocols as financial services become increasingly dependent on digital infrastructure and AI. He also stressed the need for ethical data-protection practices to ensure consumer trust in this age of AI. "Agentic AI, tokenisation, quantum, such technologies are opening new possibilities in the financial sector ... For this, I want our fintech companies to come together and set some tasks for themselves," he added In this line, the government recently formed an inter-ministerial group to develop a comprehensive cybersecurity strategy for India’s financial sector. Earlier this year, concerns emerged around Anthropic’s Mythos, an AI system capable of autonomously identifying high-severity software vulnerabilities, prompting policymakers and financial institutions to reassess the cybersecurity implications of frontier AI models. Addressing the forum, the PM outlined four broad priorities for the sector, viz stronger cybersecurity, ethical data protection, better consumer protection and closer collaboration between industry and regulators. Noting that the initial phase of India's fintech boom was largely defined by payments and digital infrastructure, he called for more fintech innovations in financial products and automated decision-making. He also underscored the need for building new products around data, fraud, cybersecurity and consumer safeguards. PM Modi also directed fintech companies to “move beyond payments”, with the next opportunity lying in areas such as credit, insurance and pensions. He also urged fintech platforms to take financial services to sections of the population that have historically had limited access to formal banking. PM Bats For UPI’s Global Expansion The PM said the next phase of UPI's growth should focus on connecting the Indian payment system with payment ecosystems of other countries. “Our next goal should be to connect it with the payment systems of those countries,” PM Modi said. As of September 2026, the homegrown payments infrastructure is live in 11 countries. Citing the India-Singapore linkage as an example, the PM said that cross-border transactions between the two countries have become almost as easy as transactions between two Indian cities. The PM also underlined that India should prioritise countries with large Indian diasporas and strong trade ties for UPI’s global expansion. “Indians are the ones who send the maximum money from abroad in the world but today, a part of the remittances goes away as transaction costs. UPI can help Indians save on these costs and the money can also reach Indian families faster,” he added. Launched in 2016 under the aegis of the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), UPI has grown from 1.78 Cr transactions in FY17 to more than 24,162 Cr transactions in FY26, an almost 13,000X increase. As per government data, transaction value has risen from ₹7,000 Cr to around ₹314 Lakh Cr over the same period. The growth accelerated further in 2026. UPI processed a record 2,451 Cr monthly transactions worth ₹29.82 Lakh Cr in August. At the heart of all this is the thriving Indian fintech economy, which is projected to cross $250 Bn in revenue by 2030. The seventh edition of the four-day fest will provide a stage to Indian fintech companies for global dialogue, collaboration and innovation in financial technology. The theme of this year's GFF is “Potential to Impact: Agentic AI, Tokenisation, Quantum - Trusted, Connected, Global Systems for Inclusive Finance.”

Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty defeated China’s He Jiting and Ren Xiangyu 11-21, 21-13, 21-17 in the China Masters 2026 final on Sunday to claim their 10th BWF World Tour title.
The victory extended the Indian pair’s head-to-head record against He and Ren to 3-0.
He Jiting and Ren Xiangyu made a blistering start, racing to a 5-0 lead as their sharp play at the net and powerful smashes put the Indians under pressure. Rankireddy and Shetty got on the board but struggled to close the gap, with the Chinese pair finding the lines consistently to lead 11-5 at the interval.
He and Ren never allowed the Indians to get closer than four points thereafter and wrapped up the opening game 21-11 in 18 minutes, with two loose shots from the Indian duo drifting long.
The second game began in similar fashion, with China taking an early 2-0 lead before Rankireddy and Shetty fought back to level at 3-3. He and Ren regained the advantage, showcasing their speed and control, but the Indians stayed in the contest and drew level at 6-6.
Rankireddy and Shetty then took control, moving into an 11-7 lead at the interval. They continued to apply pressure after the break, surging to 17-11, with Shetty’s powerful smashes proving particularly effective. Despite a late Chinese fightback, the Indians closed out the game 21-13 to level the match.
The Indians again fell behind 0-4 in the decider but rallied to level at 7-7, though the Chinese pair led 11-9 at the interval.
Trailing 17-16, Satwik and Chirag produced a stunning finish, winning five straight points to take the lead and seal the title.
The triumph marked Rankireddy and Shetty’s 10th career BWF World Tour title.

In Summary
- Apple’s new CEO John Ternus is expected to take centrestage on 9 September in Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event. This will be
- Ternus’ first appearance in an Apple event since he took over from Tim Cook.
- Apple is expected to launch new iPhones at the event, including the much-talked-about iPhone Ultra, its first foldable phone.
- As the event draws near, we write an open letter to Apple’s new CEO, requesting something that was once very much Apple – being different.
Dear John,
You will shortly be making your first public appearance as CEO at a major Apple event. Over the years, the iPhone launch pretty much sets out the tech agenda for the rest of the year. For the iPhone is not just a tech launch but a trend setter of sorts – it influences which colors, shapes, features, and functions matter in the industry in the coming days. About a decade ago, we would have laughed at the notion of a notch in any device. Until last year, orange was associated more with juice than tech. You get the idea.
Indeed, very few names have influenced our lives in the way in which Apple has over the past few decades. The brand made computers and touchscreen smartphones that were effortlessly easy to use, put thousands of songs in our pockets, created notebooks that could be carried in stationery envelopes, showed us that Bluetooth earbuds could exist without wires, added a third screen to many of our lives in the form of a tablet, got us looking at our watches for more than just the time, made us realize that there was “an app for that…”, and much more. It was seldom the first to come out with a particular product, but it often put a different spin on products, making them easier to use. It was the brand that thrived on its legendary motto, ‘Think Different’. Other brands could match Apple’s features and spec sheet, perhaps, but never the ‘feel’ or ‘vibe’ of an Apple product.
In recent times, however, this Apple feel or vibe has been getting increasingly diminished. Some would say that perhaps an “inspired” (read “copycat”) competition is closing the gap on the market leader. Perhaps. But then, it is not as if competition and “copy and paste” mode did not exist in the past. Remember how Steve Jobs went ballistic at Google for Android, claiming that it had been copied from Apple? “I’m going to destroy Android, because it’s a stolen product. I’m willing to go thermonuclear war on this,” Jobs raged when speaking of the topic, in Walter Isaacson’s biography. But even then, Apple’s products continued to be strikingly different. The competition could offer a similar appearance (camera units, straight sides, similar colors), but beneath that familiar surface, it was clear that they were just knockoffs.
That is no longer the case. Somewhere in its pursuit of market share over the past decade, Apple started losing its mystique, going from Hogwarts to Harvard. The brand’s sales volumes and capital value have shot up exponentially, but all this has come at a creative cost. Apple now seems more a part of the crowd rather than apart from it. Don’t get me wrong. Apple’s products are still very good, but while their pricing is more premium than ever, the products themselves are not as different as they used to be. In fact, in many cases, they do not even seem to be too different from their own predecessors.
The brand that championed “Think DIfferent” has been increasingly thinking similarly of late. From being among the first to popularise graphical UIs, capacitive touchscreens, app screens and face unlock systems, it has graduated to being last in line in the foldables and AI race. It might end up winning both of those contests even now, such is its market domination, but that would be a victory of volumes rather than delivered value, similar to how IBM ended up bossing the PC market in the early eighties even though it was a latecomer. IBM’s motto was incidentally “Think,” and is believed to have inspired Apple’s “Think Different.” Oh, the irony.
There has always been a large section of people who believed that most people who bought Apple products did so just to “show off the logo,” as products from other brands were just as good. For a while, this was a very unfair accusation, as in spite of their premium price tags (even more so in India, because of customs duties, we are told), Apple’s products seemed to be in a totally different league. Today, Apple still has the high ground in privacy and security and its face unlock remains unmatched, but in many other regards (yes, even in apps and interface), the brand seems content to swim in the mainstream, rather than walloping the competition from within its famous “walled garden.”
We are coming to the stage when a lot of people are actually buying Apple products for the logo on them rather than what they do. At one level, it tells us that the Apple brand has such equity that people are willing to invest large amounts in a product because it has an apple engraved on it. At another, it tells us that the products are now being defined by the brand rather than the other way around – a foldable phone is special because it comes from Apple, rather than Apple being special because it made a foldable phone.
Today, Apple is arguably the world’s greatest tech brand, but it has more money than mojo. For other brands, that would be just perfect. But since when was Apple just another brand? Mind you, money is a wonderful thing. After all, it enables one to do things and invest in ideas that don’t have a short-term payback. We did not say that; Steve Jobs did. Well, Apple has the money. Perhaps it is time for it to do things. Differently.
All this is easier said than done, of course. My colleague Akriti Rana recently wrote eloquently of how you now hold not just the reins of arguably the most high-profile tech company in the world, but also bear the burden of two massive, yet contrasting legacies. How you decide to honor them is your choice. You could choose to sail in a sea of successful sameness. Or maybe just spend more time in that walled garden.
Still, as someone whose first ever story in tech was about an Apple product (the iBook in 1999) and who confidently predicted that the first iPhone would fail (and was delighted to be proved wrong) in 2007, I have a request.
I am not asking for slimmer portfolios. Or lower price tags. I am asking for something much more basic – the experience of going to an event without having any idea of what will happen.
Of seeing a product without having seen it being leaked more often than a local municipal pipeline.
Of feeling a sense of wonder while using a product, because there is nothing else quite like it.
Of looking at the Apple logo and thinking of wizardry rather than wealth.
The universe is waiting, John Ternus. Go put a ding in it.
Regards,
Nimish Dubey

TSA brings back gate access for some people without plane tickets 25 years after 9/11
LAS VEGAS — Airport security checkpoints have been the end of the line since soon after the 9/11 attacks for most friends and relatives who want to see off departing passengers. That is changing at some U.S. airports.
The Transportation Security Administration is allowing eligible TSA PreCheck members without tickets to pass through security and enter gate areas, reviving a tradition that largely disappeared after the attacks 25 years ago this week.
"As an exclusive benefit for our most trusted travelers, this new program makes it easier to return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping along the way, bringing back the moments that once defined air travel," TSA said on its website.
The program, called Gateside by TSA PreCheck" is free, but interested members must apply online one to three days before their planned visits and receive approval before going to the airport. If approved, they can enter security using a TSA PreCheck lane with an acceptable form of identification. The passes are valid for one calendar day, but reentries are allowed on that day.
TSA says members of other trusted-traveler programs who have a Known Traveler Number also can apply for access to the gates.
The program is initially available at 13 airports, including Los Angeles International Airport, Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas and Salt Lake City International Airport, according to TSA. The agency says it plans to expand the program to more airports in the coming months.
Before the Sept. 11 attacks, individuals without tickets generally could accompany ticketed passengers to their gates. The attacks prompted sweeping changes to airport security, including restrictions on access to secure areas of airports.

If you lose a Sprite during a Battle Royale/Zero Build match in Fortnite, you can use Sprite Dust to summon it. We don’t recommend using Sprite Dust to summon common Sprites; however, if you lose your Klombo Sprite in Fortnite, given its low drop rate, summoning is easier than looking for a replacement.
Keep in mind that Mythic Sprites also cost more to summon than Rare ones. However, if you have Mastered a Sprite in Fortnite, the cost to summon them is reduced by half. Even so, avoid losing them, or you’ll end up having to spend a lot of Sprite Dust in Fortnite to get them back. We recommend limiting your use of variants such as Gold Sprites in Fortnite to the Sprite Garden.
Purchasing / Upgrading Loot Hacks
Sprite Dust in Fortnite can be used to purchase and/or upgrade Loot Hacks. This unlocks powerful weapons and items that you can come across at times, based on their drop rate. They aren’t extremely rare, but they are hard to come by.
When you upgrade Loot Hacks, it increases their drop rate, making it more likely they’ll appear in each match. The cost of upgrading Loot Hacks in Fortnite increases with each level. As such, you’ll need to save up a lot of Sprite Dust.
Sprite Services from Extraction Sites
Sprite Dust can also be used to purchase Gizmos and services from Extraction Sites in Fortnite. These are situational, but can be stocked and used anytime during Chapter 7 Season 4. That said, here’s the list and the cost in Sprite Dust.
| Gizmo/Service | Cost in Sprite Dust | 
|---|---|
| Portable Extractor | 2,500 | 
| Cheat Code Locator | 1,500 | 
| 20,000 XP | 1,000 | 
| Weapon Upgrade | 1,500 for Rare 1,800 for Epic 2,100 for Legendary 2,400 for Mythic | 
Keep in mind that stock is limited; thus, if you plan on stockpiling Fortnite Gizmos, you need to play often. However, we recommend keeping your Sprite Dust for Loot Hacks. They are still by far the most useful things to spend it on.
Easiest Method to Farm Sprite Dust in Fortnite
The best method to earn Sprite Dust in Fortnite is something we’d like to call Sprite Farming. Instead of focusing on eliminations, the main goal is to land at an offbeat Extraction Site and look for Sprites. Extract as many as you can, and then return to the main lobby.
You can easily come across Sprites from Cheat Codes, in Landmarks, and avoid players in POIs. With the numerous map changes implemented in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4, there are numerous offbeat locations to explore.
We recommend landing at the Artsy RVS Landmark in Fortnite, which is located a short distance from the Chopped Shop POI. The location is stacked with Chests, Cheat Codes, and has an Extraction Site adjacent to it. If you’re quick, you can be in and out of each match in just a few minutes.
Fortnite Sprite Summon Costs in Chapter 7 Season 4
We talked about how to summon Sprites in Fortnite using Sprite Dust, but you should also know that each Sprite has a different cost to summon. Depending on the rarity and variant, the cost varies. As such, a Rare Cheat Master Sprite in Fortnite costs more to summon than a regular Epic Sprite. Here’s how much you need to pay to summon every Sprite in Fortnite.
| Sprite Rarity | Sprite Variant | Sprite Dust Cost | 
|---|---|---|
| Mythic | Gold and Cheat Master | 2,400 | 
| Legendary | Gold and Cheat Master | 2,100 | 
| Epic | Gold and Cheat Master | 1,800 | 
| Rare | Gold and Cheat Master | 1,500 | 
| Mythic | Base Variant | 2,000 | 
| Legendary | Base Variant | 1,750 | 
| Epic | Base Variant | 1,500 | 
| Rare | Base Variant | 1,250 | 
The exception to the rule for the aforementioned table for Rare Sprites is Jonesy, Adventure, and Bush, which can be selected as your starter Sprite. The Mega Man Sprite in Fortnite is also an exception to the rule. Despite being Rare, it has a rather high summon cost of 1,750 Sprite Dust, which is similar to the X-Ray Sprite in Fortnite, which is of Legendary rarity.
That’s about everything we can tell you about Sprite Dust in Fortnite. Let us know in the comments how much Sprite Dust you’ve been able to collect thus far.
How to get Sprite Dust in Fortnite?
Extract duplicate Sprites and enter Lobby Hack (Admin Panel) Codes to get more Sprite Dust in Fortnite.
What is Sprite Dust used for in Fortnite?
Sprite Dust is used to summon lost Sprites, buy Gizmos, and purchase/upgrade Loot Hacks in Fortnite.
What is the maximum amount of Sprite Dust you can collect?
You can store up to 200,000 Sprite Dust in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4.

Huge sinkhole forms outside of Nicholas Cage’s Malibu beachfront mansion
Surrounding properties have been evacuated as at least five homes were declared unsafe for entry
A large sinkhole has opened outside a coastal Malibu mansion belonging to the actor Nicolas Cage after the driveway collapsed on Tuesday morning.
Emergency crews and utility workers responded shortly before 6am when the structural failure caused a gas leak.
SoCalGas stated the leak was secured several hours later, but natural gas was temporarily disconnected along an 85-foot (26-metre) stretch of the road as a safeguard against ongoing coastal erosion.
Representatives for Cage did not immediately reply to requests for comment. Property records indicate the estate was sold in 2024, with the former owner telling the New York Times at the time that Cage was the buyer.
The damage occurred during a Los Angeles coastal flooding advisory linked to Tropical Storm Marie, previously a hurricane. While Marie remained offshore, it brought rain and high waves to Southern California over the holiday weekend.
Officials from the city of Malibu declared at least five homes on the street unsafe for entry on Tuesday. The private neighbourhood lies between the ocean and the Pacific Coast Highway.
“Emergency personnel access is severely constrained and may be impassable, due to the large portion of the road that has collapsed,” the city wrote in the emergency declaration.
“The intact portion of the roadway is too narrow to accommodate emergency response vehicles, including fire engines and other large apparatus, creating a substantial risk to public safety and emergency response capabilities.”
Gas has been shut off in the affected area, and city officials warn that water service may also be discontinued until further notice. It is unclear how long the evacuation order will remain in place.
Cage, 62, recently starred in the Amazon series Spider-Noir, which was recently cancelled by Prime Video despite glowing and positive reviews.
The popular series won five Emmy Awards for cinematography, sound editing, stunt coordination, title design, and visual effects at Sunday's Creative Arts ceremony.
The actor has appeared in more than 100 films, winning an Oscar for Leaving Las Vegas and he will portray John Madden in a biographical film about the NFL coach and commentator out later this year.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Tobacco use is linked to infertility in women as well as poorer sperm quality and sexual function in men, according to the latest World Health Organisation (WHO) report, which further warned that second-hand smoke may also affect fertility. Women who quit smoking may have a 25% lower infertility risk than continuing smokers, it said.
The report highlighted evidence that tobacco use is associated with potentially lower chances of success for some fertility treatments. It said that evidence on newer products, including e-cigarettes, waterpipes, and smokeless tobacco, is still emerging, stating that while evidence is strongest for cigarette smoking, other tobacco and nicotine products may also pose risks to fertility and require further research.
Globally, one in six people of reproductive age will experience infertility at some point in their lifetime. Infertility is defined as the failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected sex.
40% rise in risk
The publication cites decades of evidence showing that smoking can harm women’s reproductive health. A systematic review of studies conducted between 2000 and 2026 found that women who currently smoke tobacco have a 40% higher risk of infertility compared to those who do not smoke.
The publication also notes that women who smoked tobacco in the past but are not currently smoking may have a 25% lower risk of infertility compared with women who continue to smoke, suggesting that quitting tobacco can make a meaningful difference.
The WHO stressed that infertility is not only a women’s health issue. "A recent review of 44 studies involving more than 60,000 men found that smoking was associated with reproductive dysfunction, including semen abnormalities and sexual dysfunction. The evidence indicated that men who smoke were more likely to have erectile dysfunction, ejaculation problems, and related issues such as absence of sperm in semen, poor sperm motility and abnormal sperm shape," it said.
Impact on treatments
For people using fertility treatment, tobacco smoking may reduce the chance of success. The publication cites earlier research from 21 studies, showing that cigarette smoking was linked to fewer live births and fewer pregnancies following assisted reproduction, such as in vitro fertilisation, with findings suggesting that the chances of successful outcomes may be roughly halved by cigarette smoking.
The WHO has recommended that healthcare providers inform individuals and couples planning a pregnancy about the reproductive risks of tobacco use and offer evidence-based support to help them quit. It also recommended that brief advice on quitting be consistently provided to all tobacco users in all healthcare settings.
